ourIssues.title: Update to 'Exit this page' default text may cause issues for voice control users
ourIssues.body: https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/pull/3989 updated the default content of the 'Exit this page' button to add 'Emergency' as visually-hidden text at the start of the button. Adding visually-hidden content to the start or middle of text on interactive elements can cause issues activating them for voice control users (eg Dragon, Apple Voice Control) because the label exposed to these tools ('Emergency Exit this page') doesn't match what the user will say ("Click 'Exit this page'"). Generally voice control needs an exact match on the start of the string, but anything extra at the end is fine - so making it something like `Exit this page in an emergency` would probably be OK. References: https://www.smashingmagazine.com/2022/06/voice-control-usability-considerations-partially-visually-hidden-link-names/#problems-with-partially-visually-hidden-text https://www.sarasoueidan.com/blog/accessible-text-labels/#improving-the-experience-for-screen-reader-users-whilst-keeping-it-accessible-to-speech-input-users I haven't tested yet but I have access to Dragon so I'll test in that to confirm ASAP. I just spotted this change in the v5 beta release notes and wanted to flag it as quickly as possible.

ourIssues.title: Allow multiple components to be attached to an element
ourIssues.body:
## Related component Relates to any component that is initialised with the `data-module` attribute and might cross-over with another component that uses the same element. I've outlined this with a service-specific example because it's easier to describe, but my main concern here is with other component libraries which would benefit from seamless integration with the Design System, and where service teams have less say over the implementation details. ## Context Imagine my service has a bespoke component based by [Bootstrap's Popover component](https://getbootstrap.com/docs/4.0/components/popovers/). We initialise all our components following the Design System pattern, so in this case with a `data-module="app-popover"` attribute. I want to add a popover to a button, which I also want to behave like a [Button component](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/button/). This is a problem, since the Design System doesn't support multiple modules (if that's the right term?) being initialised from one element. I can't do `data-module="govuk-button" data-module="app-popover"` because that's invalid HTML. I could do `data-module="govuk-button app-popover"` (like class attribute syntax), but that won't work because the Design System [uses exact matches](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/dd748307ca612c73c2e60548419cee94d0cd636f/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/all.mjs#L55) when looking for attributes (`app-popover` could be made to work, but `govuk-button` won't) My suggestion is that the selector for initialising components is updated to `[data-module~="${Component.moduleName}"]`, which treats the attribute as a whitespace-separated list and matches if one entry in that list is the module. It would continue to work with exact matches, as the attribute would be treated as a list of one item. ## Alternatives ### Downstream components trigger upstream behaviour In the example above, the service's Popover component could be responsible for also initialising button behaviour on the element (i.e. `(new Button(this.$module)).init()`). However, if the Popover could also be applied to other elements (e.g. links, images) we wouldn't want to add button behaviour. The Popover component could apply this conditionally, if `$this.module.tagName === 'BUTTON'`, but this leads to hidden behaviour that's hard to opt-out of. #### Using ES2015 classes From v5, this could be achieved by extending the exposed JavaScript class: ```js export class Popover extends Button { constructor($module, options) { // GOV.UK Frontend button super($module, options) // Custom button things ... } } ``` This again creates a direct dependency on the Button component, which might not be desired if the component could be used by non-button elements too. It also creates a hierarchy, which could be complex if there are more than two components: if `Popover extends Button` and `SearchToggle extends Button`, then you have the same problem making an element both a Popover and a SearchToggle. ### Encourage other departmental and service-specific components to use a different attribute/approach In the example above, the Popover component might use the `data-app-module` attribute instead. Departmental component libraries could use e.g. `data-dft-module`. Since Design System components are prefixed `govuk-` in the value, I think it's reasonable to expect others to use the attribute with a different prefix. Also, there are already other components using this attribute so changing them would require changes to dependent services. ### Require one element per component/module In the example above, the Popover could be applied to a wrapping element, for example: ```html
``` This seems unnecessarily verbose to me, and requires introducing additional HTML elements to the DOM. ## Additional information (if applicable) ### Breaking change There is a breaking change risk: if a service already has whitespace-separated names in their `data-module` attribute then this would effectively "fix" them, but it _might_ cause unexpected behaviour if they've patched around it. For example, with my Popover component above, I might have added debouncing to the Popover code because govuk-button "wasn't working" and now have duplicate/conflicting behaviour. ### Components This doesn't align with Web Components, since each element can only be one component (e.g. `` or `

ourIssues.title: Button component pseudo-element blocks mouse interactions on inner elements
ourIssues.body:
## Description of the issue

In https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/3406 there was discussion about issues with spacing when the use of abbr element was used inside the button component. This issue talks about a subsequent issue that was found in the same area of work.

We found that when a button component contains elements that have behaviour which is triggered by a mouse event such as hover, this mouse event cannot be triggered because of [the absolutely positioned psuedo-element that is used to increase the buttons target area](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/d5456e01e9aeb7167db542fb2e12cebc8a7fc374/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/button/_index.scss#L111-L128).

Compare the behaviour of a browser native button element vs a .govuk-button element.

Hovering over the `abbr` element in `<button>Contact <abbr title="Government Digital Service">GDS</abbr></button>` will produce a tooltip.

However with `<button class="govuk-button" data-module="govuk-button">Contact <abbr title="Government Digital Service">GDS</abbr></button>` hovering won't have an affect.

I have a basic codepen that demonstrates this: https://codepen.io/Kevin-Dew/pen/XWyyKXd

## Actual vs expected behaviour

Actual behaviour: mouse events do not fire for elements within a .govuk-button component
Expected behaviour: mouse events on inner elements of a button component trigger

ourIssues.title: Research improvements to disabled form control styles
ourIssues.body:
## What

We've shipped an MVP (minimum-viable product) version of disabled form controls in #1713—which aimed to make disabled styles consistent—however we still have some unanswered questions about the suitability of the disabled styles included in Frontend as a whole.

## Why

We have historically discouraged the use of disabled form controls and buttons in user-facing scenarios. Although we continue to discourage their use, we have decided to provide them to cover for situations where user research has found their use helpful or where their use can be better justified (such as an internal caseworking system). 

As we've not encouraged their use, we also haven't performed much testing or research into whether the disabled styles we use work well for end users.

## Assumptions

- Our current disabled styles aren't necessarily adequate in all contexts. For example, a value-less, disabled text input or textarea appears as an empty box, with little other affordance that it is disabled or an input.
- Although WCAG 2.1 (and, currently, 2.2) do not require a minimum contrast ratio for 'inactive' elements, we may want to ensure the visibility of disabled inputs on our own terms.
- Any changes we make to disabled styles should be applicable across all 'core' form control components: Text Input, Textarea, Select, File Upload, Checkbox, and Radios. 
  - If possible or useful, we may also want it to apply to the Button component. 

## Timebox

2 weeks

## Who is working on this?

Spike lead:

Spike buddy:

## Questions to answer

- [ ] Are our current disabled styles well understood by users?
- [ ] Are our current disabled styles still perceptable by users with vision impairment?
- [ ] Do service teams know when they shouldn't be using disabled inputs?

## Done when

- [ ] Questions have been answered or we have a clearer idea of how to get to our goal
- [ ] Findings have been reviewed and agreed with at least one other person
- [ ] Findings have been shared, e.g: via a write-up on the ticket, at a show & tell or team meeting
- [ ] Any code changes we want to make have been made
- [ ] Any documentation changes we want to make have been made

ourIssues.title: Use `!default` variables in components to allow easier overrides
Test that documented component options match the templates
ourIssues.body:
## What

Add tests that validate the documented options within our component YAML files (like [the button YAML file](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/f704053f8544e8d88acec68ca448b4cb992a76d2/src/components/button/button.yaml)) match the actual options used within the template / macro.

If the two do not match, the tests should fail.

There is as a ['work-in-progress' branch](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/tree/test-definitions) for this work which currently does this, but needs some refactoring / documentation before it can be merged.

## Why

Currently we rely on human review to ensure that the documented options match reality. During a recent [firebreak](https://insidegovuk.blog.gov.uk/2018/05/03/firebreaks-on-gov-uk/) project, we explored whether we could do anything to catch these in our CI process.

The work found a number of inaccuracies in the documentation options:

- `attributes` not documented on the breadcrumbs and select components
- `describedBy` mistakenly documented on textarea and character count components
- `footer` component YAML misformed using `arguments` instead of `params`, which means the `meta` object is not documented correctly in the Design System
- `items[].name` mistakenly documented on radios – unlike checkboxes, this can only be set globally as having a set of radios with different names doesn't make any sense
- `title` not documented on the tabs component

This highlights the need to automate these checks, so we can make sure our documentation is correct.

ourIssues.title: Macros Component API should not require internal classes for modifiers
ourIssues.body:
Macros abstract our class names, if we were to change our class names, macro usage would break for our users.

In our button examples, we pass the internal button modifier class to make a button into a start button.

We could consider passing a boolean instead so that if we choose to change how our classes work, macros still function.

For example instead of

```yaml
- name: start
  data:
    text: Start now button
    classes: 'govuk-c-button--start'
```

We could do:

```yaml
- name: start
  data:
    text: Start now button
    start: true
```

See also the GOV.UK Publishing component: http://govuk-static.herokuapp.com/component-guide/button/start_now_button

Link to code: https://github.com/alphagov/static/blob/a9a040a72d475ef7015c1c9e690a5d77687fcfd8/app/views/govuk_component/button.raw.html.erb#L1

We constructed the class based on booleans, then finally merge with `classes` and inject into the markup.

Edit: 
I put together an example showing how you can restructure the macro to avoid the confusing forking logic.

This approach only forks on individual parts of the template, which is easier to reason about.

https://glitch.com/edit/#!/flag-based-macro-approach?path=views/index.html:15:26

ourIssues.title: Propose a native HTP button to browser specs
ourIssues.body:
## What
Make a proposal to browser vendors/browser specs for them to incorporate a native hide this page button into browser software.

A potential way this could work is:
- Browsers look for an attribute on a a given page's `body` eg: `hide-this-page="true"`
- If the attribute exists, browsers display a hide this page button in the software, potentially with some messaging
- Upon activating the button, users are taken off the current website, similar to our current implementation of HTP
- Browsers can set the button to both bypass popup blocking and clear history from the domain the button was pressed on. These enhancements could potentially be managed by attributes in the `body`.

## Why
This is based on a hypothesis that by letting browser vendors handle this feature, they can ring-fence the functionality and more easily distribute it to users. During the HTP prototyping work, an issue we ran into was that certain enhancements weren't viable because they ran counter to browser rules. Examples of this were:

- Trying to erase the history of a service. We couldn't erase history completely and could only "erase" one page at a time, which didn't make a significant difference as most services are multi-page and would potentially give vulnerable users a false sense of security.
- A keyboard shortcut to activate the button. If the user uses the keyboard shortcut without interacting with the page ie: scrolling, clicking, moving focus etc, this triggers browser's popup blocker functionality as they presume this is an attempt to use malicious js to trick the user. This messes with the flow of HTP and at best confuses the user, at worst puts the user in danger.

From research into hide this page so far, it emerged that users already have existing strategies for covering their tracks and keeping anonymous online however it is often entirely down to that user to work out and manage successfully, putting them at further risk. There is an additional nuance that users may not realise they're at risk until prompted by online safety content. A broader hypothesis is that by browsers doing more to incorporate and promote online safety, it will both improve protection of users and make online safety a more prominent.

## Considerations
- This is not a proposal instead of the current HTP work but a long term solution to explore
- It may be useful to get backing on this before making the proposal from, eg, 1 or more W3C members and/or other government teams and charities
- This should be approached from the spec side over the browser vendor/software side
- This should probably be filtered into existing online anonymity and online safety spaces such as incognito mode

## Things to do
- [ ] Work out where this proposal needs to go
- [ ] Make contact with charities and gov teams who would have an interest in this
- [ ] Seek interest with w3C members
- [ ] Make proposal

ourIssues.title: HTML and Nunjucks tabs not descriptive when using JAWS
ourIssues.body: The tabs don't contain hidden text like the other elements. So, when you list them in JAWS you get a list which resembles the following: - HTML - Nunjucks - HTML - Nunjucks - HTML - Nunjucks Other elements have visually hidden text, so when you list the elements they still make sense for example: ```html Open this button example in a new window ``` When you list the links with JAWS you get a list which resembles the following: - open this button example in a new window - open this start button example in a new window - open this secondary button example in a new window ## Steps to reproduce the issue Use `CTRL + INSERT + C` to list all aria-controls and combo-boxes in JAWS. ## Suggestion Adding the same visually hidden identifier to the HTML and Nunjucks tabs so they read something like: - HTML code example for button - Nunjucks code example for button - HTML code example for start button - Nunjucks code example for start button

ourIssues.title: Agree how to ensure that users don't lose information if they follow links in the cookie banner
ourIssues.body:
## What
As part of the cookie banner work we've been thinking about how teams should handle opening links in the cookie banner if the user is completing a transactional journey and could lose information they've entered in a form if they follow links in the cookie banner.

We have some information under [Opening links in a new tab](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/styles/typography/#opening-links-in-a-new-tab) about this so we could link to it from the cookie banner guidance if we though that would be useful. The content could say something like:

> If you show the cookie banner on a page where the user enters information into a form, [open the cookies page in a new tab](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/styles/typography/#opening-links-in-a-new-tab). 

Additionally, users could lose information if interacting with the cookie banner reloads the page (server side solution when JavaScript isn't enabled or the banner doesn't progressively enhance it). We could consider recommending that once the user has consented/rejected cookies, the hide button isn't shown if JavaScript isn't enabled (JS would unhide the button)/

It's possible that there's a wider pattern here about how teams should ensure that the information users enter in forms is retained safely. 

This card should be to decide what the scope of this work is.

## Why
We should provide guidance to teams on how to making sure that users don't lose information entered in a form if they follow links in the cookie banner. 

## Who needs to know about this
Content writer, technical writer, developer, service designer?

## Further detail
As well as the cookie banner, this relates to things like links in footers. However, it's possible that the proposed wider guidance is less relevant to user interaction patterns and would be more relevant for the [Service Manual](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual). 

## Done when
- [ ] We've agreed how to help teams to make sure that users don't lose information entered in a form if they click on links in the cookie banner
- [ ] We've created a follow up card if appropriate, or captured next steps in this card

ourIssues.title: White text on panel component used for confirmation codes make it harder to copy and paste
ourIssues.body: Panels often contain reference numbers that users need to copy/paste. During research on the LPA service, users encountered problems when attempting to copy/paste this code because the copied text maintained white styling, so was not visible to the user when pasted into emails etc. This was particularly a problem for less technologically savvy users. We addressed this firstly by making the text black on a white background, and secondly by providing a "copy code" button, as shown in the attached image. I wanted to feed this back into the design system incase similar issues occur on other services.

ourIssues.title: Add example for links styled as buttons.
ourIssues.body:
The design system / button macro supports links styled as buttons - but this isn't documented as an example. The start now example is one such case, but unless a team knew it was a link, they are unlikely to find it.

For content only pages with a 'continue' button, I'd normally expect teams to use a link - but there's no example of how to do this. The page makes no mention of links.

I've seen multiple teams try to reinvent the wheel by making this happen, or trying to shim the correct behaviour - all things the design system supports.

communityIssues.title: Single page notification button can send multiple fetch requests for the same data
communityIssues.body: ## What While working on the PR to https://github.com/alphagov/govuk_publishing_components/pull/5820 we noticed that the [check-email-subscription endpoint](https://docs.publishing.service.gov.uk/repos/account-api/api.html#get-apipersonalisationcheck-email-subscription) is called twice on the page, even though the data from the API endpoint will be the same, page examples below: ### Call for evidence - View template: [views/call_for_evidence/show.html.erb](https://github.com/alphagov/frontend/blob/324c288a534267a0a489d3f14769e5ed707f9ca6/app/views/call_for_evidence/show.html.erb#L75) - Page example: https://www.gov.uk/government/calls-for-evidence/credit-union-common-bond-reform ### Consultations - View template: [views/consultation/show.html.erb](https://github.com/alphagov/frontend/blob/324c288a534267a0a489d3f14769e5ed707f9ca6/app/views/consultation/show.html.erb#L91) - Page example: https://www.gov.uk/government/consultations/soft-drinks-industry-levy ### Detailed Guide - View template: [views/detailed_guide/show.html.erb](https://github.com/alphagov/frontend/blob/324c288a534267a0a489d3f14769e5ed707f9ca6/app/views/detailed_guide/show.html.erb#L47) - Page example: https://www.gov.uk/guidance/selling-second-hand-vehicles-using-a-vat-margin-scheme ### Publication - View template: [views/publication/show.html.erb](https://github.com/alphagov/frontend/blob/324c288a534267a0a489d3f14769e5ed707f9ca6/app/views/publication/show.html.erb#L58) - Page example: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/budget-2016-documents ## Why ### Example of duplicate requests The data returned from the API endpoint will be the same, so we should only need to make a single request, even if there are several buttons on the page. ### Suggested fix We should update the single page notification button to ensure that theres only one call to the API endpoint is made, while ensuring the button location works as expected with Google Analytics.

communityIssues.title: Whitehall has some hard coded component markup
communityIssues.body:
There are a few instances in whitehall's templates where components markup has been copied and pasted, rather than calling the component directly from the gem. This introduces a maintenance burden as hard coded instances must be updated to match the component in the gem, potentially causing visual problems that could go unnoticed during a `govuk_publishing_components` dependabot update.

Components should be called directly from the gem using the `<%= render "govuk_publishing_components/components/component_name", {} %>` syntax.

[bookmarklets index lines 17 and 32](https://github.com/alphagov/whitehall/blob/main/app/views/admin/bookmarklets/index.html.erb#L17) has hard coded button markup:

- both instances appear to be hardcoded in order to apply JavaScript to the component via the `href` attribute, including Rails variables
- an alternative approach would be to move the JavaScript out of the template and into a JavaScript file, using a `js-` prefixed class passed to the component to apply event listeners, and use the [data attributes option](https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/button/with_data_attributes) to apply the Rails variables, that can be then read by the JavaScript
- it might even be possible to do something simpler, like the following:

```
<% button_href = capture do %>
  <%= render("find_in_admin").gsub(/[\r\n]/,"") %>
<% end %>

<%= render "govuk_publishing_components/components/button", {
  text: "Find in admin",
  href: "javascript:(function(){ #{button_href} })()"
} %>
```

[_accessible_attachment_field.html.erb line 3](https://github.com/alphagov/whitehall/blob/main/app/views/admin/editions/_accessible_attachment_field.html.erb#L3) includes a hard coded select component:

- looks like this is hard coded because some Rails logic is being used to determine which options inside the select should be selected or disabled
- this should be achievable by moving the logic into a presenter and relying on the [preselect](https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/select#with_preselect) and [disabled](https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/select#with_disabled_options) options on the select component

[_govspeak_help.html.erb line 22](https://github.com/alphagov/whitehall/blob/main/app/views/admin/editions/_govspeak_help.html.erb#L22) and [_style_guidance.html.erb lines 8 and 43](https://github.com/alphagov/whitehall/blob/main/app/views/admin/editions/_style_guidance.html.erb#L8) have hard coded list components:

- looks like these could just be replaced with [calls to the list component](https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/list)

[_summary_card_list.html.erb line 23](https://github.com/alphagov/whitehall/blob/main/app/views/components/_summary_card_list.html.erb#L23) has a hard coded summary list component:

- looks like there's various custom bits of data being displayed here, with some logic involved
- this looks like a direct call to the component could be used here, with the logic moved to a presenter

communityIssues.title: Whitehall overrides some component styles
communityIssues.body:
There are a few instances in whitehall's CSS where styles for gem components are being overridden, which violates our principle of [component isolation](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk_publishing_components/blob/main/docs/component_principles.md#a-component-is-isolated-when). 

If possible, these styles should either be applied directly to the components themselves (in the form of new options) or applied to parent elements of the components within the application, so they do not impact the appearance of the components themselves.

[_overrides.scss line 21](https://github.com/alphagov/whitehall/blob/main/app/assets/stylesheets/admin/_overrides.scss#L21) overrides `gem-c-summary-list` child elements:

- `.govuk-summary-list__key` is given a vertical align of top, which looks redundant and can potentially be simply removed (text is already vertically aligned to the top in this element)
- images are given `display: block`. This might be trickier to unpick although the use of this component doesn't normally include images, so this might be a custom application thing that could be added to the component defaults

[_overrides.scss line 44](https://github.com/alphagov/whitehall/blob/main/app/assets/stylesheets/admin/_overrides.scss#L44) overrides `gem-c-checkboxes` styles:

- there's a helpful comment here explaining the issue, which is to do with not showing checkboxes when JavaScript is enabled with the Add another component. The [component guide page for Add another](https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/add_another) doesn't show any examples containing checkboxes, so this could be something that could be part of the component with a documentation update

[_overrides.scss line 50](https://github.com/alphagov/whitehall/blob/main/app/assets/stylesheets/admin/_overrides.scss#L50-L59) overrides reorderable list styles:

- both overrides refer to a 'read only' version of the component, which seems like it should be an option within the component

[_document-collection-group-memberships-index.scss line 2](https://github.com/alphagov/whitehall/blob/main/app/assets/stylesheets/admin/views/_document-collection-group-memberships-index.scss#L2) overrides heading styles:

- it looks like the heading component is being positioned inline along with a list of items, presumably to make them all appear on one line together. Not sure which page this appears on, but it might be done better with some custom CSS specifically for this purpose, rather than components

[_edit-edition.scss line 33](https://github.com/alphagov/whitehall/blob/main/app/assets/stylesheets/admin/views/_edit-edition.scss#L33) overrides the warning text component:

- it's setting the margin bottom of the component to 0, which can be achieved without CSS by passing a `margin_bottom: 0` option to the component (warning text uses the [component wrapper helper](https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/warning_text#standard-options))

[_summary.scss line 47](https://github.com/alphagov/whitehall/blob/main/app/assets/stylesheets/admin/views/_summary.scss#L47) overrides the button component:

- it's setting the width of the button to `100%`
- this isn't an option on the component or in the Design System, it might be this could just be removed

communityIssues.title: layout_header does not translate into other languages properly
communityIssues.body: After `static` was removed from `frontend`, the `layout_for_public` component started to get translated on foreign language pages, which in turn translated the `layout_header` (super navigation header) component. It looks like the `Menu` button text tried to translate, but as translations don't exist for that text, it just output an empty string, making the button look broken. To fix this, we hardcoded the component to always render in English in https://github.com/alphagov/govuk_publishing_components/pull/5090. However we should fix the underlying issue so that the option to translate this component exists for the future. This also surfaces another blind spot in our visual regression tests, as if we were able to translate each component in our visual regression testing, this would have been spotted.

communityIssues.title: Audit component RTL support
communityIssues.body:
## What
Check to see which components are missing right to left language layout support. The component wrapper helper has a direction option built in and is now used by most components, but additional work may be needed in some cases to actually make the component respect that.

We could also think more generally about rtl language support in terms of layout. Should the whole page layout be reversed, or just the text within it? communityIssues.title: No search 'cancel button' styles in Firefox due to them being a non-standard CSS feature
communityIssues.body:
## What
- Most browsers have a cancel button on any `input type=search` element, which allows the user to clear any text they have entered.
- This can be styled via a CSS psuedo element called `::-webkit-search-cancel-button`
- I recently merged in a change requested by a designer to use our own cancel button styles. This was mainly because the default cancel button provided by browsers did not scale nicely when the page was zoomed in. See https://github.com/alphagov/govuk_publishing_components/pull/3673
- Firefox does not support this psuedo element as it is a non standard feature https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/::-webkit-search-cancel-button - so Firefox has no cancel buttons at all, regardless of our custom styles.
- When I asked on Slack wether we should go ahead with this change I was instructed by our Lead FE to raise this issue so that we can monitor this inconsistency, in case a search cancel button is added to Firefox in the future or the implementation in other browsers changes. https://gds.slack.com/archives/CAD0JFQ12/p1697712777367839

## Example on Chrome (cancel button available)

communityIssues.title: Cumulative layout shift on GOV.UK
communityIssues.body:
Our SpeedCurve metrics have recently (since May 25th 2023) reported an increase in the Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) on GOV.UK, which seems to be mainly to do with the cookie banner being displayed. This is most noticeable on mobile devices.

Brief investigation suggests this is not to do with any recent changes to the cookie banner (even though it was recently modified to more closely follow the Design System component) but rather a change in how SpeedCurve measures CLS. Basically, it's always been this way, we just have better reporting now.

SpeedCurve is currently reporting a CLS score of `0.6771`. Some data:

- [reporting from 27th May 2023](https://app.speedcurve.com/gds/gov-uk/test/230527_PT_0994e9befe2797c0d2e43b57a10d7b0f/)
- [reporting from 4th June 2023](https://app.speedcurve.com/gds/gov-uk/test/230604_FZ_14331823420653bbbd3ecea8b4bd108a/)
- [comparison between 24th and 25th May](https://app.speedcurve.com/gds/gov-uk/compare/?tests=230524_7W_fcc5eafb395d857094f98a580ab8d367,230525_QN_53fc15643fb3e0e960bc1f089ee13ead)

This shift is recorded at two points. Firstly when the cookie banner appears:

![Screenshot 2023-06-06 at 15 02 12](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk_publishing_components/assets/861310/f86331c1-320f-4f89-9eb7-5a9a48da69cf)

The second shift occurs as shown below. I'm not 100% sure what this shift is, it seems to be incredibly small, but it adds `0.0224` to the overall score.

![Screenshot 2023-06-06 at 15 02 17](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk_publishing_components/assets/861310/06b7e5e3-883a-42e4-8dd9-8360b8800087)

There's also a shift that occurs between the default font and Transport loading (note the line break inserted in `government services`). This might be the one above - it probably varies depending on screen width.

![Screenshot 2023-06-06 at 15 00 53](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk_publishing_components/assets/861310/5dc9b215-dbc3-49b7-b1f1-9ab41b0bc819)


## Previous work

There has been some [previous detailing of this problem](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1J8gz8fRPmPJnYk2O4bHRC79E5-p7rpSnnVWRIYodRy8/edit#heading=h.lmvvgvepxvzb) as well as some [past investigation](https://docs.google.com/document/d/11y86xkDX3Z5mKDlnseWFigES0i_ZVQifzr99e10qncw/edit#heading=h.cfu8rhxwsue9) into possible solutions.

For reference, the [Design System website](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/) uses an inline script to determine fairly quickly on page load whether the cookie banner should be shown or not, which may be another option to consider. Note that the DS does not provide JS for a cookie banner, only the HTML and CSS.

## Brief code dive

Running a lighthouse audit on a locally running GOV.UK homepage gives a CLS score of `0.285`.

Possible optimisation... moving the call to [this.showCookieMessage](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk_publishing_components/blob/main/app/assets/javascripts/govuk_publishing_components/components/cookie-banner.js#L40) from line 40 to before the call to [this.setupCookieMessage](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk_publishing_components/blob/main/app/assets/javascripts/govuk_publishing_components/components/cookie-banner.js#L17) on line 17 gets straight to showing/hiding the cookie banner ahead of showing/hiding the contents of the cookie banner (which we do so that the buttons get shown when JS is enabled but hidden when JS is not). This is basically switching one kind of CLS for another but it reduces the score to `0.272` so might be worth further investigation. I don't know why the display of these buttons isn't controlled through CSS by the `js-enabled` class, but presumably there's a reason.

Thanks to @36degrees for bringing this to our attention.

communityIssues.title: Search component button height issue when text size is increased
communityIssues.body: Noticed this on Firefox, where my browser is set to zoom text only, and I'm using a zoom greater than 100%. The search button doesn't fill the entire height of the search component. This can be seen in the component guide preview (with similar browser settings). I had a go at fixing this but it looks to be more complicated than I'd hoped. The component uses `table` and `table-cell` CSS to achieve the layout, with `table-cell` currently applied to the search input and a wrapping element on the button. I hoped that removing the wrapping element on the button and moving some styles around would fix it, but seems not. Not only does this not fix the problem but it introduces a new problem relating to the width of the input. This is currently managed by the button wrapper being set to `width: 1%` and the button itself pushing out of that by setting its own width. Also, to achieve the layout above, `appearance: auto` needs to be set (currently set to `none`) otherwise the button wraps below the input.

communityIssues.title: Introducing changes to components used in govspeak can break things

We recently had an issue caused by a change to the button component that led to a publishing problem. This was because govspeak wasn't updated to allow for the change to the button component.

Preventing similar issues in the future will need to be solved with a combination of both documentation and developer awareness. communityIssues.title: Inconsistent components API
communityIssues.body:
The component API is inconsistent across components and in comparison with `govuk-frontend`.

In the table below there is a brief comparison in how `govuk-frontend` components are aligned in API with `govuk_publishing_components`

|Component               |API |
|---                      |---  |
Accordion                 | aligned
Back link                 | aligned
Breadcrumbs               | misaligned
Button                    | slightly misaligned (start)
Character count           | slightly misaligned (nesting)
Checkboxes                | slightly misaligned (fieldset)
Date input                | slightly misaligned (fieldset)
Details                   | misaligned
Error message             | aligned
Error summary             | misaligned
Fieldset                  | misaligned
File upload               | aligned
Footer                    | aligned
Header                    | slightly misaligned (navigation_items)
Inset text                | aligned
Panel                     | misaligned
Phase banner              | misaligned
Radios                    | slightly misaligned (fieldset)
Select                    | slightly misaligned (options)
Skip link                 | aligned
Summary list              | slightly misaligned (items)
Table                     | aligned
Tabs                      | misaligned
Text input                | aligned
Textarea                  | aligned
Warning text              | slightly misaligned (iconFallbackText)

We can see a few common differences between to two API models:
- for arrays, `govuk-frontend` uses the generic `items` (in most cases) whereas `govuk_publishing_components` uses the name of the component (e.g. `attachments` for the attachment list component or `breadcrumbs` for the breadcrumbs component)
- for web addresses/paths `govuk-frontend` uses `href` whereas in `govuk_publishing_components` we often find `url` (e.g. breadcrumbs component)

It's worth mentioning that not even `govuk-frontend`'s API is consistent (e.g. `errorList` instead of `items` in the Error summary component, or differences in nesting)

A few advantages of making the API consistent:
- increases developers' confidence when calling components with arguments (without constantly checking examples in the guide)
- prototyping and production will use the same config object (can be easily copied over in both directions)
- applications can prepare the data to be fed into components consistently using helpers
- it would be easier to swap one component with another

I'm creating this to raise awareness of the differences, hopefully generate discussions around how good looks like and aim for consistency and convergency. API alignment requires at least a breaking change and some replacements across applications – which is not an easy process. For this reason, having a clear vision about how we want it to look like would save us from doing this more than once.

communityIssues.title: Feature suggestion: support a medium button size

communityIssues.title: Button styled as link in account header
communityIssues.body:
The (relatively new) account section in the header [has the option](https://github.com/nhsuk/nhsuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/nhsuk-frontend/src/nhsuk/components/header/template.njk#L140-L155) to use a <button> element which is styled like a link. This is often used for a "Log out" button - to avoid a potential security issue with using links which might cause users to be logged out without actually clicking the button.

However, when testing using screen readers in the accessibility lab, it confused us that using the shortcode for 'next form element' would jump first to "Log out".

Should we add role="link" to the button to avoid this, on the basis that it looks like a link so should behave like one? If so should it also behave like a link, for example opening a new tab if command-clicked?

Are there any other options?

* Would `<button formaction="/log-out">` behave differently from a button embedded in a form, or not?
* Alternatively we could recommend using a real link which takes you to a confirmation page that has a button on it - but this would have the down side of requiring 2 click to log out

communityIssues.title: App integration pattern for 3rd party sites and services
communityIssues.body: ## The need We believe there may be a need for guidance in the NHS App design system that outlines how 3rd party sites and services that integrate with the app should look and work – an “app integration pattern”. ## What's the problem? During some work in late 2025/early 2026, we discovered that NHS website content in the app was integrated in inconsistent ways. Some pages opened the full website in an overlay, some pages opened the full website in a web view, and some pages opened a slightly customised (with a suppressed header) version of the site in a web view. This causes a range of issues for users, such as: - integration patterns can change mid-way through a journey, leading to a jarring and confusing experience - standard website navigation elements can lead to circular journeys (for example, if users click on “My account” in the website header when they’re in the app, they’ll be prompted to go through the NHS login journey just to end up back on the app) - misleading or unhelpful terminology is shown to users (for example, links saying “NHS App” take users to pages about the NHS App rather than to the app itself and links to “profile editor” can be interpreted as being related to the user’s app profile rather than profile pages for services on the NHS website - the search bar searches the NHS website, not the app, and returns results that can be misleading in an app context - breadcrumbs take users up a level in the website hierarchy, rather than back to the previous page, causing confusing journeys and ultimately trapping users within NHS website pages when they access them from the app - lots of distracting links in the website header and footer can take users away from the task they came to the app to complete The inconsistency also causes some issues for the NHS website, such as: - analytics data is easier to gather when content is consistently integrated in a web view - journeys that involve passing across patient data work appear to more smoothy in a web view - the general direction of travel for app integrations in the future is a “custom overlay”, which is a variation on the current web view integration (not the standard overlay pattern currently used for a lot of NHS website pages) ## Our recommendations for the NHS website Our team has recommended that NHS website pages in the app should always be displayed using a web view rather than an overlay, and that NHS website teams should implement a consistent “app integration pattern” that customises global navigation elements when we detect a user is accessing the content via the NHS App. The integration pattern consists of 3 main adaptations for app users: 1. Suppressed site header – total suppression of the NHS website header, including NHS logo, account button, search bar and site navigation links 2. Simplified site footer – a reduction in the number of footer links displayed so that only essential links (terms and conditions, cookies policy and accessibility statement) are shown 3. Backwards navigation – a mechanism for allowing users to return to the previous page in their browser history (generally this means replacing the standard site breadcrumb with a “Back” link) **While some of these issues and recommendations may be specific to the NHS website, it’s likely some would apply to any other 3rd party site/service and could form the basis for more general guidance about how other organisations and services should adapt their pages for the app.**

communityIssues.title: [Feature request]: Partial Error
communityIssues.body: ### Description Within Secondary Care Services appointments and documents are populated from multiple data sources. Currently, when a PEP has an issue, the appointments or documents from that PEP will not be shown, causing an incomplete list of appointments or documents. With partial error, we are giving a user a way to refresh the data in the hopes that when a new request is sent to the PEP they will then send back the data. ### Related component This proposed component is version of the inset text with a secondary button. $ ### Context ### Alternatives Currently we have this disclaimer on top of the page. ### Additional information (if applicable) **Research Overview** Two rounds of research were conducted to inform the Partial Error component: **Round 1 – Messaging and Design Variations** - Methods: In-person moderated testing and card sorting. - Participants: 8 users. - Focus: Testing the wording, tone, and design variations of the Partial Error component. **Round 2 – Component Placement** - Methods: Unmoderated remote testing. - Participants: 30 users. - Focus: Determining the optimal placement of the component (top vs. bottom of the screen) and the colour of the inset (Blue vs. Grey vs. Red). **High-Level User Insights Language and Tone** - Participants preferred positive, reassuring language. - Words like “missing” were perceived negatively; alternatives like “showing” felt more constructive. *Calls to Action* - Having *more than one action* was important for usability. - Commonly suggested actions: “Try again” or “Contact your healthcare team.” - Most participants naturally chose “Try again” when presented with the option. *Colour and Visual Design* - Red conveys urgency and draws attention effectively. - Blue felt passive and less likely to prompt immediate action. - The inset text style of the component felt familiar and approachable. *Placement and Visibility* - Participants were more likely to notice and interact with the component when it appeared at the top of the screen. - Many missed it entirely if it was placed at the bottom, as they did not scroll down. *Key Takeaways for Component Design* - Use *positive, actionable language* to reassure users. - Include *multiple calls to action*, prioritising the most common action (“Try again”). - Leverage *colour strategically* to indicate urgency without causing alarm. - Position the component *prominently at the top* of the interface to maximise visibility. - Ensure the *visual style is familiar*, enhancing user comfort and engagement.

communityIssues.title: [Documentation]: Use case for including a back button
communityIssues.body: ### Description On Notifications and Messages, we are designing a PDF viewer that will enable users to view letters within their messages section in the NHS App. Users can view the PDF inside the app or download it. In a scenario where: - The user attempts to view OR download the letter but a service error occurs. We believe the back button is logical for the user flow. In this instance, the error is triggered by a CTA ['view letter' or 'download letter'] not the page itself so there is no risk of the user being stuck in an error loop. A 'try again' CTA is shown on the error screen, however if the service error continues the logical next step for the user will be to go back to their message. Without a back button, the user would either need to - Go to 'home', then back into 'messages' - Click 'messages' within the bottom nav to refresh ### Related documentation _No response_ ### Evidence (where applicable) _No response_

communityIssues.title: List
communityIssues.body: ## What We need a way to display app menu items that conform to app patterns. ## Why Unlike websites where you have anchor links or unordered lists, apps primary classify things as buttons. Links do exist on apps (i.e a url web resource), but they are used differently often taking the user out of the app and to a web resource on a browser. On apps, list are the primary way to display menu items. While the appearance of the list can look like a card or card link or a card panel link, they are essentially list items which can hold images, titles and a navigation destination. ## User behaviour insights The app user research teams did an accessibility test in RNIB London (June 2024). One of the findings was that users may expect 'panels' to be announced as buttons rather than links ## Details iOS describes list as >A table or list can represent data that’s organised in groups or hierarchies, and it can support user interactions like selecting, adding, deleting, and reordering. Apps and games in all platforms can use tables to present content and options; many apps use lists to express an overall information hierarchy and help people navigate it. For example, iOS Settings uses a hierarchy of lists to help people choose options, and several apps — such as Mail in iPadOS and macOS — use a table within a split view Android describes list as >Lists are continuous, vertical indexes of text and images. Many apps need to display collections of items. This document explains how you can efficiently do this in Jetpack Compose. Reference https://m3.material.io/components/lists/overview https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/lists https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/lists-and-tables https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/list ## Related Card links (Panel link) #10

communityIssues.title: Card links: border style
communityIssues.body: ### Description The current colour contrast of the page background and card links surrounding border is 1.24:1. As it does not meet the [non-text contrast](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/non-text-contrast.html) ratio of 3:1 it makes the border somewhat redundant. #### Blog post on non-text contrast of UI elements https://iknowdavehouse.medium.com/why-debate-non-text-contrast-of-ui-elements-1be4313c9e12 > Every time you design or build something, take 10 minutes to review it with all the parts of the interactive UI elements that do not meet 3:1 contrast ratio removed. > > So if your button background does not meet 3:1 remove it, if your interactive card borders do not meet 3:1 remove them… > > Then ask yourself: > > - Is the interface still understandable? > - Is the interface still as usable? > - Could I do more?

backlog.title: Download, save, print or share a confirmation, receipt, certificate, or letter at the end of a service
backlog.body:
What
A consistent pattern to fulfil the need for a user to download, save or print either a confirmation of a transaction, receipt or a certificate of completion (most commonly at the end of a service).
Why
After working for HMRC in live services and at the Home Office in build services, I have seen multiple services that have a user need to download, save or print a confirmation or receipt or certificate of completion, usually in the form of a generated PDF.
Nearly every one of these services takes a different approach and when faced with a similar problem previously as a designer on a build team, we ended up developing yet another approach due to the lack of guidance of a suggested pattern. In addition, technically lots of these services take a lot of different approaches to generating the receipt or certificate with a range of libraries used.
There could be an argument that these are somewhat different use cases so we shouldn’t conflate the pattern for them but generally it feels like all of the existing designs have a combination of letting users save/download, print or open an A4 document, usually a generated PDF. A pattern to provide guidance could help align build teams rather than letting them re-invent the wheel every time.
Related patterns and components:

#6044
#6037
#6014
#5934

Examples in existing services
[HMRC] Employment Related Securities (ERS) returns – Confirmation receipt (Live)
When the user follows the link on the page a PDF is generated PDF and opened in the browser. In older browsers that don’t support showing PDFs such as IE it just downloads.

Apparently during research, users were requesting a receipt that they could download for their records. The use case being accountants who have to keep records on their internal company systems. Print was considered but not so relevant for companies with digital record keeping where they would have to save a PDF through the print dialogue.
Unsure who the build designer was. Now being looked after by HMRC Edinburgh Live Services. Contacts are: abdirahman.mohammed@digital.hmrc.gov.uk, helen.sell@digital.hmrc.gov.uk, samuel.holyhead@digital.hmrc.gov.uk

[HMRC] Advanced Tariff Rulings (ATaR) – Save or print confirmation and other letters (Live)
Embedded in the page. Custom CSS removes the UI when printed. PDF generated when user clicks on the save button. Screenshot from the prototype for ease.

Unsure who the build designer was. Now being looked after by HMRC Edinburgh Live Services. Contacts are: abdirahman.mohammed@digital.hmrc.gov.uk, helen.sell@digital.hmrc.gov.uk, samuel.holyhead@digital.hmrc.gov.uk

[HMRC] Trusts – Confirmation receipt (Going from Live Beta into Live)
This service is just going out of beta into live and has had several sprints of research and development on the pattern. It contains a generated PDF that is downloaded to the users machine if they select they want to download. The user goes through a set of two questions pages and the file is downloaded if they choose the correct radio options.


During the handover we found out that previous designs included opening the receipt in the browser but research showed that users then closed the window which lost the token for their session as this occurs mid-flow. Apparently there is a 4 second wait when the user clicks continue to avoid overloading the PDF generator with requests. This hasn’t been an issue during testing according to the build team.
UX designer on the project build: benjamin.ingignieri@digital.hmrc.gov.uk

[Home Office] Prevent eLearning service – Certificate of completion (Closed Beta)
This service features a certificate of completion at the end of the lesson. This is to prove to managers and employers that they have completed the training.
A generated PDF that is opened in the browser via link which follows the Publishing download attachment pattern. Previous research included trying a HTML version but users struggled to save that version. PDF is opened in the browser due to security concerns about putting the users details into the front-end. User research suggests that users would expect to save this to their computer as the default behaviour. Additionally, it was found that if a green confirmation panel was used in the in the flow before this page then users would tend to close the window before reading that they can download the certificate.

UX designer on the project build: samuel.holyhead@digital.hmrc.gov.uk

[Home Office] Check someone’s immigration status (Live)
Save or print an application. This example was shared with us by Frank Ramsey and Chris O’leary at the Home Office.

Contact: frank.ramsay@digital.homeoffice.gov.uk, Chris.O'Leary@digital.homeoffice.gov.uk
Does this already exist in the design system?
In regards to existing elements in the GOV.UK design system (or other department’s design systems), while there are components suggested for saving, downloading or printing an item, I feel like this is a different problem that usually takes the form of a flow or combination of existing components.
Other thoughts on a potential pattern
Some initial thoughts about what format a pattern could take:

there seems to be a common theme that out of the actions, most users want to download a copy
seems like HTML consistently isn’t a good file format to download as most users want to store a file locally or share a file via email, etc. From research, users struggle to save a PDF via print dialogs, etc.
from research, linguistically most users refer to this as action as wanting to save the file
related – print buttons usually require javascript. It would be good to explore alternatives that fit with progressive enhancement. Embedding the content in the page and using custom CSS to remove the UI seems like a nice approach that supports the use of the print function in the browser rather than a javascript button.
sometimes download implementations open up a new blank windows in order to download the file. It would be good to explore how to avoid this.
just personal preference but the outline of the document in the ATaR example help signify which parts of the page will be printed or saved while also previewing the document. consideration would need to be given on how to signify this to users of screen readers and other assistive technology though.
in regards to generation libraries:

HMRC have a PDF generation service that they are deprecating.
some other services use pdfbox: https://pdfbox.apache.org
this is an example of how to generate an accessible PDF using pdfBox: https://github.com/martinlovell/accessible-pdfbox-example

communityIssues.title: Approach for empty components is inconsistent
communityIssues.body:
Components that require things to be passed to them can either fail silently if nothing is passed or raise an error.

Currently our approach for this varies - for example, the `attachment link` component throws an error if nothing is passed to it, but the `select` component just doesn't render anything.

It would be sensible to be consistent unless there's good reason for this variation. If we choose the option of raising an error then this should also be handled consistently across components. This would also make the component spec tests more consistent.

There might be a reason for this in some cases, e.g. where a component is used on a page and intentionally doesn't render if data for it isn't present in the content item. Any changes should be carefully checked.

communityIssues.title: Inconsistent application of `heading_size` and `heading_level`
communityIssues.body:
Some components support a `heading_size` property (values from 's' to 'xl'), but sometimes the property is defined on the top level hash and other times it is defined on the `label` property. Examples:

[input component](https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/input/with_label_as_heading):

```erb
<%= render "govuk_publishing_components/components/input", {
  label: {
    text: "This is a heading 1 and a label"
  },
  name: "name",
  heading_level: 1,
  heading_size: "l"
} %>
```

[textarea component](https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/textarea/with_label_as_page_heading):

```erb
<%= render "govuk_publishing_components/components/textarea", {
  label: {
    is_page_heading: true,
    heading_size: "xl",
    text: "Can you provide more detail?"
  },
  hint: "Please include as much information as possible.",
  name: "more-detail-error"
} %>
```

Consequently, there are examples in the wild where the config has been incorrectly applied, e.g.

- https://github.com/alphagov/whitehall/blob/3d0d0340827d8b0e32bad3823645b1ad2fabbffc/app/views/admin/attachments/_attachment_data_fields.html.erb#L10-L11
- https://github.com/alphagov/whitehall/blob/514ba658e64b3dd3b5bb12a607e47f3f0d80422c/app/views/admin/take_part_pages/_form.html.erb#L7-L24

It is difficult to know how many occurrences there are without a widespread audit.

## Proposal

1. Raise an exception if `heading_level`/`heading_size` is passed to a component in a way that it is not expecting, and
2. Decide on one way of doing things (top level, or on `label`), and migrate all components to that approach

communityIssues.title: Inconsistent components API
communityIssues.body:
The component API is inconsistent across components and in comparison with `govuk-frontend`.

In the table below there is a brief comparison in how `govuk-frontend` components are aligned in API with `govuk_publishing_components`

|Component               |API |
|---                      |---  |
Accordion                 | aligned
Back link                 | aligned
Breadcrumbs               | misaligned
Button                    | slightly misaligned (start)
Character count           | slightly misaligned (nesting)
Checkboxes                | slightly misaligned (fieldset)
Date input                | slightly misaligned (fieldset)
Details                   | misaligned
Error message             | aligned
Error summary             | misaligned
Fieldset                  | misaligned
File upload               | aligned
Footer                    | aligned
Header                    | slightly misaligned (navigation_items)
Inset text                | aligned
Panel                     | misaligned
Phase banner              | misaligned
Radios                    | slightly misaligned (fieldset)
Select                    | slightly misaligned (options)
Skip link                 | aligned
Summary list              | slightly misaligned (items)
Table                     | aligned
Tabs                      | misaligned
Text input                | aligned
Textarea                  | aligned
Warning text              | slightly misaligned (iconFallbackText)

We can see a few common differences between to two API models:
- for arrays, `govuk-frontend` uses the generic `items` (in most cases) whereas `govuk_publishing_components` uses the name of the component (e.g. `attachments` for the attachment list component or `breadcrumbs` for the breadcrumbs component)
- for web addresses/paths `govuk-frontend` uses `href` whereas in `govuk_publishing_components` we often find `url` (e.g. breadcrumbs component)

It's worth mentioning that not even `govuk-frontend`'s API is consistent (e.g. `errorList` instead of `items` in the Error summary component, or differences in nesting)

A few advantages of making the API consistent:
- increases developers' confidence when calling components with arguments (without constantly checking examples in the guide)
- prototyping and production will use the same config object (can be easily copied over in both directions)
- applications can prepare the data to be fed into components consistently using helpers
- it would be easier to swap one component with another

I'm creating this to raise awareness of the differences, hopefully generate discussions around how good looks like and aim for consistency and convergency. API alignment requires at least a breaking change and some replacements across applications – which is not an easy process. For this reason, having a clear vision about how we want it to look like would save us from doing this more than once.

ourIssues.title: Expand documentation of fieldset to discuss when to add `role="group"`
ourIssues.body:
The date component has `role="group"` on its fieldset. The fieldset component example doesn't.

Via @36degrees, this is what the [code has to say](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/6c9d8d7191edb18e8a46d2a383e311f397367946/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/date-input/template.njk#L91-L94):

* Add a paragraph of text discussing when to use it.

communityIssues.title: Whitehall overrides some component styles
communityIssues.body:
There are a few instances in whitehall's CSS where styles for gem components are being overridden, which violates our principle of [component isolation](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk_publishing_components/blob/main/docs/component_principles.md#a-component-is-isolated-when). 

If possible, these styles should either be applied directly to the components themselves (in the form of new options) or applied to parent elements of the components within the application, so they do not impact the appearance of the components themselves.

[_overrides.scss line 21](https://github.com/alphagov/whitehall/blob/main/app/assets/stylesheets/admin/_overrides.scss#L21) overrides `gem-c-summary-list` child elements:

- `.govuk-summary-list__key` is given a vertical align of top, which looks redundant and can potentially be simply removed (text is already vertically aligned to the top in this element)
- images are given `display: block`. This might be trickier to unpick although the use of this component doesn't normally include images, so this might be a custom application thing that could be added to the component defaults

[_overrides.scss line 44](https://github.com/alphagov/whitehall/blob/main/app/assets/stylesheets/admin/_overrides.scss#L44) overrides `gem-c-checkboxes` styles:

- there's a helpful comment here explaining the issue, which is to do with not showing checkboxes when JavaScript is enabled with the Add another component. The [component guide page for Add another](https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/add_another) doesn't show any examples containing checkboxes, so this could be something that could be part of the component with a documentation update

[_overrides.scss line 50](https://github.com/alphagov/whitehall/blob/main/app/assets/stylesheets/admin/_overrides.scss#L50-L59) overrides reorderable list styles:

- both overrides refer to a 'read only' version of the component, which seems like it should be an option within the component

[_document-collection-group-memberships-index.scss line 2](https://github.com/alphagov/whitehall/blob/main/app/assets/stylesheets/admin/views/_document-collection-group-memberships-index.scss#L2) overrides heading styles:

- it looks like the heading component is being positioned inline along with a list of items, presumably to make them all appear on one line together. Not sure which page this appears on, but it might be done better with some custom CSS specifically for this purpose, rather than components

[_edit-edition.scss line 33](https://github.com/alphagov/whitehall/blob/main/app/assets/stylesheets/admin/views/_edit-edition.scss#L33) overrides the warning text component:

- it's setting the margin bottom of the component to 0, which can be achieved without CSS by passing a `margin_bottom: 0` option to the component (warning text uses the [component wrapper helper](https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/warning_text#standard-options))

[_summary.scss line 47](https://github.com/alphagov/whitehall/blob/main/app/assets/stylesheets/admin/views/_summary.scss#L47) overrides the button component:

- it's setting the width of the button to `100%`
- this isn't an option on the component or in the Design System, it might be this could just be removed

communityIssues.title: Enumerate legends in Add another
communityIssues.body:
**NB: This is a breaking change**

When you use [the Add another component](https://moj-design-system.herokuapp.com/components/add-another) to add an additional item, the legend on the form is identical to the original one: in the MOJDS docs example there would be two or more legends called "Person".

This makes it hard for users with screen readers to navigate the form, because the screen reader cannot distinguish between each fieldset.

To make this clearer, we should automatically enumerate the legends by appending an index number with JavaScript. i.e. when you "add another", the original legend will become "Person 1" and the new one will be "Person 2".

In order to support services which don't want this distinction, if the form has the attribute `data-moj-add-another-enumerate="false"` then the auto-enumeration should not occur. This opt-out mechanism will need to be documented.

communityIssues.title: Back to top link fails 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum)
communityIssues.body: The [Back to top link component](https://govuk-government-frontend.herokuapp.com/component-guide/back_to_top) in government-frontend fails [2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum)](https://w3c.github.io/wcag/understanding/focus-not-obscured-minimum.html). Note: 2.4.11 is part of the new draft WCAG 2.2 criteria. The latest standard is WCAG 2.1. WCAG 2.2 isn't published yet, so this is potentially subject to change. As mentioned by Andy Sellick in his 2018 blog post ‘[Sticky elements: functionality and accessibility testing](https://technology.blog.gov.uk/2018/05/21/sticky-elements-functionality-and-accessibility-testing/)’, content can be obscured by a sticky element. 2.4.11 is specifically about focus that shouldn’t be obscured. There was an effort with this component to minimise that already as the sticky ‘Contents’ link only appears when scrolling the page but not when only tabbing through the page. Although that fixes some of the issue, that doesn’t mean that the focus never gets obscured. The sticky link still appears when scrolling via the keyboard (for example, with the arrow keys) or when accidentally scrolling with the mouse or touchpad only for a second. To replicate, open the [preview of the 'Contents list with body' component](https://govuk-government-frontend.herokuapp.com/component-guide/contents_list_with_body/default/preview), tab to the last link (‘Commencement of initial period notice’), scroll the page via the up arrow key so that the link is obscured, use tab and shift + tab to go back and forth to see how you can tab to a link that isn’t visible. communityIssues.title: Add means of extending session
communityIssues.body:
At Universal Credit we are looking to stop using our own home-rolled session timeout code and to use the one provide by hmrc-frontend instead, as recommended by the DWP Design System (https://design-system.dwp.gov.uk/patterns/manage-a-session-timeout#:~:text=This%20pattern%20uses%20the ).

However, part of the agent site is built as a Single Page Application (SPA) - users often spend a prolonged period interacting with the site without requiring loading any further pages from the server, leading to timeout warnings being issued even though the agent is still being active, and worse users being timed out thinking they had more time to act than they actually had.

The solution for us, was to auto-extend the session any time the user interacts with the page (debouncing and batching up the keep-alive requests so as not to swamp the keep-alive endpoint) 

We would like to add this functionality to the HMRC timeout dialog component and would prefer not to fork it.

A branch implementing this can be found here:
https://github.com/solidgoldpig/hmrc-frontend/tree/extend-session-on-user-interaction

communityIssues.title: Signing out leaves synchronised tabs appearing to still be signed in
communityIssues.body:
When a user chooses to sign out early, the current tab is redirected to the signed out page.

Other synchronised tabs are not redirected to the signed out page, but simply have their timeout dialog cleared.

If a user then switches to one of the other tabs, it appears as if they are still logged in when in actual fact they are not. A user could continue to interact with the page and not realise that they were not logged in until they submitted the page, potentially losing any changes made.

The correct behaviour should surely be that the user is signed out of all synchronised tabs that they have open.

communityIssues.title: Feature request: improve timeout dialog example
communityIssues.body:
I've been using the timeout dialog example in the design system for some ad-hoc testing.

Two things would help immensely:
* Don't have it show on page load - instead either after a delay, or on button press
* Show an example of what happens to existing page content

## Don't have it show on page load - instead either after a delay, or on button press
The [govuk content publishing example](https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/modal_dialogue/with_form/preview) has a button that triggers the modal. The advantage here is when testing in something like Voiceover, you're already 'inside' the page and so it better represents how it would happen in real life. With the hmrc one you get it on page load - so the voiceover focus may be on the url bar.

## Show an example of what happens to existing page content
I'm not sure it's clear what should happen to existing page content. Is it removed and replaced by the modal? does the modal appear on top? The example adds an overlay div with opacity `0.8` so I _assume_ existing content is meant to stay.

One of the accessibility acceptance criteria be that focus is trapped on the modal and you can't scroll - as there's no other content in the examples, it's hard to test if focus is truly trapped / scrolling is prevented, etc.
