backlog.title: Accessibility link
backlog.body:
What
Establish how best to name and link to information about the accessibility options available to users within services.
Is referring to 'Ease of access' (or similar) more likely to be recognised by users who could benefit from the information provided?
Why
As part of meeting the legal requirements for the accessibility, teams producing websites and applications are directed to publish an accessibility statement
Within this, services can give useful information to users about the controls available to the users, such as browser options to control text size and colours, certain assistive tools and so on.
Most services seem to do this through a link named 'Accessibility' page in the footer.
However, in a Slack discussion in the cross-government 'Accessibility' channel, members of the community shared examples where users:

do not recognise the term 'Accessibility'
do not think that it is relevant to them
do not bother to look because, from past experience, they expect it to contain technical information or jargon that isn't relevant

This means some users can miss out on information about ease of access that would make it easier for them to use a service.
Quotes from Slack discussion (as of now)
A user researcher at GDS, said:
[I've seen] "all of the above (when researching how users perceived accessibility statements for the GDS accessibility team). Particularly that users don't always associate the word with their needs, potentially consider it to be about physical access, don't expect it to contain anything useful for them, or are so used to those pages containing generic/jargony info that they don't bother to look."
A user researcher at Ministry of Justice, said:
"I’ve tested accessibility pages in the past. In usability testing users didn’t recognise the link and when prompted to look under it, didn’t think the information was relevant or helpful.
In the past, accessibility pages were largely a box-ticking exercise and had little valuable info for users. They usually consisted of a standard line about WCAG compliance (even if it was not true), HTML validation and browser keyboard shortcuts. The better ones linked to BBC’s 'my web, my way'.
I expect that even those who had looked there, over time learned not to waste their time.
Having observed recent discussions about accessibility statements, I think there’s still a risk of tick-boxing. That’s why any sample statements should include a massive caveat that they shouldn’t be copied and pasted and that you should first do the work, then write about it (in that order).
I think it would be interesting to get quant data on this with analytics."
A Front-End Developer and Accessibility Specialist at GDS, said:
"Bad discoverability was one of the reasons why Microsoft renamed their accessibility settings to “Ease of access”."
(But I don't know the source for this)
In the 'Apply for a Budgeting Loan' service, feedback about the usability of the service is broadly very positive but a small percentage of users consistently give feedback that they need larger text or for text to be read to them. For this service we know some of our user base struggle in terms of literacy and can be low in confidence and ability using technology. This service doesn't currently have an accessibility statement of its own but it seems that users have not read GOV.UK's accessibility statement about the options available to them.

ourIssues.title: Confusing use of functional colours for footer background
ourIssues.body:
## What

In the footer CSS we define `$govuk-footer-background`:

https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/6b7063b9cbf95cfbb758e4cf01e4d962b722a6eb/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/footer/_mixin.scss#L5

However that variable is never used. Instead, we then set the `background` property to `base.govuk-functional-colour(template-background)` directly:

https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/6b7063b9cbf95cfbb758e4cf01e4d962b722a6eb/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/footer/_mixin.scss#L21

Agree on which functional colour the footer should be using, and update the CSS so that it makes sense, with no unused variables.

## Why

It looks like [the intent was to use `surface-background` ](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/pull/6659#:~:text=We%27ve%20changed%20the,such%20through%20code), but from conversation on Slack it's clear we're not aligned on whether this is the right approach.

## Who needs to work on this

Developers, designers

## Who needs to review this

Developers, designers

## Done when

- [ ] We're agreed on which functional colour(s) the footer should be using, and how this might apply to other components (e.g. cookie banner)
- [ ] The CSS reflects the functional colour(s) that we want to use, and has no confusing code e.g. unused variables

ourIssues.title: Some template level svgs are hard to see when using forced colour browser extensions
ourIssues.body: ## Description of the issue When using certain forced colour made browser extensions, in this case [Dark Reader](https://darkreader.org/) which changes colours by rotating hue, certain in-page template svgs like the GOV.UK logo lockup and the OGL logo in the footer incorrectly change with the colour mode, making them functionally impossible to see with the ## Steps to reproduce the issue 1. Go to a GOV.UK service on a browser with Dark Reader installed, with Dark Reader turned off 2. Scroll down to the bottom of the page, note the OGL logo in the footer 3. Turn Dark Reader on ## Actual vs expected behaviour ### Expected The OGL logo is the same colour as the page's text colour, forced or otherwise eg: it'll be black if text is set to black, white if text is set to white. ### Actual The OGL logo is an off-black against the dark footer background ## Environment (where applicable) - Operating system: MacOS Tahoe 26.4.1 - Browser: Chrome - Browser version: 147.0.7727.117 - GOV.UK Frontend Version: >= 5.14 ## Notes What seems to be happening here is Dark Reader is adding attributes to change the colour of the SVG by rotating it's hue 180 degrees. At least for the OGL logo, this is overriding the `fill="currentcolour"` applied to the `path` of the OGL svg. That attribute is setting the svg to the page text colour, which the extension is overriding back to black. Removing `fill="currentcolour"` resolves this and, from some very shallow testing, seems to work fine without any forced colours and with other forced colour methods. It looks like there are some team tasks to do here: 1. Decide if this is something we want to try to figure out at our level or if we call this a bug in Dark Reader instead and not make it our concern 2. Investigate if removing `fill="currentcolour"` causes other unexpected problems 3. Try to understand Dark Reader's behaviour further and if there's something we're doing that's triggering Dark Reader to apply that hue rotation styling

ourIssues.title: Components assume the `govuk-visually-hidden` utility class will exist

We provide an entry points for each individual component, the idea being that users should get all of the CSS they need to use that component, and ideally nothing more.

For example, including the character count component also includes the CSS for the:

- File upload (in the JavaScript)
- Footer (in the Nunjucks template)
- Pagination (in the Nunjucks template)
- Password input (in the JavaScript)
- Summary list (in the Nunjucks template)
- Warning text (in the Nunjucks template)

## Steps to reproduce the issue

ourIssues.title: Deprecate the `govuk-device-pixel-ratio` mixin
ourIssues.body:
## What

Follow our process for [deprecating a Sass function or mixin](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/docs/contributing/managing-change.md#deprecating-a-sass-function-or-mixin) to deprecate the `govuk-device-pixel-ratio` mixin.

## Why

We haven't used the mixin internally since we updated the Royal Arms graphic in the footer to be an SVG (#5376).

[Changes in browser support](https://caniuse.com/css-media-resolution) mean that the mixin could be simplified significantly, to the point where it's not really useful to have a mixin any more:

- Opera has supported `min-resolution` since 12.1 (November 2012), and the `dppx` unit since 55 (August 2018), making the `-o-min-device-pixel-ratio` media query redundant
- Safari has supported `min-resolution` since 16.0 (September 2022), making the `-webkit-min-device-pixel-ratio` redundant
- Even Internet Explorer has supported `min-resolution` (only with `dpi` unit) since IE9

I'd suggest most users could replace the use of the mixin with just:

```scss
@media (min-resolution: 2dppx) {
```

Or, if they want to maximise browser support, use `dpi` instead:

```scss
@media (min-resolution: 192dpi) {
```

## Who needs to work on this

Developers

## Who needs to review this

Developers, tech writer

## Done when

- [ ] The mixin is marked as deprecated in the Sassdoc
- [ ] The mixin outputs a warning when called
- [ ] The deprecation is clear in the release notes

ourIssues.title: Investigate ways to deliver GOV.UK logo, footer crown and OGL logo as SVG files rather than inline
ourIssues.body:
## Related component

Header and footer

## Context

Off the back of https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/6032, I wondered if you had considered changing the way the header logo and footer crown are displayed so that they use the same method as the footer crest (https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/pull/5872), with an .svg file as a `mask-image` in CSS rather than inlining the SVG. 

This would make fixes and updates to the logo easier to roll out as they could be handled entirely as image asset and Sass changes rather than requiring developers to manually update the SVG. It would also save about 4kb of page weight on most requests as the SVG file could be cached. 

The cyan dot can be done by making the background a `linear-gradient` with hard stops between cyan and `currentColor` (to preserve forced colour compatibility). The footer crown could even reuse the same SVG file as the header logo, as the mask image can be cropped in CSS.

As in https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/pull/5872, we could fall back to displaying the SVG as a `background-image` for Edge 17 compatibility.

I've very quickly tested that this would work as expected - I'm happy to tidy it up into a draft PR if you think it's worth pursuing.

ourIssues.title: How to adapt footer for non-GOV.UK services
ourIssues.body:
## Related component

[GOV.UK footer](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/footer/)


## Context

The new rebranded footer has the crown logo at the top of it.
But the crown shouldn't be used in non-GOV.UK services, neither in the header nor the footer.

Before this change non-GOV.UK services had to change the header but not the footer, now they also have to change the footer. But we don't have any guidance for it.

We should at least add guidance similar to what we say in the ['When to use this component' section for the GOV.UK header component](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/header/#when-to-use-this-component).

And maybe we could add code options to make it easier to remove the crown.


## Alternatives

At the moment people would have to either:

* build their own footer
* or render the footer and remove the `<svg>` tag for the logo before serving it
* or remove the logo via CSS

But in either of those cases non-GOV.UK service teams need to know that they cannot use the component as is and need to change something.

ourIssues.title: Consider adding alternative text for crown and crest
ourIssues.body:
## What

Think about alternative text for the crown in the header and the footer and the crest in the footer.
We currently don't have any alternative text to describe or even mention the crown or the crest. 

The current alternative texts (not necessarily value for `alt` parameter) are:

* The crown in the header includes the word mark. It is linked and leads to the homepage. It's an`<svg>` with an `aria-label` of "GOV.UK".
* The crown in the footer does not include the word mark. It is not linked.  It's an`<svg>` with a `role="presentation". (The crown is not in the footer yet, but it will be soon.)
* The crest in the footer does not include any text (within the image itself, unless you count the motto, which is really too small to see). It is the background image of a link that goes to a National Archives page about the Crown copyright. And that link includes the text "© Crown copyright".

To summarise the alternative texts for those images...

| Image (text approximation) | Alternative text | Is in a link? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 👑 GOV.UK | GOV.UK | yes |
| 👑 |  | no |
| 🛡️ © Crown copyright | © Crown copyright | yes |

## Why

We never describe or reference the images. We should explore if doing that would be valuable to people who cannot see the images (or cannot see them well enough).

We should find out what these images do for people who can see them. And if they do anything important, we should consider those images to be meaningful and add (to) alternative text to describe them.

My (untested) assumptions:
Visually both images give the page a more official look.
They help establishing trust.
They reference something a user might want to be looking for.
And they signal the start and the end of the page.

If that is correct, they should have alternative text that conveys those things.

It's worth noting that this has never been flagged in a WCAG audit. Therefore it might not be a problem and is not an urgent thing to fix.


## Who needs to work on this

Content designer, designer, accessibility specialist, user researcher

## Who needs to review this

The team, and maybe someone from GOV.UK should be involved as well

## Done when

- [ ] Have evidence for meaning of those images to users (either through our own research or someone else's)
- [ ] Decided if those images are meaningful to our users
- [ ] If they are, write alternative text for them and implement it

ourIssues.title: Add option to footer component allowing ‘The following links open in a new tab’ guidance to be followed
ourIssues.body: ## Related component Footer ## Context My team has received a request to have one of our services's footer links open in new tabs. We want to follow the [guidance](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/styles/links/#opening-links-in-a-new-tab) for this scenario: > If you’re displaying lots of links together and want to save space and avoid repetition, consider doing both of the following: > * adding a line of text before the links saying ‘The following links open in a new tab’ > * including (opens in new tab) as part of the link text, so that part of the link text is visually hidden but still accessible to screen readers However, there's no approved html example of implementing the ‘The following links open in a new tab’ text above the links. Moreover, there's no option providing this in the nunjucks macro, which is what our team relies on. Issue [#1782](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/1782) noticed this absence back in 2020, but unfortunately nothing came of it; see also [its sibling issue](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/issues/1219) on `govuk-design-system`. I also note that the ONS Design System has an implementation in place for this accessibility principle in [their footer macro](https://service-manual.ons.gov.uk/design-system/components/footer#example.example-footer-transactional.nunjucks), an option they call `"newTabWarning"`. Perhaps this could be a model for bringing this feature into GDS? ## Alternatives In the short term we will likely have to follow whatever html implementation the team that's asking us to make this change has made at their end. However for consistency across our services, it's desirable for us to be able to use the macro in all of them, due to how they share parent templates.

ourIssues.title: Adjust components to scale with android system font size
ourIssues.body:
## What
Ensure as many of our components as possible are responding when viewing govuk-frontend web pages on android devices and adjusting android's system font size.

## Why
Govuk-frontend web pages should respect accessibility settigns and respond to them as expected.

## Steps to replicate
Tested in chrome on browserstack's Galaxy S23 instance as it's easy to notice the issue due to the device's large font size scale.

1. Go to the settings of the testing device and locate the setting to adjust device font size
2. Increase font size (recommend max in order to visualise issue more clearly)
3. Open a govuk-frontend web page on a browser on an android device eg: [the review app's announcements page](https://govuk-frontend-review.herokuapp.com/full-page-examples/announcements)

Notice that the breadcrumbs have not increased in size. Digging into the runtime styles, you will find that rem values of other elements on the page have adjusted in response to the font size change but the breadcrumbs haven't.

![Android browser showing an announcements page with scaled up font size except for the breadcrumbs element](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/assets/64783893/66ecb7d1-bf9e-459a-987c-8c85176a26b7)

## Notes
### Considerations from the spec
The likely reason this is happening can be found in CSS Mobile Text Size section of the CSS spec, specifically [2.2: Conditions that suppress adjustment](https://drafts.csswg.org/css-size-adjust/#default-adjustment-conditions). This section notes 4 reasons that would suppress text size adjustment. From initial testing, certain components can be 'fixed' by removing their block level positioning rules eg: components that have `display: inline-block`. We should be able to use `inline-block` on components and the text size adjustment not be suppressed. Recommend using the the spec in figuring out a solution.

### Impacted components
- Accordion
- Back link
- Breadcrumbs
- Button, and places consumed
    - Cookie banner buttons
    - Exit this page
- Checkboxes
- Details (not the content)
- File upload
- Some of the footer's links
- Header menu
- Notification banner
- Pagination
- Radios
- Select
- Table
- Tabs
- Tag
- Task list
- Text input, and places consumed
    - Date input
    - Password input

## Who needs to work on this
Developers

## Who needs to review this
Developers

ourIssues.title: Error Summary is not focused correctly on second form submission with NVDA
ourIssues.body:
<!--
    Please fill in as much of the template below as you’re able to. If you're unsure whether the issue already exists or how to fill in the template, open an issue anyway. Our team will help you to complete the rest.

-->

## Description of the issue
<!-- A clear and concise summary of what the bug is. -->
While using NVDA 2020.3 on Firefox 81, if an invalid form is submitted twice, focus is not set on the Error Summary.

This means that when a user tabs to the next element, it is _not_ the first error message link, but a later link on the page.

## Steps to reproduce the issue
<!-- How can we reproduce this issue? If you think it will be helpful, please provide a small code snippet and/or screenshots. -->

* Go to this full page example: http://govuk-frontend-review.herokuapp.com/full-page-examples/update-your-account-details
* Enter nothing, submit
* The page reloads with an Error Summary which is correctly focused
* Again, enter nothing and submit again
* The page reloads with focus set elsewhere. Pressing tab once moves focus to a footer link

## Actual vs expected behaviour
<!-- What is happening vs what would you expect to happen instead? -->
Focus does not appear to be set on the Error Summary - I would expect it to have focus on each form submission beyond the first.

## Environment (where applicable)
<!-- Details of your operating system, browser and the version of GOVUK Frontend you’re using may help us to reproduce your issue. -->

- Operating system: assistivLabs NVDA 2020.3 (presumably on Windows 10)
- Browser: Firefox
- Browser version: 81
- GOV.UK Frontend Version: 3.10

ourIssues.title: Test that documented component options match the templates
ourIssues.body:
## What

Add tests that validate the documented options within our component YAML files (like [the button YAML file](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/f704053f8544e8d88acec68ca448b4cb992a76d2/src/components/button/button.yaml)) match the actual options used within the template / macro.

If the two do not match, the tests should fail.

There is as a ['work-in-progress' branch](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/tree/test-definitions) for this work which currently does this, but needs some refactoring / documentation before it can be merged.

## Why

Currently we rely on human review to ensure that the documented options match reality. During a recent [firebreak](https://insidegovuk.blog.gov.uk/2018/05/03/firebreaks-on-gov-uk/) project, we explored whether we could do anything to catch these in our CI process.

The work found a number of inaccuracies in the documentation options:

- `attributes` not documented on the breadcrumbs and select components
- `describedBy` mistakenly documented on textarea and character count components
- `footer` component YAML misformed using `arguments` instead of `params`, which means the `meta` object is not documented correctly in the Design System
- `items[].name` mistakenly documented on radios – unlike checkboxes, this can only be set globally as having a set of radios with different names doesn't make any sense
- `title` not documented on the tabs component

This highlights the need to automate these checks, so we can make sure our documentation is correct.

ourIssues.title: Notification component uses `govuk-brand-colour` for border colour
ourIssues.body:
## Description of the issue

We've set our `$govuk-brand-colour` to MHCLG's teal (#00625E) and it's done the thing we expected, which is: change the header/footer border colour. But it's also changed the colour of the border on the notification component, which our designers don't like - they expected it to stay as the standard blue.

Is this intentional/expected? I can see that the header component has a separate variable, govuk-header-border-colour that is set to govuk-brand-colour - but we can't override the header border color directly because it doesn't respect a default value.

Is it expected that our notification banners should match the brand colour? To our designers it feels odd, and I can imagine if your department's colour is red and now all your notification banners are red, that would also feel odd/undesirable?

See also reference to slack thread where this was first raised (while history exists): https://ukgovernmentdigital.slack.com/archives/C6DMEH5R6/p1757328829381619. Raising/duplicating here just so I have a permalink I can reference in code while we're using a temporary workaround.

## Steps to reproduce the issue

1. Set `govuk-brand-colour` to a non-default value.
2. Render a notification banner component

## Actual vs expected behaviour

See that the border colour changes to the value you set for govuk-brand-colour, rather than the "default" blue.

ourIssues.title: WCAG 2.2: Start using a service ‖ Consistent Help
ourIssues.body:
## What

Consider adding or updating a screenshot of a start page to include visible help or contact information on the page, displayed in a consistent manner. Related to #2882. 

This is largely a usability suggestion and may not be necessary for WCAG compliance. 

### Resources

- [Start using a service pattern guidance](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/start-using-a-service/)
- [WCAG 2.2 criterion for 'Consistent Help'](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/consistent-help.html)

## Why

The new WCAG 2.2 Level A criterion 'Consistent Help' says:

> If a [Web page](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/consistent-help.html#dfn-web-page) contains any of the following help [mechanisms](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/consistent-help.html#), and those mechanisms are repeated on multiple Web pages within a [set of Web pages](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/consistent-help.html#dfn-set-of-web-pages), they occur in the same order relative to other page content, unless a change is initiated by the user:
> * Human contact details;
> * Human contact mechanism;
> * Self-help option;
> * A fully automated contact mechanism.

Although the intent of the criterion is that the contact information itself is consistently ordered with respect to the rest of the page (i.e. a help link is always in the same place in the footer, as described in #2871) we can go beyond this by advising that teams provide this information in a consistent order every time it appears.

For example, if a service has three contact mechanisms—phone, email address, post—these should be listed in the same order and format on all pages where it appears, such as the service start page, support pages, contact page, etc. 

## Who needs to work on this
- Content designer or technical writer

## Who needs to review this
- Accessibility specialist
- Content designer or technical writer

## Done when

- [ ] Guidance has been updated

ourIssues.title: Agree how to ensure that users don't lose information if they follow links in the cookie banner
ourIssues.body:
## What
As part of the cookie banner work we've been thinking about how teams should handle opening links in the cookie banner if the user is completing a transactional journey and could lose information they've entered in a form if they follow links in the cookie banner.

We have some information under [Opening links in a new tab](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/styles/typography/#opening-links-in-a-new-tab) about this so we could link to it from the cookie banner guidance if we though that would be useful. The content could say something like:

> If you show the cookie banner on a page where the user enters information into a form, [open the cookies page in a new tab](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/styles/typography/#opening-links-in-a-new-tab). 

Additionally, users could lose information if interacting with the cookie banner reloads the page (server side solution when JavaScript isn't enabled or the banner doesn't progressively enhance it). We could consider recommending that once the user has consented/rejected cookies, the hide button isn't shown if JavaScript isn't enabled (JS would unhide the button)/

It's possible that there's a wider pattern here about how teams should ensure that the information users enter in forms is retained safely. 

This card should be to decide what the scope of this work is.

## Why
We should provide guidance to teams on how to making sure that users don't lose information entered in a form if they follow links in the cookie banner. 

## Who needs to know about this
Content writer, technical writer, developer, service designer?

## Further detail
As well as the cookie banner, this relates to things like links in footers. However, it's possible that the proposed wider guidance is less relevant to user interaction patterns and would be more relevant for the [Service Manual](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual). 

## Done when

communityIssues.title: Several Instances of HTML in locale files
communityIssues.body: ## What Remove all instances of HTML in locale files. ## Why When I was working on a card to add data-tracking attributes to the copyright and license links in the footer, I noticed that the actual elements I was to add data to were actually in the locale files themselves. I was able to add a listener to the container of the link but to me it seems quite unmaintainable to have essentially 60 copies of the same elements with different text. If a class needed to be changed or an attribute then something could easily be missed. In fact there is already an issue caused by this - the `a` element in copyright_html links to a 404 in every other language apart from in `en.yml`. The instances of html in locale files are as follows: ``` opendocument_html: This file is in an OpenDocument format request_format_details_html: If you use assistive technology (such as a screen reader) and need a version of this document in a more accessible format, please email %{alternative_format_contact_email}. Please tell us what format you need. It will help us if you say what assistive technology you use. phase_banner_html: This is a new service – your feedback will help us to improve it. copyright_html: © Crown copyright licence_html: All content is available under the Open Government Licence v3.0, except where otherwise stated ``` It seems to me that most of these have the same format of `prefix` `link` `suffix`, so perhaps an alternative structure for this pattern could be ``` licence_link prefix: All content is available under the link_text: Open Government Licence v3.0 suffix: except where otherwise stated ``` and then a helper method could be used to assemble the link.

communityIssues.title: Inconsistent components API
communityIssues.body:
The component API is inconsistent across components and in comparison with `govuk-frontend`.

In the table below there is a brief comparison in how `govuk-frontend` components are aligned in API with `govuk_publishing_components`

|Component               |API |
|---                      |---  |
Accordion                 | aligned
Back link                 | aligned
Breadcrumbs               | misaligned
Button                    | slightly misaligned (start)
Character count           | slightly misaligned (nesting)
Checkboxes                | slightly misaligned (fieldset)
Date input                | slightly misaligned (fieldset)
Details                   | misaligned
Error message             | aligned
Error summary             | misaligned
Fieldset                  | misaligned
File upload               | aligned
Footer                    | aligned
Header                    | slightly misaligned (navigation_items)
Inset text                | aligned
Panel                     | misaligned
Phase banner              | misaligned
Radios                    | slightly misaligned (fieldset)
Select                    | slightly misaligned (options)
Skip link                 | aligned
Summary list              | slightly misaligned (items)
Table                     | aligned
Tabs                      | misaligned
Text input                | aligned
Textarea                  | aligned
Warning text              | slightly misaligned (iconFallbackText)

We can see a few common differences between to two API models:
- for arrays, `govuk-frontend` uses the generic `items` (in most cases) whereas `govuk_publishing_components` uses the name of the component (e.g. `attachments` for the attachment list component or `breadcrumbs` for the breadcrumbs component)
- for web addresses/paths `govuk-frontend` uses `href` whereas in `govuk_publishing_components` we often find `url` (e.g. breadcrumbs component)

It's worth mentioning that not even `govuk-frontend`'s API is consistent (e.g. `errorList` instead of `items` in the Error summary component, or differences in nesting)

A few advantages of making the API consistent:
- increases developers' confidence when calling components with arguments (without constantly checking examples in the guide)
- prototyping and production will use the same config object (can be easily copied over in both directions)
- applications can prepare the data to be fed into components consistently using helpers
- it would be easier to swap one component with another

I'm creating this to raise awareness of the differences, hopefully generate discussions around how good looks like and aim for consistency and convergency. API alignment requires at least a breaking change and some replacements across applications – which is not an easy process. For this reason, having a clear vision about how we want it to look like would save us from doing this more than once.

communityIssues.title: Remove redundant explicit role attributes from HTML5 elements
communityIssues.body:
## What

Remove the explicit role attribute on HTML elements that have the same role implicitly, including:

* the `<span>` element in the card component, which has a `text` role on the header text
* the `<nav>` element in the contents list component, which has a `navigation` role
* the `<ul>` element in the do and don't list component, which has a `list` role
* the `<footer>` element in the footer component, which has a `contentinfo` role
* the `<header>` element in the header component, which has a `banner` role
* the `<nav>` element in the pagination component, which has a `navigation` role
* the `<table>`, `<thead>`, `<tr>`, `<td>` and `<th>` elements in the table component ([see issue](https://github.com/nhsuk/nhsuk-frontend/issues/1092))

In some places we include an explicit `group` role on `<fieldset>` elements (e.g. the date input) to ensure that JAWS announces the accessible description – we should **leave this in place** unless we're able to do further investigation and understand whether this is still needed.

Update our [HTML validation rules](https://github.com/nhsuk/nhsuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/nhsuk-frontend-review/.htmlvalidate.mjs) accordingly ([see workarounds](https://github.com/nhsuk/nhsuk-frontend/commit/74aceef346383b5678b0d715ade6a8da3948f0ba)).

## Why

These have historically been set because older browsers ([noteably Internet Explorer](https://web.archive.org/web/20180103181655/https://connect.microsoft.com/IE/feedback/details/804723/html5-structural-elements-not-exposed-via-accessibility-api)) do not [map these implicit roles correctly](https://www.html5accessibility.com/).

As our browser support model has evolved, we can now remove these implicit roles.

See related issue from GOV.UK Frontend:

* https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/4708

communityIssues.title: [Feature Request] Feature Header - Secondary and Tertiary background colour variables
communityIssues.body:
The [Feature Header](https://designsystem.gov.scot/components/feature-header) component has 3 background options:
- `ds_feature-header—background`
     - Set by: `$feature-header-background` < `$ds_colour__brand`
- `ds_feature-header—background-secondary`
     - Set by: `$ds_colour__background--secondary`
- `ds_feature-header—background-tertiary`
     - Set by: `$ds_colour__background--tertiary`

The primary background is set to the Primary Brand colour by default, but this can be easily overridden by simply modifying the `$feature-header-background` variable.

Unfortunately, the secondary and tertiary options are only set by the main background colour variables, making it difficult to set custom colours for those options; as changing the main `$ds_colour__background--
{secondary/tertiary}` variables also affects many other components.

Therefore, please may I request the addition of two new intermediary variables for the secondary and tertiary feature header background colours:
- `$feature-header-background--secondary`
     - Set to `$ds_colour__background--secondary` by default
- `$feature-header-background--tertiary`
     - Set to `$ds_colour__background--tertiary` by default

This would align the secondary and tertiary options to how the primary option works, making the behaviour more consistent, and making it easier to modify the feature header background colours without affecting other components.

I know I "could" achieve this by adding custom override css, but I'd rather there be an out of the box method for achieving this.

ourIssues.title: Exit this page: Possibly note the `Clear-Site-Data` header
ourIssues.body:
### Discussed in https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/discussions/2932
Originally posted by **craigfrancis** July 9, 2023 Under the heading "Consider what to do with user session data", it might be worth noting that **some** websites might want to use the `Clear-Site-Data` header ([Specification](https://www.w3.org/TR/clear-site-data/), [MDN Article](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Clear-Site-Data)). This header helps if the user forgot to use Private Browsing Mode, and isn't familiar with clearing their browsing data (which in itself can be suspicious). This header does not clear the browsers history (as websites cannot/should-not be able to do this); but it does leave less traces of the website on the users computer (cookies, caches, localStorage, service workers, etc), which shows greater engagement with the website, and could include an active session showing a username and account details. I believe the Exit This Page link will need to use a redirect (i.e. go to a URL on the current website, which sets this header, and a Location header for the redirect). This will increase the loading time for the destination page, but loading time is always going to be a problem (and why a loading overlay is essential, because even a basic link to another website can take many seconds to begin loading - ref mobile phones with a poor connection, slow laptops running a virus checker, etc).

ourIssues.title: Devise a strategy for image performance on the website
ourIssues.body:
## What
Investigate and implement a permanent strategy for ensuring that images added to design system as part of guidance and content are as performant as possible.

## Why
To ensure that we maintain a high performing website, leveraging the HTML spec and leading by example on how to maintain a service with images.

To prevent the likelihood of content being added to the design system that negatively impacts performance.

## Who needs to work on this
Developers, Tech writers

## Things to explore

- [x] writing guidance on adding images to design system content
- [ ] make use of the HTML best practice to maximise performance eg: adding `loading="lazy"` to `img` tags
- [ ] implementing webp with fallbacks and potential automation of generation
- [ ] automate the compression of images across the website
- [ ] automate the addition of best practice markup across the website

## Notes and Considerations
- None of the pages on the website using images are performance risks currently, with an average lighthouse score of 99 for performance across all our pages with images. This work is therefore likely to provide diminishing returns in terms of actual performance gain over being an exercise in best practice.
- There is currently a mix of syntax on the website, with some pages using `img` tags added directly onto the page and some pages using the markdown image syntax (`![alt text](/img/url/)`). This is where automation is going to be particularly useful.
- Patrick Cartlidge from govuk [performed a spike into image compression on govuk](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1rAST02jvXwiAcjZKxjCDbibp1HgXCCfQPcjKt9XqINw/edit?pli=1#heading=h.idhsmtpw870d) which we could borrow from.
- 11ty have an [image markup syntax plugin](https://v1-0-1.11ty.dev/docs/plugins/image/). It's worth exploring if metalsmith have something similar or if we can borrow from 11ty's plugin.
- [Rehype](https://github.com/rehypejs/rehype) is another option for html transformation.
- We need to be aware that high DPI screens don't like blurry images, so there's a trade off to be made between image quality and image download size
- [CloudFour](https://cloudfour.com/thinks/responsive-images-101-definitions/) have a series of articles about responsive image management.

ourIssues.title: Visiting a heading within a page can have a large layout shift
ourIssues.body:
<!--
    Please fill in as much of the template below as you’re able to. If you're unsure whether the issue already exists or how to fill in the template, open an issue anyway. Our team will help you to complete the rest.

    Your issue might already exist. If so, add a comment to the existing issue instead of creating a new one. You can find existing issues here: https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/issues
-->

## Description of the issue
<!-- A clear and concise summary of what the bug is. -->

When visiting a heading within a page on the Design System website, there can be a large layout shift that causes the browser viewport to end up showing the wrong part of the page.

For example, loading the [URL for the 'Start by asking one question per page' section of the question pages pattern page](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/question-pages/#start-by-asking-one-question-per-page) in Chrome 92 can sometime result in the browser showing the 'Back links' section:

https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/503614/127671243-273b39e8-c271-4c37-ac54-9c090a678009.mp4

This behaviour is unpredictable; sometimes the browser will produce the [expected behaviour].

I have also seen this happen when visiting a page that is linked from another page within the Design System website, for instance, the guidance on when not to use a 'none' checkbox links to the 'start by asking one question per page' guidance.

<details>
<summary>Recording of Safari showing unexpected behaviour when following a link</summary>

https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/503614/127672657-48644cb4-fe9d-428e-b726-4297a598971d.mp4

</details>

## Steps to reproduce the issue
<!-- How can we reproduce this issue? If you think it will be helpful, please provide a small code snippet and/or screenshots. -->

1. Open a new browser tab
2. Visit the URL https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/question-pages/#start-by-asking-one-question-per-page

Note that this will not always produce the behaviour recorded above, sometimes it will produce the expected behaviour. However, on this page the browser fairly reliably jumps back to the same place within the page, when it does jump.

## Actual vs expected behaviour
<!-- What is happening vs what would you expect to happen instead? -->

I expect that when the page has finished loading the heading 'Start by asking one question per page' is at the top of the browser window. 

<details>
<summary>Recording of the expected behaviour in Chrome</summary>

https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/503614/127672361-df87da15-a685-4334-b715-4d166ae4a700.mp4

</details>

## Environment (where applicable)
<!-- Details of your operating system, browser and the version of GOVUK Frontend you’re using may help us to reproduce your issue. -->

I've tested locally with the URL https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/question-pages/#start-by-asking-one-question-per-page and the following browsers:

- Operating system: MacOS Catalina 10.15.7 
- Browser: Chrome 92.0.4515.107 (Official Build) (x86_64), Safari 14.1.2 (15611.3.10.1.5, 15611), Firefox 90.0.2 (64-bit)

I've also tested this in IE11 on Windows 7 using BrowserStack.

All browsers tested show similar behaviour; when loading the page for the first time it will "jump back" from the correct heading to the 'Back links' heading, but subsequent loads the browser will end up at the correct heading.

I've also tried different pages on the Design System website, with similar (if less dramatic) results.

## Notes

I'm not sure what is causing this, or if it is a problem that is affecting users, but thought I'd create an issue about it so we could discuss.

ourIssues.title: Provide guidelines on icons
ourIssues.body:
We should have some guidance, possibly on https://design-system.service.gov.uk/styles/images/ on the use of icons. This often comes up as a question.

We could mention the following:
- Icons can have accessibility issues as not all users can see them - although conversely sometimes icons can help users to understand things better. 
- Icons can be interpreted in different ways by users so that a common meaning cannot always be relied upon. We've seen in research that the meaning of an "i" in a circle which would normally communicate "information" can be interpreted in different ways. Some users thought it related to "information" but some others read it as "warning" - they might have thought about the "i" being upside down. See https://docs.google.com/document/d/1nqHmhA_IWnnmzf6JcaI2TuINbCwQoUHyzG9seZj0860/
- If icons are used, they shouldn't be the sole way of communicating something but should be supplementary to text content.
- Loading in icon fonts such as Font Awesome can have adverse effect on page loading times, especially for users on low bandwidth or older devices.

backlog.title: Download, save, print or share a confirmation, receipt, certificate, or letter at the end of a service
backlog.body:
What
A consistent pattern to fulfil the need for a user to download, save or print either a confirmation of a transaction, receipt or a certificate of completion (most commonly at the end of a service).
Why
After working for HMRC in live services and at the Home Office in build services, I have seen multiple services that have a user need to download, save or print a confirmation or receipt or certificate of completion, usually in the form of a generated PDF.
Nearly every one of these services takes a different approach and when faced with a similar problem previously as a designer on a build team, we ended up developing yet another approach due to the lack of guidance of a suggested pattern. In addition, technically lots of these services take a lot of different approaches to generating the receipt or certificate with a range of libraries used.
There could be an argument that these are somewhat different use cases so we shouldn’t conflate the pattern for them but generally it feels like all of the existing designs have a combination of letting users save/download, print or open an A4 document, usually a generated PDF. A pattern to provide guidance could help align build teams rather than letting them re-invent the wheel every time.
Related patterns and components:

#6044
#6037
#6014
#5934

Examples in existing services
[HMRC] Employment Related Securities (ERS) returns – Confirmation receipt (Live)
When the user follows the link on the page a PDF is generated PDF and opened in the browser. In older browsers that don’t support showing PDFs such as IE it just downloads.

Apparently during research, users were requesting a receipt that they could download for their records. The use case being accountants who have to keep records on their internal company systems. Print was considered but not so relevant for companies with digital record keeping where they would have to save a PDF through the print dialogue.
Unsure who the build designer was. Now being looked after by HMRC Edinburgh Live Services. Contacts are: abdirahman.mohammed@digital.hmrc.gov.uk, helen.sell@digital.hmrc.gov.uk, samuel.holyhead@digital.hmrc.gov.uk

[HMRC] Advanced Tariff Rulings (ATaR) – Save or print confirmation and other letters (Live)
Embedded in the page. Custom CSS removes the UI when printed. PDF generated when user clicks on the save button. Screenshot from the prototype for ease.

Unsure who the build designer was. Now being looked after by HMRC Edinburgh Live Services. Contacts are: abdirahman.mohammed@digital.hmrc.gov.uk, helen.sell@digital.hmrc.gov.uk, samuel.holyhead@digital.hmrc.gov.uk

[HMRC] Trusts – Confirmation receipt (Going from Live Beta into Live)
This service is just going out of beta into live and has had several sprints of research and development on the pattern. It contains a generated PDF that is downloaded to the users machine if they select they want to download. The user goes through a set of two questions pages and the file is downloaded if they choose the correct radio options.


During the handover we found out that previous designs included opening the receipt in the browser but research showed that users then closed the window which lost the token for their session as this occurs mid-flow. Apparently there is a 4 second wait when the user clicks continue to avoid overloading the PDF generator with requests. This hasn’t been an issue during testing according to the build team.
UX designer on the project build: benjamin.ingignieri@digital.hmrc.gov.uk

[Home Office] Prevent eLearning service – Certificate of completion (Closed Beta)
This service features a certificate of completion at the end of the lesson. This is to prove to managers and employers that they have completed the training.
A generated PDF that is opened in the browser via link which follows the Publishing download attachment pattern. Previous research included trying a HTML version but users struggled to save that version. PDF is opened in the browser due to security concerns about putting the users details into the front-end. User research suggests that users would expect to save this to their computer as the default behaviour. Additionally, it was found that if a green confirmation panel was used in the in the flow before this page then users would tend to close the window before reading that they can download the certificate.

UX designer on the project build: samuel.holyhead@digital.hmrc.gov.uk

[Home Office] Check someone’s immigration status (Live)
Save or print an application. This example was shared with us by Frank Ramsey and Chris O’leary at the Home Office.

Contact: frank.ramsay@digital.homeoffice.gov.uk, Chris.O'Leary@digital.homeoffice.gov.uk
Does this already exist in the design system?
In regards to existing elements in the GOV.UK design system (or other department’s design systems), while there are components suggested for saving, downloading or printing an item, I feel like this is a different problem that usually takes the form of a flow or combination of existing components.
Other thoughts on a potential pattern
Some initial thoughts about what format a pattern could take:

there seems to be a common theme that out of the actions, most users want to download a copy
seems like HTML consistently isn’t a good file format to download as most users want to store a file locally or share a file via email, etc. From research, users struggle to save a PDF via print dialogs, etc.
from research, linguistically most users refer to this as action as wanting to save the file
related – print buttons usually require javascript. It would be good to explore alternatives that fit with progressive enhancement. Embedding the content in the page and using custom CSS to remove the UI seems like a nice approach that supports the use of the print function in the browser rather than a javascript button.
sometimes download implementations open up a new blank windows in order to download the file. It would be good to explore how to avoid this.
just personal preference but the outline of the document in the ATaR example help signify which parts of the page will be printed or saved while also previewing the document. consideration would need to be given on how to signify this to users of screen readers and other assistive technology though.
in regards to generation libraries:

HMRC have a PDF generation service that they are deprecating.
some other services use pdfbox: https://pdfbox.apache.org
this is an example of how to generate an accessible PDF using pdfBox: https://github.com/martinlovell/accessible-pdfbox-example

ourIssues.title: Safari/VoiceOver reads out headings within legends twice
ourIssues.body:
<!--
    Please fill in as much of the template below as you’re able to. If you're unsure whether the issue already exists or how to fill in the template, open an issue anyway. Our team will help you to complete the rest.

    Your issue might already exist. If so, add a comment to the existing issue instead of creating a new one. You can find existing issues here:
    - an existing Github issue: https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues
    - our known validation error/warning list: https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/1280#issuecomment-509588851
-->

## Description of the issue
<!-- A clear and concise summary of what the bug is. -->

When using VoiceOver with Safari on iOS or macOS headings that are contained within legends will be read out twice.

For instance, with iOS, on the [question page example](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/question-pages/default/index.html), VoiceOver announces

> Where do you live? Heading level one. Where do you live? Landmark. Form start.

May be related to https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/2153, may be fixed by https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/1605. Raised in question page backlog discussion  https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/issues/6011#issuecomment-945603738.

## Steps to reproduce the issue
<!-- How can we reproduce this issue? If you think it will be helpful, please provide a small code snippet and/or screenshots. -->

1. On macOS, enable VoiceOver and open Safari
2. Visit https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/question-pages/default/index.html
3. Move VoiceOver to the top of the page
4. Start VoiceOver reading with keyboard shortcut Control + Option + A

## Actual vs expected behaviour
<!-- What is happening vs what would you expect to happen instead? -->

Actual behaviour:

When VoiceOver reaches the page heading, it announces
> Where do you live?, group heading level 1 Where do you live?

Expected behaviour:

VoiceOver announces the page heading 'Where do you live?' only once

## Environment (where applicable)
<!-- Details of your operating system, browser and the version of GOVUK Frontend you’re using may help us to reproduce your issue. -->

- Operating system: macOS Big Sur Version 11.6
- Browser: Safari
- Browser version: Version 15.0 (16612.1.29.41.4, 16612)
- GOV.UK Frontend Version: 3.14.0

I tried similar steps with NVDA with Firefox on Windows and JAWS with Chrome on Windows, and was unable to reproduce the issue. This issue may be a bug in VoiceOver/Safari.

ourIssues.title: Explore separating the 'core' functionality of the Character Count from the management of its configuration
ourIssues.body:
<!--

  This is a template for any issues that aren’t bug reports or new feature requests. The headings in this section provide examples of the information you might want to include, but feel free to add/delete sections where appropriate.

-->

## What

Explore extracting the core feature of the Character Count into its own class, used internally by the component and focused on:
- listening to value changes in the field it observes
- running a function to get the count
- updating the UI based on the `threshold`, a `maxlength` and the I18n messages

The original `CharacterCount` class would remain focused on managing the configuration and delegating the actual counting to that new class.

```js
// 
class CharacterCount {
  constructor(config) {
    // Do stuff with the config to figure the field to observe, the function to count, the `threshold`, `maxlength` and messages
    new CharacterCountCore({/* consistent subset of options */})
  }
}
```

Explore if we can also separate technical aspects like monitoring the value of the field and running the initial count on `show` outside of that `CharacterCountCore`.

## Why

A lot of the code in the component only manages the configuration (picking the right function based on `maxlength`/`maxwords`, ensuring the correct option takes over based on which part of the configuration defined the option). There's also some technical code (monitoring the field's value, and possibly running the initial count) which could live outside of the component so the component's instance variables remain focused on counting characters and updating the UI.

Separating the core functionality of the component from these aspect would create a better separation of concern between configuring the component, technical glue and the actual component's features, making it easier to see what's what and what can possibly be cleaned up when options are updated/removed.

## Who needs to work on this

Developers

## Who needs to review this

Developers

## Done when

- [ ] Spike to see if possible to extract such a class
- [ ] Document learnings from the spike

ourIssues.title: Some template level svgs are hard to see when using forced colour browser extensions
ourIssues.body: ## Description of the issue When using certain forced colour made browser extensions, in this case [Dark Reader](https://darkreader.org/) which changes colours by rotating hue, certain in-page template svgs like the GOV.UK logo lockup and the OGL logo in the footer incorrectly change with the colour mode, making them functionally impossible to see with the ## Steps to reproduce the issue 1. Go to a GOV.UK service on a browser with Dark Reader installed, with Dark Reader turned off 2. Scroll down to the bottom of the page, note the OGL logo in the footer 3. Turn Dark Reader on ## Actual vs expected behaviour ### Expected The OGL logo is the same colour as the page's text colour, forced or otherwise eg: it'll be black if text is set to black, white if text is set to white. ### Actual The OGL logo is an off-black against the dark footer background ## Environment (where applicable) - Operating system: MacOS Tahoe 26.4.1 - Browser: Chrome - Browser version: 147.0.7727.117 - GOV.UK Frontend Version: >= 5.14 ## Notes What seems to be happening here is Dark Reader is adding attributes to change the colour of the SVG by rotating it's hue 180 degrees. At least for the OGL logo, this is overriding the `fill="currentcolour"` applied to the `path` of the OGL svg. That attribute is setting the svg to the page text colour, which the extension is overriding back to black. Removing `fill="currentcolour"` resolves this and, from some very shallow testing, seems to work fine without any forced colours and with other forced colour methods. It looks like there are some team tasks to do here: 1. Decide if this is something we want to try to figure out at our level or if we call this a bug in Dark Reader instead and not make it our concern 2. Investigate if removing `fill="currentcolour"` causes other unexpected problems 3. Try to understand Dark Reader's behaviour further and if there's something we're doing that's triggering Dark Reader to apply that hue rotation styling

ourIssues.title: Include fingerprints in filename for image assets
ourIssues.body:
## What

Include a fingerprint in the filename for all of our image assets to make it easy for service teams to [treat them as immutable and cache them indefinitely](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Caching#cache_busting).

Update the page template and references in the stylesheet to point to the new images.

## Why

Although we allow customisation of the location of the images in both Sass (by setting `$govuk-images-path`) and Nunjucks (by setting the `assetPath` variable) it's non-trivial to change the filenames themselves – you'd need to either creatae a function that rewrites the filename in Sass or re-implement the entire `headIcons` block in Nunjucks.

Although there are only a handful of images in GOV.UK Frontend, the difficulty in adding fingerprints to them may cause issues for services with more images that are fingerprinted, preventing them from having a blanket caching strategy for all of their images.

It could also cause issues where the majority of images do have fingerprinted and teams are caching images indefinitely, without realising that our images do not have fingerprints.

## Further details

Note that if we use a hash of the file contents as part of the filename that would mean that any change to an image (including e.g. optimisations) could be a breaking change as teams would need to update the paths in their templates etc.

We could mitigate this by keeping previous versions of images between major releases, or consider using an alternative identifier that only changes if the image changes in a meaningful way (like a version number)

## Who needs to work on this

Developers

## Who needs to review this

Developers

## Done when

- [ ] Image assets in GOV.UK can be cached indefinitely (for example because they include a fingerprint in their filename that changes when the file contents change)
- [ ] References to those images have been updated
- [ ] We understand the impact on future changes to those images and what it means for versioning

ourIssues.title: WCAG 2.2: Explore how to handle focus state of short links
ourIssues.body:
## What
Figure out how to present focus states for links of 4 or fewer characters and for components which use the link styles.

## Why
During testing of components against [WCAG 2.2 criterion 2.4.13: focus appearance](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/focus-appearance.html) as part of https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/4347, it was discovered that we have several failures within components to do with parts of these components using our link decoration. The root problem is that that very short links have too small a focus area to pass the criteria. The link style itself _does_ pass the criterion, however components that use the link decoration but not the default link colour eg: breadcrumbs using black links fail this because they lose the contrast between the blue and black that links typically have.

This impacts the following components:

- [Back links](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/back-link/)
- [Breadcrumbs](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/breadcrumbs/)
- [Error summary](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/error-summary/)
- [Pagination](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/pagination/)
- [Summary list](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/summary-list/) (summary cards fail but summary lists pass)
- [Tabs](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/tabs/)

As part of this work, we have an opportunity to also update our [link guidance](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/styles/links/) to encourage users to not use short links in their content.

### Further reading
- [Testing spreadsheet (internal only)](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1PpKvhCGZJb1j0ZUUY2ZuA0CBQeu04yFD1bumiL8wGX8/edit#gid=0)
- https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/issues/3007 - related issue on focus state rationalisation
 
## Who needs to work on this
Developers, designers

## Who needs to review this
Developers, designers

## Done when

- [ ] Solution to how to present short links is devised and merged into `main`
- [ ] Link guidance is updated to advise not using short links

ourIssues.title: Consider testing our colour styles against the APCA contrast method
ourIssues.body:
## What
We have a set of 'colour' styles within our design system, which were tested for colour contrast agains the WCAG 2.x colour contrast method.

Our two sets of colour styles are:
- [main colours](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/styles/colour/#main-colours)
- the [colour palette](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/styles/colour/#colour-palette)

Consider testing these colours against the APCA method. APCA is being explored as a potential successor contrast method for WCAG 3, but the testing tools are available now.

### What it would involve
Using the [Bridge-PCA testing tool](https://www.myndex.com/BPCA/), test our colour contrasts against both the WCAG 2.x method and APCA.
- test with white background (#ffffff)
- test with black background (dark mode approximation) (#0b0c0c)
- test with white text (#ffffff)
- test with our 'black' text (#0b0c0c)

### Documentation
- [APCA 'easy intro'](https://git.apcacontrast.com/documentation/APCAeasyIntro)
- [Bridge-PCA GitHub repo](https://github.com/Myndex/bridge-pca/)

## Why
The APCA method is evidenced to do a more consistent job at matching real-world contrast needs. There's still no settled consensus on APCA's advantages and disadvantages as a tool for measuring contrast, but I figure it's probably a good enhancement to our colours.

Measuring against both methods will:
- help us potentially future-proof for WCAG 3 (but that won't be on the horizon for several more years)
- improve readability now, rather than waiting for WCAG 3

## Who needs to work on this
Developers, interaction designers, accessibility specialist
## Who needs to review this

## Done when
- [ ] test our main colours and record results
- [ ] test our colour palette and record results
- [ ] review results and decide if we want to pursue changes to any of our colours
- [ ] write up GitHub issues for any changes we decide to pursue

ourIssues.title: Investigate presence of both `/` trailed and non-trailed paths in GA
ourIssues.body:
<!--

  This is a template for any issues that aren’t bug reports or new feature requests. The headings in this section provide examples of the information you might want to include, but feel free to add/delete sections where appropriate.

-->

## What

Figure why the behaviour flow of Google Analytics revealed that we're tracking pages both with and without trailing slashes while users browse the site:
 - `/styles` and `/styles/`
 - `/patterns` and `/patterns/`
 - `/component` and `/components/`

This distinction would be fine for landing pages, as we don't control how other websites link to us. However, during navigation between pages of the design system, we should only see one format for the paths.

## Why

We likely have some form of redirect in place to make this transparent to users (at the price of an extra request, which would be great to avoid).  However, in the analytics, it muddies the data as:
- both URLs are the same page
- this doubling of pages pushes other pages out of the top X of the data, making it harder to review how users browse the Design System site

## Who needs to work on this

Developers

## Who needs to review this

Developers

## Done when

- [ ] We know why we're seeing both URLs on Google Analytics
- [ ] We've chosen and implemented a fix so we only track a single page

ourIssues.title: Iterate image guidance for ‘text in charts, diagrams and complex images
ourIssues.body:
## Related documentation
Hannah Thomas from ONS [gave feedback on the guidance](https://ukgovernmentdigital.slack.com/archives/C6DMEH5R6/p1681385024589509) on descriptive text for charts on the cross-gov Slack channel.

## Suggestion

Edited for clarity:
> Charts are a bit of an outlier [from typical ways to add descriptive text to images] because they always should come with a title. It is this title that lets a screen reader user know that there is an image.

> So our research has shown it is **better to go straight from the chart title to the text description of the chart**. Which is also why we say the chart title should start with “Figure x” and the text description should start with “Description of figure x: a line chart showing .....”

> So you should flag it is a description of the figure and you should state the type of chart

> We don’t necessarily say you have to start the text description with “Description of figure x:” - you can just start with “This line chart shows....” but feedback from stats teams was that they found it a bit **hard to separate the text description from the statistical commentary** so this was a way around it

> **Putting extra alt text in the alt attribute was found to just add unnecessary auditory clutter** when you follow this approach, and this approach was found to be better for all users - not just screen reader users - because there are an array of people who need/want/like a text description for a chart.

> [For example] colourblind users, users with dyscalculia or users who just don’t feel comfortable with charts, users with low vision who can zoom in on text but find it hard to zoom in on charts, users who need a bit of reassurance that what they have taken away from the chart is actually what the chart is showing

## Done when (possibility to start)
- [ ] Assess feedback - team, particularly accessibility expert
- [ ] Decide on the iteration we can do to existing guidance
- [ ] Respond to feedback and discuss contribution opportunities

ourIssues.title: Changing the colour palette used for graphs on GOV.UK/Design System
ourIssues.body:
## Context
<!-- What are you trying to do? Is this something you think should behave differently, or something that you currently cannot do? Is this related to an existing issue/bug? -->

The colours used in the existing charts that can be built using Govspeak do not meet the colour contrast requirements for adjacent colours (as set out in WCAG 2.1). The Analysis Function Support Team have developed accessible colour palettes to use with charts and would love to see these implemented in the charts created using Govspeak. 

I have published a webpage showing the [types of tables and charts that can be built using Govspeak](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/examples-of-visual-content-to-use-on-govuk). 

## Alternatives
<!-- Are you currently using a workaround / alternative solution instead? -->

In general statistics producers who use GOV.UK to publish content are frustrated with the technical capability they have to publish charts. Only horizontal bar charts can be created using Govspeak so they are very limited in what they can do in HTML. Many teams are still creating charts as images and then publishing them as PNGs, JPEGs or (at best) SVGs. Sometimes they publish a mix of charts created as images and charts created using Govspeak, sometimes all their charts are images. 

When it comes to colours, if they use the horizontal bar charts available in Govspeak they have no way of changing the colours. When they create charts as images they can choose whatever colours they want. 

This either leads to a mix of colour palettes being used (which isn't great), or they align all their charts with the Govspeak colour palette, which also isn't great as the adjacent colours do not meet the contrast requirements for adjacent colours, set out in WCAG 2.1. 

## Additional information (if applicable)
<!-- What evidence do you have that this meets the needs of users? It’s useful for us to know of any user research/testing you’ve done with this feature. -->

Making the Govspeak charts meet the contrast requirements set out in WCAG 2.1 won't make things 100% perfect for all users but it will definitely be an improvement for any users with access needs related to seeing adjacent colours. It is also a legal requirement. 

The colour palettes we have created are available within [this colours guidance](https://gss.civilservice.gov.uk/policy-store/data-visualisation-colours-in-charts/#section-5) (it is still technically in draft but should be signed off by the end of this week).

communityIssues.title: CLS on image elements missing explicit width and height
communityIssues.body:
We have a number of images using the [figure component](https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/figure) that currently lack width and height attributes. 

### Background

SpeedCurve originally flagged historic people images for lacking explicit width and height dimensions. Without these attributes, browsers cannot calculate the image's aspect ratio before the asset finishes downloading. This causes the page layout to jump once the image loads, resulting in poor Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) scores.

### Example pages with images missing height/width

https://www.gov.uk/guidance/notify-the-defence-accident-investigation-branch
https://www.gov.uk/government/case-studies/out-of-syria-back-into-school
https://www.gov.uk/government/how-government-works
https://www.gov.uk/government/speeches/jacqui-smith-speech-at-parliamentary-reception-for-worldskills-uk
https://www.gov.uk/foreign-travel-advice/armenia

### Relevant links 

Historic people pages PR: https://github.com/alphagov/collections/pull/4708
Related commit setting default height and width on [Image Card](https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/image_card): https://github.com/alphagov/govuk_publishing_components/commit/86450d6066fe7e5aa8fd220e93c2319de2730b62
Responsive images: https://web.dev/learn/design/responsive-images

### Proposed solution 

Where possible (e.g. decorative images), pass width and height attributes to the figure component so browsers can calculate aspect ratios. We cannot use default dimensions for all travel advice maps as they vary in sizes and this might risk distortion or clipping.

backlog.title: Suggested new component - Side menu
backlog.body:
What

Give a brief description of the style, component or pattern you want to propose.

Context:
We are in the final stages of building an e-learning service using the GDS design system. We have completed numerous rounds of user testing and already gone through one Alpha and Beta Assessment.
What:
A right-hand sidebar navigation menu which allows users to easily see their progression through a course and be able to navigate back and forth through chapters.
Current version

In-situ

Iterations from user testing

Why

Explain why you think this should be added to the GOV.UK Design System.

In our alpha assessment, we were challenged to explore if there was a user need to see their progression through the course and also to be able to navigate back and forth through the chapters. We tested various variations of a sidebar navigation similar to those found in lots of e-learning platforms. During testing, we found that some users naturally used the sidebar to return to topics earlier in the course and used it to be aware of their progression and estimate their completion time.
Design-wise, we didn’t want to reinvent the wheel so we built on existing sidebar navigation patterns from GOV.UK publishing such as the contents list on the publishing service (https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/contents_list) and the related content sidebar on many start pages. We iterated the design several times to make it simple and accessible. For instance, we made some headers in the sidebar visually hidden so they would give context to screen reader users whilst avoiding confusion for sighted users who had initially struggled with the previous design.


What evidence do you have that it's needed by multiple services across government?


In the our beta assessment, we were praised on our work developing this pattern and asked to play it back into the community:
‘the team has validated the user need to track progress within training modules, has designed a pattern that is working for their beta users, and is planning to continue iterating this pattern - the panel would encourage the team to share this pattern and research findings with the design system community’


What evidence do you have that it meets the needs of the users of those services?


We have tested and validated this component in several rounds of qual research with 5-10 people in each round, and in Private Beta testing with over 1200 people (with quant showing that people successfully use this when required, and qual feedback only positive and no negative on the latest version).
Our user testing so far has validated the need for this component and as mentioned has been praised so far by assessors. But we would love to share it with the community to get a wider perspective and possible use cases.


Have you checked that it doesn't already exist in the GOV.UK Design System?


Yes
Anything else

Include links to any examples, research or code to support your proposal, if available.

ourIssues.title: Visibility and clickability of links on white backgrounds an issue for low vision users
ourIssues.body: ## Description of the issue The link style doesn't have a sufficient contrast on a white background for low vision users and there is not enough of a visual cue to the link being clickable. This was reported by the 'Low vision' tester at the Digital Accessibility Centre (DAC), in an audit commissioned by GOV.UK Notify. They were talking about links in our side-navigation, which have no underline by default, but I think their comments apply equally to all uses of the link style. They were reporting on this side-navigation: Their comment was: > When viewing this page, I struggled to see the five links on the left-hand side of the page. > This affects me because of my eye condition the thin light blue text fades into the white > background causing them to become blurry therefore, preventing me from reading the > information provided. It would benefit me that the text is displayed in a darker colour and > made bold so they standout more clearly to read. > > The left-hand navigation links are displayed using a light blue contrast with the custom NTA > font. These links used throughout GDS products provide a difficult reading experience for > low vision users as the transparent look to the NTA font impacts text clarity. > With the difficult reading of links, using the mouse to access a required link can prove > problematic. With the mouse pointer frequently being lost, a low vision user heavily relies > on call-to-action focus to ensure correct links are being accessed. Displayed in a list, > navigating this list becomes difficult is no call-to-action focus is noticed. > In this example, an underline is presented on contact with the mouse pointer. The issue I > had with this is that I did not initially see it. The underline is thinly presented and displayed > with the same low contrast transparent blue. The call-to-action focus is not sufficient for > easy notification. > This can be improved by adding weight to the underline to produce a bolder and more > visible focus needed for accurate navigation to which would be welcomed throughout these > pages. Improved call-to-action enhances user/page interaction to increase overall UX of any > website. I think this can be summarised as the following issues: - the link style on a white background makes the text hard to read - the cursor changing over the clickable area of links is not enough of a cue to know they can be clicked - the link style on a white background makes the underline hard to see ## Steps to reproduce the issue Because the issue seems to occur for users with a visual impairment, I would guess that you would need to test with those types of users. ## Actual vs expected behaviour The tester expected to be able to read the content of the side navigation and identifying them as links but found problems reading the text and knowing they were clickable. ## Environment (where applicable) GOV.UK Notify currently uses version 2.13.0 but the tester mentions experiencing this issue on the [www.gov.uk](http://www.gov.uk/) website, so likely they were viewing pages using a more recent version. The tester was using Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge on Windows (latest versions) for the audit but they mention experiencing this issue on mobile devices and other different screens. See their comment in the description for their exact words.
