ourIssues.title: Add public API to make JavaScript components responsive to the same breakpoints as the CSS
ourIssues.body:
<!--

  This is a template for any issues that aren’t bug reports or new feature requests. The headings in this section provide examples of the information you might want to include, but feel free to add/delete sections where appropriate.

-->

## What

Create a public API so that custom components can easily observe a [MediaQueryList](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/MediaQueryList) matching one of GOV.UK Frontend's breakpoints. 

Proposed shape is two functions, in something like a `common/breakpoints` module (name up for change):
1. Make the [current `getBreakpoints` function](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/b0d62d49c76e5ce77bef7e0ed7eed6ac26f3c1d2/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/common/index.mjs#L16) public with a couple of tweaks:
   a. move the [error throwing currently do](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/tabs/tabs.mjs#L95-L100) from the components into the function
   b. this will allow to simplify the return value of the function to a string (never undefined as we'd throw if it is)
   c. cache the reading of the custom property from `document.documentElement` so we don't call `getComputedProperties` each time we need
2. Add a new `matchMedia(breakpointName, callback)` function (or better suited name) to replace the `setupResponsiveChecks` from the [Tabs](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/b0d62d49c76e5ce77bef7e0ed7eed6ac26f3c1d2/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/tabs/tabs.mjs#L92) and [ServiceNavigation components](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/b0d62d49c76e5ce77bef7e0ed7eed6ac26f3c1d2/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/service-navigation/service-navigation.mjs#L85).
   a. the function is responsible for creating a MediaQueryList observing a `min-width` media query for a given breakpoint, like the `setupResponsiveChecks` currently do, allowing components to pass in a callback that will be run when the media query is created and when there's change of whether the media query matches
   b. callback should receive either the whole MediaQueryList so it can react to whether the list matches or not 

Once those are in, use the new `matchMedia` function in our components so they don't need to create and store a MediaQueryList themselves and update their `checkSupported` static method so it checks the presence of the breakpoints and prevent initialisation of components.

## Why

It's a bit of logistics to read the breakpoint values from the DOM, throw errors and prevent component initialisation, and it's the same for both our responsive components and the mobile navigation on the Design System site.

## Who needs to work on this

Developers

## Who needs to review this

Developers

## Done when

- [ ] API for reading breakpoints has been implemented
- [ ] Component's `checkSupported` method has been updated
- [ ] Component's `setupResponsiveChecks` method has been replaced
- [ ] Frontend docs documentation for [creating your own components](https://frontend.design-system.service.gov.uk/building-your-own-javascript-components/) has an explanation on how to make components responsive
- [ ] MobileNavigationSection in the Design System site uses the public API

ourIssues.title: Resolve the border-underline issue in the service nav component
ourIssues.body: ## What Let's fix the double underline that happens when a user interacts with a link in the service navigation component. The current [service navigation](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/service-navigation/) uses both a bottom border on an active nav item, as well as a link underline on hover/focus. This creates a double line on certain states, such as active:hover and active:focus. The reasons for this are - The service name is the same size as the links, but bolded for differentiation - This means that bold cannot be used on the links, as they would then be difficult to differentiate from the service name - Forced colour mode/ high contrast mode also wipes out any subtle changes in colour (using background colours on the element to differentiate active states, for example) - This meant that there were very few elements that could be used to indicate an active:hover or active:focus state on both default and high contrast displays - Link underlines were chosen for this reason ## Why The upcoming changes to GOV.UK and its service estate are a good opportunity for us to ship some improvements to components. There is also a small chance that the service name styling will need to be updated in order to harmonise it with the GOV.UK product suite: GOV.UK Pay/ App/ One Login/ Notify etc. This isn't confirmed, though. We will also possibly be asked to update the background of the component from grey to pale blue. This is a purely visual change to refine the way that the nav looks. It would be great to do this as our components are populated across a huge number of domains and its likely that the current navigation styling will persist and even be replicated elsewhere. Although this isn't an upgrade to the usability, it is a visual refinement that will improve our reputation for design that is as attractive as it is functional. ## Who needs to work on this @mia-allers-gds, a dev, another designer if necessary, and @selfthinker for her keen eye ## Who needs to review this The team! Maybe the community? ## Done when - [ ] Thing to do

ourIssues.title: Inconsistent Nunjucks parameter names for aria-label
ourIssues.body:
There are several components which allow you to pass the text for the `aria-label` on the component's wrapper element. The names of these parameters are inconsistent despite them doing the same thing.

[Cookie banner](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/a5a50ea57175c0031168d227513b7710579d9c98/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/cookie-banner/template.njk#L4) and [service navigation](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/a5a50ea57175c0031168d227513b7710579d9c98/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/service-navigation/template.njk#L95) use `ariaLabel`. 

[Pagination](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/a5a50ea57175c0031168d227513b7710579d9c98/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/pagination/template.njk#L53) uses `landmarkLabel` and [breadcrumbs](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/a5a50ea57175c0031168d227513b7710579d9c98/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/breadcrumbs/template.njk#L14) uses `labelText`.

Pagination also [includes a visuallyHiddenText param](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/a5a50ea57175c0031168d227513b7710579d9c98/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/pagination/template.njk#L44) for pagination items. On most components, `visuallyHiddenText` params are appended to the visible text (for example [in summary card actions](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/a5a50ea57175c0031168d227513b7710579d9c98/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/summary-list/template.njk#L7)); pagination is the only example I can find where `visuallyHiddenText` is passed directly to `aria-label`, completely overriding any visual label

The documentation for the params is also structured differently. For example the docs for pagination and breadcrumbs don't mention that the value will be used as the `aria-label`, while they do for cookie banner and service navigation.

Are any of these differences intentional? I think `ariaLabel` is clearest about what the params actually do, with `[thing]AriaLabel` for labels of child elements (eg password uses `showPasswordAriaLabelText`, though again the `Text` makes that inconsistent)

ourIssues.title: Document when to use `aria-current="page"` vs `aria-current="true"`in Service Navigation guidance
ourIssues.body:
## Related documentation

The Service Navigation component supports both `aria-current"page"` and `aria-current="true"`.

All of the examples use `aria-current="true"` which is what you get when you use `active: true` with the Nunjucks maco.

Both the `current` and `active` macro options are documented for Nunjucks users, but we don't really go into detail on which to use when.

We don't provide any guidance for users of the HTML.

## Suggestion

See the discussion here: https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/issues/5983#issuecomment-3090064654

My understanding is in the reply:

> The distinction between the two is important when the items in the navigation cover multiple pages within each section. You would use:
> 
> - `aria-current="page"` when the user is on the exact same page that they would see if they clicked that link (i.e. the 'homepage' of that section)
> - `aria-current="true"` when the user is on any other page within that section

ourIssues.title: Review the use of aria-label on a <ul> element in the site navigation menu
ourIssues.body:
## What
We use an `aria-label` on our sub-navigation list `<ul>`. This causes HTML validation issues, so we need to make the call on whether we keep it as an exception, add an explicit `aria-role` to keep validation happy, or get rid of it and find another solution.

## Why
Previously, we added an `aria-label` to the main site nav's Community sub-menu to make a better experience for screenreaders:  https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/commit/4ff06e4961bcd4a147d580d1d5ac2736fe9f6ec3

Recently, we [added HTML linting](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/pull/2569), and it flagged this as `aria-label-misuse`.

If we assign an explicit `role` to the labelled list, the HTML validator is sated and complains no longer.

However, it's a bit unclear which `role` we'd want to add - `navigation` is out since this subnav is already contained within a `nav` parent, and `menu` [might not be right for this situation](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/pull/2569#discussion_r1115422380).

We could avoid this debate if we just find a solution that doesn't involve ARIA. First step would probably be to just remove the `aria-label` and test whether it reads fine in multiple screenreaders.

If it’s missing context without the aria-label, we could look at using a bit of ‘visually-hidden’ instead of an aria-label. Would need to test to see if it works consistently across all screen readers though.

## Who needs to work on this
Developer, Accessibility specialist(?)

## Who needs to review this
Developer, Accessibility specialist

## Done when

- [ ] We have a solution that is both valid HTML, and a good experience for screenreaders.
- [ ] We have implemented that solution (this will likely involve [removing the inline validation exception](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/blob/9ba07459f46a6e9738067c7ec90da6dd22f3a1b6/views/partials/_navigation.njk#L14))

communityIssues.title: Related navigation component is intrinsically tied to content item
communityIssues.body:
## What
The [related navigation component](https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/related_navigation) is built in such a way that it is tightly coupled to the expected output of the content store API. This has likely been done so that developers can pass a `content_item` instance on a given page and there isn't any need to further process the data. This has 2 emergent negative effects:

1. The component is very strict on what information it is asked to render. If you want to render something that doesn't fit the existing scope of the content API, it'll need to be built into the component.
2. The component requires rocket operator style notation to render:

```
"object_with_quotes_and_rocket_operator" => {
    "label_in_quotes" => "Some nice data",
}
```

and won't render at all if "JSON" style notation, the notation that our gem documentation generates, is used:

```
json_style_object: {
   label_without_quotes: "Some nice data",
}
```

Both of these issues make using the component on a page in the same way but not consuming explicit content item data incredibly difficult and limits our ability to built consistent templates across GOV.UK.

## Proposal
- Remove the reliance on rocket operator notation
- Remove other data checks that would block the component from rendering if content data-specific attributes weren't present
- Extended the API to allow for "custom" information to be rendered

communityIssues.title: Primary navigation outputs empty items which confuses tab navigation
communityIssues.body:
### Prerequisites

- [X] Put an X between the brackets on this line if you have done all of the following:
  - Reproduced the problem
  - Followed all applicable steps in the debugging guide
  - Checked the FAQs on the message board for common solutions
  - Checked that your issue doesn't exist: https://github.com/ministryofjustice/moj-frontend/issues
  - Checked that there is not already a package that provides the described functionality

### Description

In the Primary Navigation component it is possible to end up with empty `<li>` elements if any of the items passed to the components are conditional.

i.e. the following will results in three `<li>` and child `<a>` elements in the nav when `sample_conditional` is false.

```
{{ mojPrimaryNavigation({
  label: 'Primary navigation',
  items: [{
      text: 'item1',
      href: '/item1',
      active: true
    },
  {
    text: 'item2',
    href: '/item2',
  },
  {
    text: 'item3',
    href: '/item3',
  } if sample_conditional == true,
        ]
}) }}
```

This is a problem for tab-based navigation behaviour as well as automated tests which might reasonably expect there to only be two items in the navigation when `sample_conditional == false`. There should be a conditional guard before the elements are output.

### Steps to Reproduce

Try the above :)

**Expected behaviour:** There to only be two items in the navigation

**Actual behaviour:** There are three items in the navigation

**Reproduces how often:** 100%

### Versions

Whatever's in main right now. https://github.com/ministryofjustice/moj-frontend/blob/main/src/moj/components/primary-navigation/template.njk

backlog.title: Download, save, print or share a confirmation, receipt, certificate, or letter at the end of a service
backlog.body:
What
A consistent pattern to fulfil the need for a user to download, save or print either a confirmation of a transaction, receipt or a certificate of completion (most commonly at the end of a service).
Why
After working for HMRC in live services and at the Home Office in build services, I have seen multiple services that have a user need to download, save or print a confirmation or receipt or certificate of completion, usually in the form of a generated PDF.
Nearly every one of these services takes a different approach and when faced with a similar problem previously as a designer on a build team, we ended up developing yet another approach due to the lack of guidance of a suggested pattern. In addition, technically lots of these services take a lot of different approaches to generating the receipt or certificate with a range of libraries used.
There could be an argument that these are somewhat different use cases so we shouldn’t conflate the pattern for them but generally it feels like all of the existing designs have a combination of letting users save/download, print or open an A4 document, usually a generated PDF. A pattern to provide guidance could help align build teams rather than letting them re-invent the wheel every time.
Related patterns and components:

#6044
#6037
#6014
#5934

Examples in existing services
[HMRC] Employment Related Securities (ERS) returns – Confirmation receipt (Live)
When the user follows the link on the page a PDF is generated PDF and opened in the browser. In older browsers that don’t support showing PDFs such as IE it just downloads.

Apparently during research, users were requesting a receipt that they could download for their records. The use case being accountants who have to keep records on their internal company systems. Print was considered but not so relevant for companies with digital record keeping where they would have to save a PDF through the print dialogue.
Unsure who the build designer was. Now being looked after by HMRC Edinburgh Live Services. Contacts are: abdirahman.mohammed@digital.hmrc.gov.uk, helen.sell@digital.hmrc.gov.uk, samuel.holyhead@digital.hmrc.gov.uk

[HMRC] Advanced Tariff Rulings (ATaR) – Save or print confirmation and other letters (Live)
Embedded in the page. Custom CSS removes the UI when printed. PDF generated when user clicks on the save button. Screenshot from the prototype for ease.

Unsure who the build designer was. Now being looked after by HMRC Edinburgh Live Services. Contacts are: abdirahman.mohammed@digital.hmrc.gov.uk, helen.sell@digital.hmrc.gov.uk, samuel.holyhead@digital.hmrc.gov.uk

[HMRC] Trusts – Confirmation receipt (Going from Live Beta into Live)
This service is just going out of beta into live and has had several sprints of research and development on the pattern. It contains a generated PDF that is downloaded to the users machine if they select they want to download. The user goes through a set of two questions pages and the file is downloaded if they choose the correct radio options.


During the handover we found out that previous designs included opening the receipt in the browser but research showed that users then closed the window which lost the token for their session as this occurs mid-flow. Apparently there is a 4 second wait when the user clicks continue to avoid overloading the PDF generator with requests. This hasn’t been an issue during testing according to the build team.
UX designer on the project build: benjamin.ingignieri@digital.hmrc.gov.uk

[Home Office] Prevent eLearning service – Certificate of completion (Closed Beta)
This service features a certificate of completion at the end of the lesson. This is to prove to managers and employers that they have completed the training.
A generated PDF that is opened in the browser via link which follows the Publishing download attachment pattern. Previous research included trying a HTML version but users struggled to save that version. PDF is opened in the browser due to security concerns about putting the users details into the front-end. User research suggests that users would expect to save this to their computer as the default behaviour. Additionally, it was found that if a green confirmation panel was used in the in the flow before this page then users would tend to close the window before reading that they can download the certificate.

UX designer on the project build: samuel.holyhead@digital.hmrc.gov.uk

[Home Office] Check someone’s immigration status (Live)
Save or print an application. This example was shared with us by Frank Ramsey and Chris O’leary at the Home Office.

Contact: frank.ramsay@digital.homeoffice.gov.uk, Chris.O'Leary@digital.homeoffice.gov.uk
Does this already exist in the design system?
In regards to existing elements in the GOV.UK design system (or other department’s design systems), while there are components suggested for saving, downloading or printing an item, I feel like this is a different problem that usually takes the form of a flow or combination of existing components.
Other thoughts on a potential pattern
Some initial thoughts about what format a pattern could take:

there seems to be a common theme that out of the actions, most users want to download a copy
seems like HTML consistently isn’t a good file format to download as most users want to store a file locally or share a file via email, etc. From research, users struggle to save a PDF via print dialogs, etc.
from research, linguistically most users refer to this as action as wanting to save the file
related – print buttons usually require javascript. It would be good to explore alternatives that fit with progressive enhancement. Embedding the content in the page and using custom CSS to remove the UI seems like a nice approach that supports the use of the print function in the browser rather than a javascript button.
sometimes download implementations open up a new blank windows in order to download the file. It would be good to explore how to avoid this.
just personal preference but the outline of the document in the ATaR example help signify which parts of the page will be printed or saved while also previewing the document. consideration would need to be given on how to signify this to users of screen readers and other assistive technology though.
in regards to generation libraries:

HMRC have a PDF generation service that they are deprecating.
some other services use pdfbox: https://pdfbox.apache.org
this is an example of how to generate an accessible PDF using pdfBox: https://github.com/martinlovell/accessible-pdfbox-example

ourIssues.title: Components assume the `govuk-visually-hidden` utility class will exist
ourIssues.body:
## Description of the issue

We provide an entry points for each individual component, the idea being that users should get all of the CSS they need to use that component, and ideally nothing more.

For example, including the character count component also includes the CSS for the:

- error message
- hint
- label
- textarea

However, it does _not_ include the `govuk-visually-hidden` utility class, which is used within the Nunjucks template.

From a quick check, it looks like this affects:

- Accordion (in the JavaScript)
- Character count (in the JavaScript)
- Error message (in the Nunjucks template)
- Exit this page (in the Nunjucks template and JavaScript)
- File upload (in the JavaScript)
- Footer (in the Nunjucks template)
- Pagination (in the Nunjucks template)
- Password input (in the JavaScript)
- Summary list (in the Nunjucks template)
- Warning text (in the Nunjucks template)

## Steps to reproduce the issue

Use the component-specific entrypoint to include just the CSS for any of the components listed above, then view the component

## Actual vs expected behaviour

Visually hidden text should be hidden, but it isn't because the `govuk-visually-hidden` utility class is not included in the CSS

ourIssues.title: Pagination items not read out with mouse tracking in NVDA and Chrome
ourIssues.body:
## Description of the issue

Nothing at all is read out when hovering over items of the [pagination component](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/pagination/) with a mouse in NVDA and Chrome with mouse tracking enabled.


## Steps to reproduce the issue

1. Use NVDA with mouse tracking enabled (via Preferences > Settings... > Mouse > Enable mouse tracking)
2. Open [an example page](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/pagination/for-list-pages/) in Chrome
3. Hover over the page numbers or 'Previous'/'Next'


## Actual vs expected behaviour

Nothing is read out except the ellipsis.
It should read out the numbers and 'Previous'/'Next'.

The items all have an `aria-label`, for example, the link with the number 1 has one that says "Page 1". While most other screen readers would read the ARIA label, [NVDA intentionally does not](https://github.com/nvaccess/nvda/issues/5600). NVDA only reads what is visible on the screen when navigating via hovering with the mouse.
Therefore, it is fine that it doesn't read "Page 1", but it should read "1".


## Environment

This only happens with NVDA in Chrome.
It doesn't happen with NVDA in Firefox.
And it doesn't happen with any of the other desktop screen readers we usually test in (JAWS, VO, Narrator).

- GOV.UK Frontend Version: latest
- Operating system: Windows 10 Pro
- Browser: Chrome
- Browser version: 132
- Screen reader: NVDA
- Screen reader version: 2024.4

I assume this is either an issue in NVDA or Chrome.
I also tried an old version of NVDA (2018.1) with an old version of Chrome (64).
The issue didn't happen in that combination.


## Further findings

I've created a few [reduced test cases](https://jsbin.com/baragux) and found that the reason why this is happening is the method / hack that makes more than just the link clickable. That method uses CSS-generated content / a pseudo element that sort of goes on top of the link.

```css
.govuk-pagination__link:after {
    content: "";
    position: absolute;
    top: 0;
    right: 0;
    bottom: 0;
    left: 0;
}
```

My assumption is that NVDA doesn't "see" the text because the pseudo element is on top of it.

There is a seemingly [related issue](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/2278) where the same thing happens with checkboxes. But I don't believe it is directly related as native checkboxes without any CSS are also affected while a native list of links is not.

ourIssues.title: Add the ability to customise the classes on pagination links
ourIssues.body:
## Related component

[Pagination](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/pagination/)

## Context

Currently it isn't possible to add custom classes to individual links (neither items nor the previous/next links) within the pagination.

This limits the possibility of applying different or customised styling to them, such as [removing the visited state](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/styles/links/#links-without-a-visited-state). 

## Alternatives

If using the Nunjucks macro, these links can only be changed through writing additional CSS that hooks onto the component's wrapper. 

Otherwise, the user must use the pure HTML version of the component or fork the macro themselves.

## Additional information

This feature was requested by a user via support.

Being able to remove visited states particularly seems like a useful function for search result pages, where the URL for a page may not be unique even though the page content is totally different.

ourIssues.title: Inconsistent Nunjucks parameter names for aria-label
ourIssues.body:
There are several components which allow you to pass the text for the `aria-label` on the component's wrapper element. The names of these parameters are inconsistent despite them doing the same thing.

[Cookie banner](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/a5a50ea57175c0031168d227513b7710579d9c98/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/cookie-banner/template.njk#L4) and [service navigation](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/a5a50ea57175c0031168d227513b7710579d9c98/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/service-navigation/template.njk#L95) use `ariaLabel`. 

[Pagination](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/a5a50ea57175c0031168d227513b7710579d9c98/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/pagination/template.njk#L53) uses `landmarkLabel` and [breadcrumbs](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/a5a50ea57175c0031168d227513b7710579d9c98/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/breadcrumbs/template.njk#L14) uses `labelText`.

Pagination also [includes a visuallyHiddenText param](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/a5a50ea57175c0031168d227513b7710579d9c98/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/pagination/template.njk#L44) for pagination items. On most components, `visuallyHiddenText` params are appended to the visible text (for example [in summary card actions](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/a5a50ea57175c0031168d227513b7710579d9c98/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/summary-list/template.njk#L7)); pagination is the only example I can find where `visuallyHiddenText` is passed directly to `aria-label`, completely overriding any visual label

The documentation for the params is also structured differently. For example the docs for pagination and breadcrumbs don't mention that the value will be used as the `aria-label`, while they do for cookie banner and service navigation.

Are any of these differences intentional? I think `ariaLabel` is clearest about what the params actually do, with `[thing]AriaLabel` for labels of child elements (eg password uses `showPasswordAriaLabelText`, though again the `Text` makes that inconsistent)

ourIssues.title: Adjust components to scale with android system font size
ourIssues.body:
## What
Ensure as many of our components as possible are responding when viewing govuk-frontend web pages on android devices and adjusting android's system font size.

## Why
Govuk-frontend web pages should respect accessibility settigns and respond to them as expected.

## Steps to replicate
Tested in chrome on browserstack's Galaxy S23 instance as it's easy to notice the issue due to the device's large font size scale.

1. Go to the settings of the testing device and locate the setting to adjust device font size
2. Increase font size (recommend max in order to visualise issue more clearly)
3. Open a govuk-frontend web page on a browser on an android device eg: [the review app's announcements page](https://govuk-frontend-review.herokuapp.com/full-page-examples/announcements)

Notice that the breadcrumbs have not increased in size. Digging into the runtime styles, you will find that rem values of other elements on the page have adjusted in response to the font size change but the breadcrumbs haven't.

![Android browser showing an announcements page with scaled up font size except for the breadcrumbs element](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/assets/64783893/66ecb7d1-bf9e-459a-987c-8c85176a26b7)

## Notes
### Considerations from the spec
The likely reason this is happening can be found in CSS Mobile Text Size section of the CSS spec, specifically [2.2: Conditions that suppress adjustment](https://drafts.csswg.org/css-size-adjust/#default-adjustment-conditions). This section notes 4 reasons that would suppress text size adjustment. From initial testing, certain components can be 'fixed' by removing their block level positioning rules eg: components that have `display: inline-block`. We should be able to use `inline-block` on components and the text size adjustment not be suppressed. Recommend using the the spec in figuring out a solution.

### Impacted components
- Accordion
- Back link
- Breadcrumbs
- Button, and places consumed
    - Cookie banner buttons
    - Exit this page
- Checkboxes
- Details (not the content)
- File upload
- Some of the footer's links
- Header menu
- Notification banner
- Pagination
- Radios
- Select

- Text input, and places consumed

ourIssues.title: WCAG 2.2: Explore how to handle focus state of short links
ourIssues.body:
## What
Figure out how to present focus states for links of 4 or fewer characters and for components which use the link styles.

## Why
During testing of components against [WCAG 2.2 criterion 2.4.13: focus appearance](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/focus-appearance.html) as part of https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/4347, it was discovered that we have several failures within components to do with parts of these components using our link decoration. The root problem is that that very short links have too small a focus area to pass the criteria. The link style itself _does_ pass the criterion, however components that use the link decoration but not the default link colour eg: breadcrumbs using black links fail this because they lose the contrast between the blue and black that links typically have.

This impacts the following components:

- [Back links](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/back-link/)
- [Breadcrumbs](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/breadcrumbs/)
- [Error summary](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/error-summary/)
- [Pagination](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/pagination/)
- [Summary list](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/summary-list/) (summary cards fail but summary lists pass)
- [Tabs](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/tabs/)

As part of this work, we have an opportunity to also update our [link guidance](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/styles/links/) to encourage users to not use short links in their content.

### Further reading
- [Testing spreadsheet (internal only)](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1PpKvhCGZJb1j0ZUUY2ZuA0CBQeu04yFD1bumiL8wGX8/edit#gid=0)
- https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/issues/3007 - related issue on focus state rationalisation
 
## Who needs to work on this
Developers, designers

## Who needs to review this
Developers, designers

## Done when

- [ ] Solution to how to present short links is devised and merged into `main`
- [ ] Link guidance is updated to advise not using short links

## What

Given the following additional parameters:

```
"range": {

  "end": NUMBER,
  "current": NUMBER,
},
"page_param": STRING,
"query_string": STRING,
"anchor": STRING,
```

the Pagination component should generate a range of page links including placement of ellipses, current page styling and generated URLs to each page.

The current implementation of the Pagination component is that is just renders what it has given and does not calculation of pagination structure. communityIssues.title: Remove redundant explicit role attributes from HTML5 elements
communityIssues.body:
## What

Remove the explicit role attribute on HTML elements that have the same role implicitly, including:

* the `<span>` element in the card component, which has a `text` role on the header text
* the `<nav>` element in the contents list component, which has a `navigation` role
* the `<ul>` element in the do and don't list component, which has a `list` role
* the `<footer>` element in the footer component, which has a `contentinfo` role
* the `<header>` element in the header component, which has a `banner` role
* the `<nav>` element in the pagination component, which has a `navigation` role
* the `<table>`, `<thead>`, `<tr>`, `<td>` and `<th>` elements in the table component ([see issue](https://github.com/nhsuk/nhsuk-frontend/issues/1092))

In some places we include an explicit `group` role on `<fieldset>` elements (e.g. the date input) to ensure that JAWS announces the accessible description – we should **leave this in place** unless we're able to do further investigation and understand whether this is still needed.

Update our [HTML validation rules](https://github.com/nhsuk/nhsuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/nhsuk-frontend-review/.htmlvalidate.mjs) accordingly ([see workarounds](https://github.com/nhsuk/nhsuk-frontend/commit/74aceef346383b5678b0d715ade6a8da3948f0ba)).

## Why

These have historically been set because older browsers ([noteably Internet Explorer](https://web.archive.org/web/20180103181655/https://connect.microsoft.com/IE/feedback/details/804723/html5-structural-elements-not-exposed-via-accessibility-api)) do not [map these implicit roles correctly](https://www.html5accessibility.com/).

As our browser support model has evolved, we can now remove these implicit roles.

See related issue from GOV.UK Frontend:

* https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/4708

communityIssues.title: Pagination component uses different markup from equivalent component in GOV.UK Frontend
communityIssues.body:
There are a number of differences in the numbered pagination markup compared to that used in the equivalent component used for GOV.UK Frontend. Replacing `nhsuk` and `govuk` with `brand` so as to reduce the number of differences gives the following diff: ```diff -
+
-
- + - + - + - Previous page + Previous page -
  • - + 1
  • ⋯
  • - + 6
  • 7
  • - + 8
  • ⋯
  • - + 42
-
- + - + - + - Next page + Next page -
``` The main differences are that the NHS component: - Requires a `--numbered` modifier to enable numbered pagination styles - Includes extraneous `role="navigation"` - Uses a `div` around previous and next links - Uses `__previous` element class instead of `__prev` - Uses `__title` element class instead of `__link-title` - Doesn’t use `nhsuk-link` for pagination links Also different, but unavoidable, are the SVG icons used for previous and next arrows (and the different visually hidden class name). I’m not sure what differences there are for the block pagination variant, but a number of the above will still apply. How many of these differences are we happy with, and how many do we want to align in a future upcoming breaking release?

backlog.title: Number output
backlog.body:
What
Display the results of a calculation or the outcome of a user action.

Why
On the ‘Submit social housing lettings and sales data (CORE)’ service, we ask users to enter values for rent and other charges tenants pay.
We only need to collect the total amount, but users may be more familiar with individual values. Rather than ask them to calculate the total value themselves, we display a live calculation, which they can check before submitting the form.

Proposed solution
This component is similar to the existing text input component taking many of the same parameters (such as prefix and suffix), but uses the output element. This element is read-only and can’t be interacted with or gain focus, but instead provides semantics and accessibility features that enable user agents to announce a newly calculated value whenever it has been updated.
Results of usability testing
We initially tested this design in December 2021 and January 2022 with 10 participants. All but 1 had JavaScript enabled and were able to see the total box, but only those with JavaScript enabled would get a live calculation. They all clearly understood that the box represented a total of all values on the page, and were reassured when this value was played back on a ‘Check your answers’ screen.
However, given the possibility of a user entering the wrong total amount, and the system calculating its own value anyway, to save any confusion, we decided not to show the total amount part of the page if JavaScript is disabled.
When to use this component
Use this component when you want to give users a calculation of 2 or more numbers. While not required by the component, these should be of the same type (don’t mix currency with weights, for example). Use the prefix and suffix options to indicate what type of output is expected.
When not to use this component
You should not use this component to display alerts or other information you might place inside a live region.
How it works
This component is designed to act as a progressive enhancement, falling back to an input element if JavaScript is not available. If JavaScript is available, an input element is replaced by an output element which listens for changes on the inputs listed in its for attribute.
Try it for yourself

Demo: https://govuk-output.glitch.me/
Code: https://glitch.com/edit/#!/govuk-output

Outstanding issues and questions

This component has not been audited for its accessibility yet, and is yet to be used in a live production environment.
The output element is not supported in Internet Explorer 11. The component currently displays correctly, but doesn’t function.
Only supports addition at the moment; should it do more?
Should it be the responsibility of this component to provide a set of calculation behaviours (addition, multiplication etc.), or should this be left to individual developers who may have specific requirements?
Does there need to be an option for formatting the output, for example the number of decimal places to display?
How should invalid values be handled? Right now, if you don’t enter a number into one of the inputs, the calculated value isn’t updated.
This component may be interpreted as a disabled input; is there a better way to represent this value?

Anything else?

The number output component - CORE design history

ourIssues.title: Support standard .html/.text input for `caption` on `table` component

## Related component

Yes, https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/table/

## Context

Currently the `caption` argument in the nunjucks macro only takes a string, not the more standard "object with `html` and `text` options". This means users may not be able to pass through html they may need to unless they look into the implementation and find that html is possible to enter, but even then, users need to `| safe` the input themselves. This is unintuitive, and many other arguments in other macros have this object input pattern, rather than just a straight string.

## Alternatives

Yes, passing in a string I have put through the `safe` filter myself.

## Additional information (if applicable)

I wanted to do this myself recently as a result of an accessibility audit, so this isn't just a hypothetical, it's a real need.
I undertook making this change with AI assistance in my fork of govuk-frontend here https://github.com/ReedSoftware/govuk-frontend/pull/1 - after some talk with the GDS team, I'm aware that your stance on AI generated PRs isn't set yet, so I'm happy to leave it as a talking point or reference, but also happy to raise a PR against this change if you did decide you wanted it!

There was also some talk on the GDS channel in x-gov slack about this with @romaricpascal @selfthinker - thank you for your inputs here so far.

ourIssues.title: Add `size` option to form input component labels
ourIssues.body:
<!--

  This is a template for any issues that aren’t bug reports or new feature requests. The headings in this section provide examples of the information you might want to include, but feel free to add/delete sections where appropriate.

-->

## What

Allow form field components to receive a new `size` option in their `label` or `legend` option for easily controlling the text size of their label or legend. The option should receive a t-shirt size and set the appropriate `.govuk-label--<T_SHIRT_SIZE>` or `.govuk-fieldset__legend--<T_SHIRT_SIZE>` on the label or legend.

For components using a `label` the option should be implemented by adding a [new option to our internal Label component](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/tree/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/label) and passing the option through. For those using a `legend`, the public Fieldset component should get an update first in a similar fashion.

The affected components are:
- [Character Count](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/character-count/template.njk) (forwarding the option to Textarea)
- [Checkboxes](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/checkboxes/template.njk) (forwarding the option to either Fieldset)
- [Date Input](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/date-input/template.njk) (forwarding the option to Fieldset)
- [Fieldset](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/date-input/template.njk)
- [File Upload](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/file-upload/template.njk) (forwarding the option to Label)
- [Input](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/input/template.njk) (forwarding the option to Label)
- [Label](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/label/template.njk)
- [Password Input](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/password-input/template.njk) (forwarding the option to Input)
- [Radios](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/radios/template.njk) (forwarding the option to Fieldset)
- [Select](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/select/template.njk) (forwarding the option to Label)
- [Textarea](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/textarea/template.njk) (forwarding the option to Label)

## Why

Different components use different tags for the "title" of the field. This requires the user to understand internal nuances (is it a `label` or `legend`) to change its size. Having an option abstracting this and letting the component work out if it's `.govuk-label--...` or `.govuk-fieldset__legend--...` that's needed is much easier.

## Who needs to work on this

Developers, Tech writer

## Who needs to review this

Developers, Tech writer

## Done when

- [ ] The new option is available on all the components listed above
- [ ] The option is documented consistently across components

ourIssues.title: Improve documentation of `beforeInput(s)` and `afterInput(s)` options of our form control components
ourIssues.body:
<!--

  This is a template for any issues that aren’t bug reports or new feature requests. The headings in this section provide examples of the information you might want to include, but feel free to add/delete sections where appropriate.

-->

## What

Research and document which kind of content is OK/not OK to put in the `beforeInput(s)` and `afterInput(s)` options of our form components, introduced in #4567 to ensure all users (especially those using assistive technology) get proper access to the content.

## Why

Because the content ends up inside a form field, where the control is associated to the label/legend and any error/hint, there's a risk that content injected through `beforeInput(s)`/`afterInput(s)` options gets missed when navigating from field to field, the focus skipping over the content to the next form field. 

This means we may want to suggest restrictions as to which content is suitable for these options, possible techniques to link the content so it gets announced when navigating from field to field, and possibly a warning to test thoroughly.

## Who needs to work on this

Developers, Accessibility specialist, possibly Designers

## Who needs to review this

Developers, Accessibility specialist, possibly Designers 

## Done when

- [ ] We've clarified how to best use the `beforeInput(s)` and `afterInput(s)` options of our form components.

ourIssues.title: Adjust components to scale with android system font size
ourIssues.body:
## What
Ensure as many of our components as possible are responding when viewing govuk-frontend web pages on android devices and adjusting android's system font size.

## Why
Govuk-frontend web pages should respect accessibility settigns and respond to them as expected.

## Steps to replicate
Tested in chrome on browserstack's Galaxy S23 instance as it's easy to notice the issue due to the device's large font size scale.

1. Go to the settings of the testing device and locate the setting to adjust device font size
2. Increase font size (recommend max in order to visualise issue more clearly)
3. Open a govuk-frontend web page on a browser on an android device eg: [the review app's announcements page](https://govuk-frontend-review.herokuapp.com/full-page-examples/announcements)

Notice that the breadcrumbs have not increased in size. Digging into the runtime styles, you will find that rem values of other elements on the page have adjusted in response to the font size change but the breadcrumbs haven't.

![Android browser showing an announcements page with scaled up font size except for the breadcrumbs element](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/assets/64783893/66ecb7d1-bf9e-459a-987c-8c85176a26b7)

## Notes
### Considerations from the spec
The likely reason this is happening can be found in CSS Mobile Text Size section of the CSS spec, specifically [2.2: Conditions that suppress adjustment](https://drafts.csswg.org/css-size-adjust/#default-adjustment-conditions). This section notes 4 reasons that would suppress text size adjustment. From initial testing, certain components can be 'fixed' by removing their block level positioning rules eg: components that have `display: inline-block`. We should be able to use `inline-block` on components and the text size adjustment not be suppressed. Recommend using the the spec in figuring out a solution.

### Impacted components
- Accordion
- Back link
- Breadcrumbs
- Button, and places consumed
    - Cookie banner buttons
    - Exit this page
- Checkboxes
- Details (not the content)
- File upload
- Some of the footer's links
- Header menu
- Notification banner
- Pagination
- Radios
- Select
- Table
- Tabs
- Tag
- Task list
- Text input, and places consumed
    - Date input
    - Password input

ourIssues.title: WCAG 2.2: Investigate thickness of input focus state border
ourIssues.body:
## What
Investigate if the increased black border for the focus state of form inputs needs to be thicker.

## Why
During testing of components against [WCAG 2.2 criterion 2.4.13: focus appearance](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/focus-appearance.html) as part of https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/4347, it was discovered that several form input components that use a similar "box highlight" style focus state fail this criterion. This is because the black border isn't thick enough to meet the size requirements for this criterion and the yellow highlight can't count towards this as it's too low contrast against the white background. Increasing the black border could fix this.

This impacts the following components:
 - [Date input](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/date-input/)
 - [Select](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/select/)
 - [Text input](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/text-input/)
 - [Textarea](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/textarea/) (which will also impact [character count](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/character-count/))

It additionally effects [radios](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/radios/) and [checkboxes](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/checkboxes/) but for slightly different reasons, although it's valuable to tackle these at the same time.

### Further reading
- [Testing spreadsheet (internal only)](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1PpKvhCGZJb1j0ZUUY2ZuA0CBQeu04yFD1bumiL8wGX8/edit#gid=0)
- https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/issues/3007 - related issue on focus state rationalisation
 
## Who needs to work on this
Developers, designers

## Who needs to review this
Developers, designers

ourIssues.title: NVDA does not read hints or error messages when tabbing to checkboxes
ourIssues.body:
## Description of the issue

This is an NVDA bug, but I'm filing an issue here because it affects the accessibility of GOV.UK Frontend so I thought you may want a record of it.

When a checkbox inside a fieldset gets focus, any hint or error message associated with the fieldset should be read out after the legend and before the checkbox label. They're associated with the fieldset via `aria-describedby`. However, NVDA only reads the legend and checkbox label, not the hint or error. This means that NVDA users may be unaware that the grouping has a hint or an error.

For example, the speech output for [this example](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/checkboxes/error/index.html) with a hint and an error is:

> What is your nationality?  grouping  clickable  British  check box  not checked    including English, Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish

Note that this only affects checkboxes. Radios use the same structure and are unaffected.

[An NVDA issue for this bug](https://github.com/nvaccess/nvda/issues/12718) has been open since 2021 but unfortunately it doesn't look like there's been much progress towards a fix. It looks like [this commenter](https://github.com/nvaccess/nvda/issues/12718#issuecomment-1533364655) has also come across this issue while using GOV.UK Frontend though.

## Steps to reproduce the issue

See CodePen at https://codepen.io/matteason/pen/PoyBwYM or one of the GOV.UK Design System examples (eg [checkboxes](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/checkboxes/with-none-option-in-error/index.html))

Open NVDA, navigate to the example page and tab through the form fields

## Actual vs expected behaviour

Hints should be read for all component types in the example, but they're only read for text inputs and radios

## Environment (where applicable)

- Operating system: Windows 10
- Browser: Firefox 112.0, Chrome 112.0.5615.138
- GOV.UK Frontend Version: 4.6.0

ourIssues.title: Research improvements to disabled form control styles
ourIssues.body:
## What

We've shipped an MVP (minimum-viable product) version of disabled form controls in #1713—which aimed to make disabled styles consistent—however we still have some unanswered questions about the suitability of the disabled styles included in Frontend as a whole.

## Why

We have historically discouraged the use of disabled form controls and buttons in user-facing scenarios. Although we continue to discourage their use, we have decided to provide them to cover for situations where user research has found their use helpful or where their use can be better justified (such as an internal caseworking system). 

As we've not encouraged their use, we also haven't performed much testing or research into whether the disabled styles we use work well for end users.

## Assumptions

- Our current disabled styles aren't necessarily adequate in all contexts. For example, a value-less, disabled text input or textarea appears as an empty box, with little other affordance that it is disabled or an input.
- Although WCAG 2.1 (and, currently, 2.2) do not require a minimum contrast ratio for 'inactive' elements, we may want to ensure the visibility of disabled inputs on our own terms.
- Any changes we make to disabled styles should be applicable across all 'core' form control components: Text Input, Textarea, Select, File Upload, Checkbox, and Radios. 
  - If possible or useful, we may also want it to apply to the Button component. 

## Timebox

2 weeks

## Who is working on this?

Spike lead:

Spike buddy:

## Questions to answer

- [ ] Are our current disabled styles well understood by users?
- [ ] Are our current disabled styles still perceptable by users with vision impairment?
- [ ] Do service teams know when they shouldn't be using disabled inputs?

## Done when

- [ ] Questions have been answered or we have a clearer idea of how to get to our goal
- [ ] Findings have been reviewed and agreed with at least one other person
- [ ] Findings have been shared, e.g: via a write-up on the ticket, at a show & tell or team meeting
- [ ] Any code changes we want to make have been made
- [ ] Any documentation changes we want to make have been made

ourIssues.title: Research making the checkbox and radio button labels full width
ourIssues.body:
## What

Perform research with users as to whether making labels on checkboxes and radio buttons span the width of the container, thus increasing their touch surface, makes it easier to use these controls

## Why

Generally speaking, increasing the target area for a control makes the control easier for users to interact with.

We have some existing precendent for this in Frontend already: 

- Labels for other input types (text inputs, selects, textareas, etc.) are already full width.
- The Accordion activates expand/collapse functionality by tapping anywhere in the section header.
- The Skip Link component, when visible, is activatable by clicking anywhere in the component.

The GOV.UK team has had positive feedback when increasing target sizes for elements on the [homepage](https://insidegovuk.blog.gov.uk/2021/12/13/updating-the-gov-uk-homepage/) and [topic pages](https://insidegovuk.blog.gov.uk/2022/08/08/rolling-out-a-new-design-for-browsing-gov-uk-by-topic/) in the last year.

Various external design systems have full width checkbox and radio labels, some of which are based on or inspired by GOV.UK Frontend and have seemingly made the conscious choice to change it:

- ~~[USWDS](https://designsystem.digital.gov/components/checkbox/)~~ Update: Has since updated to no longer be full-width
- [NICE Design System](https://design-system.nice.org.uk/storybook/?path=/story/foundations-checkbox--default)
- [Transport for West Midlands Design System](https://designsystem.tfwm.org.uk/components/radios/)
- [GOLD Design System](https://gold.designsystemau.org/components/control-input/#checkbox-block) (formerly Australian Government Design System)
- [Atlassian Design System](https://atlassian.design/components/checkbox/examples)

Our inline labels date from the GOV.UK Elements days, and I couldn't immediately find any reason why they were implemented in this way at the time. We have stuck to that precedent in situations where a conflict or bug relating to the label sizing has arisen (e.g. #634).

We should validate our current approach and whether it best meets user needs when compared to alternative approaches.

## Assumptions

We've [previously found that users don't tend to click on checkbox or radio button labels](https://designnotes.blog.gov.uk/2016/11/30/weve-updated-the-radios-and-checkboxes-on-gov-uk/), even if they're styled to appear interactible. It could be assumed that the same applies here (if not moreso, as there isn't any visual indicator that interaction is possible). 

As a larger area of the screen will activate a checkbox/radio, there may be an increase in the number of accidental form inputs being made.

A seemingly 'empty' part of the page affecting a nearby input may be unexpected and cause confusion to users unless some other hint is present (e.g. a hover state). 

## Timebox
TBD

## Who is working on this?

Spike lead: TBD

Spike buddy: TBD

## Questions to answer

- [ ] Is there a tangible benefit to checkbox and radio button labels always being full width?
- [ ] Is there a tangible benefit to checkbox and radio button labels being full width in certain situations (e.g. on narrow screens)? 
- [ ] Are full width labels more likely to result in accidental and unwanted inputs?
- [ ] Is having a visually 'empty' area of the screen interactive unexpected or a source of confusion?

## Done when

- [ ] A review or prototype is produced with the modified checkbox/radio styles.
- [ ] User research has been carried out to see how these changes perform with users.
- [ ] Findings have been reviewed and shared with the team.
- [ ] Any follow up issues or actions have been written up.

ourIssues.title: Various issues under Chrome's Auto Dark Mode
ourIssues.body:
Since Chrome version 78, Google has included an experimental feature in the browser, initially named "Forced Dark Mode" and, as of writing, named "Auto Dark Mode for Web Content". 

This feature automatically modifies the appearance of webpages in order to create a "dark mode" version. This is done even if the page already supplies a "dark mode" via the `prefers-color-scheme` CSS media query. It also appears to ignore the `color-scheme` property. 

The flag comes with several different "enabled" modes (as of Chrome 99), which modify how Chrome is internally applying changes. Each mode results in subtly (sometimes radically) different resulting colours.

1. Enabled
2. Enabled with simple HSL-based inversion
3. Enabled with simple CIELAB-based inversion
4. Enabled with simple RGB-based inversion
5. Enabled with selective image inversion
6. Enabled with selective inversion of non-image elements
7. Enabled with selective inversion of everything
8. Enabled with increased text contrast

Most of these modes appear to work by first overriding neutral light background colours (such as white and light greys), and modifying any copy that it detects as existing on a modified background colour to maintain suitable contrast. Most other colours appear to be left intact. This method of alteration means that colours are not all modified in the same way: `$govuk-brand-color` in mode 1, for example, is unmodified when used as a background or border colour (#1d70b8), but is changed when it is used as a text colour (#61a1ee).

Mode 4 appears to simply invert all colours on the page, regardless of usage. 

I'm not sure how mode 1 is different from the others. It may be that this is an "automatic" mode where Chrome tries to determine which of the other seven modes works best for the given page and uses that one.

We have received at least one bug report raised by a user who was using Chrome's Auto Dark Mode feature for accessibility reasons (to make content easier to read with cataracts).

> RE the dark mode, it is now a function in Google Chrome that you can activate and it will force a dark version if the website can accommodate it. Not everyone does, BBC News for example still comes through with a traditional black text on a white background – but it works for many.

## Steps to reproduce the issue
In Google Chrome, go to `chrome://flags/#enable-force-dark` (this should jump you straight to "Auto Dark Mode for Web Contents") and enable the flag.

## Actual vs expected behaviour
Currently, a number of these modes produce colour combinations which fail the contrast requirements established in WCAG 2.1. 

Below is a non-exhaustive subset of issues currently identified in Auto Dark Mode.

### Text inputs and textareas
Text inputs are displayed with a grey background and black border in modes 1, 6, 7, and 8. This fails to meet the expected 1:3 contrast ratio for UI elements (at 1:1.68). 

![Screenshot of the design system input component, appearing grey on black.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160644743-7632dc27-cc56-4558-bd40-8fee1109717c.png)

They are displayed with a light grey background and white border in modes 3 and 5, which easily meets contrast ratio expectations.

They are displayed with the default white background and black border in all other modes.

### Input prefixes and suffixes

These are difficult to read in modes 2 and 4, where they are black on a dark grey background (1:3.23).

![Screenshot of the design system input prefix and suffix example, where the text is black on dark grey.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160646813-ac2ad0a1-083d-4ca0-b571-b1ecacd450e4.png)

These are much more difficult to read in modes 3 and 5, which renders it as black on an even darker grey (1.22).

![Screenshot of the design system input prefix and suffix example. The text is visually imperceptible from the background.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160650473-9c6f3529-5a06-4408-b20e-242b1c66a08e.png)

These are displayed with adequate contrast in other modes.

### Checkboxes and radio buttons
The border and selection states of checkboxes and radio buttons do not have sufficient contrast in modes 1, 6, 7, and 8 (at a pretty much imperceptible contrast ratio of 1:1.04)

![Screenshot of the design system checkbox component, illustrating insufficient contrast between the checkboxes and background, which are both dark grey.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160644218-1fc50370-249e-4e47-b73a-eab9a8b8ea34.png)

They are displayed with white borders and selection states in all other modes.

### Select

In modes 1, 6, 7, and 8, select boxes are rendered with a dark grey background and dark grey border (1:1.04).

![Screenshot of the design system select component, which appears to just be white text with no border or icon.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160648934-5554f80a-1794-40e1-a9b7-a7c16df83d29.png)

They are rendered with a black background and white border in all other modes.

### Skiplinks

In modes 1, 2, 6, and 7, skiplinks are rendered as white on focus-colour yellow, which does not meet contrast requirements (1:1.34).

![Screenshot of a white link on a bright yellow background.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160649767-19aecf58-2ea6-4517-9852-283a4c91f922.png)

In mode 4, it is white on light blue, which is also below expectations (1:3.24).

![Screenshot of a white link on a bright blue background.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160649982-3f7999be-3540-40c5-8d00-7b9350407360.png)

In mode 8, it is white on focus-color yellow, but additionally has a black text shadow/stroke effect applied, which makes it difficult to read.

![Screenshot of a white link with a thin, pixellated black shadow surrounding it, on a bright yellow background.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160650309-a61034bd-d400-4ca3-b312-db890c382f19.png)

This is displayed with adequate contrast (albeit, in white on brown) in all other modes.

### Iconography

Most iconography fails to meet contrast requirements in virtually all modes. This includes:
- the open and close arrows on the Accordion component.
- the arrow on the Back link component.
- the arrows on the Breadcrumbs component.
- the exclamation icon on the Warning text component.

### Other components
The good news is that, for the most part, the majority of other components we have in GOV.UK Frontend are not as badly affected as those above, with various components such as Inset text, Error summary, and Notification banner maintaining their necessary visual presence and suitable contrast even with modified colours. 

## Environment
The results specified here were taken in Chrome 99, running on macOS 15.3, whilst the operating system was set to light mode. 

Interestingly, Chrome DevTools does not give any indication that a change to the page's appearance has taken place. All HTML and CSS content, including the user agent stylesheet, computed styles, and those returned through JavaScript, appear unmodified and are not aligned with the page's actual appearance when Auto Dark Mode is enabled.

Anything interactive:

ourIssues.title: Why do checkboxes and radios have transparent backgrounds?
ourIssues.body:
The following came from a question I asked on the design system slack channel.
https://ukgovernmentdigital.slack.com/archives/C6DMEH5R6/p1572279335253200

**TLDR:** checkboxes and radios have transparent backgrounds. This means they don't stand out visually against non white panels as text input elements do.

From thread:
---------
does anyone know why the checkboxes (and I assume radio buttons) have transparent backgrounds? Rather than a white background (which would probably be the default browser rendering of a standard checkbox).
**GOV checkbox (with transparent background):**
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/23551105/67845990-5e27a280-faf8-11e9-8e33-0bb7e1f6b0b5.png)
**Default checkbox (without GOV styling):**
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/23551105/67846092-86af9c80-faf8-11e9-8571-995a80aa3825.png)

**Anon 1:** 
I suspect that’s because they’re custom rendered rather than native checkboxes, and we want to support users who change their text and background colours.

11 replies

**Anon 2:**
Hi Dave,
This decision pre-dates the design system so I'll need to do a bit of digging to see if we can find out why - but my guess is something along the lines of what **Anon 1** said. Will come back to you.
Have you seen any problems around this, or are you just wondering?
After some investigation - it appears that his is the pertinent commit: https://github.com/alphagov/govuk_elements/commit/4972b81697fbf5b9ac12a211010c623e625ab3ab

**Dave Haigh**
I am looking at using small checkboxes as a filter for a list. The filters are located on a light grey panel (similar to the call to action blocks on GOV.UK guidance pages). As you can see in the screenshot the checkbox doesn’t stand out well as the background is transparent.

Im not sure on the answer to this but… should the scenario be:
- If user HAS NOT specified any browser background colour then they should be white;
- Else if user HAS a specified background colour in certain modes then they should be either transparent or that colour (when in that mode)
1. Is the above correct?
2. Is it possible?
3.Also, some other elements do not respect user specified background colours such as text inputs (they’re always white). Why are only the checks and radios transparent?

i’ve specified my background colour to be red (in any mode) in this screenshot:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/23551105/67846236-c5455700-faf8-11e9-868f-432708c3a31f.png)

**Anon 3**
I don’t really have a good answer for you other than that the radios and checkboxes in the Design System are based on those introduced in Elements back in 2016 by people that no longer work here. As **Anon 2** said, we don’t have the context of every historical decision. We could definitely look at changing that behaviour, but we’d need to test thoroughly to make sure they still work in all of these sorts of scenarios.

ourIssues.title: Expand documentation of fieldset to discuss when to add `role="group"`

communityIssues.title: Using `true` as a default parameter value is confusing
communityIssues.body:
In the search component, there is an [option to prevent the label from appearing inside the text input][1].

The parameter that does this - `inline_label` - defaults to `true`. To set the label to appear above, you need to set that parameter to `false`.

```erb
<%= render "govuk_publishing_components/components/search", {
  inline_label: false,
} %>
```

This makes sense when using component itself, but does leave things a little confusing when updating the component markup.

An unwritten but useful convention is for components to set any parameters with defaults at the top of the component partial:

```erb
<%
  margin_bottom ||= 2
  inverse_background ||= false
  some_other_thing ||= "marmalade"
%>
```

This means that the defaults are easily found and in one place in the component, rather than being spread out across the markup.

The `||=` assignment operator is a shorthand for:

```ruby
value = value ? value : default_value
```

So when a falsey value needs to be passed in it can't override the default - so a parameter which is `true` by default can't be listed at the top of the component.

Because it's not declared at the top of the partial, a check needs to be done before the variable is used. This usually means that `local_assigns.include?(:variable_name)` is used. If the variable was declared with `||=` then this wouldn't need to be used.

**For these reasons, should a convention be added to avoid `true` as a default value for a parameter in components?**

There may be components that have a default that seems to require `true` as a default - for example, a component that has a border visible by default. This could have a `show_border` parameter that is true - but flipping the name round and having an `omit_border` that defaults to `false` gives the same end result without needing the default to be `true`.

[1]: https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/search/stop_the_label_appearing_inline

communityIssues.title: Inconsistent components API
communityIssues.body:
The component API is inconsistent across components and in comparison with `govuk-frontend`.

In the table below there is a brief comparison in how `govuk-frontend` components are aligned in API with `govuk_publishing_components`

|Component               |API |
|---                      |---  |
Accordion                 | aligned
Back link                 | aligned
Breadcrumbs               | misaligned
Button                    | slightly misaligned (start)
Character count           | slightly misaligned (nesting)
Checkboxes                | slightly misaligned (fieldset)
Date input                | slightly misaligned (fieldset)
Details                   | misaligned
Error message             | aligned
Error summary             | misaligned
Fieldset                  | misaligned
File upload               | aligned
Footer                    | aligned
Header                    | slightly misaligned (navigation_items)
Inset text                | aligned
Panel                     | misaligned
Phase banner              | misaligned
Radios                    | slightly misaligned (fieldset)
Select                    | slightly misaligned (options)
Skip link                 | aligned
Summary list              | slightly misaligned (items)
Table                     | aligned
Tabs                      | misaligned
Text input                | aligned
Textarea                  | aligned
Warning text              | slightly misaligned (iconFallbackText)

We can see a few common differences between to two API models:
- for arrays, `govuk-frontend` uses the generic `items` (in most cases) whereas `govuk_publishing_components` uses the name of the component (e.g. `attachments` for the attachment list component or `breadcrumbs` for the breadcrumbs component)
- for web addresses/paths `govuk-frontend` uses `href` whereas in `govuk_publishing_components` we often find `url` (e.g. breadcrumbs component)

It's worth mentioning that not even `govuk-frontend`'s API is consistent (e.g. `errorList` instead of `items` in the Error summary component, or differences in nesting)

A few advantages of making the API consistent:
- increases developers' confidence when calling components with arguments (without constantly checking examples in the guide)
- prototyping and production will use the same config object (can be easily copied over in both directions)
- applications can prepare the data to be fed into components consistently using helpers
- it would be easier to swap one component with another

I'm creating this to raise awareness of the differences, hopefully generate discussions around how good looks like and aim for consistency and convergency. API alignment requires at least a breaking change and some replacements across applications – which is not an easy process. For this reason, having a clear vision about how we want it to look like would save us from doing this more than once.

backlog.title: Right-to-left (RTL) language support
backlog.body:
What
Add support for right-to-left (RTL) languages to GOV.UK Frontend components.
Why
A number of pages on GOV.UK are made available in RTL languages, however they tend to insert RTL content into the same layout used by left-to-right (LTR) languages instead of mirroring the entire interface, as is typical for RTL languages. For example, in RTL languages a right-pointing arrow indicates moving backwards, whereas a left-pointing arrow indicates progress.
RTL languages are currently in use in various areas of GOV.UK. (Google search results are for a rough indication of how widely used each language is.)

Arabic (Google search results, example page)
Persian (Farsi) (Google search results, example page)
Dari Persian (Google search results, example page)
Hebrew (Google search results, example page)
Pashto (Google search results, example page)
Shahmukhi Punjabi (Google search results, example page)
Urdu (Google search results, example page)

GOV.UK's lack of RTL support produces unexpected layouts in situation where RTL languages are already in use (though many of these instances are with publishing components and not Frontend):

Announcements (Arabic)

The email and RSS notification links are misaligned and have incorrect margins.


Screening tests for you and your baby (Urdu)

Page metadata appears reversed (value appears before key) due to left floats.
Date format appears scrambled due to trying to automatically interpolate LTR content into an RTL context.
Email alerts button has incorrect margins.


COVID-19 lateral flow test instructions (Arabic)

Indent text component doesn't appear indented, as the indent is on the wrong side.



There are some situations where RTL language content has only been made available in PDF format, potentially due to restrictions with creating this content in HTML, which creates an accessibility barrier for end users. For example, detention rights are available in English as a HTML page but must be downloaded as a PDF for Arabic, Farsi and Urdu speakers.

ourIssues.title: Add the ability to customise the classes on pagination links
ourIssues.body:
## Related component

[Pagination](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/pagination/)

## Context

Currently it isn't possible to add custom classes to individual links (neither items nor the previous/next links) within the pagination.

This limits the possibility of applying different or customised styling to them, such as [removing the visited state](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/styles/links/#links-without-a-visited-state). 

## Alternatives

If using the Nunjucks macro, these links can only be changed through writing additional CSS that hooks onto the component's wrapper. 

Otherwise, the user must use the pure HTML version of the component or fork the macro themselves.

## Additional information

This feature was requested by a user via support.

Being able to remove visited states particularly seems like a useful function for search result pages, where the URL for a page may not be unique even though the page content is totally different.

ourIssues.title: Improve the `title`s for pattern guidance pages
ourIssues.body:
## Context

Pattern pages with compound titles do not have the entire title included within the `title` element.

|Page `h1`|Page `title`|
|:-|:-|
|Ask users for Bank Details|Bank details|
|Ask users for Email addresses|Email addresses|
|Help users to Confirm an email address|Confirm an email address|
|Help users to Exit a page quickly|Exit a page quickly|

This can cause confusion, as some pages on the Design System website can have similar or identical `title`s in browser tabs and search result listings. 

|Pattern page `title`|Non-pattern page `title`|
|:-|:-|
|Cookies page|[Cookies](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/cookies/)|
|Dates|[Date input](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/date-input/)|
|Exit a page quickly|[Exit this page](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/exit-this-page/)|
|Passwords|Password input [in development]|

In instances where a pattern has a compound title (i.e. "Ask users for...", "Help users to...") these should be included in the page `title`. 

It may also be useful to include the name of the parent section ("Styles", "Components", "Patterns", etc.) somewhere within the page `title` on these child pages.

## Alternatives

Currently you must either look at the page's URL or click through to visit the page in order to see whether it is the desired page. 

## Additional information

Raised by a working group member during a working group meeting.
