ourIssues.title: Enhanced File Upload banner does not update on browser Back/Forward in Chrome&Edge
ourIssues.body:
## Description of the issue

in Chrome or Edge, when a user navigates Back or Forward to a page with a File Upload component on it, any preexisting value in the hidden file input is not shown correctly in the file upload component's banner

## Steps to reproduce the issue

In Chrome or Edge:

1. navigate to https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/file-upload/enhanced/
1. choose a file, either by the button or by dragging & dropping
1. simulate the user submitting the form and having a file actually be uploaded by changing the address bar to [www.gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/)
1. use the browser's Back button to return to the upload-a-single-file example

## Actual vs expected behaviour

Expected behaviour: the banner shows the file name chosen in step 2
Actual behaviour: the banner shows 'No file chosen'

The reason I expect the filename to appear in the banner is that the filename is actually populated by the browser in the hidden file input tag. This can be verified by opening the browser console and executing the following: `document.querySelector('input[type="file"]').value`

Therefore, if the user were to press Continue again, they'd be uploading the previously-chosen file.

This doesn't happen in Firefox or Safari because they don't populate the `files` property of file input tags on browser navigation.

## Environment (where applicable)

- Operating system: N/A
- Browser: Chrome+Edge, not Firefox or Safari
- Browser version: latest (Chrome 153)
- GOV.UK Frontend Version: 6.5.0

ourIssues.title: Radios: selected dot renders off-centre and lopsided at fractional zoom/display scaling — a CSS mitigation that bounds the error (follow-up to #5104)
Summary list: Allow customisation of full action link content
ourIssues.body: ## What Currently, action links in the Summary list have a hardcoded content order of the action name (`html` or `text`), followed by an area of visually hidden text (`visuallyHiddenText`). The visually hidden text includes a hardcoded space separating it from the prior text, and is usually the same or similar to the key for the current row. For example: ```html change name delete address ``` ## Why This fixed ordering doesn't accommodate localisation into languages where this text appears in a different order. For example, in German we might have this: ```html Namen ändern Adresse löschen ``` Having a hardcoded space is also undesirable in certain languages, such as Chinese: ```html 更换名字 删除名称 ``` Although it is currently possible for services to pass HTML into the action links and ignore the `visuallyHiddenText` parameter completely, we may want to investigate methods of either making `visuallyHiddenText` work with other languages, or removing the use of a dedicated/hardcoded parameter in favour of using the `html` parameter. ## Who needs to work on this Developers ## Who needs to review this Developers ## Done when - [ ] Investigate ways that `visuallyHiddenText` could work with non-English languages. - [ ] Make changes to the Nunjucks template and related tests, if we decide to make modifications. - [ ] Document any changes to Nunjucks parameters.

ourIssues.title: Handle `caller` in test fixtures
Make it easier to add a hint or an error message to a fieldset
ourIssues.body:
## What

If you want to use the fieldset component to group related fields, for example asking for a street address, you need to take care of including the hint / error message components separately and do extra work to associate them with the fieldset.

We do not provide any examples or guidance on how to do this, and it would be easy to get wrong (for example, by not creating the association with the fieldset)

It therefore seems like it would be useful if the fieldset component accepted `hint` and `errorMessage` objects and took care of this association itself.

## Why

This was requested by @edwardhorsford in https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/issues/778#issuecomment-459047140.

## Additional information

The radios, checkbox and date input components all use hints and error messages which are then associated with the fieldset using `aria-describedby`. However, this logic is handled (and therefore duplicated) within the individual components.

Moving this logic to the fieldset component _might_ allow us to simplify the repeated logic in the radios, checkboxes and date input components. However, it's not clear what should happen to the hint / error message [if you do not include a fieldset](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/62d3de38036b858b1dd85c5bd8c027830fab5a3d/src/components/date-input/template.njk#L79-L96).

ourIssues.title: Consider replacing 'Town or city' in address with 'Address line 3'

@christopherthomasdesign wrote

_"We're going to separate the 'address line x' change from the county field one so that we can make this change straight away. We should hopefully reach a conclusion on the county field soon."_

In your discussions about the county field, you may wish to refer to a previous pull request that applied the 'Address line x' format for all lines. https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/pull/1369

In effect, 'Town or city' would become 'Address line 3' and is less prescriptive about what should be in it. The field has always tolerated input of 'York, Yorkshire' but the current label might appear to discourage it.

Let me be clear, I am not currently lobbying for this change myself. I'm merely stating it as an option to consider in your discussions. It may be a change that somebody else wants to lobby for. I hope that helps your discussion.

ourIssues.title: Typography for labels on patterns with multiple fields
ourIssues.body:
Where patterns have multiple fields on a single page (rather than just one, where the label or legend doubles as the `<h1>`), it is currently unclear what typographic weight should be applied to the field labels (or legends).

[Addresses](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/addresses/) and [Bank details](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/bank-details/) suggest using regular weight, Address lookup (the video) and [Payment card details](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/payment-card-details/) suggest using `s`.

The Getting started page has a section on [styling options for labels and legends](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/get-started/labels-legends-headings/#styling-options-for-labels-and-legends) which also suggest that `m` is an option if needed.

Should the patterns in the Design System have consistency between them in typography (ie all use `s` or regular)? Or is there a reason for the differences?  And should those pages make clear whether the typography in the patterns can be changed if necessary, or whether they should be copied exactly as they are?

ourIssues.title: Iterate image guidance for ‘text in charts, diagrams and complex images
ourIssues.body:
## Related documentation
Hannah Thomas from ONS [gave feedback on the guidance](https://ukgovernmentdigital.slack.com/archives/C6DMEH5R6/p1681385024589509) on descriptive text for charts on the cross-gov Slack channel.

## Suggestion

Edited for clarity:
> Charts are a bit of an outlier [from typical ways to add descriptive text to images] because they always should come with a title. It is this title that lets a screen reader user know that there is an image.

> So our research has shown it is **better to go straight from the chart title to the text description of the chart**. Which is also why we say the chart title should start with “Figure x” and the text description should start with “Description of figure x: a line chart showing .....”

> So you should flag it is a description of the figure and you should state the type of chart

> We don’t necessarily say you have to start the text description with “Description of figure x:” - you can just start with “This line chart shows....” but feedback from stats teams was that they found it a bit **hard to separate the text description from the statistical commentary** so this was a way around it

> **Putting extra alt text in the alt attribute was found to just add unnecessary auditory clutter** when you follow this approach, and this approach was found to be better for all users - not just screen reader users - because there are an array of people who need/want/like a text description for a chart.

> [For example] colourblind users, users with dyscalculia or users who just don’t feel comfortable with charts, users with low vision who can zoom in on text but find it hard to zoom in on charts, users who need a bit of reassurance that what they have taken away from the chart is actually what the chart is showing

## Done when (possibility to start)
- [ ] Assess feedback - team, particularly accessibility expert
- [ ] Decide on the iteration we can do to existing guidance
- [ ] Respond to feedback and discuss contribution opportunities

communityIssues.title: The experimental chart component's accessibility criteria needs more detail

We have reintroduced the [experimental Chart component ](https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/chart)as part of some exploratory work we are doing in the Patterns & Pages team.

During the review, we realised that the accessibility criteria is quite small for the component. Currently, it says:

```
Charts must:

use line colours with a contrast ratio higher than 4.5:1 against the background colour to meet WCAG AA
contain a heading and description so that skip links and semantics are accurate
```

However we suspect that there would be a lot more criteria to make a chart accessible, so we've raised this issue so that we remember to populate it with more stuff.

As we are adding this component to the next accessibility audit, we're expecting the outcome of that to inform the criteria. We could also base the criteria off of the [GSS guidance](https://analysisfunction.civilservice.gov.uk/policy-store/data-visualisation-charts/).

backlog.title: Suggested new component - Side menu
backlog.body:
What

Give a brief description of the style, component or pattern you want to propose.

Context:
We are in the final stages of building an e-learning service using the GDS design system. We have completed numerous rounds of user testing and already gone through one Alpha and Beta Assessment.
What:
A right-hand sidebar navigation menu which allows users to easily see their progression through a course and be able to navigate back and forth through chapters.
Current version

In-situ

Iterations from user testing

Why

Explain why you think this should be added to the GOV.UK Design System.

In our alpha assessment, we were challenged to explore if there was a user need to see their progression through the course and also to be able to navigate back and forth through the chapters. We tested various variations of a sidebar navigation similar to those found in lots of e-learning platforms. During testing, we found that some users naturally used the sidebar to return to topics earlier in the course and used it to be aware of their progression and estimate their completion time.
Design-wise, we didn’t want to reinvent the wheel so we built on existing sidebar navigation patterns from GOV.UK publishing such as the contents list on the publishing service (https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/contents_list) and the related content sidebar on many start pages. We iterated the design several times to make it simple and accessible. For instance, we made some headers in the sidebar visually hidden so they would give context to screen reader users whilst avoiding confusion for sighted users who had initially struggled with the previous design.


What evidence do you have that it's needed by multiple services across government?


In the our beta assessment, we were praised on our work developing this pattern and asked to play it back into the community:
‘the team has validated the user need to track progress within training modules, has designed a pattern that is working for their beta users, and is planning to continue iterating this pattern - the panel would encourage the team to share this pattern and research findings with the design system community’


What evidence do you have that it meets the needs of the users of those services?


We have tested and validated this component in several rounds of qual research with 5-10 people in each round, and in Private Beta testing with over 1200 people (with quant showing that people successfully use this when required, and qual feedback only positive and no negative on the latest version).
Our user testing so far has validated the need for this component and as mentioned has been praised so far by assessors. But we would love to share it with the community to get a wider perspective and possible use cases.


Have you checked that it doesn't already exist in the GOV.UK Design System?


Yes
Anything else

Include links to any examples, research or code to support your proposal, if available.

ourIssues.title: File upload breaks on input ids containing quotes (unescaped selector in findLabel)
ourIssues.body:
## Summary

`FileUpload.findLabel()` interpolates the raw input id into `document.querySelector(`label[for="..."]`)`, so an id containing a double quote (e.g. `a"b`, legal HTML) throws an uncaught `SyntaxError: Invalid selector` instead of resolving the label — breaking component init. Verified with the real module under jsdom: `findLabel()` with input id `a"b` throws; the label exists in the DOM.

Same unescaped-interpolation class as #7395 (error summary/checkboxes) and #7397 (tabs), different component — no `CSS.escape` on this path.

## Expected

Escape the id with `CSS.escape()`, like the sibling fixes.

ourIssues.title: Uncaught selector errors for ids/names containing quotes (error summary, checkboxes)
ourIssues.body:
## Summary

Clicking an error-summary link (or toggling an exclusive checkbox) throws an uncaught `SyntaxError: Invalid selector` when the target's `id`/`name` contains quote characters, because both components interpolate raw values into `querySelector`/`querySelectorAll`:

- Error summary: `` document.querySelector(`label[for='${id}']`) `` breaks for ids like `child's-name` (legal HTML5). The throw aborts the click handler before focus/scroll, verified with the real module under jsdom.
- Checkboxes: `` querySelectorAll(`input[type="checkbox"][name="${name}"]`) `` (×2 call sites) breaks for names like `a"b`. The exclusive ("None of these") unchecking never runs, so a contradictory state can be submitted.

No `CSS.escape` is used anywhere in `src/`. Related #1808/#1809 fixed other interpolation paths but left these two open.

## Expected

Escape the interpolated values with `CSS.escape()` (supported by every browser in the support matrix) so special-character ids/names keep working.

ourIssues.title: WCAG 2.2: Explore how to handle focus state of short links
ourIssues.body:
## What
Figure out how to present focus states for links of 4 or fewer characters and for components which use the link styles.

## Why
During testing of components against [WCAG 2.2 criterion 2.4.13: focus appearance](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/focus-appearance.html) as part of https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/4347, it was discovered that we have several failures within components to do with parts of these components using our link decoration. The root problem is that that very short links have too small a focus area to pass the criteria. The link style itself _does_ pass the criterion, however components that use the link decoration but not the default link colour eg: breadcrumbs using black links fail this because they lose the contrast between the blue and black that links typically have.

This impacts the following components:

- [Back links](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/back-link/)
- [Breadcrumbs](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/breadcrumbs/)
- [Error summary](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/error-summary/)
- [Pagination](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/pagination/)
- [Summary list](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/summary-list/) (summary cards fail but summary lists pass)
- [Tabs](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/tabs/)

As part of this work, we have an opportunity to also update our [link guidance](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/styles/links/) to encourage users to not use short links in their content.

### Further reading
- [Testing spreadsheet (internal only)](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1PpKvhCGZJb1j0ZUUY2ZuA0CBQeu04yFD1bumiL8wGX8/edit#gid=0)
- https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/issues/3007 - related issue on focus state rationalisation
 
## Who needs to work on this
Developers, designers

## Who needs to review this
Developers, designers

## Done when

- [ ] Solution to how to present short links is devised and merged into `main`
- [ ] Link guidance is updated to advise not using short links

ourIssues.title: Various issues under Chrome's Auto Dark Mode
ourIssues.body:
Since Chrome version 78, Google has included an experimental feature in the browser, initially named "Forced Dark Mode" and, as of writing, named "Auto Dark Mode for Web Content". 

This feature automatically modifies the appearance of webpages in order to create a "dark mode" version. This is done even if the page already supplies a "dark mode" via the `prefers-color-scheme` CSS media query. It also appears to ignore the `color-scheme` property. 

The flag comes with several different "enabled" modes (as of Chrome 99), which modify how Chrome is internally applying changes. Each mode results in subtly (sometimes radically) different resulting colours.

1. Enabled
2. Enabled with simple HSL-based inversion
3. Enabled with simple CIELAB-based inversion
4. Enabled with simple RGB-based inversion
5. Enabled with selective image inversion
6. Enabled with selective inversion of non-image elements
7. Enabled with selective inversion of everything
8. Enabled with increased text contrast

Most of these modes appear to work by first overriding neutral light background colours (such as white and light greys), and modifying any copy that it detects as existing on a modified background colour to maintain suitable contrast. Most other colours appear to be left intact. This method of alteration means that colours are not all modified in the same way: `$govuk-brand-color` in mode 1, for example, is unmodified when used as a background or border colour (#1d70b8), but is changed when it is used as a text colour (#61a1ee).

Mode 4 appears to simply invert all colours on the page, regardless of usage. 

I'm not sure how mode 1 is different from the others. It may be that this is an "automatic" mode where Chrome tries to determine which of the other seven modes works best for the given page and uses that one.

We have received at least one bug report raised by a user who was using Chrome's Auto Dark Mode feature for accessibility reasons (to make content easier to read with cataracts).

> RE the dark mode, it is now a function in Google Chrome that you can activate and it will force a dark version if the website can accommodate it. Not everyone does, BBC News for example still comes through with a traditional black text on a white background – but it works for many.

## Steps to reproduce the issue
In Google Chrome, go to `chrome://flags/#enable-force-dark` (this should jump you straight to "Auto Dark Mode for Web Contents") and enable the flag.

## Actual vs expected behaviour
Currently, a number of these modes produce colour combinations which fail the contrast requirements established in WCAG 2.1. 

Below is a non-exhaustive subset of issues currently identified in Auto Dark Mode.

### Text inputs and textareas
Text inputs are displayed with a grey background and black border in modes 1, 6, 7, and 8. This fails to meet the expected 1:3 contrast ratio for UI elements (at 1:1.68). 

![Screenshot of the design system input component, appearing grey on black.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160644743-7632dc27-cc56-4558-bd40-8fee1109717c.png)

They are displayed with a light grey background and white border in modes 3 and 5, which easily meets contrast ratio expectations.

They are displayed with the default white background and black border in all other modes.

### Input prefixes and suffixes

These are difficult to read in modes 2 and 4, where they are black on a dark grey background (1:3.23).

![Screenshot of the design system input prefix and suffix example, where the text is black on dark grey.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160646813-ac2ad0a1-083d-4ca0-b571-b1ecacd450e4.png)

These are much more difficult to read in modes 3 and 5, which renders it as black on an even darker grey (1.22).

![Screenshot of the design system input prefix and suffix example. The text is visually imperceptible from the background.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160650473-9c6f3529-5a06-4408-b20e-242b1c66a08e.png)

These are displayed with adequate contrast in other modes.

### Checkboxes and radio buttons
The border and selection states of checkboxes and radio buttons do not have sufficient contrast in modes 1, 6, 7, and 8 (at a pretty much imperceptible contrast ratio of 1:1.04)

![Screenshot of the design system checkbox component, illustrating insufficient contrast between the checkboxes and background, which are both dark grey.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160644218-1fc50370-249e-4e47-b73a-eab9a8b8ea34.png)

They are displayed with white borders and selection states in all other modes.

### Select

In modes 1, 6, 7, and 8, select boxes are rendered with a dark grey background and dark grey border (1:1.04).

![Screenshot of the design system select component, which appears to just be white text with no border or icon.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160648934-5554f80a-1794-40e1-a9b7-a7c16df83d29.png)

They are rendered with a black background and white border in all other modes.

### Skiplinks

In modes 1, 2, 6, and 7, skiplinks are rendered as white on focus-colour yellow, which does not meet contrast requirements (1:1.34).

![Screenshot of a white link on a bright yellow background.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160649767-19aecf58-2ea6-4517-9852-283a4c91f922.png)

In mode 4, it is white on light blue, which is also below expectations (1:3.24).

![Screenshot of a white link on a bright blue background.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160649982-3f7999be-3540-40c5-8d00-7b9350407360.png)

In mode 8, it is white on focus-color yellow, but additionally has a black text shadow/stroke effect applied, which makes it difficult to read.

![Screenshot of a white link with a thin, pixellated black shadow surrounding it, on a bright yellow background.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160650309-a61034bd-d400-4ca3-b312-db890c382f19.png)

This is displayed with adequate contrast (albeit, in white on brown) in all other modes.

### Iconography

Most iconography fails to meet contrast requirements in virtually all modes. This includes:
- the open and close arrows on the Accordion component.
- the arrow on the Back link component.
- the arrows on the Breadcrumbs component.
- the exclamation icon on the Warning text component.

### Other components
The good news is that, for the most part, the majority of other components we have in GOV.UK Frontend are not as badly affected as those above, with various components such as Inset text, Error summary, and Notification banner maintaining their necessary visual presence and suitable contrast even with modified colours. 

## Environment
The results specified here were taken in Chrome 99, running on macOS 15.3, whilst the operating system was set to light mode. 

Interestingly, Chrome DevTools does not give any indication that a change to the page's appearance has taken place. All HTML and CSS content, including the user agent stylesheet, computed styles, and those returned through JavaScript, appear unmodified and are not aligned with the page's actual appearance when Auto Dark Mode is enabled.

ourIssues.title: Improve inconsistent screenreader behaviours for error summary/notification banner
ourIssues.body:
## What
The error summary and notification banner components are implemented in similar ways: using `role=‘alert’`, `aria-labelledby` and moving focus to the component with JavaScript. However, in our own testing and testing done by others, we have noticed that screenreader behaviour when announcing these components is extremely inconsistent ([link to testing spreadsheet here](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1KrgPdKf8M6zsNZcRPUG0r7H1-1aREW5QgnjhhfVHIag/edit?usp=sharing)).

We could investigate the following as some starting points:

- [ ] Test if we can reliably and consistently reproduce any of the issues below 
- [ ] Whether we're using `role='alert'` and `aria-labelledby` in the correct way
- [ ] If there are any other solutions to this problem that perform more consistently
- [ ] If the behaviour of `aria-live` / `role='alert'` is adequately defined in the specs

## Context
When building the notification banner component, it was flagged that `aria-labelledby` was redundant for the error summary component (and therefore on the alert versions of the notification banner too). However, when we tested this in various assistive tech, we found that removing `aria-labelledby` could 1) change the behaviour a lot (especially in Voiceover on Mac), and 2) in general, announcing of error summary/notification banner is extremely inconsistent between different screenreaders. 

In the short term, we decided not to remove aria-labelledbyfrom the error summary, and instead to add aria-labelledby to notification banners to make them consistent with the error summary.

## Related Issues

- [Inconsistent announcing of error summary/notification banner](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/1954)
- [Error summary is not focused correctly on second form submission with NVDA](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/2055)
- [Links within error summary are not consistently read out (Safari + Voiceover on MacOS Catalina)](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/2072)

This W3C issue is also slightly related and something we may want to follow up on if we think that the aria properties we're using need to be better defined in the spec, i.e: how things *should* behave on page load: https://github.com/w3c/aria/issues/1360

ourIssues.title: Error Summary is not focused correctly on second form submission with NVDA
ourIssues.body:

ourIssues.title: Consider changing or removing focus state for error summary and notification banner
ourIssues.body: ## What Decide on whether the notification banner, which is automatically focused when the page loads (for the error and success variants), should have a focus state and what it should look like. Decide whether the same treatment should be applied to the existing error summary component which behaves in the same way. ## Why We need to understand whether WCAG 2.1 1.4.11 Non-text contrast applies to this element. It's programatically focused on page load, but is not keyboard-operable – once focus has left the error summary, you cannot navigate back to it using the keyboard. The proposed 2.4.11 focus visible (at time of writing) [explicitly only applies to keyboard operable controls](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/focus-appearance-minimum.html#keyboard-focus): > Some elements can take focus (such as the target of a skip link), however, it is only when the element is operable by keyboard controls that this criterion applies. If this logic applies to 1.4.11, then the focus state of the error summary / notification banner does not need to meet contrast – in which case, is the yellow outline actually helpful? Or should we remove it entirely? If the focus state does need to meet contrast, then we need to revisit the focus state for both the error summary and the new notification banner component. ## Further detail The error summary currently has a yellow outline when focused. The proposed notification banner component will also take focus on page load (for the error and success variants), so we will presumably want to use the same approach. However, the yellow outline does not meet 3:1 colour contrast against the white background. Other components use a black border when focused (which then means it meets contrast), but because the error summary is focused on page load we want to preserve the border colour so that it suggests an error / success state as appropriate. ## Done when - [x] Understand how WCAG 2.4.11 applies to the notification banner and error summary components - [ ] Decide on focus state for notification banner - [ ] Decide on focus state for error summary

communityIssues.title: Use the utility functions and classes exported by `govuk-frontend`
Inconsistent components API
communityIssues.body:
The component API is inconsistent across components and in comparison with `govuk-frontend`.

In the table below there is a brief comparison in how `govuk-frontend` components are aligned in API with `govuk_publishing_components`

|Component               |API |
|---                      |---  |
Accordion                 | aligned
Back link                 | aligned
Breadcrumbs               | misaligned
Button                    | slightly misaligned (start)
Character count           | slightly misaligned (nesting)
Checkboxes                | slightly misaligned (fieldset)
Date input                | slightly misaligned (fieldset)
Details                   | misaligned
Error message             | aligned
Error summary             | misaligned
Fieldset                  | misaligned
File upload               | aligned
Footer                    | aligned
Header                    | slightly misaligned (navigation_items)
Inset text                | aligned
Panel                     | misaligned
Phase banner              | misaligned
Radios                    | slightly misaligned (fieldset)
Select                    | slightly misaligned (options)
Skip link                 | aligned
Summary list              | slightly misaligned (items)
Table                     | aligned
Tabs                      | misaligned
Text input                | aligned
Textarea                  | aligned
Warning text              | slightly misaligned (iconFallbackText)

We can see a few common differences between to two API models:
- for arrays, `govuk-frontend` uses the generic `items` (in most cases) whereas `govuk_publishing_components` uses the name of the component (e.g. `attachments` for the attachment list component or `breadcrumbs` for the breadcrumbs component)
- for web addresses/paths `govuk-frontend` uses `href` whereas in `govuk_publishing_components` we often find `url` (e.g. breadcrumbs component)

It's worth mentioning that not even `govuk-frontend`'s API is consistent (e.g. `errorList` instead of `items` in the Error summary component, or differences in nesting)

A few advantages of making the API consistent:
- increases developers' confidence when calling components with arguments (without constantly checking examples in the guide)
- prototyping and production will use the same config object (can be easily copied over in both directions)
- applications can prepare the data to be fed into components consistently using helpers
- it would be easier to swap one component with another

I'm creating this to raise awareness of the differences, hopefully generate discussions around how good looks like and aim for consistency and convergency. API alignment requires at least a breaking change and some replacements across applications – which is not an easy process. For this reason, having a clear vision about how we want it to look like would save us from doing this more than once.

communityIssues.title: Uplift NHS components to align with GOV
communityIssues.body:
Following the release of [nhsuk-frontend v10](https://github.com/nhsuk/nhsuk-frontend/releases/tag/v10.0.0), we can now uplift components to incorporate features and fixes present in GOV components that are missing from NHS components.

backlog.title: Contribution submission for Exit this page component
backlog.body:
Formerly known as 'Hide this page component'
What
What are we proposing
We are looking to implement a component, using the existing button component, that allows vulnerable users of a Government service to quickly and safely hide the page and reduce the risk of Domestic Abuse incidents.
The functionality behind the component would allow a user to quickly hide the current page and open a new, ambiguous webpage, such as BBC Weather or another such website. This would lower the risk of drawing attention to browsing habits from a perpetrator.
Why
Why are we proposing this design pattern?

Domestic abuse is physical, sexual, psychological or financial abuse that takes place within an intimate or family-type relationship and that forms a pattern of forceful and controlling behaviour. This can include forced marriage and so-called ‘honour-based crimes.” Domestic abuse may include a range of abusive behaviours, not all of which are in themselves inherently ‘violent’

The biggest risk to a victim of Domestic Abuse is homicide and serious physical assaults - this is at its greatest risk when a victim is planning to flee or escape from the perpetrator. Often, one of the first things a victim will do is to speak to someone to make a disclosure about abuse. The second thing they will do is research and find help online, often using Government services.
We need to ensure that the risk is minimised for users when using online services. Although victims and survivors can be aware of the risks, it is the Government's responsibility to protect individuals using a service. Therefore, it is crucial that there is a consistency of approach in design and functionality across Government with this component.
What evidence do you have that it's needed by multiple services across government?
From conversations between the Department for Work and Pensions, Ministry of Justice, the Cabinet Office and Scottish Government, it is already clear that other services need to ensure that this design is available.
Services are already responding to the rise in Domestic Abuse during COVID-19 by building their own minimum viable solutions to allow users to quickly hide their webpages.
There are areas of the Government site, such as “Domestic Abuse: How to get help”, that a high risk user would access for support that does not include a way to hide their browsing. This is putting those users of this service at risk.
What evidence do you have that it meets the needs of the users of those services?
Speaking with subject matter experts (SME), it is critical that we offer this feature on the GOV.UK website. It is a feature that is provided by other organisations, such as:

Scottish Government - Domestic Abuse page
Refuge
Women’s Aid
Victim Support

Each website has varied design implementations, but ultimately addresses the same user need of being able to hide browsing habits quickly.
The Ministry of Justice have carried out some initial research with an SME to establish whether the proposed solution meets the user needs.
Have you checked that it doesn't already exist in the GOV.UK Design System?
There are no outstanding issues or tickets in the Design System backlog that refer to this type of component.
Anything else
What else has been done
The MoJ have iterated twice on the design component on our live service - looking at language, design and functionality.
There are several designs that are considered minimum viable products which have been released by the DWP (Child Maintenance Service) - Cabinet Office (Coronavirus Support) and the MoJ (Legal Aid Agency). The expediency of these releases has been due to the fact that by not having something, we are putting our users at risk.
The MoJ have carried out some early rounds of testing with an SME that have looked at design, functionality and various use cases from a range of user scenarios. This has all been documented and shared with DWP and CO to share research and findings.
Designs
We looked to extend the GOV.UK Button component to act as the interactive element that a user would press to exit the website.
The Design System suggests using red for any destructive actions undertaken on a GOV.UK website - as the intention for the 'Hide this page' button was essentially closing the webpage down, it would be deemed destructive. This has been adopted by DWP and the Scottish Government.
We decided to utilise the additional space available in the 1/3 column, which is usually reserved for additional information as it allowed us to present the button within immediate view for the user.
The button would then be "sticky" in position at the top of the page on smaller devices. This prevents any conflict with the GOV.UK 'Contents' link that is positioned at the bottom of the screen. It also removes potential accidental presses by a user who doesn't need to use it.
Feedback from SME on the design

Victims of Domestic Abuse are used to using their reptilian brain and are in fight or flight mode so the red would be a trigger for them to draw their to attention to it - Comment from SME

Content
The language used in the button has recently been changed in order to create a more unified style as we continue to work with DWP, Cabinet Office and the Scottish Government. The use of 'Hide this page' presented more of a sense of immediacy, as well as being more descriptive of what the button actually does when the user interacts with it, so we have moved away from the original 'Quick Exit'.
We also use a keyboard function for the user to be able to interact with the button which is controlled by pressing the 'Esc' key.
Behaviour and Functionality
We have explored several types of behaviour for the button, however in order to provide the greatest amount of safety for users we decided to implement functionality similar to other charities and organisations.
When a user interacts with the button, they are sent to a new browser tab that opens BBC Weather. The original tab that they were on doesn't close, but redirects to Google.
This component does not prescribe which websites are to be linked to. That is best done by the individual services and their user research combined with the knowledge of their user base. Google and BBC Weather are good neutral examples pending further research.
Accessibility
The Legal Aid Agency have had an Accessibility Audit on their service and this highlighted some improvements to the component. These were:

Ensuring the button text accurately describes it's purpose
Ensure the instruction "(Or press 'Esc' key)" is presented to all users when presented as a sticky element
Include visually hidden text at the top of the page to help users of assistive technology be aware of the leave page functionality
Differentiate betwixt mobile displays and PC displays zoomed in, so the information about using the escape key is not hidden for non-mobile narrow displays

These changes have been implemented in the latest version of the component, however we will be looking to further test the accessibility of the component as we continue to iterate on it.
MoJ Data Analytics
The 'Hide this page' button has been running as an MVP on the Check Legal Aid service since 14 April 2020. It has been used with a fair amount of frequency, however at present we are are yet to analyse the data in more detail.
The gaps in data recording were due to changes on the back-end of our service that caused GA to drop out.
Graph data since 14 April 2020

The below graph data also shows variations in spikes and lower use through the pandemic

Examples



MoJ
DWP

Cabinet Office

backlog.title: Suggested new component - Side menu
backlog.body:
What

Give a brief description of the style, component or pattern you want to propose.

Context:
We are in the final stages of building an e-learning service using the GDS design system. We have completed numerous rounds of user testing and already gone through one Alpha and Beta Assessment.
What:
A right-hand sidebar navigation menu which allows users to easily see their progression through a course and be able to navigate back and forth through chapters.
Current version

In-situ

Iterations from user testing

Why

Explain why you think this should be added to the GOV.UK Design System.

In our alpha assessment, we were challenged to explore if there was a user need to see their progression through the course and also to be able to navigate back and forth through the chapters. We tested various variations of a sidebar navigation similar to those found in lots of e-learning platforms. During testing, we found that some users naturally used the sidebar to return to topics earlier in the course and used it to be aware of their progression and estimate their completion time.
Design-wise, we didn’t want to reinvent the wheel so we built on existing sidebar navigation patterns from GOV.UK publishing such as the contents list on the publishing service (https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/contents_list) and the related content sidebar on many start pages. We iterated the design several times to make it simple and accessible. For instance, we made some headers in the sidebar visually hidden so they would give context to screen reader users whilst avoiding confusion for sighted users who had initially struggled with the previous design.


What evidence do you have that it's needed by multiple services across government?


In the our beta assessment, we were praised on our work developing this pattern and asked to play it back into the community:
‘the team has validated the user need to track progress within training modules, has designed a pattern that is working for their beta users, and is planning to continue iterating this pattern - the panel would encourage the team to share this pattern and research findings with the design system community’


What evidence do you have that it meets the needs of the users of those services?


We have tested and validated this component in several rounds of qual research with 5-10 people in each round, and in Private Beta testing with over 1200 people (with quant showing that people successfully use this when required, and qual feedback only positive and no negative on the latest version).
Our user testing so far has validated the need for this component and as mentioned has been praised so far by assessors. But we would love to share it with the community to get a wider perspective and possible use cases.


Have you checked that it doesn't already exist in the GOV.UK Design System?


Yes
Anything else

Include links to any examples, research or code to support your proposal, if available.

backlog.title: Indeterminate progress indicator
Accessibility link
backlog.body:
What
Establish how best to name and link to information about the accessibility options available to users within services.
Is referring to 'Ease of access' (or similar) more likely to be recognised by users who could benefit from the information provided?
Why
As part of meeting the legal requirements for the accessibility, teams producing websites and applications are directed to publish an accessibility statement
Within this, services can give useful information to users about the controls available to the users, such as browser options to control text size and colours, certain assistive tools and so on.
Most services seem to do this through a link named 'Accessibility' page in the footer.
However, in a Slack discussion in the cross-government 'Accessibility' channel, members of the community shared examples where users:

do not recognise the term 'Accessibility'
do not think that it is relevant to them
do not bother to look because, from past experience, they expect it to contain technical information or jargon that isn't relevant

This means some users can miss out on information about ease of access that would make it easier for them to use a service.
Quotes from Slack discussion (as of now)
A user researcher at GDS, said:
[I've seen] "all of the above (when researching how users perceived accessibility statements for the GDS accessibility team). Particularly that users don't always associate the word with their needs, potentially consider it to be about physical access, don't expect it to contain anything useful for them, or are so used to those pages containing generic/jargony info that they don't bother to look."
A user researcher at Ministry of Justice, said:
"I’ve tested accessibility pages in the past. In usability testing users didn’t recognise the link and when prompted to look under it, didn’t think the information was relevant or helpful.
In the past, accessibility pages were largely a box-ticking exercise and had little valuable info for users. They usually consisted of a standard line about WCAG compliance (even if it was not true), HTML validation and browser keyboard shortcuts. The better ones linked to BBC’s 'my web, my way'.
I expect that even those who had looked there, over time learned not to waste their time.
Having observed recent discussions about accessibility statements, I think there’s still a risk of tick-boxing. That’s why any sample statements should include a massive caveat that they shouldn’t be copied and pasted and that you should first do the work, then write about it (in that order).
I think it would be interesting to get quant data on this with analytics."
A Front-End Developer and Accessibility Specialist at GDS, said:
"Bad discoverability was one of the reasons why Microsoft renamed their accessibility settings to “Ease of access”."
(But I don't know the source for this)
In the 'Apply for a Budgeting Loan' service, feedback about the usability of the service is broadly very positive but a small percentage of users consistently give feedback that they need larger text or for text to be read to them. For this service we know some of our user base struggle in terms of literacy and can be low in confidence and ability using technology. This service doesn't currently have an accessibility statement of its own but it seems that users have not read GOV.UK's accessibility statement about the options available to them.

It's a bit strange given that this component is called a phase banner, and there are [questions about whether the phase banner is the right place to ask for feedback](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/issues/4972#issuecomment-1898717662), but this is an easy change to match how the component is being used in some places.

ourIssues.title: Check if we need a mixin for getting specific font maps from the typography scale
ourIssues.body:
## What
Get feedback from the community to assess if there's a need for a mixin to target a specific font map within the typography scale. Instead of collecting and setting all `font-size`'s and `line-height`'s by breakpoint, this would find a specific map within a specified scale point map based on a specified breakpoint within that map.

## Why
This was an initial proposal following https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/3837 however we came to the conclusion that we don't have enough evidence to know if this is necessary. We additionally think that most scenarios that would need this would be solved by [the wider typography scale work](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/issues/2289) and better documentation.

To assess these hypotheses and see if this mixin would still be useful, we will ask the community about if the new scale is meeting their needs.

Designers, Researchers

## Done when

- [x] An initial release of the new scale has been launched
- [ ] The community have been surveyed for if the new scale is useful or if there are other features they need
- [ ] A decision has been made on if this feature is needed and issues have been raised to carry out the work if necessary

ourIssues.title: Safari/VoiceOver: Grouped radios read out incorrect information
ourIssues.body: ## Description of the issue When using Mac's VoiceOver functionality on a group of radio buttons that have conditionally rendered elements the feedback from the voice over is often incorrect. How it is in correct seems to be dependant on the browser being used, as I have observed consistent but different behaviour on different browsers. When using Chrome VO will say that there is more radio buttons than there are, and will also say that the select button is n+1. In a scenario where there are 3 radio buttons and the first is selected VO will read "2 of 4 selected" when it should be "1 of 3 selected". When using VO on the same elements in Safari a similar behaviour is seen but it seems to be able to count the correct number of radio buttons. In the same scenario as before it will readout "2 of 3 selected" when it should be "1 of 3 selected". I am personally unable to check other browsers or voice over software for further testing. TL:DR Mac's Voice Over says there are more radio buttons within a group than there are when using the conditional reveal. ## Steps to reproduce the issue 1. Navigate to [Radio Conditional Reveal example](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/radios/conditional-reveal/index.html) in either Chrome or Safari on a Mac. 2. Turn on Mac's VoiceOver 3. Select radio buttons and observe the VO's output 4. Repeat step three if behavior stated is not observed ## Actual vs expected behaviour Voice over reads "X of Y selected" vs "X+1 of Y+1 selected" (Chrome) or "X+1 of Y selected" (Safari). ## Environment (where applicable) - Operating system: - Browser: Safari 16.3 (18614.4.6.1.6), Chrome 108.0.5359.124 - GOV.UK Frontend Version: 4.0.1

ourIssues.title: Research making the checkbox and radio button labels full width
ourIssues.body:
## What

Perform research with users as to whether making labels on checkboxes and radio buttons span the width of the container, thus increasing their touch surface, makes it easier to use these controls

## Why

Generally speaking, increasing the target area for a control makes the control easier for users to interact with.

We have some existing precendent for this in Frontend already: 

- Labels for other input types (text inputs, selects, textareas, etc.) are already full width.
- The Accordion activates expand/collapse functionality by tapping anywhere in the section header.
- The Skip Link component, when visible, is activatable by clicking anywhere in the component.

The GOV.UK team has had positive feedback when increasing target sizes for elements on the [homepage](https://insidegovuk.blog.gov.uk/2021/12/13/updating-the-gov-uk-homepage/) and [topic pages](https://insidegovuk.blog.gov.uk/2022/08/08/rolling-out-a-new-design-for-browsing-gov-uk-by-topic/) in the last year.

Various external design systems have full width checkbox and radio labels, some of which are based on or inspired by GOV.UK Frontend and have seemingly made the conscious choice to change it:

- ~~[USWDS](https://designsystem.digital.gov/components/checkbox/)~~ Update: Has since updated to no longer be full-width
- [NICE Design System](https://design-system.nice.org.uk/storybook/?path=/story/foundations-checkbox--default)
- [Transport for West Midlands Design System](https://designsystem.tfwm.org.uk/components/radios/)
- [GOLD Design System](https://gold.designsystemau.org/components/control-input/#checkbox-block) (formerly Australian Government Design System)
- [Atlassian Design System](https://atlassian.design/components/checkbox/examples)

Our inline labels date from the GOV.UK Elements days, and I couldn't immediately find any reason why they were implemented in this way at the time. We have stuck to that precedent in situations where a conflict or bug relating to the label sizing has arisen (e.g. #634).

We should validate our current approach and whether it best meets user needs when compared to alternative approaches.

## Assumptions

We've [previously found that users don't tend to click on checkbox or radio button labels](https://designnotes.blog.gov.uk/2016/11/30/weve-updated-the-radios-and-checkboxes-on-gov-uk/), even if they're styled to appear interactible. It could be assumed that the same applies here (if not moreso, as there isn't any visual indicator that interaction is possible). 

As a larger area of the screen will activate a checkbox/radio, there may be an increase in the number of accidental form inputs being made.

A seemingly 'empty' part of the page affecting a nearby input may be unexpected and cause confusion to users unless some other hint is present (e.g. a hover state). 

## Timebox
TBD

## Who is working on this?

Spike lead: TBD

Spike buddy: TBD

## Questions to answer

- [ ] Is there a tangible benefit to checkbox and radio button labels always being full width?
- [ ] Is there a tangible benefit to checkbox and radio button labels being full width in certain situations (e.g. on narrow screens)? 
- [ ] Are full width labels more likely to result in accidental and unwanted inputs?
- [ ] Is having a visually 'empty' area of the screen interactive unexpected or a source of confusion?

## Done when

- [ ] A review or prototype is produced with the modified checkbox/radio styles.
- [ ] User research has been carried out to see how these changes perform with users.
- [ ] Findings have been reviewed and shared with the team.
- [ ] Any follow up issues or actions have been written up.

ourIssues.title: Revisit how we do pre-releases and our expectations from them
ourIssues.body:
<!--

  This is a template for any issues that aren’t bug reports or new feature requests. The headings in this section provide examples of the information you might want to include, but feel free to add/delete sections where appropriate.

-->

## What
One of our actions from the v4.0.0 retro was to clarify our expectations of pre-releases. For v4.0.0, it seemed like the majority of people who interacted with the pre-release looked mainly at the release notes - we're not sure if they tried out the pre-release in their own service. 

We also had feedback from one user saying that they expected the pre-release to be published via `npm`.

## Why
Pre-releases seem like a useful way to get feedback from users and have more confidence before publishing a release, especially a breaking one. But as a team, we're not sure we're getting the most out of them that we could be.

## Who needs to work on this

## Who needs to review this

## Ideas

We could:

- [ ] Investigate publishing pre-releases via `npm` and how that would work for us. What benefits would it provide?
- [ ] Gather feedback from users on why they have/haven't interacted with pre-releases in the past
- [ ] As a team, decide on our expectations from pre-releases, i.e: if we publish a pre-release, we want at least [x] number of users to provide feedback
- [ ] As a team, decide how pre-releases fit into our release process so that we can plan them in earlier

## What

ourIssues.title: Update macros content to specify when you use `text` or `html`
ourIssues.body:
## What
While working on cookie banner macros, I got some feedback that could apply to all other macros content.

A reviewer asked why users should choose either `text` or `html`, as we hadn't specified this in the cookie content. I then learned that if users ever attempt to pass both `text` and `html`,  `html` will win every time.

We then decided to add this sentence to the `html` Description: "If you are not passing HTML, use `text`."

All of our components contain `text` and `html` options. However, it's only in the cookie banner content that we explain when to use one or the other.

If we updated the other components to match, it would entail 28 issues and pull requests. I'm happy to make those changes, but I'd like to find out from the team whether you consider it a good use of time. Or should we investigate whether there are other changes that apply across the board? Then wait until we have a comprehensive list of changes to make?

To clarify for users when they should use either `text` or `html`.

Technical Writer, Developers, Delivery Manager

ourIssues.title: Improve Language Navigation guidance on not losing data in forms when navigating between languages
ourIssues.body:
<!--

  This is a template for any issues that aren’t bug reports or new feature requests. The headings in this section provide examples of the information you might want to include, but feel free to add/delete sections where appropriate.

-->

## What

Improve Language Navigation guidance on not losing data in forms when using the component so that it's clearer what the behaviour should be

> Make sure the user does not lose any data they’ve entered when they navigate to another language. Do not ask the user to re-enter information they’ve already given.

https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/language-navigation/

## Why

We have [had some feedback ](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/discussions/5620#discussioncomment-18582218)that it's not clear in practice if this means keeping the users currently inputted data on a page or just keeping the data from the overall user journey.

Since this is a non-standard thing to do, we think it's likely other developers will wonder what they're aiming for.

There's some potential improvements to this:
- improving the guidance so it's clear that it includes users' un-submitted input 
- guidance around explaining at a high level how to achieve this functionality, similar to what we do for Cookie banner and Form validation (for developers)

## Background

This content was originally added in response to HMRC's welsh language toggle guidance. They detailed why they chose to keep data between page views in some feedback of note:

> welsh users will toggle back and forth between languages to ensure understanding of unfamiliar words and/or to check that both journeys are the same

> welsh speakers familiar with uncommon english specific to the context benefit from both the ability to toggle easily, and from these terms being shown in brackets within the welsh service (to avoid having to do as much switching)

> users prefer english/welsh toggle to whole journey language switching and absence of feature to toggle within service (only being able to select at start) tested negatively

https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/discussions/5351#discussioncomment-17278309

Content designer, developer

Content designer, developer

ourIssues.title: Transitioning Access QR Codes to Apple & Google Wallets
ourIssues.body:
We are working on a project that allows users to fill in a publicly accessible form to apply for access to maritime locations across the UK. Once a user completes an application, they receive a reference number and a QR code is shown at the end of the form. This information is also sent to them via a confirmation email.

To streamline operations on-site, this user flow allows applicants to present the QR code to be scanned by a secondary system, rather than having to manually present or read out a reference number. Currently, a user can have multiple QR codes and must download or screenshot them if they want to keep them handy on their mobile device.

During recent user testing, multiple participants raised that they would highly prefer to store these QR codes directly within their device’s native wallet (Apple Wallet and Google Wallet) for easier access and management when arriving at a maritime location.

Following this feedback, we built a proof of concept (PoC) that successfully allows users to download and add a wallet item for both iOS and Android. We have consulted the Government Digital Service (GDS) on our research and approach, and they have agreed that this is a sensible direction.

While we are aware of and have engaged with the [GOV.UK](http://gov.uk/) Wallet team, we believe that in the short term, having this native wallet functionality integrated directly into our service makes the most sense for our users.

Certificate & Licensing Management
To create and distribute native wallet items, both Apple and Google require signed certificates linked to developer licences. For our PoC, we funded and used our own team’s developer licence. However, for a production-ready solution, we believe the long-term enterprise licences, billing, and cryptographic signing keys should be managed centrally by the Home Office. We need to identify exactly which team or department handles this central governance.

Questions & Guidance Requested
To bridge the gap between our engineering team and corporate security and to move this wallet integration forward we are seeking guidance on the following:

Community Knowledge: Has anyone else in the GDS/wider government ecosystem built a similar native wallet workflow? If so, could you point us in their direction so we can learn more about their architectural approach, licensing setup, and the challenges they faced?
Licensing, Funding, & Governance Contact: Strategically, we need the official enterprise developer licences and associated billing to be handled at the departmental level. Who or which team within the Home Office should we reach out to in order to arrange central provisioning, corporate funding/billing, and security approval for these official accounts?

ourIssues.title: Replace the Figma community file with a new contribution
ourIssues.body:
## What
We have a joint contribution from MoJ and GDS to replace the existing Figma community file. The new Figma contribution will aim to be up to date with the GOV.UK Design System, including the updated brand. We will replace the existing one linked in the [community resources page](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/community/resources-and-tools/) with this new contribution and let users know about the changes. 

## Why
The existing [Figma community file](https://www.figma.com/design/NWuFffKvPQhl3aJ9nKU0p3/GOV.UK-Design-System?node-id=23-233&p=f) is out of date. It was last updated in 2023. The new version will aim to be in sync with the GOV.UK Design System. It also takes advantage of and applies newer features available from Figma and should better meet the needs of users. 


## Background


@nnagewad and @murrlipp have been working together to create an updated version of the Design System on Figma. The Design System did a [first pass](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/issues/4738) at this contribution and provided some feedback earlier in the year. It’s now at a stage that MoJ are planning to adopt this new version. 

This new version isn’t ready for wider sharing yet. It still requires some designers to road test. It should also include the upcoming Design System changes planned for V6.0 to ensure users don’t need to adopt and update in quick succession. 

## Decisions made

- @nnagewad and @murrlipp will ask some designers to road test the new version and make any necessary changes
- MoJ will adopt the new version and make it available as a community file
- MoJ rollout is not dependent on including changes to V6.0 
- The new version will not be published as a community file until it includes the changes from GOV.UK Frontend V6.0
- MoJ will aim to help maintain and update the Figma file, which GDS will be a contributor to. 
- DS will replace the existing Figma community file with the new contribution
- DS will communicate the initial changes to the community
- DS and MoJ won’t actively provide user support for the new Figma contribution. However, we will review this decision after we see how users respond.. 

## Tasks still to do

- Setup ways of working with contributors
- Create a delivery and comms plan so that MoJ and DS can align timing and expectations
- Write comms to tell users about the changes
- Decide what to do about the existing community file and let the previous contributor know what's happening
- Decide what how comms will work with future updates to the Figma file
- Decide if Design System should provide more guidance on how to use Figma and what that would be (Example from [MoJ Design System](https://design-patterns.service.justice.gov.uk/prototyping/prototyping-methods/))

ourIssues.title: Iterate image guidance for ‘text in charts, diagrams and complex images
ourIssues.body:
## Related documentation
Hannah Thomas from ONS [gave feedback on the guidance](https://ukgovernmentdigital.slack.com/archives/C6DMEH5R6/p1681385024589509) on descriptive text for charts on the cross-gov Slack channel.

## Suggestion

Edited for clarity:
> Charts are a bit of an outlier [from typical ways to add descriptive text to images] because they always should come with a title. It is this title that lets a screen reader user know that there is an image.

> So our research has shown it is **better to go straight from the chart title to the text description of the chart**. Which is also why we say the chart title should start with “Figure x” and the text description should start with “Description of figure x: a line chart showing .....”

> So you should flag it is a description of the figure and you should state the type of chart

> We don’t necessarily say you have to start the text description with “Description of figure x:” - you can just start with “This line chart shows....” but feedback from stats teams was that they found it a bit **hard to separate the text description from the statistical commentary** so this was a way around it

> **Putting extra alt text in the alt attribute was found to just add unnecessary auditory clutter** when you follow this approach, and this approach was found to be better for all users - not just screen reader users - because there are an array of people who need/want/like a text description for a chart.

> [For example] colourblind users, users with dyscalculia or users who just don’t feel comfortable with charts, users with low vision who can zoom in on text but find it hard to zoom in on charts, users who need a bit of reassurance that what they have taken away from the chart is actually what the chart is showing

## Done when (possibility to start)
- [ ] Assess feedback - team, particularly accessibility expert
- [ ] Decide on the iteration we can do to existing guidance
- [ ] Respond to feedback and discuss contribution opportunities

communityIssues.title: Including our JavaScript in an application is confusing
communityIssues.body:
Our [JavaScript usage documentation](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk_publishing_components/blob/main/docs/install-and-use.md#5-include-and-configure-javascript) offers two options for using the components gem JS.

For individual components include:

- `dependencies.js`
- `lib.js`
- (plus individual component JS as required)

For all components:

- `dependencies.js`
- `all_components.js`

However, [all_components.js](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk_publishing_components/blob/main/app/assets/javascripts/govuk_publishing_components/all_components.js) includes `lib.js` already, which is a bit confusing and could be streamlined, perhaps by moving the `lib.js` import into `dependencies`, or just including the contents of `lib.js` in dependencies.

For reference all of our public facing applications are using the individual model:

App | dependencies.js | lib.js
---- | ------ | -----
`frontend` | Y | Y
[finder-frontend](https://github.com/alphagov/finder-frontend/blob/main/app/assets/javascripts/application.js#L12-L13) imports | Y | Y
[collections](https://github.com/alphagov/collections/blob/main/app/assets/javascripts/application.js#L1-L2) | Y | Y
[smart answers](https://github.com/alphagov/smart-answers/blob/main/app/assets/javascripts/application.js#L1-L2) | Y | Y
[email-alert-frontend](https://github.com/alphagov/email-alert-frontend/blob/main/app/assets/javascripts/application.js#L1-L2) | Y | Y
[feedback](https://github.com/alphagov/feedback/blob/main/app/assets/javascripts/application.js#L1-L2) | Y | Y

`frontend` is a little confusing because `application.js` imports `dependencies` and its own dependencies file, which then imports `lib`.

communityIssues.title: Several Instances of HTML in locale files
communityIssues.body: ## What Remove all instances of HTML in locale files. ## Why When I was working on a card to add data-tracking attributes to the copyright and license links in the footer, I noticed that the actual elements I was to add data to were actually in the locale files themselves. I was able to add a listener to the container of the link but to me it seems quite unmaintainable to have essentially 60 copies of the same elements with different text. If a class needed to be changed or an attribute then something could easily be missed. In fact there is already an issue caused by this - the `a` element in copyright_html links to a 404 in every other language apart from in `en.yml`. The instances of html in locale files are as follows: ``` opendocument_html: This file is in an OpenDocument format request_format_details_html: If you use assistive technology (such as a screen reader) and need a version of this document in a more accessible format, please email %{alternative_format_contact_email}. Please tell us what format you need. It will help us if you say what assistive technology you use. phase_banner_html: This is a new service – your feedback will help us to improve it. copyright_html: © Crown copyright licence_html: All content is available under the Open Government Licence v3.0, except where otherwise stated ``` It seems to me that most of these have the same format of `prefix` `link` `suffix`, so perhaps an alternative structure for this pattern could be ``` licence_link prefix: All content is available under the link_text: Open Government Licence v3.0 suffix: except where otherwise stated ``` and then a helper method could be used to assemble the link.

What

We are looking to implement a component that is a hybrid version of: Selects, Checkboxes and Search boxes. The multi-select component provides the following functionality:

A select like component that can store a large list of selectable items in a collapsable control
The ability to search for items and order the most relevant items to the top of the list

Expanded state of the multi-select component with a dynamic search bar at the top of the component (default focus), select/deselect all items underneath; followed by a list of remaining items with 2 items having been selected

Why

The need for a multi-select component is required for making large lists of items (30+ items) searchable and selectable. By integrating a multi-select component within the GOV.UK Design System, we are supporting the functionality required by users to traverse and select large lists of items efficiently.

Enhances the user interface by minimising the display space through the implementation of collapsable filters

ourIssues.title: Consider adding documentation on `select[multiple]`
ourIssues.body:
The `<select>` HTML element has an alternative mode that allows for selecting multiple values, also known as a multi-select listbox. This is enabled using the `multiple` flag. We don't explicitly support using `multiple` with our Nunjucks macro, however service teams can still enable it through the attributes parameter. 

We do not support `multiple` in our CSS and discourage using it for a few reasons:
- Using multi-select is complicated, requiring the user to hold down one or more keyboard keys (<kbd>⌘ Cmd</kbd>/<kbd>⌃ Ctrl</kbd> or <kbd>⇧ Shift</kbd>) whilst clicking on options. This is difficult to convey and usually not well understood by users.
- Multi-select cannot be easily used with keyboard navigation alone, practically requiring a pointer device to use.
- Multi-select is not (to my knowledge) well supported by assistive technologies.

We may also want to include information on the `size` attribute, which we also do not support in Frontend's code, although it doesn't have the same pitfalls as `multiple`. 

## Related documentation
[Select](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/select/)

## Suggestion
A user has suggested adding documentation about `select[multiple]`; specifically, adding information on why we discourage using it and don't support it: https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/3317 

In most situations, we would probably recommend using [a list of checkboxes](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/checkboxes/) instead.

## Evidence (where applicable)

- [`<select>` your poison](https://www.24a11y.com/2019/select-your-poison/) on [24 Accessibility](https://www.24a11y.com/)

ourIssues.body:
<!--

  This is a template for any issues that aren’t bug reports or new feature requests. The headings in this section provide examples of the information you might want to include, but feel free to add/delete sections where appropriate.

-->

## What

Replace `sass-color-helpers` with an alternative way to [check contrast of organisation colours](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/dea97c0d6af0b0391e374d3467916c91096200e8/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/settings/colours.unit.test.js#L226).

> 2. using the Sass compilation to extract values from the organisation colours (CSS declarations are very close to JSON properties) and then run computations in JavaScript

## Why

`sass-color-helpers` relies on a few Sass features that are deprecated (global builtins, colour functions, slash divisions) and the library hasn't seen any activity in the last few years.

## Who needs to work on this

Developers

Developers

ourIssues.title: Implement responsive typography using CSS custom properties
ourIssues.body:
<!--

  This is a template for any issues that aren’t bug reports or new feature requests. The headings in this section provide examples of the information you might want to include, but feel free to add/delete sections where appropriate.

-->

## What

In a similar way that we're moving to custom properties to [implement print text](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/6363) and [implement responsive spacing](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/6480), use custom properties to implement responsive typography. This includes:
- checking the two following steps are enough to ensure the current features of responsive typography would be fully ported to custom properties
- outputing `--govuk-responsive-typography-<SIZE>-font-size` and `--govuk-responsive-typography-<SIZE>-line-height` custom properties in core/govuk-frontend-properties, with their corresponding @media query adjusting their value. Note that:
   - we may need to do more than bluntly looping and outputing the custom properties directly followed by an @media statement to avoid Sass' warning about Mixed declarations)
   - the code outputing the media queries doesn't simply output the raw `line-height` but does [computations to turn it into a relative line height](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/helpers/_typography.scss#L197-L206)
- updating the `govuk-font-size` mixin to output declarations for `font-size` (and `line-height` if `$line-height` is true), each using a `var()` call to reference the appropriate custom properties for the requested size. The mixin should still error if the requested size is unavailable or throw deprecation warnings if the size is deprecated, as well as allow the size to be set as `!important`.


## Why

Responsive typography outputs a media query for each use of `govuk-font-size`. Moving to custom properties means we'll use a single media query in a single place, which should result in less code in the compiled CSS.

## Who needs to work on this

Developers, Tech writers

## Who needs to review this

Developers, Tech writers

## Done when

- [ ] Plan outlined above has been double checked for completeness and
- [ ] Custom properties for each size of the typography scale are output on `:root`, with their associated media query and without triggering mixed-decls warnings from Sass
- [ ] The `govuk-font-size` mixin has been updated to output `var()` values.

ourIssues.title: Implement responsive spacing using custom properties
ourIssues.body:
<!--

  This is a template for any issues that aren’t bug reports or new feature requests. The headings in this section provide examples of the information you might want to include, but feel free to add/delete sections where appropriate.

-->

## What

In a similar way that we're moving to [custom properties to implement print text](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/6363), use custom properties to implement responsive spacing. This includes:
- outputing `--govuk-responsive-spacing-<LEVEL>` custom properties in `core/govuk-frontend-properties`, with their corresponding `@media` query adjusting their value (note that we may need to do more than bluntly looping and outputing the custom properties directly followed by an `@media` statement to avoid [Sass' warning about Mixed declarations](https://sass-lang.com/documentation/breaking-changes/mixed-decls/))
- adding a `govuk-responsive-spacing` function to output the `var()` statement, throwing an error if the scale level is not set
- deprecating the `govuk-responsive-margin` and `govuk-responsive-padding` mixins
- replacing the use of `govuk-responsive-margin` and `govuk-responsive-padding` mixins with `margin-...` and `padding-...` properties and calls to `govuk-responsive-spacing` and `calc()`.

## Why

Responsive spacing outputs a media query for each use of `govuk-responsive-margin` and `govuk-responsive-padding`. Moving to custom properties means we'll use a single media query, which should result in less code.

## Who needs to work on this

Developers, Tech writer

## Who needs to review this

Developers, Tech writer

## Done when

- [ ] Custom properties for each responsive spacing level are output on `:root`, with their associated media query and without triggering `mixed-decls` warnings from Sass
- [ ] `govuk-responsive-margin` and `govuk-responsive-padding` mixins have been deprecated
- [ ] We have a `govuk-responsive-spacing` option generating a `var()` statement to access the appropriate scale of the responsive spacing (and throwing an error if the requested scale does not exist)
- [ ] Internal calls to `govuk-responsive-margin` and `govuk-responsive-padding` have been replaced by native `margin-...` and `padding-...` CSS properties calling the `govuk-responsive-spacing` function.
- [ ] CHANGELOG explains users how to migrate to the new `govuk-responsive-spacing` option

[Govspeak](https://govspeak-preview.publishing.service.gov.uk/guide) is a set of additions to markdown sytax that allows for adding certain components from the GOVUK design system into markdown content.

This would likely mean we'd have to change the markdown processor for the whole site from `markdown-it` to `marked`, which has an existing govspeak plugin: https://github.com/x-govuk/marked-govspeak
