This would give us a bit more flexibility of markup / formatting options available within the guidance, and make adding them easier for content editors.

- Content Designer
- Developer

backlog.title: Custom error and fail pages
backlog.body:
Sometimes a service will need to tell the user about an error and will need more space to describe the problem than the typical error summary and error message allows for.
This is typically where the error isn't as simple as validation but because the data provided conflicts with other data already in the system.
Reasons you might want this:

You want to link to guidance or to another page in the service
Fixing the error might take more than editing the data in the field - eg the entire section is wrong
There's a number of choices for how to proceed

In these cases I've typically made what I've called 'bespoke fail pages' - an error page to cover the specific situation.
Sharing here in case it helps anyone else and in the hopes something gets added to the design system at some point.

backlog.title: Error messages: add guidance on how to write good ones
backlog.body:
What
Every service needs to validate what people type in and select. This update will explain how to write error messages for everyone.
View the draft guidance
View the code in GitHub
Why
#6028 and #6026 tell you how to display an error message summary and field-level error messages. There needs to be guidance that:

shows how these components work together
documents error message content design principles
gives examples of what content should be used in error messages

This is needed across every government service to improve consistency within and between services. It is important to have error messages that work for everyone and give enough information to help people easily recover.
Anything else
I drafted some principles and presented them at ConCon 6 in September 2016. I then had a lot of comments from people in different departments and made changes to the draft. This includes principles, and suggested content for the error summary box and error messages.

ourIssues.title: Components assume the `govuk-visually-hidden` utility class will exist
ourIssues.body:
## Description of the issue

We provide an entry points for each individual component, the idea being that users should get all of the CSS they need to use that component, and ideally nothing more.

For example, including the character count component also includes the CSS for the:

- error message
- hint
- label
- textarea

However, it does _not_ include the `govuk-visually-hidden` utility class, which is used within the Nunjucks template.

From a quick check, it looks like this affects:

- Accordion (in the JavaScript)
- Character count (in the JavaScript)
- Error message (in the Nunjucks template)
- Exit this page (in the Nunjucks template and JavaScript)
- File upload (in the JavaScript)
- Footer (in the Nunjucks template)
- Pagination (in the Nunjucks template)
- Password input (in the JavaScript)
- Summary list (in the Nunjucks template)
- Warning text (in the Nunjucks template)

## Steps to reproduce the issue

Use the component-specific entrypoint to include just the CSS for any of the components listed above, then view the component

## Actual vs expected behaviour

Visually hidden text should be hidden, but it isn't because the `govuk-visually-hidden` utility class is not included in the CSS

ourIssues.title: NVDA does not read hints or error messages when tabbing to checkboxes
ourIssues.body:
## Description of the issue

This is an NVDA bug, but I'm filing an issue here because it affects the accessibility of GOV.UK Frontend so I thought you may want a record of it.

When a checkbox inside a fieldset gets focus, any hint or error message associated with the fieldset should be read out after the legend and before the checkbox label. They're associated with the fieldset via `aria-describedby`. However, NVDA only reads the legend and checkbox label, not the hint or error. This means that NVDA users may be unaware that the grouping has a hint or an error.

For example, the speech output for [this example](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/checkboxes/error/index.html) with a hint and an error is:

> What is your nationality?  grouping  clickable  British  check box  not checked    including English, Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish

Note that this only affects checkboxes. Radios use the same structure and are unaffected.

[An NVDA issue for this bug](https://github.com/nvaccess/nvda/issues/12718) has been open since 2021 but unfortunately it doesn't look like there's been much progress towards a fix. It looks like [this commenter](https://github.com/nvaccess/nvda/issues/12718#issuecomment-1533364655) has also come across this issue while using GOV.UK Frontend though.

## Steps to reproduce the issue

See CodePen at https://codepen.io/matteason/pen/PoyBwYM or one of the GOV.UK Design System examples (eg [checkboxes](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/checkboxes/with-none-option-in-error/index.html))

Open NVDA, navigate to the example page and tab through the form fields

## Actual vs expected behaviour

Hints should be read for all component types in the example, but they're only read for text inputs and radios

## Environment (where applicable)

- Operating system: Windows 10
- Browser: Firefox 112.0, Chrome 112.0.5615.138
- GOV.UK Frontend Version: 4.6.0

ourIssues.title: Error message: Remove hardcoded content order
ourIssues.body: ## What Error messages currently contain a fixed content order, which is hardcoded into the component's Nunjucks template. This is composed of a block of visually-hidden text (`visuallyHiddenText`, defaults to 'Error') followed by a colon (:), a hardcoded space, then the configured error message (`html` or `text`). This prefixes the message with 'error' for screen readers, so that the context of the message announced up-front and is easier to understand. For example, the component may currently output this text: ```html Error: Enter an event name ``` ## Why Having a hardcoded content order can make it more difficult to appropriately localise the string. In particular, the currently hardcoded colon and space characters are incompatible with certain languages. Some logographic written languages—such as Chinese and Japanese—use a fixed-width colon character that fits better alongside logograms, and don't include a space after it. ```html 错误：输入事件名称 エラー：イベント名を入力してください ``` Translators may also find that the 'Error' label being visible is more useful to their target users—as red does not indicate incorrectness or danger in all cultures (it symbolises happiness and prosperity in Chinese culture, for example). Although it is currently possible for services to pass HTML into the error message and remove the initial 'Error:' section by setting `visuallyHiddenText` to `false`, we may want to investigate methods of either making `visuallyHiddenText` work with other languages, incorporating the colon and space into the editable area, or removing the use of a dedicated parameter and hardcoded text in favour of only using the `html` parameter. ## Who needs to work on this Developers ## Who needs to review this Developers ## Done when - [ ] Investigate methods of making the error message support non-English languages. - [ ] Make changes to the Nunjucks template and related tests, if we decide to make modifications. - [ ] Document any changes to Nunjucks parameters.

ourIssues.title: Textarea hints and error messages are not read out if a value is already present (JAWS/Chrome)
ourIssues.body:
## Description of the issue
When using JAWS, moving focus to a textarea that already has a populated value does not read out any elements associated with the textarea by `aria-describedby`.

## Steps to reproduce the issue
1. Create an instance of the textarea or character count component that: (a) has a default value of any length; (b) has an associated hint, error message, or both; and (c) does not have a threshold, if it's a character count. 
2. With JAWS running, navigate to the page in Chrome.
3. Apply focus to the textarea using either keyboard or mouse.
4. Listen to what JAWS reads out.

An existing example can be found in [the character count's error state example](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/character-count/error/index.html) in the design system. I've also made [a bare minimum example as a fiddle](https://jsfiddle.net/querkmachine/3z6drbto/).

## Actual vs expected behaviour
Actual behaviour: JAWS will read out the input label and that it is a textarea that currently contains text.

Expected behaviour: JAWS will read out the label, that it is a textarea that currently contains text, plus any hints and error messages associated with the input via `aria-describedby`.

The issue does not appear to occur with `<input>` elements (be they empty or populated), or with empty `<textarea>`s.

## Environment 
- Operating system: Windows 10
- Browser: Google Chrome
- Browser version: 99
- GOV.UK Frontend Version: 4.0.1

Tested in both JAWS 2021.2103.174 and JAWS 2022.2202.38. 

I could not reproduce this in Firefox or IE when using JAWS, and not in any browser when using NVDA 2021.2.

ourIssues.title: Consider updating hints and error messages to use paragraphs
ourIssues.body:
## What Consider updating hints and error messages to use paragraphs rather than spans and divs. https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/d5a3fa8c5e61dbc7ca0f7a8429cc8e6716ee7c32/src/govuk/components/error-message/template.njk#L3-L6 https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/d5a3fa8c5e61dbc7ca0f7a8429cc8e6716ee7c32/src/govuk/components/hint/template.njk#L1-L4 ## Why As raised by a user on x-gov Slack: > the error message is in a tag. Is there a reason why a `` is used, rather than a `
` or `

`, for example? The reason I ask is because I’ve been doing some testing with JAWS and I’ve found that there’s no pause between reading the hint text and the error message. So JAWS reads “For example 12 11 2007 error colon the date your passport was issued must be in the past”. Using a `

` didn’t make a difference, but using a `

` resulted in a pause between the hint text and the error message, so potentially making it a little clearer. It looks like hints used to be paragraphs, but [were changed to spans when the hints were moved inside the label](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk_elements/commit/5f631c113840bfd4cc3ed81de8fb311638457a92#diff-1968332cde003a71f281b5d33445bcb3a43d2ac1cee565f6bc0e0a0144cfb846) – presumably as [only phrasing content is permitted within a `label`](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/forms.html#the-label-element). Error messages, when they were added later, were also spans inside the label. We recently [updated hints to use divs rather than spans](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/commit/d92d3c8a990730213430b686d239fc7b278530a9) so that they can be used with flow content (for example multiple paragraph tags, or a list) Since [we moved hints and error messages out of the labels](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/pull/681), we should consider whether they should now by marked up as paragraphs instead. ## Who needs to know about this Developers, designers ## Done when - [x] Tested alternate form controls with error messages and hints marked up as paragraphs in assistive technologies - [x] Identified other potential issues cause by changing hints and error messages to paragraphs - [ ] Decision made and code change made - [ ] Check if the changelog for https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/1856 needs updating as a result of this work

ourIssues.title: Legend (and hint and error message) for the group of radios / checkboxes announced when focusing a conditionally revealed field whilst using VoiceOver
ourIssues.body:
Conditionally revealed controls are inside the `<fieldset>` that wraps the radios / checkboxes.

This could potentially cause confusion, as in VoiceOver the legend (and any other text associated with the fieldset using `aria-describedby`, such as a hint or error message) is read out when focusing the conditionally revealed content.

![Screenshot 2020-10-16 at 13 03 20](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/121939/96256125-fe980080-0faf-11eb-9da5-289e0c39a63e.png)

For example, when focusing the conditionally revealed 'email address' field in the example from the Design System (above), Voiceover with Safari (14) on macOS (10.15.7) announces:

> "Email address, edit text, How would you like to be contacted? Select all options that are relevant to you. You are currently on a text field. To enter text in this field, type."

The hint text "Select all options that are relevant to you" applies to the set of checkboxes, and does not make sense in the context of the email address field.

ourIssues.title: Investigate issue with error message offset for users without convergent vision
ourIssues.body: ## Background Issue first discussed [on the backlog](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/issues/6026#issuecomment-591360096). ## Summary of issue The main finding was that a participant in research who doesn’t have convergent vision found inputting the second password difficult since the field was offset to the right (with the error styling applied). This is what they saw when the page reloaded after they input the wrong password: ### Markup used in prototype I’ve had a look at the markup used for the fields in the prototype which all looks correct. I can share the link/credentials for the prototype. ## My transcript of research audio _(Shared with consent of research participant)_ [Researcher asks participant to enter (made up) passwords in a form] **Participant:** Oh so it wasn’t the same password. For some reason this is difficult for me. Another reason to use password managers is that it’s quite hard for me to do that [enter password manually]. I’m good I’m there. For some reason I mistyped the password and what it does is it offsets just because of the way that the UI works, it offsets the password boxes and puts it in a different colour which for me doesn’t really help. Most of what we have on any of these when you’re using green is [inaudible] for me anyway. This has actually highlighted it in a form of orange which is fine but it offsets it from the password boxes. So what that means to me is that I’ve got to use convergent vision which I don’t have. So it took me three attempts to get that right, just because I can’t align my vision with two things one of which is offset, it’s just very hard for me. **Researcher:** That’s interesting thank you. If you click back we’ll be able to see that issue. **Participant:** Yeah I was wondering about that. So that’s _in red with green_* and I know the green’s generally used but that as a visual cue doesn’t help me in fact confuses. So we tend to use greyscale if we can’t use colour but we would use a colour blind palette for it and we’ve changed all of our UI to do that now since the accessibility directive. But can you see how it’s slightly offset? So I navigate between this password and this password, it’s actually to the right which means that my vision can’t make that adjustment easily so it took me three attempts because the password box is actually offset to the right. — _*Spoke to the researcher: they think that this comment referred to the fact that the red for used for error messages is not a “pure” red so could contain hints of colours . However it’s worth noting that the prototype used the legacy red (#b10e1e). As we don’t rely on colour to communicate things and the colour the participant saw isn’t the current one not going to take any further action on this for now. Although their comment about using grayscale colours is interesting!_ ## Done when - [x] We've discussed as a team how to approach the issue - [x] We've created a follow up issue, if appropriate

ourIssues.title: Make it easier to add a hint or an error message to a fieldset
ourIssues.body:
## What

If you want to use the fieldset component to group related fields, for example asking for a street address, you need to take care of including the hint / error message components separately and do extra work to associate them with the fieldset.

We do not provide any examples or guidance on how to do this, and it would be easy to get wrong (for example, by not creating the association with the fieldset)

It therefore seems like it would be useful if the fieldset component accepted `hint` and `errorMessage` objects and took care of this association itself.

## Why

This was requested by @edwardhorsford in https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/issues/778#issuecomment-459047140.

## Additional information

The radios, checkbox and date input components all use hints and error messages which are then associated with the fieldset using `aria-describedby`. However, this logic is handled (and therefore duplicated) within the individual components.

Moving this logic to the fieldset component _might_ allow us to simplify the repeated logic in the radios, checkboxes and date input components. However, it's not clear what should happen to the hint / error message [if you do not include a fieldset](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/62d3de38036b858b1dd85c5bd8c027830fab5a3d/src/components/date-input/template.njk#L79-L96).

ourIssues.title: HTML lint and link check skip the 404 and generic error pages
ourIssues.body:
`npm run lint:html` validates `build/**/index.html`, so `build/404.html` and `build/errors/generic.html` are never validated. `npm run check-links` crawls from `build/sitemap.xml`; `404.njk` sets `ignoreInSitemap` and no page links to it, so links on the 404 page are never checked either. Netlify serves the 404 page to everyone who reaches a missing URL. Reproduction: add `

a

b x

` under the h1 in `src/404.njk`, then `npm run build`. `npm run lint:html` returns 0 and `npm run check-links` returns 0. `npx html-validate build/404.html` directly returns 1 (duplicate ID). The same lines in `src/contact.njk` make both commands return 1. Tested at bf1d72c5. Suggested fix: widen the lint glob to `build/**/*.html` (or add the two error pages explicitly), and add `build/404.html` and `build/errors/generic.html` as extra entry points for hyperlink. Both pages pass today, so the change would not turn CI red.

ourIssues.title: Replace what's new Mailchimp signup form with a custom signup form using server-side validation
ourIssues.body:
## What

The 'what's new' email signup form should use GOV.UK Design System components, including using server-side validation to show form errors to the user.

As currently the Design System website is a set of static pages, this will require an additional server app to be able to:

1. serve the HTML form (possibly?)
2. receive the form submission
3. validate the form submission
4. generate a page with error messages and serve it to the user OR
5.  submit the request to the Mailchimp API

There are a number of ways to achieve this; the first part of this epic will be to choose one that fits our needs.

## Why

Currently the 'what's new' mailing list signup form is a regular hosted Mailchimp form. This has a number of downsides:

- the form HTML has accessibility issues
- the form error handling has accessibility issues
- the form design is not consistent with GOV.UK Design System
- the solution is tied to Mailchimp

We looked at using an embedded Mailchimp form, but this would require using JavaScript to do input validation and error handling.

We used the Mailchimp signup form as a 'minimum viable product' for the initial launch of the 'what's new' feature because: a) we had tested it in user research and found that users were able to complete the journey b) we hadn't yet got usage analytics to validate that an email list fulfils the user need.

However, for a permanent solution, server side validation is the best and only way to get an accessible and consistent experience for all users.

## Who needs to know about this

Product manager, Developer, User researcher (possibly)

## Done when

- [ ] we've scoped out the different options for server-side validation, and chosen one
- [ ] the 'what's new' signup form uses Design System components (design has already been done, see commit [5bca1b64a](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/blob/5bca1b64acb67a372f9cec84e37ba42277fd92dc/src/email-updates.njk))
- [ ] we have a server-side validation solution for the form input
- [ ] the form and validation are connected so that form errors are shown to the user using Design System components

communityIssues.title: Use Ruby object deconstruction to remove reassignment of variables
communityIssues.body:
## What

Rename attributes such as `data_attributes` and `aria_attributes` to `data` and `aria`. Then use the Ruby object deconstruction to reference these. 

### More details 

#### 'Parent' component

Instead of 

```
data_attributes ||= {}

<%= tag(h1) data: data_attributes %>
```
use this

```
data ||= {}

<%= tag(h1) data: %>
```

#### Child component

Instead of

```
error_message ||= nil

<%= render "govuk_publishing_components/components/error_message", text: error_message %>
```

use this

```
error ||= {}

<%= render "govuk_publishing_components/components/error_message",  **error_message %>
```

#### Child element

Instead of 

```
atom_element_classes = "some-class"

<%= tag(atom_element) class: atom_element_classes %>
```

use this

```
atom_element_attributes = {}
atom_element_attributes[:class] = "some-class"

<%= tag(atom_element, **atom_element_attributes) %>
```



## Why

We now consistently use the `tag_helper` throughout govuk_publishing_components instead of Ruby templating syntax. It's confusing that the `tag_helper` parameters and the partial template parameters are named differently, even though they are usually used in the same way. If we use the same parameter names then we can take advantage of the syntax which would make the code more readable and calling the partials more intuitive.

communityIssues.title: Inconsistent components API
communityIssues.body:
The component API is inconsistent across components and in comparison with `govuk-frontend`.

In the table below there is a brief comparison in how `govuk-frontend` components are aligned in API with `govuk_publishing_components`

|Component               |API |
|---                      |---  |
Accordion                 | aligned
Back link                 | aligned
Breadcrumbs               | misaligned
Button                    | slightly misaligned (start)
Character count           | slightly misaligned (nesting)
Checkboxes                | slightly misaligned (fieldset)
Date input                | slightly misaligned (fieldset)
Details                   | misaligned
Error message             | aligned
Error summary             | misaligned
Fieldset                  | misaligned
File upload               | aligned
Footer                    | aligned
Header                    | slightly misaligned (navigation_items)
Inset text                | aligned
Panel                     | misaligned
Phase banner              | misaligned
Radios                    | slightly misaligned (fieldset)
Select                    | slightly misaligned (options)
Skip link                 | aligned
Summary list              | slightly misaligned (items)
Table                     | aligned
Tabs                      | misaligned
Text input                | aligned
Textarea                  | aligned
Warning text              | slightly misaligned (iconFallbackText)

We can see a few common differences between to two API models:
- for arrays, `govuk-frontend` uses the generic `items` (in most cases) whereas `govuk_publishing_components` uses the name of the component (e.g. `attachments` for the attachment list component or `breadcrumbs` for the breadcrumbs component)
- for web addresses/paths `govuk-frontend` uses `href` whereas in `govuk_publishing_components` we often find `url` (e.g. breadcrumbs component)

It's worth mentioning that not even `govuk-frontend`'s API is consistent (e.g. `errorList` instead of `items` in the Error summary component, or differences in nesting)

A few advantages of making the API consistent:
- increases developers' confidence when calling components with arguments (without constantly checking examples in the guide)
- prototyping and production will use the same config object (can be easily copied over in both directions)
- applications can prepare the data to be fed into components consistently using helpers
- it would be easier to swap one component with another

I'm creating this to raise awareness of the differences, hopefully generate discussions around how good looks like and aim for consistency and convergency. API alignment requires at least a breaking change and some replacements across applications – which is not an easy process. For this reason, having a clear vision about how we want it to look like would save us from doing this more than once.

backlog.title: Inbox pattern for mail, tasks or notifications
backlog.body:
What
Inbox design patterns for mail or notifications are common in commercial applications. The most pervasive patterns are a three-panel fluid layout for large & medium-sized screens and tabbed navigation with card components representing discrete messages for mobile.
We're testing the possibility of a cross-government inbox pattern to enable more rapid communication between departments and citizens.
Several components within the design system could be used to build an inbox-type experience. Modern inbox patterns are quite complex, setting a high standard for user interaction. Similar to driving a car—which is complex but, once mastered, offers significant benefits—these inbox patterns may not be easy or intuitive at first (or even accessible). However, their continuous development and widespread use have made them the standard way to manage complex tasks.
Why
Design System
Even though this will not be a reusable component it could be a keystone design pattern that connects to, possibly impacting, other patterns within the design system. This needs consideration from the design system community and input from other research and experiences.
Depending on the level of service integration into the inbox, many of the existing Design system components will be used including form design components and general service interactions.
Some related patterns would be

https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/summary-list/
https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/complete-multiple-tasks/
https://design-system.service.gov.uk/styles/layout/

And has the potential to impact some existing patterns changing them altogether

https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/contact-a-department-or-service-team/
https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/check-a-service-is-suitable/
https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/create-accounts/

There may also be existing inbox patterns that have been designed and tested internally for civil servants and gov departments that we can learn from when designing for a wider group of users.
Needs
The primary need is for citizens to receive communications from government departments that cover legal and functional requirements to implement policy. The government needs an official way to send these communications to individuals and organisations. Currently, this is done through physical letters sent to a mailbox at the person's residence, which is verified to be connected to their identity.
Although we have not yet researched the specific needs, we have a few initial assumptions that we will test during our work:

Persistent and Recoverable Communication: Citizens need a reliable way to receive government communications that won't be lost, destroyed, or missed (e.g., when moving). Physical letters can fail to meet this need.
Control Over Communication Preferences: Citizens should be able to manage their communication preferences with the entire government, rather than dealing with each department individually. This is especially important for those who need assistance or special accommodations.
Timely Action on Important Matters: Citizens need to act quickly on important issues. Physical mail can take up to a week for a round trip, delaying responses and potentially causing anxiety or stress for citizens. For the government, this leads to longer service delivery and issue resolution times.
Confirmation of Receipt: Government departments need to confirm that citizens have received communications, as this could affect their responses.

Anything else
Denmark has had a citizen mailbox since 2007 using a standard inbox design pattern and currently, the paradigm is being tested in Scotland.

https://en.digst.dk/systems/digital-post-app/
https://www.civtech.scot/demo-day-9-netcompany

This would connect and need to work with other Gov platforms

Gov.UK One login
Gov.UK Notify (has previously done some research on communicating with citizens)
Gov.UK Pay

Additional related components and issues
Generalised patterns such as cards and lists will be relevant in this work

https://design.education.gov.uk/design-system/dfe-frontend/components/card
https://designsystem.parliament.uk/components/cards/card/
#5852
UKHomeOffice/design-system#377

Mobile inbox patterns

https://www.simform.com/mobile-patterns/iphone/mailbox

Design History
A design history based on this work
https://github.com/alphagov/gov-mailbox-design-history
Figma file exploring the pattern
Figma file examining the inbox pattern
https://www.figma.com/design/zOdvURuLtLklNjP2f7zun0/GDS-Inbox-design-pattern-proposal?node-id=0-1&t=YTftxtJJQa2NG28c-1
GDS Inbox pattern.pdf

ourIssues.title: Components assume the `govuk-visually-hidden` utility class will exist
ourIssues.body:
## Description of the issue

We provide an entry points for each individual component, the idea being that users should get all of the CSS they need to use that component, and ideally nothing more.

For example, including the character count component also includes the CSS for the:

- error message

- label
- textarea

However, it does _not_ include the `govuk-visually-hidden` utility class, which is used within the Nunjucks template.

From a quick check, it looks like this affects:

- Accordion (in the JavaScript)
- Character count (in the JavaScript)
- Error message (in the Nunjucks template)
- Exit this page (in the Nunjucks template and JavaScript)
- File upload (in the JavaScript)
- Footer (in the Nunjucks template)
- Pagination (in the Nunjucks template)
- Password input (in the JavaScript)
- Summary list (in the Nunjucks template)
- Warning text (in the Nunjucks template)

## Steps to reproduce the issue

Use the component-specific entrypoint to include just the CSS for any of the components listed above, then view the component

Visually hidden text should be hidden, but it isn't because the `govuk-visually-hidden` utility class is not included in the CSS

ourIssues.title: Consider increasing contrast between `border` functional colour and page background
ourIssues.body:
<!--
    Please fill in as much of the template below as you’re able to. If you're unsure whether the issue already exists or how to fill in the template, open an issue anyway. Our team will help you to complete the rest.

## Description of the issue

The [border colour](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/styles/colour/#:~:text=border,-#cecece) (#cecece) has a contrast ratio of 2:1:1 with the [body-background](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/styles/colour/#:~:text=body-background) (#ffffff) colour. It's worth noting that the auditor raised this as a usability issue, not a WCAG fail. They raised it against Notify's use of the summary list component but I've framed this around the 2 colours mentioned because it will apply to other components/patterns.

## Steps to reproduce the issue

Use a colour contrast checker like [webaim's online checker](https://webaim.org/resources/contrastchecker/) to check the 2 colours.

The border colour should have a ratio of 3:1 with the body-background colour.

ourIssues.title: Inconsistent Nunjucks parameter names for aria-label
ourIssues.body:
There are several components which allow you to pass the text for the `aria-label` on the component's wrapper element. The names of these parameters are inconsistent despite them doing the same thing.

[Cookie banner](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/a5a50ea57175c0031168d227513b7710579d9c98/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/cookie-banner/template.njk#L4) and [service navigation](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/a5a50ea57175c0031168d227513b7710579d9c98/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/service-navigation/template.njk#L95) use `ariaLabel`. 

[Pagination](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/a5a50ea57175c0031168d227513b7710579d9c98/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/pagination/template.njk#L53) uses `landmarkLabel` and [breadcrumbs](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/a5a50ea57175c0031168d227513b7710579d9c98/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/breadcrumbs/template.njk#L14) uses `labelText`.

Pagination also [includes a visuallyHiddenText param](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/a5a50ea57175c0031168d227513b7710579d9c98/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/pagination/template.njk#L44) for pagination items. On most components, `visuallyHiddenText` params are appended to the visible text (for example [in summary card actions](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/a5a50ea57175c0031168d227513b7710579d9c98/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/summary-list/template.njk#L7)); pagination is the only example I can find where `visuallyHiddenText` is passed directly to `aria-label`, completely overriding any visual label

The documentation for the params is also structured differently. For example the docs for pagination and breadcrumbs don't mention that the value will be used as the `aria-label`, while they do for cookie banner and service navigation.

Are any of these differences intentional? I think `ariaLabel` is clearest about what the params actually do, with `[thing]AriaLabel` for labels of child elements (eg password uses `showPasswordAriaLabelText`, though again the `Text` makes that inconsistent)

ourIssues.title: WCAG 2.2: Explore how to handle focus state of short links
ourIssues.body:
## What
Figure out how to present focus states for links of 4 or fewer characters and for components which use the link styles.

## Why
During testing of components against [WCAG 2.2 criterion 2.4.13: focus appearance](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/focus-appearance.html) as part of https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/4347, it was discovered that we have several failures within components to do with parts of these components using our link decoration. The root problem is that that very short links have too small a focus area to pass the criteria. The link style itself _does_ pass the criterion, however components that use the link decoration but not the default link colour eg: breadcrumbs using black links fail this because they lose the contrast between the blue and black that links typically have.

This impacts the following components:

- [Back links](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/back-link/)
- [Breadcrumbs](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/breadcrumbs/)
- [Error summary](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/error-summary/)
- [Pagination](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/pagination/)
- [Summary list](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/summary-list/) (summary cards fail but summary lists pass)
- [Tabs](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/tabs/)

As part of this work, we have an opportunity to also update our [link guidance](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/styles/links/) to encourage users to not use short links in their content.

### Further reading
- [Testing spreadsheet (internal only)](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1PpKvhCGZJb1j0ZUUY2ZuA0CBQeu04yFD1bumiL8wGX8/edit#gid=0)
- https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/issues/3007 - related issue on focus state rationalisation
 
## Who needs to work on this
Developers, designers

## Who needs to review this
Developers, designers

## Done when

- [ ] Solution to how to present short links is devised and merged into `main`
- [ ] Link guidance is updated to advise not using short links

ourIssues.title: Summary list: Allow customisation of full action link content
ourIssues.body: ## What Currently, action links in the Summary list have a hardcoded content order of the action name (`html` or `text`), followed by an area of visually hidden text (`visuallyHiddenText`). The visually hidden text includes a hardcoded space separating it from the prior text, and is usually the same or similar to the key for the current row. For example: ```html change name delete address ``` ## Why This fixed ordering doesn't accommodate localisation into languages where this text appears in a different order. For example, in German we might have this: ```html Namen ändern Adresse löschen ``` Having a hardcoded space is also undesirable in certain languages, such as Chinese: ```html 更换名字 删除名称 ``` Although it is currently possible for services to pass HTML into the action links and ignore the `visuallyHiddenText` parameter completely, we may want to investigate methods of either making `visuallyHiddenText` work with other languages, or removing the use of a dedicated/hardcoded parameter in favour of using the `html` parameter. ## Who needs to work on this Developers ## Who needs to review this Developers ## Done when - [ ] Investigate ways that `visuallyHiddenText` could work with non-English languages. - [ ] Make changes to the Nunjucks template and related tests, if we decide to make modifications. - [ ] Document any changes to Nunjucks parameters.

ourIssues.title: How to populate items arrays with dynamic data
ourIssues.body:
I have a common challenge when using the macros that I've got array data for my items, but populating it in to the `items` array in the macros is tricky as I've got n items - determined by what the user has added.

Transforming existing array data to the form needed by macros isn't so easy or obvious in Nunjucks - I wonder if there's anything we can do - either sub-macros / some guidance about how to generate the array.

As an example, I've got this page:
![Screenshot 2019-08-16 at 12 02 03](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2204224/63164417-4627a300-c020-11e9-931f-fcc53f5d329f.png)

The items in my summary list come from the user so are _n_ in length. I'd like something where I can use a `for` to loop over my data to do whatever I need to it.

For my above example, for ease of prototyping I'm just calling the entire summaryList macro again - this doesn't produce great markup, but is ok-enough for now.

What do teams do in this case? is there anything the macros could do (or new macros?) to make this easier?

ourIssues.title: Support for conditionally showing items / rows when passing data in macros
ourIssues.body: ## What I've frequently wanted to conditionally show or hide a single item in an array used the macros - such as the summary list or radios. At the moment this is rather awkward to do - but could be much simpler, especially for prototyping. You can *almost* achieve this by adding logic at the end of the item, like so: ```js items: [ { value: "admin", text: "Edit, view and manage", checked: false, hint: { text: "Edit the full case as well as manage case permissions" } }, { value: "edit", text: "Edit and view", checked: true, hint: { text: "Edit the full case" } } if foo == "bar" ] ``` However, because of [#1494](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/1494) it doesn't work. Even if it did, it might not be so obvious. @GrilloPress suggested a flag on the item might work: ```js "display": variableTrueOrNotMate ``` ## My use case: I have a page of radios. When the user first runs through it, it has one less option than when they run through again (and have the option of removing). The page is the same - I want to be able to conditionally show the last option based on data. First time: Second time: If #1494 does get fixed, it does support this _sortof_ - I'm not sure it's obvious / explicit though. Would be good to see if this is an issue others have come across.

communityIssues.title: Whitehall has some hard coded component markup
communityIssues.body:
There are a few instances in whitehall's templates where components markup has been copied and pasted, rather than calling the component directly from the gem. This introduces a maintenance burden as hard coded instances must be updated to match the component in the gem, potentially causing visual problems that could go unnoticed during a `govuk_publishing_components` dependabot update.

Components should be called directly from the gem using the `<%= render "govuk_publishing_components/components/component_name", {} %>` syntax.

[bookmarklets index lines 17 and 32](https://github.com/alphagov/whitehall/blob/main/app/views/admin/bookmarklets/index.html.erb#L17) has hard coded button markup:

- both instances appear to be hardcoded in order to apply JavaScript to the component via the `href` attribute, including Rails variables
- an alternative approach would be to move the JavaScript out of the template and into a JavaScript file, using a `js-` prefixed class passed to the component to apply event listeners, and use the [data attributes option](https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/button/with_data_attributes) to apply the Rails variables, that can be then read by the JavaScript
- it might even be possible to do something simpler, like the following:

```
<% button_href = capture do %>
  <%= render("find_in_admin").gsub(/[\r\n]/,"") %>
<% end %>

<%= render "govuk_publishing_components/components/button", {
  text: "Find in admin",
  href: "javascript:(function(){ #{button_href} })()"
} %>
```

[_accessible_attachment_field.html.erb line 3](https://github.com/alphagov/whitehall/blob/main/app/views/admin/editions/_accessible_attachment_field.html.erb#L3) includes a hard coded select component:

- looks like this is hard coded because some Rails logic is being used to determine which options inside the select should be selected or disabled
- this should be achievable by moving the logic into a presenter and relying on the [preselect](https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/select#with_preselect) and [disabled](https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/select#with_disabled_options) options on the select component

[_govspeak_help.html.erb line 22](https://github.com/alphagov/whitehall/blob/main/app/views/admin/editions/_govspeak_help.html.erb#L22) and [_style_guidance.html.erb lines 8 and 43](https://github.com/alphagov/whitehall/blob/main/app/views/admin/editions/_style_guidance.html.erb#L8) have hard coded list components:

- looks like these could just be replaced with [calls to the list component](https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/list)

[_summary_card_list.html.erb line 23](https://github.com/alphagov/whitehall/blob/main/app/views/components/_summary_card_list.html.erb#L23) has a hard coded summary list component:

- looks like there's various custom bits of data being displayed here, with some logic involved
- this looks like a direct call to the component could be used here, with the logic moved to a presenter

communityIssues.title: Inconsistent components API
communityIssues.body:
The component API is inconsistent across components and in comparison with `govuk-frontend`.

In the table below there is a brief comparison in how `govuk-frontend` components are aligned in API with `govuk_publishing_components`

|Component               |API |
|---                      |---  |
Accordion                 | aligned
Back link                 | aligned
Breadcrumbs               | misaligned
Button                    | slightly misaligned (start)
Character count           | slightly misaligned (nesting)
Checkboxes                | slightly misaligned (fieldset)
Date input                | slightly misaligned (fieldset)
Details                   | misaligned
Error message             | aligned
Error summary             | misaligned
Fieldset                  | misaligned
File upload               | aligned
Footer                    | aligned
Header                    | slightly misaligned (navigation_items)
Inset text                | aligned
Panel                     | misaligned
Phase banner              | misaligned
Radios                    | slightly misaligned (fieldset)
Select                    | slightly misaligned (options)
Skip link                 | aligned
Summary list              | slightly misaligned (items)
Table                     | aligned
Tabs                      | misaligned
Text input                | aligned
Textarea                  | aligned
Warning text              | slightly misaligned (iconFallbackText)

We can see a few common differences between to two API models:
- for arrays, `govuk-frontend` uses the generic `items` (in most cases) whereas `govuk_publishing_components` uses the name of the component (e.g. `attachments` for the attachment list component or `breadcrumbs` for the breadcrumbs component)
- for web addresses/paths `govuk-frontend` uses `href` whereas in `govuk_publishing_components` we often find `url` (e.g. breadcrumbs component)

It's worth mentioning that not even `govuk-frontend`'s API is consistent (e.g. `errorList` instead of `items` in the Error summary component, or differences in nesting)

A few advantages of making the API consistent:
- increases developers' confidence when calling components with arguments (without constantly checking examples in the guide)
- prototyping and production will use the same config object (can be easily copied over in both directions)
- applications can prepare the data to be fed into components consistently using helpers
- it would be easier to swap one component with another

I'm creating this to raise awareness of the differences, hopefully generate discussions around how good looks like and aim for consistency and convergency. API alignment requires at least a breaking change and some replacements across applications – which is not an easy process. For this reason, having a clear vision about how we want it to look like would save us from doing this more than once.

backlog.title: Right-to-left (RTL) language support
backlog.body:
What
Add support for right-to-left (RTL) languages to GOV.UK Frontend components.
Why
A number of pages on GOV.UK are made available in RTL languages, however they tend to insert RTL content into the same layout used by left-to-right (LTR) languages instead of mirroring the entire interface, as is typical for RTL languages. For example, in RTL languages a right-pointing arrow indicates moving backwards, whereas a left-pointing arrow indicates progress.
RTL languages are currently in use in various areas of GOV.UK. (Google search results are for a rough indication of how widely used each language is.)

Arabic (Google search results, example page)
Persian (Farsi) (Google search results, example page)
Dari Persian (Google search results, example page)
Hebrew (Google search results, example page)
Pashto (Google search results, example page)
Shahmukhi Punjabi (Google search results, example page)
Urdu (Google search results, example page)

GOV.UK's lack of RTL support produces unexpected layouts in situation where RTL languages are already in use (though many of these instances are with publishing components and not Frontend):

Announcements (Arabic)

The email and RSS notification links are misaligned and have incorrect margins.


Screening tests for you and your baby (Urdu)

Page metadata appears reversed (value appears before key) due to left floats.
Date format appears scrambled due to trying to automatically interpolate LTR content into an RTL context.
Email alerts button has incorrect margins.


COVID-19 lateral flow test instructions (Arabic)

Indent text component doesn't appear indented, as the indent is on the wrong side.



There are some situations where RTL language content has only been made available in PDF format, potentially due to restrictions with creating this content in HTML, which creates an accessibility barrier for end users. For example, detention rights are available in English as a HTML page but must be downloaded as a PDF for Arabic, Farsi and Urdu speakers.

Test all of our components in screen readers with mouse tracking.

ourIssues.title: Adjust components to scale with android system font size
ourIssues.body:
## What
Ensure as many of our components as possible are responding when viewing govuk-frontend web pages on android devices and adjusting android's system font size.

## Why
Govuk-frontend web pages should respect accessibility settigns and respond to them as expected.

## Steps to replicate
Tested in chrome on browserstack's Galaxy S23 instance as it's easy to notice the issue due to the device's large font size scale.

1. Go to the settings of the testing device and locate the setting to adjust device font size
2. Increase font size (recommend max in order to visualise issue more clearly)
3. Open a govuk-frontend web page on a browser on an android device eg: [the review app's announcements page](https://govuk-frontend-review.herokuapp.com/full-page-examples/announcements)

Notice that the breadcrumbs have not increased in size. Digging into the runtime styles, you will find that rem values of other elements on the page have adjusted in response to the font size change but the breadcrumbs haven't.

![Android browser showing an announcements page with scaled up font size except for the breadcrumbs element](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/assets/64783893/66ecb7d1-bf9e-459a-987c-8c85176a26b7)

## Notes
### Considerations from the spec
The likely reason this is happening can be found in CSS Mobile Text Size section of the CSS spec, specifically [2.2: Conditions that suppress adjustment](https://drafts.csswg.org/css-size-adjust/#default-adjustment-conditions). This section notes 4 reasons that would suppress text size adjustment. From initial testing, certain components can be 'fixed' by removing their block level positioning rules eg: components that have `display: inline-block`. We should be able to use `inline-block` on components and the text size adjustment not be suppressed. Recommend using the the spec in figuring out a solution.

### Impacted components
- Accordion
- Back link
- Breadcrumbs
- Button, and places consumed
    - Cookie banner buttons
    - Exit this page
- Checkboxes
- Details (not the content)
- File upload
- Some of the footer's links
- Header menu
- Notification banner
- Pagination
- Radios
- Select
- Table
- Tabs
- Tag
- Task list
- Text input, and places consumed
    - Date input
    - Password input

## Who needs to work on this
Developers

## Who needs to review this
Developers

ourIssues.title: Explore 'versioning' parts of guidance
ourIssues.body:
## What

Explore the idea of 'versioning' guidance aka: identifying certain parts of our guidance based on if it pertains to a specific version of Frontend.

Examples of things that could be 'versioned':

- Components (when the component was introduced)
- Patterns (the minimum version you need to use a given pattern based on which components it users)
- Nunjucks macro options
- specific features or functionality on guidance pages
- 'announcement' guidance where we want to advertise a specific change eg: in version x.y.z we introduced this feature we want you to be aware of...

In addition, explore a consistent visual language for communicating versioning across the website.

## Why

- To help us communicate to users when features became available in Frontend
- To encourage users to think about the version of Frontend in their service
- To codify times we've established visual language for specific bits of work but retired that thing afterwards, meaning we're redoing that design work over and over

Designers, Developers, Content designers

## Who needs to review this

Designers, Developers, Content designers

- [ ] Assessed the value of those ideas
- [ ] Explored those ideas in more detail
- [ ] Investigated a visual language for versioning based on the outcome of spiking those ideas

ourIssues.title: The names of some patterns can cause confusion when they appear as part of a sentence
ourIssues.body:
## What
Feedback from the cross-government working group following publication of '[Help users to understand the impact of an emergency on your service](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/understand-the-impact-of-an-emergency/)' to add single quotation marks when we reference page names.

Although feedback is for the emergency banner pattern this would also apply to all content on the Design System.

## Why

The pattern names are long, and this can make sentences that they appear in confusing to read. Starting the pattern name with an upper case letter is not sufficient, because it doesn't explicitly indicate the _end_ of the name.

Some options:
- live with it
- put quotes around pattern names
- put quotes around all document names
- put quotes around problematic instances only
- replace the name with a pronoun like 'this' or 'the pattern'

## Who needs to know about this

Stephen, Tim

backlog.title: Video Relay Service (VRS)
backlog.body:
What
A component to link to Video Relay Service (VRS).
Why
Departments are starting to provide Video Relay Service for people who need sign language interpretation, and it's becoming more popular across all departments.
Because it's new we are seeing a pattern emerging where people just stick a link on the start page.
However, when talking to @timpaul  about it, we discussed that there isn't a lot of research around it to know if people know what "Video Relay Service" actually is. Also, some people are BSL monoglots, which means they may not even be able to read a link written in English
Suggestion
There is a common icon for sign language which could probably be incorporated into a component similar to the back link, so that even if people don't know what VRS is, or they can't read the written English, they can still find the sign language interpretation feature.


Edit: Original image is not recommended as it is associated with ALS (American Sign Language) rather than BSL, based on NHS research.

ourIssues.title: Enhanced File Upload banner does not update on browser Back/Forward in Chrome&Edge
ourIssues.body:
## Description of the issue

in Chrome or Edge, when a user navigates Back or Forward to a page with a File Upload component on it, any preexisting value in the hidden file input is not shown correctly in the file upload component's banner

## Steps to reproduce the issue

In Chrome or Edge:

1. navigate to https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/file-upload/enhanced/
1. choose a file, either by the button or by dragging & dropping
1. simulate the user submitting the form and having a file actually be uploaded by changing the address bar to [www.gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/)
1. use the browser's Back button to return to the upload-a-single-file example

## Actual vs expected behaviour

Expected behaviour: the banner shows the file name chosen in step 2
Actual behaviour: the banner shows 'No file chosen'

The reason I expect the filename to appear in the banner is that the filename is actually populated by the browser in the hidden file input tag. This can be verified by opening the browser console and executing the following: `document.querySelector('input[type="file"]').value`

Therefore, if the user were to press Continue again, they'd be uploading the previously-chosen file.

This doesn't happen in Firefox or Safari because they don't populate the `files` property of file input tags on browser navigation.

## Environment (where applicable)

- Operating system: N/A
- Browser: Chrome+Edge, not Firefox or Safari
- Browser version: latest (Chrome 153)
- GOV.UK Frontend Version: 6.5.0

ourIssues.title: Adjust components to scale with android system font size
ourIssues.body:
## What
Ensure as many of our components as possible are responding when viewing govuk-frontend web pages on android devices and adjusting android's system font size.

## Why
Govuk-frontend web pages should respect accessibility settigns and respond to them as expected.

## Steps to replicate
Tested in chrome on browserstack's Galaxy S23 instance as it's easy to notice the issue due to the device's large font size scale.

1. Go to the settings of the testing device and locate the setting to adjust device font size
2. Increase font size (recommend max in order to visualise issue more clearly)
3. Open a govuk-frontend web page on a browser on an android device eg: [the review app's announcements page](https://govuk-frontend-review.herokuapp.com/full-page-examples/announcements)

Notice that the breadcrumbs have not increased in size. Digging into the runtime styles, you will find that rem values of other elements on the page have adjusted in response to the font size change but the breadcrumbs haven't.

![Android browser showing an announcements page with scaled up font size except for the breadcrumbs element](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/assets/64783893/66ecb7d1-bf9e-459a-987c-8c85176a26b7)

## Notes
### Considerations from the spec
The likely reason this is happening can be found in CSS Mobile Text Size section of the CSS spec, specifically [2.2: Conditions that suppress adjustment](https://drafts.csswg.org/css-size-adjust/#default-adjustment-conditions). This section notes 4 reasons that would suppress text size adjustment. From initial testing, certain components can be 'fixed' by removing their block level positioning rules eg: components that have `display: inline-block`. We should be able to use `inline-block` on components and the text size adjustment not be suppressed. Recommend using the the spec in figuring out a solution.

### Impacted components
- Accordion
- Back link
- Breadcrumbs
- Button, and places consumed
    - Cookie banner buttons
    - Exit this page
- Checkboxes
- Details (not the content)
- File upload
- Some of the footer's links
- Header menu
- Notification banner
- Pagination
- Radios
- Select
- Table
- Tabs
- Tag
- Task list
- Text input, and places consumed
    - Date input
    - Password input

Developers

Developers

ourIssues.title: WCAG 2.2: Explore how to handle focus state of short links
ourIssues.body:
## What
Figure out how to present focus states for links of 4 or fewer characters and for components which use the link styles.

## Why
During testing of components against [WCAG 2.2 criterion 2.4.13: focus appearance](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/focus-appearance.html) as part of https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/4347, it was discovered that we have several failures within components to do with parts of these components using our link decoration. The root problem is that that very short links have too small a focus area to pass the criteria. The link style itself _does_ pass the criterion, however components that use the link decoration but not the default link colour eg: breadcrumbs using black links fail this because they lose the contrast between the blue and black that links typically have.

This impacts the following components:

- [Back links](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/back-link/)
- [Breadcrumbs](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/breadcrumbs/)
- [Error summary](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/error-summary/)
- [Pagination](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/pagination/)
- [Summary list](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/summary-list/) (summary cards fail but summary lists pass)
- [Tabs](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/tabs/)

As part of this work, we have an opportunity to also update our [link guidance](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/styles/links/) to encourage users to not use short links in their content.

### Further reading
- [Testing spreadsheet (internal only)](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1PpKvhCGZJb1j0ZUUY2ZuA0CBQeu04yFD1bumiL8wGX8/edit#gid=0)
- https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/issues/3007 - related issue on focus state rationalisation
 
## Who needs to work on this
Developers, designers

## Who needs to review this
Developers, designers

## Done when

- [ ] Solution to how to present short links is devised and merged into `main`
- [ ] Link guidance is updated to advise not using short links

ourIssues.title: Various issues under Chrome's Auto Dark Mode
ourIssues.body:
Since Chrome version 78, Google has included an experimental feature in the browser, initially named "Forced Dark Mode" and, as of writing, named "Auto Dark Mode for Web Content". 

This feature automatically modifies the appearance of webpages in order to create a "dark mode" version. This is done even if the page already supplies a "dark mode" via the `prefers-color-scheme` CSS media query. It also appears to ignore the `color-scheme` property. 

The flag comes with several different "enabled" modes (as of Chrome 99), which modify how Chrome is internally applying changes. Each mode results in subtly (sometimes radically) different resulting colours.

1. Enabled
2. Enabled with simple HSL-based inversion
3. Enabled with simple CIELAB-based inversion
4. Enabled with simple RGB-based inversion
5. Enabled with selective image inversion
6. Enabled with selective inversion of non-image elements
7. Enabled with selective inversion of everything
8. Enabled with increased text contrast

Most of these modes appear to work by first overriding neutral light background colours (such as white and light greys), and modifying any copy that it detects as existing on a modified background colour to maintain suitable contrast. Most other colours appear to be left intact. This method of alteration means that colours are not all modified in the same way: `$govuk-brand-color` in mode 1, for example, is unmodified when used as a background or border colour (#1d70b8), but is changed when it is used as a text colour (#61a1ee).

Mode 4 appears to simply invert all colours on the page, regardless of usage. 

I'm not sure how mode 1 is different from the others. It may be that this is an "automatic" mode where Chrome tries to determine which of the other seven modes works best for the given page and uses that one.

We have received at least one bug report raised by a user who was using Chrome's Auto Dark Mode feature for accessibility reasons (to make content easier to read with cataracts).

> RE the dark mode, it is now a function in Google Chrome that you can activate and it will force a dark version if the website can accommodate it. Not everyone does, BBC News for example still comes through with a traditional black text on a white background – but it works for many.

## Steps to reproduce the issue
In Google Chrome, go to `chrome://flags/#enable-force-dark` (this should jump you straight to "Auto Dark Mode for Web Contents") and enable the flag.

## Actual vs expected behaviour
Currently, a number of these modes produce colour combinations which fail the contrast requirements established in WCAG 2.1. 

Below is a non-exhaustive subset of issues currently identified in Auto Dark Mode.

### Text inputs and textareas
Text inputs are displayed with a grey background and black border in modes 1, 6, 7, and 8. This fails to meet the expected 1:3 contrast ratio for UI elements (at 1:1.68). 

![Screenshot of the design system input component, appearing grey on black.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160644743-7632dc27-cc56-4558-bd40-8fee1109717c.png)

They are displayed with a light grey background and white border in modes 3 and 5, which easily meets contrast ratio expectations.

They are displayed with the default white background and black border in all other modes.

### Input prefixes and suffixes

These are difficult to read in modes 2 and 4, where they are black on a dark grey background (1:3.23).

![Screenshot of the design system input prefix and suffix example, where the text is black on dark grey.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160646813-ac2ad0a1-083d-4ca0-b571-b1ecacd450e4.png)

These are much more difficult to read in modes 3 and 5, which renders it as black on an even darker grey (1.22).

![Screenshot of the design system input prefix and suffix example. The text is visually imperceptible from the background.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160650473-9c6f3529-5a06-4408-b20e-242b1c66a08e.png)

These are displayed with adequate contrast in other modes.

### Checkboxes and radio buttons
The border and selection states of checkboxes and radio buttons do not have sufficient contrast in modes 1, 6, 7, and 8 (at a pretty much imperceptible contrast ratio of 1:1.04)

![Screenshot of the design system checkbox component, illustrating insufficient contrast between the checkboxes and background, which are both dark grey.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160644218-1fc50370-249e-4e47-b73a-eab9a8b8ea34.png)

They are displayed with white borders and selection states in all other modes.

### Select

In modes 1, 6, 7, and 8, select boxes are rendered with a dark grey background and dark grey border (1:1.04).

![Screenshot of the design system select component, which appears to just be white text with no border or icon.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160648934-5554f80a-1794-40e1-a9b7-a7c16df83d29.png)

They are rendered with a black background and white border in all other modes.

### Skiplinks

In modes 1, 2, 6, and 7, skiplinks are rendered as white on focus-colour yellow, which does not meet contrast requirements (1:1.34).

![Screenshot of a white link on a bright yellow background.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160649767-19aecf58-2ea6-4517-9852-283a4c91f922.png)

In mode 4, it is white on light blue, which is also below expectations (1:3.24).

![Screenshot of a white link on a bright blue background.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160649982-3f7999be-3540-40c5-8d00-7b9350407360.png)

In mode 8, it is white on focus-color yellow, but additionally has a black text shadow/stroke effect applied, which makes it difficult to read.

![Screenshot of a white link with a thin, pixellated black shadow surrounding it, on a bright yellow background.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160650309-a61034bd-d400-4ca3-b312-db890c382f19.png)

This is displayed with adequate contrast (albeit, in white on brown) in all other modes.

### Iconography

Most iconography fails to meet contrast requirements in virtually all modes. This includes:
- the open and close arrows on the Accordion component.
- the arrow on the Back link component.
- the arrows on the Breadcrumbs component.
- the exclamation icon on the Warning text component.

### Other components
The good news is that, for the most part, the majority of other components we have in GOV.UK Frontend are not as badly affected as those above, with various components such as Inset text, Error summary, and Notification banner maintaining their necessary visual presence and suitable contrast even with modified colours. 

## Environment
The results specified here were taken in Chrome 99, running on macOS 15.3, whilst the operating system was set to light mode. 

Interestingly, Chrome DevTools does not give any indication that a change to the page's appearance has taken place. All HTML and CSS content, including the user agent stylesheet, computed styles, and those returned through JavaScript, appear unmodified and are not aligned with the page's actual appearance when Auto Dark Mode is enabled.

ourIssues.title: Consider larger elements for a bigger touch/target size
ourIssues.body:
## Related component
Anything interactive:
 - Buttons

Larger elements are easy to use, whether that's on a touch device like a phone, or using a mouse or other input device.

ourIssues.title: Visiting a heading within a page can have a large layout shift
ourIssues.body:
<!--
    Please fill in as much of the template below as you’re able to. If you're unsure whether the issue already exists or how to fill in the template, open an issue anyway. Our team will help you to complete the rest.

    Your issue might already exist. If so, add a comment to the existing issue instead of creating a new one. You can find existing issues here: https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/issues
-->

## Description of the issue
<!-- A clear and concise summary of what the bug is. -->

When visiting a heading within a page on the Design System website, there can be a large layout shift that causes the browser viewport to end up showing the wrong part of the page.

For example, loading the [URL for the 'Start by asking one question per page' section of the question pages pattern page](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/question-pages/#start-by-asking-one-question-per-page) in Chrome 92 can sometime result in the browser showing the 'Back links' section:

https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/503614/127671243-273b39e8-c271-4c37-ac54-9c090a678009.mp4

This behaviour is unpredictable; sometimes the browser will produce the [expected behaviour].

I have also seen this happen when visiting a page that is linked from another page within the Design System website, for instance, the guidance on when not to use a 'none' checkbox links to the 'start by asking one question per page' guidance.

<details>
<summary>Recording of Safari showing unexpected behaviour when following a link</summary>

https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/503614/127672657-48644cb4-fe9d-428e-b726-4297a598971d.mp4

</details>

## Steps to reproduce the issue
<!-- How can we reproduce this issue? If you think it will be helpful, please provide a small code snippet and/or screenshots. -->

1. Open a new browser tab
2. Visit the URL https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/question-pages/#start-by-asking-one-question-per-page

Note that this will not always produce the behaviour recorded above, sometimes it will produce the expected behaviour. However, on this page the browser fairly reliably jumps back to the same place within the page, when it does jump.

## Actual vs expected behaviour
<!-- What is happening vs what would you expect to happen instead? -->

I expect that when the page has finished loading the heading 'Start by asking one question per page' is at the top of the browser window. 

<details>
<summary>Recording of the expected behaviour in Chrome</summary>

https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/503614/127672361-df87da15-a685-4334-b715-4d166ae4a700.mp4

</details>

## Environment (where applicable)
<!-- Details of your operating system, browser and the version of GOVUK Frontend you’re using may help us to reproduce your issue. -->

I've tested locally with the URL https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/question-pages/#start-by-asking-one-question-per-page and the following browsers:

- Operating system: MacOS Catalina 10.15.7 
- Browser: Chrome 92.0.4515.107 (Official Build) (x86_64), Safari 14.1.2 (15611.3.10.1.5, 15611), Firefox 90.0.2 (64-bit)

I've also tested this in IE11 on Windows 7 using BrowserStack.

All browsers tested show similar behaviour; when loading the page for the first time it will "jump back" from the correct heading to the 'Back links' heading, but subsequent loads the browser will end up at the correct heading.

I've also tried different pages on the Design System website, with similar (if less dramatic) results.

## Notes

I'm not sure what is causing this, or if it is a problem that is affecting users, but thought I'd create an issue about it so we could discuss.

communityIssues.title: Footnote links and their backlinks are too small
communityIssues.body: [Footnotes within the Govspeak component](https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/govspeak#footnotes) currently don't fail [2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum)](https://w3c.github.io/wcag/understanding/target-size-minimum.html). But that is only because there is an exception for interactive elements within inline text. Note: 2.5.8 is part of the new draft WCAG 2.2 criteria. The latest standard is WCAG 2.1. WCAG 2.2 isn't published yet, so this is potentially subject to change. But the small size of footnotes is still an accessibility issue, they are very difficult to click on with a mouse or finger on a touch device, especially for people with motor impairments. That’s worse when footnotes or backlinks are close to another link or footnote (which can also look different in other viewports). When testing the smallest footnote link was only 5.62 x 18.5px and the backlink was 19 x 23.5px. There is a worse example of footnotes under [Specialist content](https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/govspeak#specialist_content). Screenshots of footnotes and backlinks with their dimensions: This was fixed in some areas on www.gov.uk already (e.g. partly [in this Govspeak PR](https://github.com/alphagov/govspeak/pull/192)) by changing: * ‘1’ to ‘[footnote 1]’ (although a shorter '[note 1]' might also work) * ‘↩’ to ‘Go to where this is referenced’ (although that was later changed to be in an aria-label and not visible text, there would need to be a bit more text or spacing to make the link wider) That also shows that there is an issue of footnotes currently being inconsistent across www.gov.uk.

communityIssues.title: Inconsistent components API
communityIssues.body:
The component API is inconsistent across components and in comparison with `govuk-frontend`.

In the table below there is a brief comparison in how `govuk-frontend` components are aligned in API with `govuk_publishing_components`

|Component               |API |
|---                      |---  |
Accordion                 | aligned
Back link                 | aligned
Breadcrumbs               | misaligned
Button                    | slightly misaligned (start)
Character count           | slightly misaligned (nesting)
Checkboxes                | slightly misaligned (fieldset)
Date input                | slightly misaligned (fieldset)
Details                   | misaligned
Error message             | aligned
Error summary             | misaligned
Fieldset                  | misaligned
File upload               | aligned
Footer                    | aligned
Header                    | slightly misaligned (navigation_items)
Inset text                | aligned
Panel                     | misaligned
Phase banner              | misaligned
Radios                    | slightly misaligned (fieldset)
Select                    | slightly misaligned (options)
Skip link                 | aligned
Summary list              | slightly misaligned (items)
Table                     | aligned
Tabs                      | misaligned
Text input                | aligned
Textarea                  | aligned
Warning text              | slightly misaligned (iconFallbackText)

We can see a few common differences between to two API models:
- for arrays, `govuk-frontend` uses the generic `items` (in most cases) whereas `govuk_publishing_components` uses the name of the component (e.g. `attachments` for the attachment list component or `breadcrumbs` for the breadcrumbs component)
- for web addresses/paths `govuk-frontend` uses `href` whereas in `govuk_publishing_components` we often find `url` (e.g. breadcrumbs component)

It's worth mentioning that not even `govuk-frontend`'s API is consistent (e.g. `errorList` instead of `items` in the Error summary component, or differences in nesting)

A few advantages of making the API consistent:
- increases developers' confidence when calling components with arguments (without constantly checking examples in the guide)
- prototyping and production will use the same config object (can be easily copied over in both directions)
- applications can prepare the data to be fed into components consistently using helpers
- it would be easier to swap one component with another

I'm creating this to raise awareness of the differences, hopefully generate discussions around how good looks like and aim for consistency and convergency. API alignment requires at least a breaking change and some replacements across applications – which is not an easy process. For this reason, having a clear vision about how we want it to look like would save us from doing this more than once.
