ourIssues.title: Improve Language Navigation guidance on not losing data in forms when navigating between languages
ourIssues.body:
<!--

  This is a template for any issues that aren’t bug reports or new feature requests. The headings in this section provide examples of the information you might want to include, but feel free to add/delete sections where appropriate.

-->

## What

Improve Language Navigation guidance on not losing data in forms when using the component so that it's clearer what the behaviour should be

> Make sure the user does not lose any data they’ve entered when they navigate to another language. Do not ask the user to re-enter information they’ve already given.

https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/language-navigation/

## Why

We have [had some feedback ](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/discussions/5620#discussioncomment-18582218)that it's not clear in practice if this means keeping the users currently inputted data on a page or just keeping the data from the overall user journey.

Since this is a non-standard thing to do, we think it's likely other developers will wonder what they're aiming for.

There's some potential improvements to this:
- improving the guidance so it's clear that it includes users' un-submitted input 
- guidance around explaining at a high level how to achieve this functionality, similar to what we do for Cookie banner and Form validation (for developers)

## Background

This content was originally added in response to HMRC's welsh language toggle guidance. They detailed why they chose to keep data between page views in some feedback of note:

> welsh users will toggle back and forth between languages to ensure understanding of unfamiliar words and/or to check that both journeys are the same

> welsh speakers familiar with uncommon english specific to the context benefit from both the ability to toggle easily, and from these terms being shown in brackets within the welsh service (to avoid having to do as much switching)

> users prefer english/welsh toggle to whole journey language switching and absence of feature to toggle within service (only being able to select at start) tested negatively

https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/discussions/5351#discussioncomment-17278309

## Who needs to work on this

Content designer, developer

## Who needs to review this

Content designer, developer

## Done when

- [ ] the guidance is clearer on exactly what data should be persisted
- [ ] we've considered if extended guidance is appropriate

communityIssues.title: Multi-file upload component: Adoption questions for Bulk Upload service
communityIssues.body:
## Context

We are building a bulk upload feature for our service. We've been looking at the [multi-file upload component](https://github.com/ministryofjustice/moj-frontend/tree/main/src/moj/components/multi-file-upload) as our design starting point.

We've built a technical proof of concept in React that demonstrates multi-file upload feasibility, and we now need to bring this into a GDS-compliant, user-tested design prototype. We'd like to understand the component's current status and capabilities before we proceed.

## Our use case

- **Users:** Internal operations managers
- **Action:** Upload up to 10 documents at once
- **File types:** PDF, JPEG, PNG (additional file types: xlsx, docs, msg)
- **Max file size:** 1GB (PDF), 100MB (images)
- **Key requirement:** Per-file status reporting (success/fail with reason) and error recovery

## Questions
### 1. Component maturity and approval status

Is the multi-file upload component considered production-ready and approved for use in live government services? We noticed the last commit was approximately 11 months ago — is this because it's stable, or is active development paused?

### 2. Per-file error handling

Does the component (or a newer unreleased version) support per-file error states? Specifically, we need to handle:

- File too large (exceeds size limit)
- Wrong file type (not in accepted list)
- Virus detected (failed scanning)
- Duplicate file warning (filename already exists in the collection)
- Network timeout / upload failure
- **Partial batch success** (e.g., 8 of 10 files succeed, 2 fail with individual reasons)

Are any of these handled out of the box, or would we need to extend the component?

### 3. GOV.UK Prototype Kit compatibility

Is there a Prototype Kit-compatible version of this component? We need to present designs at a Service review and ideally want to use the Prototype Kit for our interactive prototype. If not, is Figma + the component's HTML/CSS sufficient for demonstration purposes?

### 4. Confirmation step

Our governance requires users to review their file selection and confirm before upload begins (to prevent accidental wrong uploads). Does the component support an intermediate confirmation step between file selection and upload initiation?

### 5. Additional patterns

Does the MoJ Design System have documented patterns for:
- Upload progress indicators (per-file)
- Recovery flows when some files in a batch fail
- Post-upload metadata assignment (user categorises files after they've uploaded)

### 6. Known limitations or alternatives

Are there any known limitations, planned deprecation, or alternative components we should consider? We're aware the component doesn't currently support:
- Folder structure retention
- Custom confirmation dialogs
- Bad file type preview/rejection before upload

Are any of these on the roadmap?

## Our timeline

We're targeting a release in soon. Any guidance — even a quick pointer to the right documentation or person — would be hugely appreciated.

## Happy to contribute back

If we extend the component for our use case (error states, confirmation step), we'd be happy to contribute those patterns back to the MoJ Design System if that would be useful.

**Component:** `src/moj/components/multi-file-upload`

communityIssues.title: Multi-file upload component: Allow additional parameters to be submitted when uploading files
communityIssues.body:
<!--

Have you read the Code of Conduct? By filing an Issue, you are expected to comply with it, including treating everyone with respect:

https://github.com/ministryofjustice/moj-frontend/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md

Do you want to ask a question? Are you looking for support? You can [contact the Design System team](https://design-patterns.service.justice.gov.uk/community/help-and-feedback).

---

Keep in mind that this code is customisable. Please consider the following options before filing this issue:

* Tweak the project's configuration, styles, etcetera.
* Install a community package.
* Create a package or enhance an existing package.

If none of these options is appropriate for the feature you want, please explain why that's the case by filling out the issue template below.

Also, note that the team has finite resources, so it's unlikely that we'll work on feature requests. If we're interested in a particular feature, however, we'll follow up and ask you to submit an RFC to talk about it in more detail.

-->

## Summary

It would be useful to be able to include extra parameters in `formData` in requests sent by the multi-file upload component. This could be done by making an additional hook available, called something like `uploadFileParamsHook` (similar to the existing `uploadFileExitHook` and `uploadFileErrorHook`) which would allow `formData` to be amended as required.

## Motivation

We use the multi-file upload component in two places in the CCCD application. In each of those places we include an additional parameter (`form_id`) in the AJAX request sent by the component. This allows our documents controller to identify where the request has come from and treat the uploaded file differently depending on the source. Our previous approach to uploading files allowed us to add this parameter to `formData`, however the current implementation of the multi-file upload component does not allow `formData` to be altered, which has made adopting the component more difficult.

## Describe alternatives you've considered

At the moment we are overriding the `uploadFile` function locally to add this functionality. While this works, we ideally do not want to overwrite what comes from moj-frontend as this means we start to deviate from a common approach could result in us missing updates or bug fixes.

## Additional context

We have partially implemented this in our current solution [here](https://github.com/ministryofjustice/Claim-for-Crown-Court-Defence/blob/master/app/webpack/javascripts/modules/Modules.MultiFileUpload.js).

We define:
```
      uploadFileParamsHook: function (_uploader, formData) {
        const formIdElement = document.querySelector('#claim_form_id')
        if (formIdElement) { formData.append('document[form_id]', formIdElement.value) }
      },
```

and call it in our overrided `uploadFile` function:
```
this.params.uploadFileParamsHook(this, formData)
```

If `uploadFileParamsHook` were added to the moj-frontend package, we would be able to remove our customisation of the `uploadFile` function.

I’d be happy to help with a pull request for this change if you are open to adding this feature.

communityIssues.title: Big number text-only variant is announced as two separate items by VoiceOver and TalkBack
communityIssues.body:
## What
iOS and Mac VoiceOver, and Android TalkBack currently read the value (e.g., "82") and the label (e.g., "Open consultations") of the [big number component text-only version](https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/big_number) as two separate elements. They should be wrapped/marked up so the entire phrase is announced as one single item or link.

[We fixed the issue for JAWS and NVDA recently](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk_publishing_components/pull/5458), there's more detail on that PR on what we looked at. VoiceOver and TalkBack also read the link version of the big number as one item. However, we didn't find a solution for VoiceOver and TalkBack when big number isn't a link. 

It might be that it's not possible to fix this for all the combinations of screen readers we support. In that case we might want to look at redesigning the component to support it being announced as one item.

## Why
This issue was raised in the 2025 GOV.UK accessibility audit:

> When a text within a semantic element such as a link or a heading is split across multiple child elements, this can mean that instead of being relayed all in one go, it is relayed in pieces, with the ‘link’ or ‘heading’ role relayed after each piece, as if they were separate links or separate headings. For example, screen reader users may encounter only ‘66’, followed by ‘Open consultations’ and assume that these are separate links with different destinations.

When testing this on VoiceOver, however, "1M" is announced as "one metre" rather than "one million".

I've only tested in VoiceOver so I'm unsure if this issue is specific to VO or replicated across other assistive tech.

ourIssues.title: File upload breaks on input ids containing quotes (unescaped selector in findLabel)
ourIssues.body:
## Summary

`FileUpload.findLabel()` interpolates the raw input id into `document.querySelector(`label[for="..."]`)`, so an id containing a double quote (e.g. `a"b`, legal HTML) throws an uncaught `SyntaxError: Invalid selector` instead of resolving the label — breaking component init. Verified with the real module under jsdom: `findLabel()` with input id `a"b` throws; the label exists in the DOM.

Same unescaped-interpolation class as #7395 (error summary/checkboxes) and #7397 (tabs), different component — no `CSS.escape` on this path.

## Expected

Escape the id with `CSS.escape()`, like the sibling fixes.

ourIssues.title: Uncaught selector errors for ids/names containing quotes (error summary, checkboxes)
ourIssues.body:
## Summary

Clicking an error-summary link (or toggling an exclusive checkbox) throws an uncaught `SyntaxError: Invalid selector` when the target's `id`/`name` contains quote characters, because both components interpolate raw values into `querySelector`/`querySelectorAll`:

- Error summary: `` document.querySelector(`label[for='${id}']`) `` breaks for ids like `child's-name` (legal HTML5). The throw aborts the click handler before focus/scroll, verified with the real module under jsdom.
- Checkboxes: `` querySelectorAll(`input[type="checkbox"][name="${name}"]`) `` (×2 call sites) breaks for names like `a"b`. The exclusive ("None of these") unchecking never runs, so a contradictory state can be submitted.

No `CSS.escape` is used anywhere in `src/`. Related #1808/#1809 fixed other interpolation paths but left these two open.

## Expected

Escape the interpolated values with `CSS.escape()` (supported by every browser in the support matrix) so special-character ids/names keep working.

backlog.title: Invite users to a private or public beta
backlog.body:
What
When testing a new version of a service, it's important to limit the number of users that use it at first.
First with an opt-in approach at Private Beta. One way of doing this would be sending out an email if you know users email before they use the service, although this is increasingly difficult to GDPR. You can promote the Private Beta ahead of time using social media and other advertising channels and collect contact details of people who are interested. Another (less public) way is to find users through professional networks they are members of. This is particularly useful for services where people are using it as part of their job.
Then, at Public Beta the service can move to an opt-out approach. The new service becomes the default promoted option, but there should include a link to the old legacy service as there may be unforeseen issues with the new service not found in Private Beta which means some users need to use the old version.
These are high-level principles – It would be good if people can populate the comments on this issue with real-life examples and how well the approach worked to de-risk the rollout of services and help teams learn and iterate.
Why


What evidence do you have that it's needed by multiple services across government?


This is something that all new government services need to do to follow the agile delivery phases.


What evidence do you have that it meets the needs of the users of those services?


I've personally not seen methodical evidence per se for this approach although it makes sense logically and is commonly used across government. As mentioned above, it would be great if people have any evidence for its efficacy.


Have you checked that it doesn't already exist in the GOV.UK Design System?


Yes
Anything else

Include links to any examples, research or code to support your proposal, if available.

Arguably this belongs more in the Service Manual than the Design System. There is already a page about how the beta phase works, but I think the detail of implementation belongs more in the Design System.

ourIssues.title: Problems with New Transport font for vision impaired users
ourIssues.body:
## Description of the issue

The New Transport font, now used across www.gov.uk and any site on the `.service.gov.uk` domain, can be hard to read for vision impaired users. Those affected have to use custom stylesheets or forced colour modes (Windows High Contrast Mode or changing colours in Firefox) to achieve a high enough contrast.

This was reported by the 'Low vision' tester at the Digital Accessibility Centre (DAC), in an audit commissioned by GOV.UK Notify.

Their comment was:

> The font used for GOV.UK provides little in terms of legibility experienced by some user
> groups such the Vision impaired, Elderly and dyslexic. As a vision impaired user, who does
> not rely on assistive technology, the font provides a lightly rendered grey, translucent
> display which allows the contrast to be affected by the background glare creating a grey and
> difficult to focus reading platform despite the measured high contrast. The reading and
> absorption of information is impacted particularly during longer periods of navigation.
> The New Transport font or GDS transport as it is alternatively referred to, is a digitalised
> version of the road traffic signs seen across Britain’s roads. When viewed on Gov.uk, for me,
> the digitalization does not transfer well. When analysed, the contrast ratio returned a 19.6:1
> ratio. This contrast should look black however the opaque styling of the font reduces this
> appearance as background glare appears to leak through the font body.
> 
> As a result, for a low vision perspective, this impacts on the ability to read successfully for
> periods of time as reading fatigue quickly sets in making larger bodies of text difficult to
> read and absorb its information.
> As with the traffic signs, the heavier font and increased size renders well with the white text
> set on a deep blue background seen on UK motorways. The lighter, thinner digital version
> bears no resemblance to the physical seen on our roads. As a result, improvement in clarity
> with additional weight, up to 500 together with a #000000 hex code, may provide all users a
> better-rounded and less transparent readable font which should provide a sharper text
> appearance capable of absorbing background glare to improve prolonged reading and
> overall UX. These improvements will also relate to mobile devices where currently a
> negative reading experience prevails.
> 
> As a result, I personally must use the GOV.UK products with a custom stylesheet to improve
> the font appearance and increase overall UX.
> 
> [Talking about using a custom stylesheet to force all text into the Franklin Gothic Medium font]
> The heavier font provides an example of a sharper text appearance with a truer contrast
> enabling improved reading experience. With no alternative stylesheets available on any GOV.UK
> pages, this will only be available to experienced users with the knowledge to create their own
> stylesheet and therefore cannot be relied upon for all users.
> 
> Other options include inverting contrast via the Windows operating system and using the
> shortcut keys shift>alt>print-screen to provide a high-viz version of the screen. This
> eliminates glare and provides sharper text appearance which improves the ability to read
> and absorb the page information.
> 
> This however may hide some functionality and only effective on Edge and IE browsers.
> Other browsers rely on add-ons to do this which are not as effective.
> The font quality differs depending on the screen resolution as higher quality monitors
> provide a better view however, the font does not improve when viewed on lower quality or
> lower resolution screens. This also impacts on mobile devices where the font is naturally
> smaller.
> providing text/contrast options via alternative stylesheets or widgets within the GDS
> platforms are recommended to help all users establish an improved custom, Gov.Uk
> experience and provide a personalised platform to suit a user’s needs.

I can share the full audit and contact details for DAC if required.

## Steps to reproduce the issue

Because the issue seems to occur for users with a visual impairment, I would guess that you would need to test with those types of users.

## Actual vs expected behaviour

The tester expected to be able to read the text without issue but found problems related to how the design of the font interacted with their view of the web page.

## Environment (where applicable)

GOV.UK Notify currently uses version 2.13.0 but the tester mentions experiencing this issue on the www.gov.uk website, so likely they were viewing pages using a more recent version.

The tester was using Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge on Windows (latest versions) for the audit but they mention experiencing this issue on mobile devices and other different screens. See their comment in the description for their exact words.

ourIssues.title: WCAG 2.2: Start using a service ‖ Consistent Help
ourIssues.body:
## What

Consider adding or updating a screenshot of a start page to include visible help or contact information on the page, displayed in a consistent manner. Related to #2882. 

This is largely a usability suggestion and may not be necessary for WCAG compliance. 

### Resources

- [Start using a service pattern guidance](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/start-using-a-service/)
- [WCAG 2.2 criterion for 'Consistent Help'](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/consistent-help.html)

## Why

The new WCAG 2.2 Level A criterion 'Consistent Help' says:

> If a [Web page](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/consistent-help.html#dfn-web-page) contains any of the following help [mechanisms](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/consistent-help.html#), and those mechanisms are repeated on multiple Web pages within a [set of Web pages](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/consistent-help.html#dfn-set-of-web-pages), they occur in the same order relative to other page content, unless a change is initiated by the user:
> * Human contact details;
> * Human contact mechanism;
> * Self-help option;
> * A fully automated contact mechanism.

Although the intent of the criterion is that the contact information itself is consistently ordered with respect to the rest of the page (i.e. a help link is always in the same place in the footer, as described in #2871) we can go beyond this by advising that teams provide this information in a consistent order every time it appears.

For example, if a service has three contact mechanisms—phone, email address, post—these should be listed in the same order and format on all pages where it appears, such as the service start page, support pages, contact page, etc. 

## Who needs to work on this
- Content designer or technical writer

## Who needs to review this
- Accessibility specialist
- Content designer or technical writer

## Done when

- [ ] Guidance has been updated

backlog.title: Contribution submission for Exit this page component
backlog.body:
Formerly known as 'Hide this page component'
What
What are we proposing
We are looking to implement a component, using the existing button component, that allows vulnerable users of a Government service to quickly and safely hide the page and reduce the risk of Domestic Abuse incidents.
The functionality behind the component would allow a user to quickly hide the current page and open a new, ambiguous webpage, such as BBC Weather or another such website. This would lower the risk of drawing attention to browsing habits from a perpetrator.
Why
Why are we proposing this design pattern?

Domestic abuse is physical, sexual, psychological or financial abuse that takes place within an intimate or family-type relationship and that forms a pattern of forceful and controlling behaviour. This can include forced marriage and so-called ‘honour-based crimes.” Domestic abuse may include a range of abusive behaviours, not all of which are in themselves inherently ‘violent’

The biggest risk to a victim of Domestic Abuse is homicide and serious physical assaults - this is at its greatest risk when a victim is planning to flee or escape from the perpetrator. Often, one of the first things a victim will do is to speak to someone to make a disclosure about abuse. The second thing they will do is research and find help online, often using Government services.
We need to ensure that the risk is minimised for users when using online services. Although victims and survivors can be aware of the risks, it is the Government's responsibility to protect individuals using a service. Therefore, it is crucial that there is a consistency of approach in design and functionality across Government with this component.
What evidence do you have that it's needed by multiple services across government?
From conversations between the Department for Work and Pensions, Ministry of Justice, the Cabinet Office and Scottish Government, it is already clear that other services need to ensure that this design is available.
Services are already responding to the rise in Domestic Abuse during COVID-19 by building their own minimum viable solutions to allow users to quickly hide their webpages.
There are areas of the Government site, such as “Domestic Abuse: How to get help”, that a high risk user would access for support that does not include a way to hide their browsing. This is putting those users of this service at risk.
What evidence do you have that it meets the needs of the users of those services?
Speaking with subject matter experts (SME), it is critical that we offer this feature on the GOV.UK website. It is a feature that is provided by other organisations, such as:

Scottish Government - Domestic Abuse page
Refuge
Women’s Aid
Victim Support

Each website has varied design implementations, but ultimately addresses the same user need of being able to hide browsing habits quickly.
The Ministry of Justice have carried out some initial research with an SME to establish whether the proposed solution meets the user needs.
Have you checked that it doesn't already exist in the GOV.UK Design System?
There are no outstanding issues or tickets in the Design System backlog that refer to this type of component.
Anything else
What else has been done
The MoJ have iterated twice on the design component on our live service - looking at language, design and functionality.
There are several designs that are considered minimum viable products which have been released by the DWP (Child Maintenance Service) - Cabinet Office (Coronavirus Support) and the MoJ (Legal Aid Agency). The expediency of these releases has been due to the fact that by not having something, we are putting our users at risk.
The MoJ have carried out some early rounds of testing with an SME that have looked at design, functionality and various use cases from a range of user scenarios. This has all been documented and shared with DWP and CO to share research and findings.
Designs
We looked to extend the GOV.UK Button component to act as the interactive element that a user would press to exit the website.
The Design System suggests using red for any destructive actions undertaken on a GOV.UK website - as the intention for the 'Hide this page' button was essentially closing the webpage down, it would be deemed destructive. This has been adopted by DWP and the Scottish Government.
We decided to utilise the additional space available in the 1/3 column, which is usually reserved for additional information as it allowed us to present the button within immediate view for the user.
The button would then be "sticky" in position at the top of the page on smaller devices. This prevents any conflict with the GOV.UK 'Contents' link that is positioned at the bottom of the screen. It also removes potential accidental presses by a user who doesn't need to use it.
Feedback from SME on the design

Victims of Domestic Abuse are used to using their reptilian brain and are in fight or flight mode so the red would be a trigger for them to draw their to attention to it - Comment from SME

Content
The language used in the button has recently been changed in order to create a more unified style as we continue to work with DWP, Cabinet Office and the Scottish Government. The use of 'Hide this page' presented more of a sense of immediacy, as well as being more descriptive of what the button actually does when the user interacts with it, so we have moved away from the original 'Quick Exit'.
We also use a keyboard function for the user to be able to interact with the button which is controlled by pressing the 'Esc' key.
Behaviour and Functionality
We have explored several types of behaviour for the button, however in order to provide the greatest amount of safety for users we decided to implement functionality similar to other charities and organisations.
When a user interacts with the button, they are sent to a new browser tab that opens BBC Weather. The original tab that they were on doesn't close, but redirects to Google.
This component does not prescribe which websites are to be linked to. That is best done by the individual services and their user research combined with the knowledge of their user base. Google and BBC Weather are good neutral examples pending further research.
Accessibility
The Legal Aid Agency have had an Accessibility Audit on their service and this highlighted some improvements to the component. These were:

Ensuring the button text accurately describes it's purpose
Ensure the instruction "(Or press 'Esc' key)" is presented to all users when presented as a sticky element
Include visually hidden text at the top of the page to help users of assistive technology be aware of the leave page functionality
Differentiate betwixt mobile displays and PC displays zoomed in, so the information about using the escape key is not hidden for non-mobile narrow displays

These changes have been implemented in the latest version of the component, however we will be looking to further test the accessibility of the component as we continue to iterate on it.
MoJ Data Analytics
The 'Hide this page' button has been running as an MVP on the Check Legal Aid service since 14 April 2020. It has been used with a fair amount of frequency, however at present we are are yet to analyse the data in more detail.
The gaps in data recording were due to changes on the back-end of our service that caused GA to drop out.
Graph data since 14 April 2020

The below graph data also shows variations in spikes and lower use through the pandemic

backlog.title: Suggested new component - Side menu
backlog.body:
What

Give a brief description of the style, component or pattern you want to propose.

Context:
We are in the final stages of building an e-learning service using the GDS design system. We have completed numerous rounds of user testing and already gone through one Alpha and Beta Assessment.
What:
A right-hand sidebar navigation menu which allows users to easily see their progression through a course and be able to navigate back and forth through chapters.
Current version

In-situ

Iterations from user testing

Why

Explain why you think this should be added to the GOV.UK Design System.

In our alpha assessment, we were challenged to explore if there was a user need to see their progression through the course and also to be able to navigate back and forth through the chapters. We tested various variations of a sidebar navigation similar to those found in lots of e-learning platforms. During testing, we found that some users naturally used the sidebar to return to topics earlier in the course and used it to be aware of their progression and estimate their completion time.
Design-wise, we didn’t want to reinvent the wheel so we built on existing sidebar navigation patterns from GOV.UK publishing such as the contents list on the publishing service (https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/contents_list) and the related content sidebar on many start pages. We iterated the design several times to make it simple and accessible. For instance, we made some headers in the sidebar visually hidden so they would give context to screen reader users whilst avoiding confusion for sighted users who had initially struggled with the previous design.


What evidence do you have that it's needed by multiple services across government?


In the our beta assessment, we were praised on our work developing this pattern and asked to play it back into the community:
‘the team has validated the user need to track progress within training modules, has designed a pattern that is working for their beta users, and is planning to continue iterating this pattern - the panel would encourage the team to share this pattern and research findings with the design system community’


What evidence do you have that it meets the needs of the users of those services?


We have tested and validated this component in several rounds of qual research with 5-10 people in each round, and in Private Beta testing with over 1200 people (with quant showing that people successfully use this when required, and qual feedback only positive and no negative on the latest version).
Our user testing so far has validated the need for this component and as mentioned has been praised so far by assessors. But we would love to share it with the community to get a wider perspective and possible use cases.


Have you checked that it doesn't already exist in the GOV.UK Design System?


Yes
Anything else

Include links to any examples, research or code to support your proposal, if available.

ourIssues.title: Components assume the `govuk-visually-hidden` utility class will exist
ourIssues.body:
## Description of the issue

We provide an entry points for each individual component, the idea being that users should get all of the CSS they need to use that component, and ideally nothing more.

For example, including the character count component also includes the CSS for the:

- error message
- hint
- label
- textarea

However, it does _not_ include the `govuk-visually-hidden` utility class, which is used within the Nunjucks template.

From a quick check, it looks like this affects:

- Accordion (in the JavaScript)
- Character count (in the JavaScript)
- Error message (in the Nunjucks template)
- Exit this page (in the Nunjucks template and JavaScript)
- File upload (in the JavaScript)
- Footer (in the Nunjucks template)
- Pagination (in the Nunjucks template)
- Password input (in the JavaScript)
- Summary list (in the Nunjucks template)
- Warning text (in the Nunjucks template)

## Steps to reproduce the issue

Use the component-specific entrypoint to include just the CSS for any of the components listed above, then view the component

## Actual vs expected behaviour

Visually hidden text should be hidden, but it isn't because the `govuk-visually-hidden` utility class is not included in the CSS

ourIssues.title: Add option to footer component allowing ‘The following links open in a new tab’ guidance to be followed
ourIssues.body: ## Related component Footer ## Context My team has received a request to have one of our services's footer links open in new tabs. We want to follow the [guidance](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/styles/links/#opening-links-in-a-new-tab) for this scenario: > If you’re displaying lots of links together and want to save space and avoid repetition, consider doing both of the following: > * adding a line of text before the links saying ‘The following links open in a new tab’ > * including (opens in new tab) as part of the link text, so that part of the link text is visually hidden but still accessible to screen readers However, there's no approved html example of implementing the ‘The following links open in a new tab’ text above the links. Moreover, there's no option providing this in the nunjucks macro, which is what our team relies on. Issue [#1782](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/1782) noticed this absence back in 2020, but unfortunately nothing came of it; see also [its sibling issue](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/issues/1219) on `govuk-design-system`. I also note that the ONS Design System has an implementation in place for this accessibility principle in [their footer macro](https://service-manual.ons.gov.uk/design-system/components/footer#example.example-footer-transactional.nunjucks), an option they call `"newTabWarning"`. Perhaps this could be a model for bringing this feature into GDS? ## Alternatives In the short term we will likely have to follow whatever html implementation the team that's asking us to make this change has made at their end. However for consistency across our services, it's desirable for us to be able to use the macro in all of them, due to how they share parent templates.

ourIssues.title: Update to 'Exit this page' default text may cause issues for voice control users
ourIssues.body: https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/pull/3989 updated the default content of the 'Exit this page' button to add 'Emergency' as visually-hidden text at the start of the button. Adding visually-hidden content to the start or middle of text on interactive elements can cause issues activating them for voice control users (eg Dragon, Apple Voice Control) because the label exposed to these tools ('Emergency Exit this page') doesn't match what the user will say ("Click 'Exit this page'"). Generally voice control needs an exact match on the start of the string, but anything extra at the end is fine - so making it something like `Exit this page in an emergency` would probably be OK. References: https://www.smashingmagazine.com/2022/06/voice-control-usability-considerations-partially-visually-hidden-link-names/#problems-with-partially-visually-hidden-text https://www.sarasoueidan.com/blog/accessible-text-labels/#improving-the-experience-for-screen-reader-users-whilst-keeping-it-accessible-to-speech-input-users I haven't tested yet but I have access to Dragon so I'll test in that to confirm ASAP. I just spotted this change in the v5 beta release notes and wanted to flag it as quickly as possible.

ourIssues.title: Error message: Remove hardcoded content order
ourIssues.body: ## What Error messages currently contain a fixed content order, which is hardcoded into the component's Nunjucks template. This is composed of a block of visually-hidden text (`visuallyHiddenText`, defaults to 'Error') followed by a colon (:), a hardcoded space, then the configured error message (`html` or `text`). This prefixes the message with 'error' for screen readers, so that the context of the message announced up-front and is easier to understand. For example, the component may currently output this text: ```html Error: Enter an event name ``` ## Why Having a hardcoded content order can make it more difficult to appropriately localise the string. In particular, the currently hardcoded colon and space characters are incompatible with certain languages. Some logographic written languages—such as Chinese and Japanese—use a fixed-width colon character that fits better alongside logograms, and don't include a space after it. ```html 错误：输入事件名称 エラー：イベント名を入力してください ``` Translators may also find that the 'Error' label being visible is more useful to their target users—as red does not indicate incorrectness or danger in all cultures (it symbolises happiness and prosperity in Chinese culture, for example). Although it is currently possible for services to pass HTML into the error message and remove the initial 'Error:' section by setting `visuallyHiddenText` to `false`, we may want to investigate methods of either making `visuallyHiddenText` work with other languages, incorporating the colon and space into the editable area, or removing the use of a dedicated parameter and hardcoded text in favour of only using the `html` parameter. ## Who needs to work on this Developers ## Who needs to review this Developers ## Done when - [ ] Investigate methods of making the error message support non-English languages. - [ ] Make changes to the Nunjucks template and related tests, if we decide to make modifications. - [ ] Document any changes to Nunjucks parameters.

ourIssues.title: Summary list: Allow customisation of full action link content
ourIssues.body: ## What Currently, action links in the Summary list have a hardcoded content order of the action name (`html` or `text`), followed by an area of visually hidden text (`visuallyHiddenText`). The visually hidden text includes a hardcoded space separating it from the prior text, and is usually the same or similar to the key for the current row. For example: ```html change name delete address ``` ## Why This fixed ordering doesn't accommodate localisation into languages where this text appears in a different order. For example, in German we might have this: ```html Namen ändern Adresse löschen ``` Having a hardcoded space is also undesirable in certain languages, such as Chinese: ```html 更换名字 删除名称 ``` Although it is currently possible for services to pass HTML into the action links and ignore the `visuallyHiddenText` parameter completely, we may want to investigate methods of either making `visuallyHiddenText` work with other languages, or removing the use of a dedicated/hardcoded parameter in favour of using the `html` parameter. ## Who needs to work on this Developers ## Who needs to review this Developers ## Done when - [ ] Investigate ways that `visuallyHiddenText` could work with non-English languages. - [ ] Make changes to the Nunjucks template and related tests, if we decide to make modifications. - [ ] Document any changes to Nunjucks parameters.

ourIssues.title: Ability to group radio buttons / checkboxes within sub-headings
ourIssues.body:
Hi.

I'm wondering how best to support radio buttons (and checkboxes) which have sub-groups with headings?

Currently, you can use multiple `govukRadios` macros which share the same `name` attribute, however because they use a `data-module` attribute to scope the conditional reveals, these don't work properly across the groups.

Alternatively, you can using a single macro and put headings in using `divider`s, but these don't currently support HTML markup.

On a related not, it's unclear whether the best output would be nested `<fieldset>`s with `<legend>`s, or a single `<fieldset>` with headings and either aria attributes or visually-hidden prefixes to associate labels with their headings.

ourIssues.title: Review the use of aria-label on a <ul> element in the site navigation menu
ourIssues.body:
## What
We use an `aria-label` on our sub-navigation list `<ul>`. This causes HTML validation issues, so we need to make the call on whether we keep it as an exception, add an explicit `aria-role` to keep validation happy, or get rid of it and find another solution.

## Why
Previously, we added an `aria-label` to the main site nav's Community sub-menu to make a better experience for screenreaders:  https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/commit/4ff06e4961bcd4a147d580d1d5ac2736fe9f6ec3

Recently, we [added HTML linting](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/pull/2569), and it flagged this as `aria-label-misuse`.

If we assign an explicit `role` to the labelled list, the HTML validator is sated and complains no longer.

However, it's a bit unclear which `role` we'd want to add - `navigation` is out since this subnav is already contained within a `nav` parent, and `menu` [might not be right for this situation](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/pull/2569#discussion_r1115422380).

We could avoid this debate if we just find a solution that doesn't involve ARIA. First step would probably be to just remove the `aria-label` and test whether it reads fine in multiple screenreaders.

If it’s missing context without the aria-label, we could look at using a bit of ‘visually-hidden’ instead of an aria-label. Would need to test to see if it works consistently across all screen readers though.

## Who needs to work on this
Developer, Accessibility specialist(?)

## Who needs to review this
Developer, Accessibility specialist

## Done when

- [ ] We have a solution that is both valid HTML, and a good experience for screenreaders.
- [ ] We have implemented that solution (this will likely involve [removing the inline validation exception](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/blob/9ba07459f46a6e9738067c7ec90da6dd22f3a1b6/views/partials/_navigation.njk#L14))

ourIssues.title: HTML and Nunjucks tabs not descriptive when using JAWS
ourIssues.body: The tabs don't contain hidden text like the other elements. So, when you list them in JAWS you get a list which resembles the following: - HTML - Nunjucks - HTML - Nunjucks - HTML - Nunjucks Other elements have visually hidden text, so when you list the elements they still make sense for example: ```html Open this button example in a new window ``` When you list the links with JAWS you get a list which resembles the following: - open this button example in a new window - open this start button example in a new window - open this secondary button example in a new window ## Steps to reproduce the issue Use `CTRL + INSERT + C` to list all aria-controls and combo-boxes in JAWS. ## Suggestion Adding the same visually hidden identifier to the HTML and Nunjucks tabs so they read something like: - HTML code example for button - Nunjucks code example for button - HTML code example for start button - Nunjucks code example for start button

ourIssues.title: Details - last child margin rule misses nested elements

## Description of the issue If we have `

` or `

    ` elements inside a Details block, then their bottom margin is removed by a rule which looks like this in the browser: ``` .govuk-details__text>:last-child { margin-bottom: 0; } ``` which comes from [here](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/4fb2d91b86a0d807902b09d070ffc38f16442f97/src/govuk/components/details/_index.scss#L85) The problem we are having is that if the `

    ` or `

      ` element is nested, e.g. inside a `
      ` or another `
        ` then it escapes this rule and the bottom margin is wrong. This general issue is discussed here: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/31457798/best-usage-of-css-last-child-selector-in-nested-elements ## Steps to reproduce the issue Page content like this is mis-styled: ``` {% macro no_nino_details() %}

        {{ "no_nino__explanation" | translate }}

        ...
        • {{ "document__birth_marriage_etc" | translate }}

            ...
          • {{ "benefits__other" | translate }}

communityIssues.body:
## What:

The auditor has suggested that links in the [document list](https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/document_list) appear like headings because they are bigger and bold and are heading some content. Therefore they should also be headings in the code.

**Example URLs:**

* https://www.gov.uk/contact
* https://www.gov.uk/corporate-information
* https://www.gov.uk/search/all

Another one that was flagged up but shows where it definitely doesn't make any sense to "fix" is https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/brexit-guidance.

But sometimes they are more clearly heading things, other times they aren't. They’re not always heading something useful (like just a date on the Brexit guidance) and would be bad as headings in that case. Although inconsistency would be worse, if some were headings and others weren’t.

This needs some investigation and might not need any fixing.

Anika's advice would be to probably NOT make them headings, or at the very least think very hard about it first.

## Why:

Many screen reader users are used to navigating via headings. Having headings here might make it slightly easier to navigate and understand the content but too many headings are not good for accessibility either. Too little or too much structure makes a page harder to navigate. It's about getting the right balance.

## Prioritisation score: `3`

Reach: `3`, Severity: `2`, Effort: `2`

backlog.title: Contribution submission for Exit this page component
backlog.body:
Formerly known as 'Hide this page component'
What
What are we proposing
We are looking to implement a component, using the existing button component, that allows vulnerable users of a Government service to quickly and safely hide the page and reduce the risk of Domestic Abuse incidents.
The functionality behind the component would allow a user to quickly hide the current page and open a new, ambiguous webpage, such as BBC Weather or another such website. This would lower the risk of drawing attention to browsing habits from a perpetrator.
Why
Why are we proposing this design pattern?

Domestic abuse is physical, sexual, psychological or financial abuse that takes place within an intimate or family-type relationship and that forms a pattern of forceful and controlling behaviour. This can include forced marriage and so-called ‘honour-based crimes.” Domestic abuse may include a range of abusive behaviours, not all of which are in themselves inherently ‘violent’

The biggest risk to a victim of Domestic Abuse is homicide and serious physical assaults - this is at its greatest risk when a victim is planning to flee or escape from the perpetrator. Often, one of the first things a victim will do is to speak to someone to make a disclosure about abuse. The second thing they will do is research and find help online, often using Government services.
We need to ensure that the risk is minimised for users when using online services. Although victims and survivors can be aware of the risks, it is the Government's responsibility to protect individuals using a service. Therefore, it is crucial that there is a consistency of approach in design and functionality across Government with this component.
What evidence do you have that it's needed by multiple services across government?
From conversations between the Department for Work and Pensions, Ministry of Justice, the Cabinet Office and Scottish Government, it is already clear that other services need to ensure that this design is available.
Services are already responding to the rise in Domestic Abuse during COVID-19 by building their own minimum viable solutions to allow users to quickly hide their webpages.
There are areas of the Government site, such as “Domestic Abuse: How to get help”, that a high risk user would access for support that does not include a way to hide their browsing. This is putting those users of this service at risk.
What evidence do you have that it meets the needs of the users of those services?
Speaking with subject matter experts (SME), it is critical that we offer this feature on the GOV.UK website. It is a feature that is provided by other organisations, such as:

Scottish Government - Domestic Abuse page
Refuge
Women’s Aid
Victim Support

Each website has varied design implementations, but ultimately addresses the same user need of being able to hide browsing habits quickly.
The Ministry of Justice have carried out some initial research with an SME to establish whether the proposed solution meets the user needs.
Have you checked that it doesn't already exist in the GOV.UK Design System?
There are no outstanding issues or tickets in the Design System backlog that refer to this type of component.
Anything else
What else has been done
The MoJ have iterated twice on the design component on our live service - looking at language, design and functionality.
There are several designs that are considered minimum viable products which have been released by the DWP (Child Maintenance Service) - Cabinet Office (Coronavirus Support) and the MoJ (Legal Aid Agency). The expediency of these releases has been due to the fact that by not having something, we are putting our users at risk.
The MoJ have carried out some early rounds of testing with an SME that have looked at design, functionality and various use cases from a range of user scenarios. This has all been documented and shared with DWP and CO to share research and findings.
Designs
We looked to extend the GOV.UK Button component to act as the interactive element that a user would press to exit the website.
The Design System suggests using red for any destructive actions undertaken on a GOV.UK website - as the intention for the 'Hide this page' button was essentially closing the webpage down, it would be deemed destructive. This has been adopted by DWP and the Scottish Government.
We decided to utilise the additional space available in the 1/3 column, which is usually reserved for additional information as it allowed us to present the button within immediate view for the user.
The button would then be "sticky" in position at the top of the page on smaller devices. This prevents any conflict with the GOV.UK 'Contents' link that is positioned at the bottom of the screen. It also removes potential accidental presses by a user who doesn't need to use it.
Feedback from SME on the design

Victims of Domestic Abuse are used to using their reptilian brain and are in fight or flight mode so the red would be a trigger for them to draw their to attention to it - Comment from SME

Content
The language used in the button has recently been changed in order to create a more unified style as we continue to work with DWP, Cabinet Office and the Scottish Government. The use of 'Hide this page' presented more of a sense of immediacy, as well as being more descriptive of what the button actually does when the user interacts with it, so we have moved away from the original 'Quick Exit'.
We also use a keyboard function for the user to be able to interact with the button which is controlled by pressing the 'Esc' key.
Behaviour and Functionality
We have explored several types of behaviour for the button, however in order to provide the greatest amount of safety for users we decided to implement functionality similar to other charities and organisations.
When a user interacts with the button, they are sent to a new browser tab that opens BBC Weather. The original tab that they were on doesn't close, but redirects to Google.
This component does not prescribe which websites are to be linked to. That is best done by the individual services and their user research combined with the knowledge of their user base. Google and BBC Weather are good neutral examples pending further research.
Accessibility
The Legal Aid Agency have had an Accessibility Audit on their service and this highlighted some improvements to the component. These were:

Ensuring the button text accurately describes it's purpose
Ensure the instruction "(Or press 'Esc' key)" is presented to all users when presented as a sticky element
Include visually hidden text at the top of the page to help users of assistive technology be aware of the leave page functionality
Differentiate betwixt mobile displays and PC displays zoomed in, so the information about using the escape key is not hidden for non-mobile narrow displays

These changes have been implemented in the latest version of the component, however we will be looking to further test the accessibility of the component as we continue to iterate on it.
MoJ Data Analytics
The 'Hide this page' button has been running as an MVP on the Check Legal Aid service since 14 April 2020. It has been used with a fair amount of frequency, however at present we are are yet to analyse the data in more detail.
The gaps in data recording were due to changes on the back-end of our service that caused GA to drop out.
Graph data since 14 April 2020

The below graph data also shows variations in spikes and lower use through the pandemic

Examples



MoJ
DWP

ourIssues.title: VoiceOver on Safari cannot navigate into open Accordion section text content
ourIssues.body:
## Description of the issue

VoiceOver users in Safari browsers are not able to access the text content of open accordion sections. They are only able to access links.

Originally raised by [this zendesk ticket (internal to team only)](https://govuk.zendesk.com/agent/tickets/6881808?brand_id=3194076).

## Steps to reproduce the issue

Using VoiceOver on a Safari browser:

1. go to the [default Accordion example](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/accordion/default/)
2. navigate to one of the Accordion sections
3. open the section
4. attempt to navigate further down into the contents of the section

## Actual vs expected behaviour

Expected behaviour is that VoiceOver navigates into the section content and reads it out normally. Instead it skips the open section and continues to the next section heading.

You can also try this with the [example with summaries](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/accordion/with-summary-section/) where all the sections only contain links which are navigable using VoiceOver.

## Environment (where applicable)

- Operating system: MacOS 26.7
- Browser: Safari desktop
- Browser version: 26.7
- GOV.UK Frontend Version: At least 4.5.0

## Additional information

The reason for this is very likely the Accordion using `hidden="until-found` as an enhancement which we introduced in 4.5.0 via https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/pull/3053. There _was_ a [WebKit bug raised regarding this](https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=310623) which noted an error with `hidden="until-found"` in Safari not properly updating the accessibility tree in response to content expanding or collapsing. It's listed as solved but from testing is not fixed. The solution to this bug may therefore simply be to push for this getting fixed again.

ourIssues.title: Support standard .html/.text input for `caption` on `table` component
ourIssues.body:
## Related component

Yes, https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/table/

## Context

Currently the `caption` argument in the nunjucks macro only takes a string, not the more standard "object with `html` and `text` options". This means users may not be able to pass through html they may need to unless they look into the implementation and find that html is possible to enter, but even then, users need to `| safe` the input themselves. This is unintuitive, and many other arguments in other macros have this object input pattern, rather than just a straight string.

## Alternatives

Yes, passing in a string I have put through the `safe` filter myself.

## Additional information (if applicable)

I wanted to do this myself recently as a result of an accessibility audit, so this isn't just a hypothetical, it's a real need.
I undertook making this change with AI assistance in my fork of govuk-frontend here https://github.com/ReedSoftware/govuk-frontend/pull/1 - after some talk with the GDS team, I'm aware that your stance on AI generated PRs isn't set yet, so I'm happy to leave it as a talking point or reference, but also happy to raise a PR against this change if you did decide you wanted it!

There was also some talk on the GDS channel in x-gov slack about this with @romaricpascal @selfthinker - thank you for your inputs here so far.

ourIssues.title: Consider wrapping Task list onto a single column on narrow viewports
ourIssues.body: ## Related component [Task list](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/task-list/) ## Context Historically (even before it was part of the GOV.UK Design System), the Task list component has retained a two column layout across all viewport sizes, with each row displaying the task name and detail on the left and status on the right. This was originally contributed when our default font size on mobile devices was 16px equivalent, which worked quite well, with space for roughly 3 to 5 words per line. However, the new typography scale increased the font size to 19px equivalent, which became the default in Frontend 6.0.0. This has resulted in long names or detail being squashed into long, narrow, somewhat harder to read columns with anywhere from 1 to 3 words per line. We might want to update the component so that the content is displayed in a single column on narrow viewports. |Old type scale|New type scale| |:-:|:-:| ||| ## Alternatives This problem is somewhat dependent on the text of the status labels. Rows with longer statuses naturally get more squashed than shorter ones, and the shorter the task name and detail, the less there is to squash. Thus one way to 'avoid' the issue is to place less text in the component. ## Additional information (if applicable) Only started being an issue in 5.2.0, if the user enabled the new typography scale. As of 6.0.0 this is the default scale.

ourIssues.title: Add the ability to customise the classes on pagination links
ourIssues.body:
## Related component

[Pagination](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/pagination/)

## Context

Currently it isn't possible to add custom classes to individual links (neither items nor the previous/next links) within the pagination.

This limits the possibility of applying different or customised styling to them, such as [removing the visited state](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/styles/links/#links-without-a-visited-state). 

## Alternatives

If using the Nunjucks macro, these links can only be changed through writing additional CSS that hooks onto the component's wrapper. 

Otherwise, the user must use the pure HTML version of the component or fork the macro themselves.

## Additional information

This feature was requested by a user via support.

Being able to remove visited states particularly seems like a useful function for search result pages, where the URL for a page may not be unique even though the page content is totally different.

ourIssues.title: Consider adding functionality to Exit this page to accept an array of redirects and use one at random
ourIssues.body:
## Related component

- [Exit this page](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/exit-this-page/)

## Context

Following a recent blog post I made about the Exit this Page component, a commenter suggested that users _always_ being directed to BBC Weather could raise suspicion in a vulnerable user. This is especially the case if they need to use the exit functionality several times in a relatively short period and are redirected to BBC Weather every time. 

To counter this, we could allow services to pass an array of multiple services into the EtP component and have the component choose one of these at random upon each activation to redirect to.

## Alternatives

A service could write server-side code to change the target for the EtP button on each page load, 

## Additional information (if applicable)

There would still need to be a 'main' redirect that exists as the `href` of the link used as a no-JS fallback. I'm not sure we have a defined format for passing an array via `data-*` attributes either, so this functionality may have to be limited to JavaScript configuration.

ourIssues.title: Add content to Skip link guidance about problem caused by preservation of fragment identifiers between pages
ourIssues.body:
The skip link component adds a `#main-content` fragment identifier to the current URL. This can persist across pages causing an unexpected jump to the main content area on load. I'd like to add a warning about this to the guidance, along with tips about ways teams could write their code to avoid this. 

## Related component

https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/skip-link/

## Context

This problem has been seen to happen in the following scenario:
- the skip link was used, thereby adding `#main-content` to the current URL
- you leave the page via a successful form submission
- the form doesn't set the `action` attribute and so POSTs to the current URL
- the server uses [the POST -> Redirect -> GET pattern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post/Redirect/Get) to navigate to the next page

Given all that, the browser will preserve `#main-content` in the new URL[^1] causing the next page to jump to the start of the main content area when it loads.

This was picked up as an issue by the Digital Accessibility Centre (DAC) in a recent audit of GOV.UK Notify[^2], who stated that it failed [the WCAG 2.4.3 (Focus Order) success criteria](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG20/Understanding/focus-order).

Given [the POST -> Redirect -> GET pattern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post/Redirect/Get) is so commonly used in web apps, I think there's some value in making teams aware of this problem and helping them write their code in a way that stops it happening.

## Alternatives

N/A

## Additional information (if applicable)

Suggested changes, to stop the problem occurring are:
- setting the `action` attribute on the `<form>` tag to match the current URL, without `#main-content`
- setting the URL for the next page explicitly using the [Content-Location](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Content-Location) header

## References

[^1]: This is correct behaviour, as defined in [Handling of fragment identifiers in redirected URLs](https://www.w3.org/Protocols/HTTP/Fragment/draft-bos-http-redirect-00.txt)
[^2]: Issue 'ID: DAC_Focus_order_01' on page 19 of [the audit report](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jRkkL3AZj-7Q0uo7yfHUv_JF9q0Ecw6g/view?usp=sharing) (needs a GDS Google account for access)

ourIssues.title: Allow multiple components to be attached to an element
ourIssues.body:
## Related component Relates to any component that is initialised with the `data-module` attribute and might cross-over with another component that uses the same element. I've outlined this with a service-specific example because it's easier to describe, but my main concern here is with other component libraries which would benefit from seamless integration with the Design System, and where service teams have less say over the implementation details. ## Context Imagine my service has a bespoke component based by [Bootstrap's Popover component](https://getbootstrap.com/docs/4.0/components/popovers/). We initialise all our components following the Design System pattern, so in this case with a `data-module="app-popover"` attribute. I want to add a popover to a button, which I also want to behave like a [Button component](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/button/). This is a problem, since the Design System doesn't support multiple modules (if that's the right term?) being initialised from one element. I can't do `data-module="govuk-button" data-module="app-popover"` because that's invalid HTML. I could do `data-module="govuk-button app-popover"` (like class attribute syntax), but that won't work because the Design System [uses exact matches](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/dd748307ca612c73c2e60548419cee94d0cd636f/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/all.mjs#L55) when looking for attributes (`app-popover` could be made to work, but `govuk-button` won't) My suggestion is that the selector for initialising components is updated to `[data-module~="${Component.moduleName}"]`, which treats the attribute as a whitespace-separated list and matches if one entry in that list is the module. It would continue to work with exact matches, as the attribute would be treated as a list of one item. ## Alternatives ### Downstream components trigger upstream behaviour In the example above, the service's Popover component could be responsible for also initialising button behaviour on the element (i.e. `(new Button(this.$module)).init()`). However, if the Popover could also be applied to other elements (e.g. links, images) we wouldn't want to add button behaviour. The Popover component could apply this conditionally, if `$this.module.tagName === 'BUTTON'`, but this leads to hidden behaviour that's hard to opt-out of. #### Using ES2015 classes From v5, this could be achieved by extending the exposed JavaScript class: ```js export class Popover extends Button { constructor($module, options) { // GOV.UK Frontend button super($module, options) // Custom button things ... } } ``` This again creates a direct dependency on the Button component, which might not be desired if the component could be used by non-button elements too. It also creates a hierarchy, which could be complex if there are more than two components: if `Popover extends Button` and `SearchToggle extends Button`, then you have the same problem making an element both a Popover and a SearchToggle. ### Encourage other departmental and service-specific components to use a different attribute/approach In the example above, the Popover component might use the `data-app-module` attribute instead. Departmental component libraries could use e.g. `data-dft-module`. Since Design System components are prefixed `govuk-` in the value, I think it's reasonable to expect others to use the attribute with a different prefix. Also, there are already other components using this attribute so changing them would require changes to dependent services. ### Require one element per component/module In the example above, the Popover could be applied to a wrapping element, for example: ```html
``` This seems unnecessarily verbose to me, and requires introducing additional HTML elements to the DOM. ## Additional information (if applicable) ### Breaking change There is a breaking change risk: if a service already has whitespace-separated names in their `data-module` attribute then this would effectively "fix" them, but it _might_ cause unexpected behaviour if they've patched around it. For example, with my Popover component above, I might have added debouncing to the Popover code because govuk-button "wasn't working" and now have duplicate/conflicting behaviour. ### Components This doesn't align with Web Components, since each element can only be one component (e.g. `` or `

ourIssues.title: Allow pre-selecting a specific tab when using the tabs component
ourIssues.body:
## Related component

Tabs

## Context

Unless you pass the ID for a specific tab as part of the anchor in the URL, the tabs component assumes that you always want the first tab to be visible:

https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/19015c3df291db1653ea94793bfcbd95cbdd4063/src/govuk/components/tabs/tabs.mjs#L76-L78

If you're using the Nunjucks macro, the `--selected` modifier is always added to the first tab:

https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/19015c3df291db1653ea94793bfcbd95cbdd4063/src/govuk/components/tabs/template.njk#L14

However, if the user is using the HTML they can put the `--selected` modifier on whichever tab they like – but because of the assumption in the JavaScript, the tab to be visible on page load, but as soon as the JavaScript kicks the user will be switched back to the first tab.

I'd suggest:

- if any of the tabs have the `--selected` modifier on page load, the JavaScript should keep the first tab with that class as the active tab
- the Nunjucks macro should be extended to allow the user to set a specific tab as selected (but should default to the first tab as it does currently).

## Alternatives

One alternative is to include the ID of the target tab in the URL when linking to the page, but that results in the viewport being scrolled to the top of the tab, cutting off the top of the page.

## Additional information (if applicable)

This came up when supporting a user on Slack, who (quite rightly) expected to be able to set the active tab by moving the `--selected` modifier class, and was surprised when that didn't work.

ourIssues.title: Allow `govuk-font-size` to be called with a 't-shirt size' for `$size`
ourIssues.body:
## Context

We have the concept of 't-shirt sizes' (`xl`, `l`, `m`, `s`, `xs`) for text, for example headings, labels, legends, table captions.

They use consistent font sizes, but the mapping of t-shirt size to underlying font size is not defined anywhere in the codebase – it's just defined in each place individually and kept in sync.

For example, `xl` maps to a font size of 48 (on desktop):

https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/34806961fffb5e3b43de9fbda5f9a08f376ec196/src/govuk/core/_typography.scss#L11-L19

https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/34806961fffb5e3b43de9fbda5f9a08f376ec196/src/govuk/components/table/_index.scss#L53-L56

https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/34806961fffb5e3b43de9fbda5f9a08f376ec196/src/govuk/components/label/_index.scss#L13-L16

https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/34806961fffb5e3b43de9fbda5f9a08f376ec196/src/govuk/components/fieldset/_index.scss#L37-L40

We should consider updating `govuk-typography-responsive` to accept a t-shirt size, and automatically use the underlying size from the `$govuk-typography-scale`.

This would also allow calls to govuk-font to accept a t-shirt size, for example:

```scss
@include govuk-font($size: xl, $weight: bold);
```

This would also provide a way for components (ours, and downstream) to match with the heading sizes without, for example, needing to extend a heading class.

## Alternatives

Without this, we need to keep the various 't-shirt-sized' components in the codebase in sync manually, and there is no easy way for consumers to use the xl, l sizing in their own codebase without manually keeping them in sync.

## Additional information (if applicable)

This does introduce another (optional) layer of abstraction, but it feels like a useful one?

We might also want to consider extending the typography overrides to provide e.g. `govuk-!-font-size-xl` classes.

ourIssues.title: Make it easier to add a hint or an error message to a fieldset
ourIssues.body:
## What

If you want to use the fieldset component to group related fields, for example asking for a street address, you need to take care of including the hint / error message components separately and do extra work to associate them with the fieldset.

We do not provide any examples or guidance on how to do this, and it would be easy to get wrong (for example, by not creating the association with the fieldset)

It therefore seems like it would be useful if the fieldset component accepted `hint` and `errorMessage` objects and took care of this association itself.

## Why

This was requested by @edwardhorsford in https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/issues/778#issuecomment-459047140.

## Additional information

The radios, checkbox and date input components all use hints and error messages which are then associated with the fieldset using `aria-describedby`. However, this logic is handled (and therefore duplicated) within the individual components.

Moving this logic to the fieldset component _might_ allow us to simplify the repeated logic in the radios, checkboxes and date input components. However, it's not clear what should happen to the hint / error message [if you do not include a fieldset](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/62d3de38036b858b1dd85c5bd8c027830fab5a3d/src/components/date-input/template.njk#L79-L96).

ourIssues.title: Tweak design of button component on mobile (and maybe desktop, too)
ourIssues.body:
Currently our button components default to full width on smaller (mobile) screens. Because of this, its possible that the buttons are not as noticeable by users — many people have mentioned that they look like banners, not buttons, and this makes them easy to skip over.

Additionally, the top and bottom padding on the full width buttons is quite small which makes the text more difficult to read.

## Context

To solve the above issues and to generally improve the look of the buttons, we could:
- Make them responsive the width of the text, not the screen
- Improve the padding to make locating the text easier

## Alternatives

N/A

## Additional information (if applicable)

It would be great to do this around the time of the rebrand rollout, and ahead of the app release. Apps have chunkier buttons than our component and it would be beneficial for users if we brought them closer together

ourIssues.title: Improve the `title`s for pattern guidance pages
ourIssues.body:
## Context

Pattern pages with compound titles do not have the entire title included within the `title` element.

|Page `h1`|Page `title`|
|:-|:-|
|Ask users for Bank Details|Bank details|
|Ask users for Email addresses|Email addresses|
|Help users to Confirm an email address|Confirm an email address|
|Help users to Exit a page quickly|Exit a page quickly|

This can cause confusion, as some pages on the Design System website can have similar or identical `title`s in browser tabs and search result listings. 

|Pattern page `title`|Non-pattern page `title`|
|:-|:-|
|Cookies page|[Cookies](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/cookies/)|
|Dates|[Date input](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/date-input/)|
|Exit a page quickly|[Exit this page](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/exit-this-page/)|
|Passwords|Password input [in development]|

In instances where a pattern has a compound title (i.e. "Ask users for...", "Help users to...") these should be included in the page `title`. 

It may also be useful to include the name of the parent section ("Styles", "Components", "Patterns", etc.) somewhere within the page `title` on these child pages.

## Alternatives

Currently you must either look at the page's URL or click through to visit the page in order to see whether it is the desired page. 

## Additional information

Raised by a working group member during a working group meeting.

ourIssues.title: Changing the colour palette used for graphs on GOV.UK/Design System
ourIssues.body:
## Context
<!-- What are you trying to do? Is this something you think should behave differently, or something that you currently cannot do? Is this related to an existing issue/bug? -->

The colours used in the existing charts that can be built using Govspeak do not meet the colour contrast requirements for adjacent colours (as set out in WCAG 2.1). The Analysis Function Support Team have developed accessible colour palettes to use with charts and would love to see these implemented in the charts created using Govspeak. 

I have published a webpage showing the [types of tables and charts that can be built using Govspeak](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/examples-of-visual-content-to-use-on-govuk). 

## Alternatives
<!-- Are you currently using a workaround / alternative solution instead? -->

In general statistics producers who use GOV.UK to publish content are frustrated with the technical capability they have to publish charts. Only horizontal bar charts can be created using Govspeak so they are very limited in what they can do in HTML. Many teams are still creating charts as images and then publishing them as PNGs, JPEGs or (at best) SVGs. Sometimes they publish a mix of charts created as images and charts created using Govspeak, sometimes all their charts are images. 

When it comes to colours, if they use the horizontal bar charts available in Govspeak they have no way of changing the colours. When they create charts as images they can choose whatever colours they want. 

This either leads to a mix of colour palettes being used (which isn't great), or they align all their charts with the Govspeak colour palette, which also isn't great as the adjacent colours do not meet the contrast requirements for adjacent colours, set out in WCAG 2.1. 

## Additional information (if applicable)
<!-- What evidence do you have that this meets the needs of users? It’s useful for us to know of any user research/testing you’ve done with this feature. -->

Making the Govspeak charts meet the contrast requirements set out in WCAG 2.1 won't make things 100% perfect for all users but it will definitely be an improvement for any users with access needs related to seeing adjacent colours. It is also a legal requirement. 

The colour palettes we have created are available within [this colours guidance](https://gss.civilservice.gov.uk/policy-store/data-visualisation-colours-in-charts/#section-5) (it is still technically in draft but should be signed off by the end of this week).
