ourIssues.title: It's not clear if the cookie banner should appear on the cookies page itself
ourIssues.body:
Raised by a user on Slack. They weren't sure whether a cookie banner should appear on a service's cookie page, and had seen varying implementations in different services.

## Related documentation

[Cookie banner component](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/cookie-banner/)
[Cookies page pattern](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/cookies-page/)

## Suggestion

Explain what the approach should be.

We have some logic to stop the cookie banner showing on the cookies page in the Design System:
https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/blob/main/src/javascripts/components/cookie-banner.mjs#L22

So it's a case of explaining that this is how it should work, and why.

## Evidence (where applicable)

Passports doesn't show the cookie banner – https://www.passport.service.gov.uk/help/cookies-setting
JSA does - https://www.apply-for-new-style-jsa.dwp.gov.uk/citizen-ui/cookies-policy

ourIssues.title: Agree how to ensure that users don't lose information if they follow links in the cookie banner
ourIssues.body:
## What
As part of the cookie banner work we've been thinking about how teams should handle opening links in the cookie banner if the user is completing a transactional journey and could lose information they've entered in a form if they follow links in the cookie banner.

We have some information under [Opening links in a new tab](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/styles/typography/#opening-links-in-a-new-tab) about this so we could link to it from the cookie banner guidance if we though that would be useful. The content could say something like:

> If you show the cookie banner on a page where the user enters information into a form, [open the cookies page in a new tab](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/styles/typography/#opening-links-in-a-new-tab). 

Additionally, users could lose information if interacting with the cookie banner reloads the page (server side solution when JavaScript isn't enabled or the banner doesn't progressively enhance it). We could consider recommending that once the user has consented/rejected cookies, the hide button isn't shown if JavaScript isn't enabled (JS would unhide the button)/

It's possible that there's a wider pattern here about how teams should ensure that the information users enter in forms is retained safely. 

This card should be to decide what the scope of this work is.

## Why
We should provide guidance to teams on how to making sure that users don't lose information entered in a form if they follow links in the cookie banner. 

## Who needs to know about this
Content writer, technical writer, developer, service designer?

## Further detail
As well as the cookie banner, this relates to things like links in footers. However, it's possible that the proposed wider guidance is less relevant to user interaction patterns and would be more relevant for the [Service Manual](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual). 

## Done when
- [ ] We've agreed how to help teams to make sure that users don't lose information entered in a form if they click on links in the cookie banner
- [ ] We've created a follow up card if appropriate, or captured next steps in this card

communityIssues.title: Cumulative layout shift on GOV.UK
communityIssues.body:
Our SpeedCurve metrics have recently (since May 25th 2023) reported an increase in the Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) on GOV.UK, which seems to be mainly to do with the cookie banner being displayed. This is most noticeable on mobile devices.

Brief investigation suggests this is not to do with any recent changes to the cookie banner (even though it was recently modified to more closely follow the Design System component) but rather a change in how SpeedCurve measures CLS. Basically, it's always been this way, we just have better reporting now.

SpeedCurve is currently reporting a CLS score of `0.6771`. Some data:

- [reporting from 27th May 2023](https://app.speedcurve.com/gds/gov-uk/test/230527_PT_0994e9befe2797c0d2e43b57a10d7b0f/)
- [reporting from 4th June 2023](https://app.speedcurve.com/gds/gov-uk/test/230604_FZ_14331823420653bbbd3ecea8b4bd108a/)
- [comparison between 24th and 25th May](https://app.speedcurve.com/gds/gov-uk/compare/?tests=230524_7W_fcc5eafb395d857094f98a580ab8d367,230525_QN_53fc15643fb3e0e960bc1f089ee13ead)

This shift is recorded at two points. Firstly when the cookie banner appears:

![Screenshot 2023-06-06 at 15 02 12](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk_publishing_components/assets/861310/f86331c1-320f-4f89-9eb7-5a9a48da69cf)

The second shift occurs as shown below. I'm not 100% sure what this shift is, it seems to be incredibly small, but it adds `0.0224` to the overall score.

![Screenshot 2023-06-06 at 15 02 17](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk_publishing_components/assets/861310/06b7e5e3-883a-42e4-8dd9-8360b8800087)

There's also a shift that occurs between the default font and Transport loading (note the line break inserted in `government services`). This might be the one above - it probably varies depending on screen width.

![Screenshot 2023-06-06 at 15 00 53](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk_publishing_components/assets/861310/5dc9b215-dbc3-49b7-b1f1-9ab41b0bc819)


## Previous work

There has been some [previous detailing of this problem](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1J8gz8fRPmPJnYk2O4bHRC79E5-p7rpSnnVWRIYodRy8/edit#heading=h.lmvvgvepxvzb) as well as some [past investigation](https://docs.google.com/document/d/11y86xkDX3Z5mKDlnseWFigES0i_ZVQifzr99e10qncw/edit#heading=h.cfu8rhxwsue9) into possible solutions.

For reference, the [Design System website](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/) uses an inline script to determine fairly quickly on page load whether the cookie banner should be shown or not, which may be another option to consider. Note that the DS does not provide JS for a cookie banner, only the HTML and CSS.

## Brief code dive

Running a lighthouse audit on a locally running GOV.UK homepage gives a CLS score of `0.285`.

Possible optimisation... moving the call to [this.showCookieMessage](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk_publishing_components/blob/main/app/assets/javascripts/govuk_publishing_components/components/cookie-banner.js#L40) from line 40 to before the call to [this.setupCookieMessage](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk_publishing_components/blob/main/app/assets/javascripts/govuk_publishing_components/components/cookie-banner.js#L17) on line 17 gets straight to showing/hiding the cookie banner ahead of showing/hiding the contents of the cookie banner (which we do so that the buttons get shown when JS is enabled but hidden when JS is not). This is basically switching one kind of CLS for another but it reduces the score to `0.272` so might be worth further investigation. I don't know why the display of these buttons isn't controlled through CSS by the `js-enabled` class, but presumably there's a reason.

Thanks to @36degrees for bringing this to our attention.

backlog.title: Help users know how long something might take (time estimation)
backlog.body:
What
It may or may not be helpful to help users understand how long something might take, for example:

to complete a form
to get a response
to read some guidance

It's arguably helpful for people to know roughly how long something might take so they can plan their time. However on the other hand, things can take longer or shorter depending on the user's situation, disability, etc.
If we do give estimated times, it would be good to discuss and standardise on how we estimate those times.
Why
This is something we currently do on Start pages, and Confirmation pages

backlog.title: Suggested new component - Side menu
backlog.body:
What

Give a brief description of the style, component or pattern you want to propose.

Context:
We are in the final stages of building an e-learning service using the GDS design system. We have completed numerous rounds of user testing and already gone through one Alpha and Beta Assessment.
What:
A right-hand sidebar navigation menu which allows users to easily see their progression through a course and be able to navigate back and forth through chapters.
Current version

In-situ

Iterations from user testing

Why

Explain why you think this should be added to the GOV.UK Design System.

In our alpha assessment, we were challenged to explore if there was a user need to see their progression through the course and also to be able to navigate back and forth through the chapters. We tested various variations of a sidebar navigation similar to those found in lots of e-learning platforms. During testing, we found that some users naturally used the sidebar to return to topics earlier in the course and used it to be aware of their progression and estimate their completion time.
Design-wise, we didn’t want to reinvent the wheel so we built on existing sidebar navigation patterns from GOV.UK publishing such as the contents list on the publishing service (https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/contents_list) and the related content sidebar on many start pages. We iterated the design several times to make it simple and accessible. For instance, we made some headers in the sidebar visually hidden so they would give context to screen reader users whilst avoiding confusion for sighted users who had initially struggled with the previous design.


What evidence do you have that it's needed by multiple services across government?


In the our beta assessment, we were praised on our work developing this pattern and asked to play it back into the community:
‘the team has validated the user need to track progress within training modules, has designed a pattern that is working for their beta users, and is planning to continue iterating this pattern - the panel would encourage the team to share this pattern and research findings with the design system community’


What evidence do you have that it meets the needs of the users of those services?


We have tested and validated this component in several rounds of qual research with 5-10 people in each round, and in Private Beta testing with over 1200 people (with quant showing that people successfully use this when required, and qual feedback only positive and no negative on the latest version).
Our user testing so far has validated the need for this component and as mentioned has been praised so far by assessors. But we would love to share it with the community to get a wider perspective and possible use cases.


Have you checked that it doesn't already exist in the GOV.UK Design System?


Yes
Anything else

Include links to any examples, research or code to support your proposal, if available.

backlog.title: Video Relay Service (VRS)
backlog.body:
What
A component to link to Video Relay Service (VRS).
Why
Departments are starting to provide Video Relay Service for people who need sign language interpretation, and it's becoming more popular across all departments.
Because it's new we are seeing a pattern emerging where people just stick a link on the start page.
However, when talking to @timpaul  about it, we discussed that there isn't a lot of research around it to know if people know what "Video Relay Service" actually is. Also, some people are BSL monoglots, which means they may not even be able to read a link written in English
Suggestion
There is a common icon for sign language which could probably be incorporated into a component similar to the back link, so that even if people don't know what VRS is, or they can't read the written English, they can still find the sign language interpretation feature.


Edit: Original image is not recommended as it is associated with ALS (American Sign Language) rather than BSL, based on NHS research.

backlog.title: Help users to find the right service for them
backlog.body:
What
There are many examples of government services which serve similar (or the same) needs for people with slightly different circumstances.
In the case where we can rely on most users navigating to a high-level Start Page, but not to the individual service variants, we can ask users questions about themselves to and then present them with the options available to them.
n.b. This is related to the "Check a service is suitable for you" pattern but different in content. That pattern starts with a user thinking that a service is suitable for them, but possibly being incorrect. This pattern starts with a user needing a problem to be solved but not necessarily having any idea what their options are for solving it.
Why
I'm not sure which services this is currently part of, but I have a hunch that it should be part of more. I've seen some services early in development that are Brexit-related that do things like this, but can't currently put much info about them on here.
One live example is "Find out if you can settle in the UK".

backlog.title: Make a Joint Application
backlog.body:
What
A pattern for multiple users to submit an application together, which they may have joint liability for.
We've been specifically designing a service where users need to see everything the other person submits as they are taking out a loan together.
This interaction has been tested from both applicants' perspectives in multiple rounds of Alpha testing on our service:

First user completes application, submitting the information about their self and their partner.
At the end of the application, the first user is given a unique code to give to the second applicant.
The second applicant receives a link to the second applicant's start page, where they must enter the unique code.
Their bit of the application is essentially checking the details submitted by the first applicant, using the check your answers pattern. If they do change any of the answers, the first applicant will receive an email and go through the same process until both applicants have seen the information being submitted.

We first considered designing it so that each applicant fills in their own info, but then realised that would need much more back and forth between the applicants for most people. Users in our research said they'd probably either know the information about their partner, or be sat with them when making the application. We're also considering adding the ability to skip the pages that asking for your partner's information as we test more in Beta.
We can update here with more information from our Beta when we have it.
Why
There are various services in Government that need to applied for my multiple users, for example married couples, who may be doing something they are both liable for like buying a house, or maybe filing for a divorce, applying for Universal Credit, etc.
Anything else
I can link individuals to our research reports on this interaction if needed.

backlog.title: Before you start page
backlog.body:
What
An information page that immediately follows a start page. It helps users understand what they need to do before they start using the service.
Why
Qualitative research for Carer's Allowance found that GOV.UK content alone wasn't making people aware that applying for Carer's Allowance may (in certain circumstances) affect the benefits of the person they care for. Data analysis found that people were dropping out of the service when this was made clear to them later in their journey.
Anything else

Before you start: DWP design patterns

ourIssues.title: WCAG 2.2: Start using a service ‖ Consistent Help
ourIssues.body:
## What

Consider adding or updating a screenshot of a start page to include visible help or contact information on the page, displayed in a consistent manner. Related to #2882. 

This is largely a usability suggestion and may not be necessary for WCAG compliance. 

### Resources

- [Start using a service pattern guidance](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/start-using-a-service/)
- [WCAG 2.2 criterion for 'Consistent Help'](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/consistent-help.html)

## Why

The new WCAG 2.2 Level A criterion 'Consistent Help' says:

> If a [Web page](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/consistent-help.html#dfn-web-page) contains any of the following help [mechanisms](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/consistent-help.html#), and those mechanisms are repeated on multiple Web pages within a [set of Web pages](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/consistent-help.html#dfn-set-of-web-pages), they occur in the same order relative to other page content, unless a change is initiated by the user:
> * Human contact details;
> * Human contact mechanism;
> * Self-help option;
> * A fully automated contact mechanism.

Although the intent of the criterion is that the contact information itself is consistently ordered with respect to the rest of the page (i.e. a help link is always in the same place in the footer, as described in #2871) we can go beyond this by advising that teams provide this information in a consistent order every time it appears.

For example, if a service has three contact mechanisms—phone, email address, post—these should be listed in the same order and format on all pages where it appears, such as the service start page, support pages, contact page, etc. 

## Who needs to work on this
- Content designer or technical writer

## Who needs to review this
- Accessibility specialist
- Content designer or technical writer

## Done when

- [ ] Guidance has been updated

backlog.title: Native apps
backlog.body:
What
Native mobile apps for government – things like the GOV.UK ID Check app and the HMRC app.
Use this space to share things like:

any broad design principles you've used when working on apps
things you've learnt from testing mobile apps with users

ourIssues.title: Module name missing for some `new ElementError()` calls
ourIssues.body:
<!--
    Please fill in as much of the template below as you’re able to. If you're unsure whether the issue already exists or how to fill in the template, open an issue anyway. Our team will help you to complete the rest.

    Your issue might already exist. If so, add a comment to the existing issue instead of creating a new one. You can find existing issues here:
    - an existing Github issue: https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues
    - known validation errors or warnings: https://github.com/orgs/alphagov/projects/37
-->

## Description of the issue

Component `ElementError` messages were [updated to use `moduleName` suffixes](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/pull/5338):

```console
govuk-accordion: Root element (`$root`) is not of type HTMLElement
govuk-button: Root element (`$root`) already initialised
govuk-checkboxes: Form inputs (`<input type="checkbox">`) not found
govuk-exit-this-page: Root element (`$root`) is not of type HTMLElement
...
```

But the following error messages were missed:

```console
Password input: Form field (`.govuk-js-password-input-input`) must be of type `password`.
Password input: Button (`.govuk-js-password-input-toggle`) must be of type `button`.
Skip link: Target link (`href="#example"`) has no hash fragment
```

They use older plain english component names and not `moduleName`

<!-- A clear and concise summary of what the bug is. -->

## Steps to reproduce the issue

Trigger one of the errors shown above where `moduleName` is not used

## Actual vs expected behaviour

All component-level errors should log the correct `moduleName` for better error reporting

E.g. `Password input:` → `govuk-password-input:`

ourIssues.title: Add content to Skip link guidance about problem caused by preservation of fragment identifiers between pages
ourIssues.body:
The skip link component adds a `#main-content` fragment identifier to the current URL. This can persist across pages causing an unexpected jump to the main content area on load. I'd like to add a warning about this to the guidance, along with tips about ways teams could write their code to avoid this. 

## Related component

https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/skip-link/

## Context

This problem has been seen to happen in the following scenario:
- the skip link was used, thereby adding `#main-content` to the current URL
- you leave the page via a successful form submission
- the form doesn't set the `action` attribute and so POSTs to the current URL
- the server uses [the POST -> Redirect -> GET pattern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post/Redirect/Get) to navigate to the next page

Given all that, the browser will preserve `#main-content` in the new URL[^1] causing the next page to jump to the start of the main content area when it loads.

This was picked up as an issue by the Digital Accessibility Centre (DAC) in a recent audit of GOV.UK Notify[^2], who stated that it failed [the WCAG 2.4.3 (Focus Order) success criteria](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG20/Understanding/focus-order).

Given [the POST -> Redirect -> GET pattern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post/Redirect/Get) is so commonly used in web apps, I think there's some value in making teams aware of this problem and helping them write their code in a way that stops it happening.

## Alternatives

N/A

## Additional information (if applicable)

Suggested changes, to stop the problem occurring are:
- setting the `action` attribute on the `<form>` tag to match the current URL, without `#main-content`
- setting the URL for the next page explicitly using the [Content-Location](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Content-Location) header

## References

[^1]: This is correct behaviour, as defined in [Handling of fragment identifiers in redirected URLs](https://www.w3.org/Protocols/HTTP/Fragment/draft-bos-http-redirect-00.txt)
[^2]: Issue 'ID: DAC_Focus_order_01' on page 19 of [the audit report](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jRkkL3AZj-7Q0uo7yfHUv_JF9q0Ecw6g/view?usp=sharing) (needs a GDS Google account for access)

ourIssues.title: Research making the checkbox and radio button labels full width
ourIssues.body:
## What

Perform research with users as to whether making labels on checkboxes and radio buttons span the width of the container, thus increasing their touch surface, makes it easier to use these controls

## Why

Generally speaking, increasing the target area for a control makes the control easier for users to interact with.

We have some existing precendent for this in Frontend already: 

- Labels for other input types (text inputs, selects, textareas, etc.) are already full width.
- The Accordion activates expand/collapse functionality by tapping anywhere in the section header.
- The Skip Link component, when visible, is activatable by clicking anywhere in the component.

The GOV.UK team has had positive feedback when increasing target sizes for elements on the [homepage](https://insidegovuk.blog.gov.uk/2021/12/13/updating-the-gov-uk-homepage/) and [topic pages](https://insidegovuk.blog.gov.uk/2022/08/08/rolling-out-a-new-design-for-browsing-gov-uk-by-topic/) in the last year.

Various external design systems have full width checkbox and radio labels, some of which are based on or inspired by GOV.UK Frontend and have seemingly made the conscious choice to change it:

- ~~[USWDS](https://designsystem.digital.gov/components/checkbox/)~~ Update: Has since updated to no longer be full-width
- [NICE Design System](https://design-system.nice.org.uk/storybook/?path=/story/foundations-checkbox--default)
- [Transport for West Midlands Design System](https://designsystem.tfwm.org.uk/components/radios/)
- [GOLD Design System](https://gold.designsystemau.org/components/control-input/#checkbox-block) (formerly Australian Government Design System)
- [Atlassian Design System](https://atlassian.design/components/checkbox/examples)

Our inline labels date from the GOV.UK Elements days, and I couldn't immediately find any reason why they were implemented in this way at the time. We have stuck to that precedent in situations where a conflict or bug relating to the label sizing has arisen (e.g. #634).

We should validate our current approach and whether it best meets user needs when compared to alternative approaches.

## Assumptions

We've [previously found that users don't tend to click on checkbox or radio button labels](https://designnotes.blog.gov.uk/2016/11/30/weve-updated-the-radios-and-checkboxes-on-gov-uk/), even if they're styled to appear interactible. It could be assumed that the same applies here (if not moreso, as there isn't any visual indicator that interaction is possible). 

As a larger area of the screen will activate a checkbox/radio, there may be an increase in the number of accidental form inputs being made.

A seemingly 'empty' part of the page affecting a nearby input may be unexpected and cause confusion to users unless some other hint is present (e.g. a hover state). 

## Timebox
TBD

## Who is working on this?

Spike lead: TBD

Spike buddy: TBD

## Questions to answer

- [ ] Is there a tangible benefit to checkbox and radio button labels always being full width?
- [ ] Is there a tangible benefit to checkbox and radio button labels being full width in certain situations (e.g. on narrow screens)? 
- [ ] Are full width labels more likely to result in accidental and unwanted inputs?
- [ ] Is having a visually 'empty' area of the screen interactive unexpected or a source of confusion?

## Done when

- [ ] A review or prototype is produced with the modified checkbox/radio styles.
- [ ] User research has been carried out to see how these changes perform with users.
- [ ] Findings have been reviewed and shared with the team.
- [ ] Any follow up issues or actions have been written up.

ourIssues.title: Various issues under Chrome's Auto Dark Mode
ourIssues.body:
Since Chrome version 78, Google has included an experimental feature in the browser, initially named "Forced Dark Mode" and, as of writing, named "Auto Dark Mode for Web Content". 

This feature automatically modifies the appearance of webpages in order to create a "dark mode" version. This is done even if the page already supplies a "dark mode" via the `prefers-color-scheme` CSS media query. It also appears to ignore the `color-scheme` property. 

The flag comes with several different "enabled" modes (as of Chrome 99), which modify how Chrome is internally applying changes. Each mode results in subtly (sometimes radically) different resulting colours.

1. Enabled
2. Enabled with simple HSL-based inversion
3. Enabled with simple CIELAB-based inversion
4. Enabled with simple RGB-based inversion
5. Enabled with selective image inversion
6. Enabled with selective inversion of non-image elements
7. Enabled with selective inversion of everything
8. Enabled with increased text contrast

Most of these modes appear to work by first overriding neutral light background colours (such as white and light greys), and modifying any copy that it detects as existing on a modified background colour to maintain suitable contrast. Most other colours appear to be left intact. This method of alteration means that colours are not all modified in the same way: `$govuk-brand-color` in mode 1, for example, is unmodified when used as a background or border colour (#1d70b8), but is changed when it is used as a text colour (#61a1ee).

Mode 4 appears to simply invert all colours on the page, regardless of usage. 

I'm not sure how mode 1 is different from the others. It may be that this is an "automatic" mode where Chrome tries to determine which of the other seven modes works best for the given page and uses that one.

We have received at least one bug report raised by a user who was using Chrome's Auto Dark Mode feature for accessibility reasons (to make content easier to read with cataracts).

> RE the dark mode, it is now a function in Google Chrome that you can activate and it will force a dark version if the website can accommodate it. Not everyone does, BBC News for example still comes through with a traditional black text on a white background – but it works for many.

## Steps to reproduce the issue
In Google Chrome, go to `chrome://flags/#enable-force-dark` (this should jump you straight to "Auto Dark Mode for Web Contents") and enable the flag.

## Actual vs expected behaviour
Currently, a number of these modes produce colour combinations which fail the contrast requirements established in WCAG 2.1. 

Below is a non-exhaustive subset of issues currently identified in Auto Dark Mode.

### Text inputs and textareas
Text inputs are displayed with a grey background and black border in modes 1, 6, 7, and 8. This fails to meet the expected 1:3 contrast ratio for UI elements (at 1:1.68). 

![Screenshot of the design system input component, appearing grey on black.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160644743-7632dc27-cc56-4558-bd40-8fee1109717c.png)

They are displayed with a light grey background and white border in modes 3 and 5, which easily meets contrast ratio expectations.

They are displayed with the default white background and black border in all other modes.

### Input prefixes and suffixes

These are difficult to read in modes 2 and 4, where they are black on a dark grey background (1:3.23).

![Screenshot of the design system input prefix and suffix example, where the text is black on dark grey.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160646813-ac2ad0a1-083d-4ca0-b571-b1ecacd450e4.png)

These are much more difficult to read in modes 3 and 5, which renders it as black on an even darker grey (1.22).

![Screenshot of the design system input prefix and suffix example. The text is visually imperceptible from the background.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160650473-9c6f3529-5a06-4408-b20e-242b1c66a08e.png)

These are displayed with adequate contrast in other modes.

### Checkboxes and radio buttons
The border and selection states of checkboxes and radio buttons do not have sufficient contrast in modes 1, 6, 7, and 8 (at a pretty much imperceptible contrast ratio of 1:1.04)

![Screenshot of the design system checkbox component, illustrating insufficient contrast between the checkboxes and background, which are both dark grey.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160644218-1fc50370-249e-4e47-b73a-eab9a8b8ea34.png)

They are displayed with white borders and selection states in all other modes.

### Select

In modes 1, 6, 7, and 8, select boxes are rendered with a dark grey background and dark grey border (1:1.04).

![Screenshot of the design system select component, which appears to just be white text with no border or icon.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160648934-5554f80a-1794-40e1-a9b7-a7c16df83d29.png)

They are rendered with a black background and white border in all other modes.

### Skiplinks

In modes 1, 2, 6, and 7, skiplinks are rendered as white on focus-colour yellow, which does not meet contrast requirements (1:1.34).

![Screenshot of a white link on a bright yellow background.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160649767-19aecf58-2ea6-4517-9852-283a4c91f922.png)

In mode 4, it is white on light blue, which is also below expectations (1:3.24).

![Screenshot of a white link on a bright blue background.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160649982-3f7999be-3540-40c5-8d00-7b9350407360.png)

In mode 8, it is white on focus-color yellow, but additionally has a black text shadow/stroke effect applied, which makes it difficult to read.

![Screenshot of a white link with a thin, pixellated black shadow surrounding it, on a bright yellow background.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160650309-a61034bd-d400-4ca3-b312-db890c382f19.png)

This is displayed with adequate contrast (albeit, in white on brown) in all other modes.

### Iconography

Most iconography fails to meet contrast requirements in virtually all modes. This includes:
- the open and close arrows on the Accordion component.
- the arrow on the Back link component.
- the arrows on the Breadcrumbs component.
- the exclamation icon on the Warning text component.

### Other components
The good news is that, for the most part, the majority of other components we have in GOV.UK Frontend are not as badly affected as those above, with various components such as Inset text, Error summary, and Notification banner maintaining their necessary visual presence and suitable contrast even with modified colours. 

## Environment
The results specified here were taken in Chrome 99, running on macOS 15.3, whilst the operating system was set to light mode. 

Interestingly, Chrome DevTools does not give any indication that a change to the page's appearance has taken place. All HTML and CSS content, including the user agent stylesheet, computed styles, and those returned through JavaScript, appear unmodified and are not aligned with the page's actual appearance when Auto Dark Mode is enabled.

ourIssues.title: Consider changing or removing focus state for error summary and notification banner
ourIssues.body: ## What Decide on whether the notification banner, which is automatically focused when the page loads (for the error and success variants), should have a focus state and what it should look like. Decide whether the same treatment should be applied to the existing error summary component which behaves in the same way. ## Why We need to understand whether WCAG 2.1 1.4.11 Non-text contrast applies to this element. It's programatically focused on page load, but is not keyboard-operable – once focus has left the error summary, you cannot navigate back to it using the keyboard. The proposed 2.4.11 focus visible (at time of writing) [explicitly only applies to keyboard operable controls](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/focus-appearance-minimum.html#keyboard-focus): > Some elements can take focus (such as the target of a skip link), however, it is only when the element is operable by keyboard controls that this criterion applies. If this logic applies to 1.4.11, then the focus state of the error summary / notification banner does not need to meet contrast – in which case, is the yellow outline actually helpful? Or should we remove it entirely? If the focus state does need to meet contrast, then we need to revisit the focus state for both the error summary and the new notification banner component. ## Further detail The error summary currently has a yellow outline when focused. The proposed notification banner component will also take focus on page load (for the error and success variants), so we will presumably want to use the same approach. However, the yellow outline does not meet 3:1 colour contrast against the white background. Other components use a black border when focused (which then means it meets contrast), but because the error summary is focused on page load we want to preserve the border colour so that it suggests an error / success state as appropriate. ## Done when - [x] Understand how WCAG 2.4.11 applies to the notification banner and error summary components - [ ] Decide on focus state for notification banner - [ ] Decide on focus state for error summary

communityIssues.title: The experimental chart component's accessibility criteria needs more detail

We have reintroduced the [experimental Chart component ](https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/chart)as part of some exploratory work we are doing in the Patterns & Pages team.

During the review, we realised that the accessibility criteria is quite small for the component. Currently, it says:

```
Charts must:

use line colours with a contrast ratio higher than 4.5:1 against the background colour to meet WCAG AA
contain a heading and description so that skip links and semantics are accurate
```

However we suspect that there would be a lot more criteria to make a chart accessible, so we've raised this issue so that we remember to populate it with more stuff.

As we are adding this component to the next accessibility audit, we're expecting the outcome of that to inform the criteria. We could also base the criteria off of the [GSS guidance](https://analysisfunction.civilservice.gov.uk/policy-store/data-visualisation-charts/).

communityIssues.title: Inconsistent components API
communityIssues.body:
The component API is inconsistent across components and in comparison with `govuk-frontend`.

In the table below there is a brief comparison in how `govuk-frontend` components are aligned in API with `govuk_publishing_components`

|Component               |API |
|---                      |---  |
Accordion                 | aligned
Back link                 | aligned
Breadcrumbs               | misaligned
Button                    | slightly misaligned (start)
Character count           | slightly misaligned (nesting)
Checkboxes                | slightly misaligned (fieldset)
Date input                | slightly misaligned (fieldset)
Details                   | misaligned
Error message             | aligned
Error summary             | misaligned
Fieldset                  | misaligned
File upload               | aligned
Footer                    | aligned
Header                    | slightly misaligned (navigation_items)
Inset text                | aligned
Panel                     | misaligned
Phase banner              | misaligned
Radios                    | slightly misaligned (fieldset)
Select                    | slightly misaligned (options)
Skip link                 | aligned
Summary list              | slightly misaligned (items)
Table                     | aligned
Tabs                      | misaligned
Text input                | aligned
Textarea                  | aligned
Warning text              | slightly misaligned (iconFallbackText)

We can see a few common differences between to two API models:
- for arrays, `govuk-frontend` uses the generic `items` (in most cases) whereas `govuk_publishing_components` uses the name of the component (e.g. `attachments` for the attachment list component or `breadcrumbs` for the breadcrumbs component)
- for web addresses/paths `govuk-frontend` uses `href` whereas in `govuk_publishing_components` we often find `url` (e.g. breadcrumbs component)

It's worth mentioning that not even `govuk-frontend`'s API is consistent (e.g. `errorList` instead of `items` in the Error summary component, or differences in nesting)

A few advantages of making the API consistent:
- increases developers' confidence when calling components with arguments (without constantly checking examples in the guide)
- prototyping and production will use the same config object (can be easily copied over in both directions)
- applications can prepare the data to be fed into components consistently using helpers
- it would be easier to swap one component with another

I'm creating this to raise awareness of the differences, hopefully generate discussions around how good looks like and aim for consistency and convergency. API alignment requires at least a breaking change and some replacements across applications – which is not an easy process. For this reason, having a clear vision about how we want it to look like would save us from doing this more than once.

backlog.title: Toggle switch component
backlog.body:
What
An on/off toggle button that allows the user to make a change to that page immediately, without the need to submit an answer or navigate away from the current page.
Why
On the 'Video appointment service' project, there was a user need to change a setting on the page (microphone - on/off and camera - on/off). We have done 5 rounds of research with a variety of iterations and users and have concluded that a toggle switch design is the most recognisable, usable and understandable. We initially tested with components already in the GOV.UK design system (buttons with text, buttons with icons and text and radio buttons) but users with low digital confidence struggled to know the current state of the buttons, and radios and checkboxes are an input that needs submitting, rather than having an immediate effect on the page. (https://www.nngroup.com/articles/toggle-switch-guidelines/)
In our latest round of research, everyone understood and could use the toggle buttons designed. They have also been thoroughly accessibility tested. I have not seen any other examples of toggles across government services (except for the NHS app).
It is worth noting they currently rely on javascript which is acceptable on the 'Video appointment service' as javascript is required to take part in the video appointment.
Anything else
Mural board on iterations and high level research findings:


Addition of colour and shape has been found to increase understanding of current state.

backlog.title: Contribution submission for Exit this page component
backlog.body:
Formerly known as 'Hide this page component'
What
What are we proposing
We are looking to implement a component, using the existing button component, that allows vulnerable users of a Government service to quickly and safely hide the page and reduce the risk of Domestic Abuse incidents.
The functionality behind the component would allow a user to quickly hide the current page and open a new, ambiguous webpage, such as BBC Weather or another such website. This would lower the risk of drawing attention to browsing habits from a perpetrator.
Why
Why are we proposing this design pattern?

Domestic abuse is physical, sexual, psychological or financial abuse that takes place within an intimate or family-type relationship and that forms a pattern of forceful and controlling behaviour. This can include forced marriage and so-called ‘honour-based crimes.” Domestic abuse may include a range of abusive behaviours, not all of which are in themselves inherently ‘violent’

The biggest risk to a victim of Domestic Abuse is homicide and serious physical assaults - this is at its greatest risk when a victim is planning to flee or escape from the perpetrator. Often, one of the first things a victim will do is to speak to someone to make a disclosure about abuse. The second thing they will do is research and find help online, often using Government services.
We need to ensure that the risk is minimised for users when using online services. Although victims and survivors can be aware of the risks, it is the Government's responsibility to protect individuals using a service. Therefore, it is crucial that there is a consistency of approach in design and functionality across Government with this component.
What evidence do you have that it's needed by multiple services across government?
From conversations between the Department for Work and Pensions, Ministry of Justice, the Cabinet Office and Scottish Government, it is already clear that other services need to ensure that this design is available.
Services are already responding to the rise in Domestic Abuse during COVID-19 by building their own minimum viable solutions to allow users to quickly hide their webpages.
There are areas of the Government site, such as “Domestic Abuse: How to get help”, that a high risk user would access for support that does not include a way to hide their browsing. This is putting those users of this service at risk.
What evidence do you have that it meets the needs of the users of those services?
Speaking with subject matter experts (SME), it is critical that we offer this feature on the GOV.UK website. It is a feature that is provided by other organisations, such as:

Scottish Government - Domestic Abuse page
Refuge
Women’s Aid
Victim Support

Each website has varied design implementations, but ultimately addresses the same user need of being able to hide browsing habits quickly.
The Ministry of Justice have carried out some initial research with an SME to establish whether the proposed solution meets the user needs.
Have you checked that it doesn't already exist in the GOV.UK Design System?
There are no outstanding issues or tickets in the Design System backlog that refer to this type of component.
Anything else
What else has been done
The MoJ have iterated twice on the design component on our live service - looking at language, design and functionality.
There are several designs that are considered minimum viable products which have been released by the DWP (Child Maintenance Service) - Cabinet Office (Coronavirus Support) and the MoJ (Legal Aid Agency). The expediency of these releases has been due to the fact that by not having something, we are putting our users at risk.
The MoJ have carried out some early rounds of testing with an SME that have looked at design, functionality and various use cases from a range of user scenarios. This has all been documented and shared with DWP and CO to share research and findings.
Designs
We looked to extend the GOV.UK Button component to act as the interactive element that a user would press to exit the website.
The Design System suggests using red for any destructive actions undertaken on a GOV.UK website - as the intention for the 'Hide this page' button was essentially closing the webpage down, it would be deemed destructive. This has been adopted by DWP and the Scottish Government.
We decided to utilise the additional space available in the 1/3 column, which is usually reserved for additional information as it allowed us to present the button within immediate view for the user.
The button would then be "sticky" in position at the top of the page on smaller devices. This prevents any conflict with the GOV.UK 'Contents' link that is positioned at the bottom of the screen. It also removes potential accidental presses by a user who doesn't need to use it.
Feedback from SME on the design

Victims of Domestic Abuse are used to using their reptilian brain and are in fight or flight mode so the red would be a trigger for them to draw their to attention to it - Comment from SME

Content
The language used in the button has recently been changed in order to create a more unified style as we continue to work with DWP, Cabinet Office and the Scottish Government. The use of 'Hide this page' presented more of a sense of immediacy, as well as being more descriptive of what the button actually does when the user interacts with it, so we have moved away from the original 'Quick Exit'.
We also use a keyboard function for the user to be able to interact with the button which is controlled by pressing the 'Esc' key.
Behaviour and Functionality
We have explored several types of behaviour for the button, however in order to provide the greatest amount of safety for users we decided to implement functionality similar to other charities and organisations.
When a user interacts with the button, they are sent to a new browser tab that opens BBC Weather. The original tab that they were on doesn't close, but redirects to Google.
This component does not prescribe which websites are to be linked to. That is best done by the individual services and their user research combined with the knowledge of their user base. Google and BBC Weather are good neutral examples pending further research.
Accessibility
The Legal Aid Agency have had an Accessibility Audit on their service and this highlighted some improvements to the component. These were:

Ensuring the button text accurately describes it's purpose
Ensure the instruction "(Or press 'Esc' key)" is presented to all users when presented as a sticky element
Include visually hidden text at the top of the page to help users of assistive technology be aware of the leave page functionality
Differentiate betwixt mobile displays and PC displays zoomed in, so the information about using the escape key is not hidden for non-mobile narrow displays

These changes have been implemented in the latest version of the component, however we will be looking to further test the accessibility of the component as we continue to iterate on it.
MoJ Data Analytics
The 'Hide this page' button has been running as an MVP on the Check Legal Aid service since 14 April 2020. It has been used with a fair amount of frequency, however at present we are are yet to analyse the data in more detail.
The gaps in data recording were due to changes on the back-end of our service that caused GA to drop out.
Graph data since 14 April 2020

The below graph data also shows variations in spikes and lower use through the pandemic

Examples



MoJ
DWP












SCOT.GOV
Cabinet Office




Image to follow

backlog.title: Multi File Upload
backlog.body:
What

I am looking to propose a Multi File upload pattern that currently does not exist in GDS. Currently, there are variations from HMRC and the MoJ which is most closely related to our use case for UKHSA. I have contacted govuk-design-system-support@digital.cabinet-office.gov.uk. who asked me to start a new issues.

Why

Explain why you think this should be added to the GOV.UK Design System.


The pattern would allow users to upload multiple files at once, review the uploaded files, and remove unwanted files, in it's MVP format with possible other features being explored.
There is currently no other pattern in GDS that meets a users need to upload a bulk amount of files at once.
There is also a current issue on GitHub 'upload file component has no visual target area when dragging and dropping a file'.
We have use cases where users need to upload multiple files at once, over 100 files in one submission. After our research, the NPIS team and the user-centred design team from UKHSA have concluded that no component in GDS meets the users needs.



What evidence do you have that it's needed by multiple services across the government?
Research shows multiple file upload patterns being used by HMRC and MoJ. There are further use cases within UKHSA.




What evidence do you have that it meets the needs of the users of those services?
The file upload component proposal build on what is being used by the MoJ and addresses accessibility concerns from the MoJ patterns. For examples, the use of green and red colours to distinguish if a file is ready uploaded and ticks and cross icons that could present problems with screen readers. Futher research has shows users want to know more details on upload space available and the number of files uploaded giving more clarity to the user.




Have you checked that it doesn't already exist in the GOV.UK Design System?
Yes


Anything else

Include links to any examples, research or code to support your proposal, if available.

ourIssues.title: VoiceOver on Safari cannot navigate into open Accordion section text content
ourIssues.body:
## Description of the issue

VoiceOver users in Safari browsers are not able to access the text content of open accordion sections. They are only able to access links.

Originally raised by [this zendesk ticket (internal to team only)](https://govuk.zendesk.com/agent/tickets/6881808?brand_id=3194076).

## Steps to reproduce the issue

Using VoiceOver on a Safari browser:

1. go to the [default Accordion example](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/accordion/default/)
2. navigate to one of the Accordion sections
3. open the section
4. attempt to navigate further down into the contents of the section

## Actual vs expected behaviour

Expected behaviour is that VoiceOver navigates into the section content and reads it out normally. Instead it skips the open section and continues to the next section heading.

You can also try this with the [example with summaries](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/accordion/with-summary-section/) where all the sections only contain links which are navigable using VoiceOver.

## Environment (where applicable)

- Operating system: MacOS 26.7
- Browser: Safari desktop
- Browser version: 26.7
- GOV.UK Frontend Version: At least 4.5.0

## Additional information

The reason for this is very likely the Accordion using `hidden="until-found` as an enhancement which we introduced in 4.5.0 via https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/pull/3053. There _was_ a [WebKit bug raised regarding this](https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=310623) which noted an error with `hidden="until-found"` in Safari not properly updating the accessibility tree in response to content expanding or collapsing. It's listed as solved but from testing is not fixed. The solution to this bug may therefore simply be to push for this getting fixed again.

ourIssues.title: Components assume the `govuk-visually-hidden` utility class will exist
ourIssues.body:
## Description of the issue

We provide an entry points for each individual component, the idea being that users should get all of the CSS they need to use that component, and ideally nothing more.

For example, including the character count component also includes the CSS for the:

- error message
- hint
- label
- textarea

However, it does _not_ include the `govuk-visually-hidden` utility class, which is used within the Nunjucks template.

From a quick check, it looks like this affects:

- Accordion (in the JavaScript)
- Character count (in the JavaScript)
- Error message (in the Nunjucks template)
- Exit this page (in the Nunjucks template and JavaScript)
- File upload (in the JavaScript)
- Footer (in the Nunjucks template)
- Pagination (in the Nunjucks template)
- Password input (in the JavaScript)
- Summary list (in the Nunjucks template)
- Warning text (in the Nunjucks template)

## Steps to reproduce the issue

Use the component-specific entrypoint to include just the CSS for any of the components listed above, then view the component

## Actual vs expected behaviour

Visually hidden text should be hidden, but it isn't because the `govuk-visually-hidden` utility class is not included in the CSS

ourIssues.title: Adjust components to scale with android system font size
ourIssues.body:
## What
Ensure as many of our components as possible are responding when viewing govuk-frontend web pages on android devices and adjusting android's system font size.

## Why
Govuk-frontend web pages should respect accessibility settigns and respond to them as expected.

## Steps to replicate
Tested in chrome on browserstack's Galaxy S23 instance as it's easy to notice the issue due to the device's large font size scale.

1. Go to the settings of the testing device and locate the setting to adjust device font size
2. Increase font size (recommend max in order to visualise issue more clearly)
3. Open a govuk-frontend web page on a browser on an android device eg: [the review app's announcements page](https://govuk-frontend-review.herokuapp.com/full-page-examples/announcements)

Notice that the breadcrumbs have not increased in size. Digging into the runtime styles, you will find that rem values of other elements on the page have adjusted in response to the font size change but the breadcrumbs haven't.

![Android browser showing an announcements page with scaled up font size except for the breadcrumbs element](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/assets/64783893/66ecb7d1-bf9e-459a-987c-8c85176a26b7)

## Notes
### Considerations from the spec
The likely reason this is happening can be found in CSS Mobile Text Size section of the CSS spec, specifically [2.2: Conditions that suppress adjustment](https://drafts.csswg.org/css-size-adjust/#default-adjustment-conditions). This section notes 4 reasons that would suppress text size adjustment. From initial testing, certain components can be 'fixed' by removing their block level positioning rules eg: components that have `display: inline-block`. We should be able to use `inline-block` on components and the text size adjustment not be suppressed. Recommend using the the spec in figuring out a solution.

### Impacted components
- Accordion
- Back link
- Breadcrumbs
- Button, and places consumed
    - Cookie banner buttons
    - Exit this page
- Checkboxes
- Details (not the content)
- File upload
- Some of the footer's links
- Header menu
- Notification banner
- Pagination
- Radios
- Select
- Table
- Tabs
- Tag
- Task list
- Text input, and places consumed
    - Date input
    - Password input

Developers

ourIssues.body:
## What

Perform research with users as to whether making labels on checkboxes and radio buttons span the width of the container, thus increasing their touch surface, makes it easier to use these controls

## Why

Generally speaking, increasing the target area for a control makes the control easier for users to interact with.

We have some existing precendent for this in Frontend already: 

- Labels for other input types (text inputs, selects, textareas, etc.) are already full width.
- The Accordion activates expand/collapse functionality by tapping anywhere in the section header.
- The Skip Link component, when visible, is activatable by clicking anywhere in the component.

The GOV.UK team has had positive feedback when increasing target sizes for elements on the [homepage](https://insidegovuk.blog.gov.uk/2021/12/13/updating-the-gov-uk-homepage/) and [topic pages](https://insidegovuk.blog.gov.uk/2022/08/08/rolling-out-a-new-design-for-browsing-gov-uk-by-topic/) in the last year.

Various external design systems have full width checkbox and radio labels, some of which are based on or inspired by GOV.UK Frontend and have seemingly made the conscious choice to change it:

- ~~[USWDS](https://designsystem.digital.gov/components/checkbox/)~~ Update: Has since updated to no longer be full-width
- [NICE Design System](https://design-system.nice.org.uk/storybook/?path=/story/foundations-checkbox--default)
- [Transport for West Midlands Design System](https://designsystem.tfwm.org.uk/components/radios/)
- [GOLD Design System](https://gold.designsystemau.org/components/control-input/#checkbox-block) (formerly Australian Government Design System)
- [Atlassian Design System](https://atlassian.design/components/checkbox/examples)

Our inline labels date from the GOV.UK Elements days, and I couldn't immediately find any reason why they were implemented in this way at the time. We have stuck to that precedent in situations where a conflict or bug relating to the label sizing has arisen (e.g. #634).

We should validate our current approach and whether it best meets user needs when compared to alternative approaches.

## Assumptions

We've [previously found that users don't tend to click on checkbox or radio button labels](https://designnotes.blog.gov.uk/2016/11/30/weve-updated-the-radios-and-checkboxes-on-gov-uk/), even if they're styled to appear interactible. It could be assumed that the same applies here (if not moreso, as there isn't any visual indicator that interaction is possible). 

As a larger area of the screen will activate a checkbox/radio, there may be an increase in the number of accidental form inputs being made.

A seemingly 'empty' part of the page affecting a nearby input may be unexpected and cause confusion to users unless some other hint is present (e.g. a hover state). 

## Timebox
TBD

## Who is working on this?

Spike lead: TBD

Spike buddy: TBD

## Questions to answer

- [ ] Is there a tangible benefit to checkbox and radio button labels always being full width?
- [ ] Is there a tangible benefit to checkbox and radio button labels being full width in certain situations (e.g. on narrow screens)? 
- [ ] Are full width labels more likely to result in accidental and unwanted inputs?
- [ ] Is having a visually 'empty' area of the screen interactive unexpected or a source of confusion?

## Done when

- [ ] A review or prototype is produced with the modified checkbox/radio styles.
- [ ] User research has been carried out to see how these changes perform with users.
- [ ] Findings have been reviewed and shared with the team.
- [ ] Any follow up issues or actions have been written up.

ourIssues.title: Various issues under Chrome's Auto Dark Mode
ourIssues.body:
Since Chrome version 78, Google has included an experimental feature in the browser, initially named "Forced Dark Mode" and, as of writing, named "Auto Dark Mode for Web Content". 

This feature automatically modifies the appearance of webpages in order to create a "dark mode" version. This is done even if the page already supplies a "dark mode" via the `prefers-color-scheme` CSS media query. It also appears to ignore the `color-scheme` property. 

The flag comes with several different "enabled" modes (as of Chrome 99), which modify how Chrome is internally applying changes. Each mode results in subtly (sometimes radically) different resulting colours.

1. Enabled
2. Enabled with simple HSL-based inversion
3. Enabled with simple CIELAB-based inversion
4. Enabled with simple RGB-based inversion
5. Enabled with selective image inversion
6. Enabled with selective inversion of non-image elements
7. Enabled with selective inversion of everything
8. Enabled with increased text contrast

Most of these modes appear to work by first overriding neutral light background colours (such as white and light greys), and modifying any copy that it detects as existing on a modified background colour to maintain suitable contrast. Most other colours appear to be left intact. This method of alteration means that colours are not all modified in the same way: `$govuk-brand-color` in mode 1, for example, is unmodified when used as a background or border colour (#1d70b8), but is changed when it is used as a text colour (#61a1ee).

Mode 4 appears to simply invert all colours on the page, regardless of usage. 

I'm not sure how mode 1 is different from the others. It may be that this is an "automatic" mode where Chrome tries to determine which of the other seven modes works best for the given page and uses that one.

We have received at least one bug report raised by a user who was using Chrome's Auto Dark Mode feature for accessibility reasons (to make content easier to read with cataracts).

> RE the dark mode, it is now a function in Google Chrome that you can activate and it will force a dark version if the website can accommodate it. Not everyone does, BBC News for example still comes through with a traditional black text on a white background – but it works for many.

## Steps to reproduce the issue
In Google Chrome, go to `chrome://flags/#enable-force-dark` (this should jump you straight to "Auto Dark Mode for Web Contents") and enable the flag.

## Actual vs expected behaviour
Currently, a number of these modes produce colour combinations which fail the contrast requirements established in WCAG 2.1. 

Below is a non-exhaustive subset of issues currently identified in Auto Dark Mode.

### Text inputs and textareas
Text inputs are displayed with a grey background and black border in modes 1, 6, 7, and 8. This fails to meet the expected 1:3 contrast ratio for UI elements (at 1:1.68). 

![Screenshot of the design system input component, appearing grey on black.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160644743-7632dc27-cc56-4558-bd40-8fee1109717c.png)

They are displayed with a light grey background and white border in modes 3 and 5, which easily meets contrast ratio expectations.

They are displayed with the default white background and black border in all other modes.

### Input prefixes and suffixes

These are difficult to read in modes 2 and 4, where they are black on a dark grey background (1:3.23).

![Screenshot of the design system input prefix and suffix example, where the text is black on dark grey.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160646813-ac2ad0a1-083d-4ca0-b571-b1ecacd450e4.png)

These are much more difficult to read in modes 3 and 5, which renders it as black on an even darker grey (1.22).

![Screenshot of the design system input prefix and suffix example. The text is visually imperceptible from the background.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160650473-9c6f3529-5a06-4408-b20e-242b1c66a08e.png)

These are displayed with adequate contrast in other modes.

### Checkboxes and radio buttons
The border and selection states of checkboxes and radio buttons do not have sufficient contrast in modes 1, 6, 7, and 8 (at a pretty much imperceptible contrast ratio of 1:1.04)

![Screenshot of the design system checkbox component, illustrating insufficient contrast between the checkboxes and background, which are both dark grey.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160644218-1fc50370-249e-4e47-b73a-eab9a8b8ea34.png)

They are displayed with white borders and selection states in all other modes.

### Select

In modes 1, 6, 7, and 8, select boxes are rendered with a dark grey background and dark grey border (1:1.04).

![Screenshot of the design system select component, which appears to just be white text with no border or icon.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160648934-5554f80a-1794-40e1-a9b7-a7c16df83d29.png)

They are rendered with a black background and white border in all other modes.

### Skiplinks

In modes 1, 2, 6, and 7, skiplinks are rendered as white on focus-colour yellow, which does not meet contrast requirements (1:1.34).

![Screenshot of a white link on a bright yellow background.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160649767-19aecf58-2ea6-4517-9852-283a4c91f922.png)

In mode 4, it is white on light blue, which is also below expectations (1:3.24).

![Screenshot of a white link on a bright blue background.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160649982-3f7999be-3540-40c5-8d00-7b9350407360.png)

In mode 8, it is white on focus-color yellow, but additionally has a black text shadow/stroke effect applied, which makes it difficult to read.

![Screenshot of a white link with a thin, pixellated black shadow surrounding it, on a bright yellow background.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160650309-a61034bd-d400-4ca3-b312-db890c382f19.png)

This is displayed with adequate contrast (albeit, in white on brown) in all other modes.

### Iconography

Most iconography fails to meet contrast requirements in virtually all modes. This includes:
- the open and close arrows on the Accordion component.
- the arrow on the Back link component.
- the arrows on the Breadcrumbs component.
- the exclamation icon on the Warning text component.

### Other components
The good news is that, for the most part, the majority of other components we have in GOV.UK Frontend are not as badly affected as those above, with various components such as Inset text, Error summary, and Notification banner maintaining their necessary visual presence and suitable contrast even with modified colours. 

## Environment
The results specified here were taken in Chrome 99, running on macOS 15.3, whilst the operating system was set to light mode. 

Interestingly, Chrome DevTools does not give any indication that a change to the page's appearance has taken place. All HTML and CSS content, including the user agent stylesheet, computed styles, and those returned through JavaScript, appear unmodified and are not aligned with the page's actual appearance when Auto Dark Mode is enabled.

ourIssues.title: Improve support for Windows High Contrast Mode and Internet Explorer 11
ourIssues.body:
<!--

  This is a template for any issues that aren’t bug reports or new feature requests. The headings in this section provide examples of the information you might want to include, but feel free to add/delete sections where appropriate.

-->

This builds on work by @chris-gds for the accordion component refresh in #2257.

## What

Add media feature `-ms-high-contrast` to media queries that change styles for Windows High Contrast Mode.

Add CSS property `-ms-high-contrast-adjust` where property `forced-color-adjust` is used.

For example, see draft PR #2290 

## Why

Internet Explorer 11 doesn't support the [`forced-colors` media feature](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@media/forced-colors) or the [`forced-color-adjust` property](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/forced-color-adjust), but it has equivalents in [`-ms-high-contrast`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@media/-ms-high-contrast) and [`-ms-high-contrast-adjust`](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/hh771863(v=vs.85)).

We can port fixes for High Contrast Mode such as improved focus states for radios and checkboxes (https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/pull/2264) that currently work in Edge / Chrome / Opera but not Internet Explorer.

According to the 2018 WebAIM survey of users with low vision, a higher percentage use Internet Explorer than Edge.

## Who needs to know about this

Devs

## Done when

- [x] GOV.UK Frontend has support for Windows High Contrast Mode and Internet Explorer 11 #2290 
- [ ] Documented how to add tweaks for Windows High Contrast Mode and other forced colour modes in future

ourIssues.title: Add guidance around print styles and behaviour
ourIssues.body:
## Related documentation

No existing equivalent.

Should likely be a new page, but could be spread across several pages (colours, typography, accordion, tabs, details, etc.) otherwise. 

## Suggestion

The Design System doesn't currently provide any guidance relating to print styles. The only mention of them is on the [layout styles](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/styles/layout/), where there's a override class specific to hiding elements when printed.

This is a question that comes up on support channels and is discussed on Slack semi-frequently, and we have made various choices when developing styles and components that are undocumented. This guidance could also be useful for teams developing new components built on Frontend's code. 

### Things that could be documented

**Remember printing is expensive.** Ink and paper are not free (ink especially) for both users and the environment. Where possible, we should minimise how much of each is used by hiding superfluous elements on the page when printing (e.g. the site's navigation) and making considered decisions over the use and quantity of colour.

**Maintain the page's current state.** A user is often printing the page because they need a hard copy of some piece of information. This could be a particular section on a guidance page, a reference number for an application, or the answers they've provided to a service. Generally, don't alter parts page the user is likely to want to print, when they print it (e.g. expanding or collapsing accordion sections, changing tabs, blanking form inputs).

**Remove background colours.** Don't rely on the presence of a background colour for text contrast. If anything, we likely want to encourage proactively removing background colours to ensure the readability of any text placed on top of them. Use borders to preserve the separation and grouping of elements instead.[^FE]

**Don't use colour to convey information.** Pages may be printed in greyscale, making it difficult to determine the colours of elements. Supplement with text labels, shapes or patterns.

**Use system fonts.** Printers can occassionally struggle to correctly understand web font formats. Reset to a system font or font keyword (e.g. `sans-serif`) to avoid this issue.[^FE]

**Provide context for invisible information.** Some information is usually only visible within a browser, such as a tooltip expanding on an `<abbr>` or the browser status bar showing the URL that a link directs to. When printed, this important information can be lost. Use print styles to re-insert this content on the page.[^FE]

[^FE]: Already a thing GOV.UK Frontend or Frontend components do. Still good to include so teams don't inadvertently override it or forget to implement or test in their own styles.

### Caveats

A user's individual printer configuration will change what the output looks like, and each browser additionally handles things differently when printing, such as whether they respect media queries and what breakpoints they use for calculating them. In this regard, a content author doesn't have a huge amount of control over how some aspects of a page look when printed. Related issue: https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/3441

communityIssues.title: Inconsistent components API
communityIssues.body:
The component API is inconsistent across components and in comparison with `govuk-frontend`.

In the table below there is a brief comparison in how `govuk-frontend` components are aligned in API with `govuk_publishing_components`

|Component               |API |
|---                      |---  |
Accordion                 | aligned
Back link                 | aligned
Breadcrumbs               | misaligned
Button                    | slightly misaligned (start)
Character count           | slightly misaligned (nesting)
Checkboxes                | slightly misaligned (fieldset)
Date input                | slightly misaligned (fieldset)
Details                   | misaligned
Error message             | aligned
Error summary             | misaligned
Fieldset                  | misaligned
File upload               | aligned
Footer                    | aligned
Header                    | slightly misaligned (navigation_items)
Inset text                | aligned
Panel                     | misaligned
Phase banner              | misaligned
Radios                    | slightly misaligned (fieldset)
Select                    | slightly misaligned (options)
Skip link                 | aligned
Summary list              | slightly misaligned (items)
Table                     | aligned
Tabs                      | misaligned
Text input                | aligned
Textarea                  | aligned
Warning text              | slightly misaligned (iconFallbackText)

We can see a few common differences between to two API models:
- for arrays, `govuk-frontend` uses the generic `items` (in most cases) whereas `govuk_publishing_components` uses the name of the component (e.g. `attachments` for the attachment list component or `breadcrumbs` for the breadcrumbs component)
- for web addresses/paths `govuk-frontend` uses `href` whereas in `govuk_publishing_components` we often find `url` (e.g. breadcrumbs component)

It's worth mentioning that not even `govuk-frontend`'s API is consistent (e.g. `errorList` instead of `items` in the Error summary component, or differences in nesting)

A few advantages of making the API consistent:
- increases developers' confidence when calling components with arguments (without constantly checking examples in the guide)
- prototyping and production will use the same config object (can be easily copied over in both directions)
- applications can prepare the data to be fed into components consistently using helpers
- it would be easier to swap one component with another

I'm creating this to raise awareness of the differences, hopefully generate discussions around how good looks like and aim for consistency and convergency. API alignment requires at least a breaking change and some replacements across applications – which is not an easy process. For this reason, having a clear vision about how we want it to look like would save us from doing this more than once.
