ourIssues.title: Improve documentation of `beforeInput(s)` and `afterInput(s)` options of our form control components
ourIssues.body:
<!--

  This is a template for any issues that aren’t bug reports or new feature requests. The headings in this section provide examples of the information you might want to include, but feel free to add/delete sections where appropriate.

-->

## What

Research and document which kind of content is OK/not OK to put in the `beforeInput(s)` and `afterInput(s)` options of our form components, introduced in #4567 to ensure all users (especially those using assistive technology) get proper access to the content.

## Why

Because the content ends up inside a form field, where the control is associated to the label/legend and any error/hint, there's a risk that content injected through `beforeInput(s)`/`afterInput(s)` options gets missed when navigating from field to field, the focus skipping over the content to the next form field. 

This means we may want to suggest restrictions as to which content is suitable for these options, possible techniques to link the content so it gets announced when navigating from field to field, and possibly a warning to test thoroughly.

## Who needs to work on this

Developers, Accessibility specialist, possibly Designers

## Who needs to review this

Developers, Accessibility specialist, possibly Designers 

## Done when

- [ ] We've clarified how to best use the `beforeInput(s)` and `afterInput(s)` options of our form components.

ourIssues.title: Research improvements to disabled form control styles
ourIssues.body:
## What

We've shipped an MVP (minimum-viable product) version of disabled form controls in #1713—which aimed to make disabled styles consistent—however we still have some unanswered questions about the suitability of the disabled styles included in Frontend as a whole.

## Why

We have historically discouraged the use of disabled form controls and buttons in user-facing scenarios. Although we continue to discourage their use, we have decided to provide them to cover for situations where user research has found their use helpful or where their use can be better justified (such as an internal caseworking system). 

As we've not encouraged their use, we also haven't performed much testing or research into whether the disabled styles we use work well for end users.

## Assumptions

- Our current disabled styles aren't necessarily adequate in all contexts. For example, a value-less, disabled text input or textarea appears as an empty box, with little other affordance that it is disabled or an input.
- Although WCAG 2.1 (and, currently, 2.2) do not require a minimum contrast ratio for 'inactive' elements, we may want to ensure the visibility of disabled inputs on our own terms.
- Any changes we make to disabled styles should be applicable across all 'core' form control components: Text Input, Textarea, Select, File Upload, Checkbox, and Radios. 
  - If possible or useful, we may also want it to apply to the Button component. 

## Timebox

2 weeks

## Who is working on this?

Spike lead:

Spike buddy:

## Questions to answer

- [ ] Are our current disabled styles well understood by users?
- [ ] Are our current disabled styles still perceptable by users with vision impairment?
- [ ] Do service teams know when they shouldn't be using disabled inputs?

## Done when

- [ ] Questions have been answered or we have a clearer idea of how to get to our goal
- [ ] Findings have been reviewed and agreed with at least one other person
- [ ] Findings have been shared, e.g: via a write-up on the ticket, at a show & tell or team meeting
- [ ] Any code changes we want to make have been made
- [ ] Any documentation changes we want to make have been made

ourIssues.title: Consider updating hints and error messages to use paragraphs
ourIssues.body:
## What Consider updating hints and error messages to use paragraphs rather than spans and divs. https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/d5a3fa8c5e61dbc7ca0f7a8429cc8e6716ee7c32/src/govuk/components/error-message/template.njk#L3-L6 https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/d5a3fa8c5e61dbc7ca0f7a8429cc8e6716ee7c32/src/govuk/components/hint/template.njk#L1-L4 ## Why As raised by a user on x-gov Slack: > the error message is in a tag. Is there a reason why a `` is used, rather than a `
` or `

`, for example? The reason I ask is because I’ve been doing some testing with JAWS and I’ve found that there’s no pause between reading the hint text and the error message. So JAWS reads “For example 12 11 2007 error colon the date your passport was issued must be in the past”. Using a `

` didn’t make a difference, but using a `

` resulted in a pause between the hint text and the error message, so potentially making it a little clearer. It looks like hints used to be paragraphs, but [were changed to spans when the hints were moved inside the label](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk_elements/commit/5f631c113840bfd4cc3ed81de8fb311638457a92#diff-1968332cde003a71f281b5d33445bcb3a43d2ac1cee565f6bc0e0a0144cfb846) – presumably as [only phrasing content is permitted within a `label`](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/forms.html#the-label-element). Error messages, when they were added later, were also spans inside the label. We recently [updated hints to use divs rather than spans](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/commit/d92d3c8a990730213430b686d239fc7b278530a9) so that they can be used with flow content (for example multiple paragraph tags, or a list) Since [we moved hints and error messages out of the labels](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/pull/681), we should consider whether they should now by marked up as paragraphs instead. ## Who needs to know about this Developers, designers ## Done when - [x] Tested alternate form controls with error messages and hints marked up as paragraphs in assistive technologies - [x] Identified other potential issues cause by changing hints and error messages to paragraphs - [ ] Decision made and code change made - [ ] Check if the changelog for https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/1856 needs updating as a result of this work

ourIssues.title: The expanded/collapsed state of conditional reveals is not available to all assistive technologies
ourIssues.body:
## What

As part of an internal accessibility audit of GOV.UK, conditional reveals† was flagged as failing WCAG 4.1.2:

> **4.1.2 Name, Role, Value**: For all user interface components (including but not limited to: form elements, links and components generated by scripts), the name and role can be programmatically determined; states, properties, and values that can be set by the user can be programmatically set; and notification of changes to these items is available to user agents, including assistive technologies. (Level A)

It was flagged as failing because:
- the additional 'role' of the checkbox or radio button is not clear
- changes to the expanded ‘state’ of the radio buttons is not available to assistive tech, and so users may be unaware that something else has changed on the page as a result of selecting a radio.

We use `aria-expanded` on these controls, but that is technically invalid according to the spec, which [only allows `aria-expanded` on certain roles](https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria-1.1/#aria-expanded). Some screen readers still announce the expanded state, but those that don’t have no reason to implement it because it’s against the spec. ARIA 1.2 (which is currently in draft) extends support of aria-expanded to checkboxes but not radios.

The fact that `aria-expanded` is not valid is recorded as a separate but related issue (https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/979).

As of [September 2019](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/979#issuecomment-528932826), this is known to affect:

- Voiceover (https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/989)
- JAWS (https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/935)

### Update

As of June 2021, we [removed conditional reveals from our accessibility statement](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/issues/6042#issuecomment-871527458).

---

† The [page being audited](https://webarchive.nationalarchives.gov.uk/20200911014618/https://www.gov.uk/email-signup?link=/world/switzerland) uses the conditional reveals in an unusual way, as what’s being revealed is effectively contextual help (like a hint) that would help the user to make the right choice. Whereas the way we intend the component to be used is [to reveal additional form controls that ‘follow on’ from the initial question](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/radios/#conditionally-revealing-content). We think that revealing text in this way is 'worse' in terms of accessibility, so we have a separate issue to discourage users from using conditional reveals to reveal text (https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/issues/1362)

backlog.title: Passwordless login
backlog.body:
What
Let users edit their information without a password, by sending them a secure link to their email address when they want to login.
Why
The problem with passwords
Passwords are both annoying for users and rarely anymore secure than just using an email link – Arguably, it's even less secure than using an email link. This is because users often use the same password for everything, so if their password to some insecure online shop (for example) gets leaked, then also their password for a critical GOV.UK service gets leaked.
The argument against passwordless systems is usually that the email becomes the single point of defence, so if a hacker has access to your email they have access to everything. This would be true, but passwords don't protect against that as they always need a way to 'reset' them, and the mechanism to do that is basically the email link which is the passwordless system itself.
Besides this, is the point that email accounts are generally built to be more secure than the average shopfront anyway. So if it's the choice between your email account being your one way in, and a password which is shared between all the insecure websites you use, the email wins everytime.
Of course, the best way to protect an account completely is to have a unique password for every account. But we all know that users don't do this, and the more we keep getting them to remember different passwords for everything the less likely they are to make different ones. One solution is to use an app like OnePassword which stores lots of passwords for you, but that will only ever be something that more technically literate users use. Many users of GOV.UK are much more likely to use a paper password store if they do use different passwords, which has it's own security problems.
The solution
It's essentially the "Forgot your password" function, without the bit where people try and fail to remember their password.
This is already in use on GOV.UK for 'Manage your email subscriptions'.


Admittedly, this service is potentially more well suited than most to this kind of logging in as the user is starting in their email inbox anyway when they start their journey. (i.e When they realise they want to change their subscriptions.)
However, the pattern is also in use across many private sector services including Slack. (Which I believe also includes an option to create a password for quicker login, but deters users from this as a default.)

I think it would be good for more services to be experimenting with this as a login method and collecting their research findings here.
Some links to other people making this argument

https://auth0.com/blog/is-passwordless-authentication-more-secure-than-passwords/
https://swoopnow.com/passwordless-login/#security

backlog.title: 'Select / Unselect all' functionality?
backlog.body:
I am working as a SD on the HMRC help and support email service (along with a UR - a team of two). The user logs into the service with their email address, and that email address is then matched with email subscriptions from various HOD data stores. The user is presented with a list of their current email subscriptions, with the checkboxes ticked by default. They are also presented, below that, with a lis of H&S topics which may also be of interest to them (ie topics to which they are not currently subscribed, with the checkboxes unticked). There are a total of 18 topics.
In some cases, eg an Agent/Accountant, the list of subscribed topics may be quite long.
If a user is subscribed to many topics, and therefore has a lot of checkboxes ticked, is there a pattern to allow for 'uncheck all'?
This is the sort of thing we'd like to do...

ourIssues.title: Have a way to prevent tables from overflowing by breaking words
ourIssues.body: If you have a table containing a long string, such as an email address, then it can cause the table to extend beyond the width of its container: Adding the [`govuk-!-text-break-word` class](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/styles/font-override-classes/#breaking-up-long-words) makes no difference in this scenario. Ideally, the table would follow the pattern of the summary list component (which also looks table-like), and would have its contents break across multiple lines if needed to prevent the table overflowing.

ourIssues.title: Legend (and hint and error message) for the group of radios / checkboxes announced when focusing a conditionally revealed field whilst using VoiceOver
ourIssues.body:
Conditionally revealed controls are inside the `<fieldset>` that wraps the radios / checkboxes.

This could potentially cause confusion, as in VoiceOver the legend (and any other text associated with the fieldset using `aria-describedby`, such as a hint or error message) is read out when focusing the conditionally revealed content.

![Screenshot 2020-10-16 at 13 03 20](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/121939/96256125-fe980080-0faf-11eb-9da5-289e0c39a63e.png)

For example, when focusing the conditionally revealed 'email address' field in the example from the Design System (above), Voiceover with Safari (14) on macOS (10.15.7) announces:

> "Email address, edit text, How would you like to be contacted? Select all options that are relevant to you. You are currently on a text field. To enter text in this field, type."

The hint text "Select all options that are relevant to you" applies to the set of checkboxes, and does not make sense in the context of the email address field.

ourIssues.title: Improve the `title`s for pattern guidance pages
ourIssues.body:
## Context

Pattern pages with compound titles do not have the entire title included within the `title` element.

|Page `h1`|Page `title`|
|:-|:-|
|Ask users for Bank Details|Bank details|
|Ask users for Email addresses|Email addresses|
|Help users to Confirm an email address|Confirm an email address|
|Help users to Exit a page quickly|Exit a page quickly|

This can cause confusion, as some pages on the Design System website can have similar or identical `title`s in browser tabs and search result listings. 

|Pattern page `title`|Non-pattern page `title`|
|:-|:-|
|Cookies page|[Cookies](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/cookies/)|
|Dates|[Date input](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/date-input/)|
|Exit a page quickly|[Exit this page](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/exit-this-page/)|
|Passwords|Password input [in development]|

In instances where a pattern has a compound title (i.e. "Ask users for...", "Help users to...") these should be included in the page `title`. 

It may also be useful to include the name of the parent section ("Styles", "Components", "Patterns", etc.) somewhere within the page `title` on these child pages.

## Alternatives

Currently you must either look at the page's URL or click through to visit the page in order to see whether it is the desired page. 

## Additional information

Raised by a working group member during a working group meeting.

ourIssues.title: Investigate making it clearer that the Design System email address is not a generic government helpline
ourIssues.body:
Adding as I think we've discussed this before but never written it up.

## What

We very frequently receive emails from members of the public who have encountered issues with a GOV.UK service (or a government service generally) and are seeking support or updates. 

This is despite displaying a warning on our [get in touch](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/get-in-touch/) page stating that we are unable to help with these queries and providing instructions on how to contact the relevant government departments. 

## Why

This is not a high-volume issue (around a dozen emails a week or fewer), but it's a persistent one.

Members of the public often include Personally Identifying Information in these emails, unnecessarily exposing Design System team members to PII and requiring every member of the team to manually delete the offending emails from their inboxes to comply with data protection laws. In Zendesk, it also means that we need to go through the data redaction process before we can proceed to forward the ticket to user support.

In addition to dealing with the irrelevant ticket, these additional PII tasks are distracting for the whole team. They don't always happen in a timely fashion (if at all) due to members being on leave or on non-working days.

By reducing the quantity of unrelated support emails the team receives, we can alleviate this source frustration and help avoid unnecessarily holding personal data. 

A non-exhaustive list of potential ways to resolve this:

- Remove the contact page from search engine results, as (assumedly) this is where members of the public are finding it.
- Rewrite and/or reformat the existing warning text to make it _extremely_ explicit that we do not provide support or information to members of the public.
  - Consider harsher language in general, such as saying that emails from the public will be deleted and not responded to. 
- Use a more visually prominent component, such as a [Notification banner](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/notification-banner/), or bespoke styling, to display the warning.
- Consider not displaying the email address or link unless a user performs an action acknowledging the warning.

## Who needs to work on this

- Content designers
- Developers (potentially)
- Designers (potentially)

## Who needs to review this

- Content designers

## Done when

- [ ] Thing to do

ourIssues.title: WCAG 2.2: Start using a service ‖ Consistent Help
ourIssues.body:
## What

Consider adding or updating a screenshot of a start page to include visible help or contact information on the page, displayed in a consistent manner. Related to #2882. 

This is largely a usability suggestion and may not be necessary for WCAG compliance. 

### Resources

- [Start using a service pattern guidance](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/start-using-a-service/)
- [WCAG 2.2 criterion for 'Consistent Help'](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/consistent-help.html)

## Why

The new WCAG 2.2 Level A criterion 'Consistent Help' says:

> If a [Web page](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/consistent-help.html#dfn-web-page) contains any of the following help [mechanisms](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/consistent-help.html#), and those mechanisms are repeated on multiple Web pages within a [set of Web pages](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/consistent-help.html#dfn-set-of-web-pages), they occur in the same order relative to other page content, unless a change is initiated by the user:
> * Human contact details;
> * Human contact mechanism;
> * Self-help option;
> * A fully automated contact mechanism.

Although the intent of the criterion is that the contact information itself is consistently ordered with respect to the rest of the page (i.e. a help link is always in the same place in the footer, as described in #2871) we can go beyond this by advising that teams provide this information in a consistent order every time it appears.

For example, if a service has three contact mechanisms—phone, email address, post—these should be listed in the same order and format on all pages where it appears, such as the service start page, support pages, contact page, etc. 

## Who needs to work on this
- Content designer or technical writer

## Who needs to review this
- Accessibility specialist
- Content designer or technical writer

## Done when

- [ ] Guidance has been updated

ourIssues.title: Styling headings / labels / legends
ourIssues.body:
I've been struggling a bit with styling of headings / labels / legends - and finding classes to do the styling. I think partly this is because to make something bold and a certain size, I need to use different classes depending on the element it is. It's tripped me up a few times now.

I find styling tricky because:
* Many component examples only show components with a non-bold small label. But in _most_ cases I need to override this.
* The section on `typography` doesn't include the classes you'd need

For instance in this example:
![screenshot 2019-03-04 at 16 54 38](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2204224/53748934-3cf5b000-3e9e-11e9-99c0-433fdc0dfba8.png)

I wanted to make the label for `Email address` larger and bold.

What I want it to look like:
![screenshot 2019-03-04 at 16 48 00](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2204224/53749472-59461c80-3e9f-11e9-87f4-937b3bb45995.png)

Talking with @adamsilver, I reckon in _most_ cases where a _thing_ is not page-per-thing, we're going to want to make the label larger and bold.

My solution so far has been to go to the question pages which have some more examples of different sizes with bold questions.

@nickcolley pointed me at [this getting started 'Making labels and legends headings' page](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/get-started/labels-legends-headings/). Which covers some more options. I think partly my issue is I expected the classes to be documented in `/typography`, not in 'getting started' guidance.

Some suggestions:
* For basic styling things like font weight / size, can details of the classes be put in `/styles/typography` ?
* For many patterns I'd consider two further examples: one with the pattern as if it's page per thing (with large label or legend), and one with a larger bold heading applied (like they are in the question pages pattern).

ourIssues.title: Add `size` option to form input component labels
ourIssues.body:
<!--

  This is a template for any issues that aren’t bug reports or new feature requests. The headings in this section provide examples of the information you might want to include, but feel free to add/delete sections where appropriate.

-->

## What

Allow form field components to receive a new `size` option in their `label` or `legend` option for easily controlling the text size of their label or legend. The option should receive a t-shirt size and set the appropriate `.govuk-label--<T_SHIRT_SIZE>` or `.govuk-fieldset__legend--<T_SHIRT_SIZE>` on the label or legend.

For components using a `label` the option should be implemented by adding a [new option to our internal Label component](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/tree/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/label) and passing the option through. For those using a `legend`, the public Fieldset component should get an update first in a similar fashion.

The affected components are:
- [Character Count](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/character-count/template.njk) (forwarding the option to Textarea)
- [Checkboxes](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/checkboxes/template.njk) (forwarding the option to either Fieldset)
- [Date Input](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/date-input/template.njk) (forwarding the option to Fieldset)
- [Fieldset](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/date-input/template.njk)
- [File Upload](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/file-upload/template.njk) (forwarding the option to Label)
- [Input](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/input/template.njk) (forwarding the option to Label)
- [Label](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/label/template.njk)
- [Password Input](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/password-input/template.njk) (forwarding the option to Input)
- [Radios](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/radios/template.njk) (forwarding the option to Fieldset)
- [Select](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/select/template.njk) (forwarding the option to Label)
- [Textarea](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/textarea/template.njk) (forwarding the option to Label)

## Why

Different components use different tags for the "title" of the field. This requires the user to understand internal nuances (is it a `label` or `legend`) to change its size. Having an option abstracting this and letting the component work out if it's `.govuk-label--...` or `.govuk-fieldset__legend--...` that's needed is much easier.

## Who needs to work on this

Developers, Tech writer

## Who needs to review this

Developers, Tech writer

## Done when

- [ ] The new option is available on all the components listed above
- [ ] The option is documented consistently across components

ourIssues.body: ## What A user requested that we make [labels and legends as page headings](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/get-started/labels-legends-headings/) support the use of [captions](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/styles/typography/#headings-with-captions). communityIssues.title: Back to top link fails 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum)
communityIssues.body: The [Back to top link component](https://govuk-government-frontend.herokuapp.com/component-guide/back_to_top) in government-frontend fails [2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum)](https://w3c.github.io/wcag/understanding/focus-not-obscured-minimum.html). Note: 2.4.11 is part of the new draft WCAG 2.2 criteria. The latest standard is WCAG 2.1. WCAG 2.2 isn't published yet, so this is potentially subject to change. As mentioned by Andy Sellick in his 2018 blog post ‘[Sticky elements: functionality and accessibility testing](https://technology.blog.gov.uk/2018/05/21/sticky-elements-functionality-and-accessibility-testing/)’, content can be obscured by a sticky element. 2.4.11 is specifically about focus that shouldn’t be obscured. There was an effort with this component to minimise that already as the sticky ‘Contents’ link only appears when scrolling the page but not when only tabbing through the page. Although that fixes some of the issue, that doesn’t mean that the focus never gets obscured. The sticky link still appears when scrolling via the keyboard (for example, with the arrow keys) or when accidentally scrolling with the mouse or touchpad only for a second. To replicate, open the [preview of the 'Contents list with body' component](https://govuk-government-frontend.herokuapp.com/component-guide/contents_list_with_body/default/preview), tab to the last link (‘Commencement of initial period notice’), scroll the page via the up arrow key so that the link is obscured, use tab and shift + tab to go back and forth to see how you can tab to a link that isn’t visible. ourIssues.title: Consider applying custom print styles to Button component
ourIssues.body: Spun off from #7364. ## Related component - [Button](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/button/) ## Context When printing a page, all major browsers allow the user to remove background colours and background images, with the intent of reducing the amount of ink or toner needed to print the page, often as the default setting. This is a fairly brute force process, working similarly to setting `background: transparent !important` on every element of the page. In some browsers, white coloured text is altered to be light grey on any element with the background removed. However, this can still provide insufficient levels of contrast. In combination, this means that when a page is printed with this option set, buttons come out not looking much like buttons at all. They lack the button-defining 'box', text contrast on most of them is low, there's little visual difference between primary, secondary and warning buttons, and the chevron on start buttons becomes invisible. Above screenshot is from Chromium. PDF versions of each major desktop browser. - [Chromium (Chrome, Edge)](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/31270305/Chrome.-.Button.states.pdf) - [Firefox](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/31270304/Firefox.-.Button.states.pdf) - [Safari](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/31270303/Safari.-.Button.states.pdf) Whilst this probably isn't a major issue (button text should be self-explanatory anyway), we could restore some distinction to the buttons by adding print styles to: - proactively remove the background colours from each button, rather than leaving it up to user configuration, and ensure that buttons have a contrasting text colour - add visible borders around each button - use some other aspect of the button (such as the border) to convey the primary/secondary/warning colours

ourIssues.title: Add documentation on best practices for deduplicating CSS classes and using `initAll`

ourIssues.title: Macros Component API should not require internal classes for modifiers
ourIssues.body:
Macros abstract our class names, if we were to change our class names, macro usage would break for our users.

In our button examples, we pass the internal button modifier class to make a button into a start button.

We could consider passing a boolean instead so that if we choose to change how our classes work, macros still function.

For example instead of

```yaml
- name: start
  data:
    text: Start now button
    classes: 'govuk-c-button--start'
```

We could do:

```yaml
- name: start
  data:
    text: Start now button
    start: true
```

See also the GOV.UK Publishing component: http://govuk-static.herokuapp.com/component-guide/button/start_now_button

Link to code: https://github.com/alphagov/static/blob/a9a040a72d475ef7015c1c9e690a5d77687fcfd8/app/views/govuk_component/button.raw.html.erb#L1

We constructed the class based on booleans, then finally merge with `classes` and inject into the markup.

Edit: 
I put together an example showing how you can restructure the macro to avoid the confusing forking logic.

This approach only forks on individual parts of the template, which is easier to reason about.

https://glitch.com/edit/#!/flag-based-macro-approach?path=views/index.html:15:26

ourIssues.title: Add guidance on empty table cells to Table component
ourIssues.body:
## Related documentation

* [Table component](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/table/)

## Suggestion

Add guidance on how users should handle cells that don't have any data.

## Evidence (where applicable)

GDS's content design guidance states that cells should never be empty, but instead explicitly state they contain no data: https://www.gov.uk/guidance/content-design/tables

There is also guidance that column and row headings should never be empty, and should always contain descriptive content unless it's the top-left most cell. 

Our component softly implies this by having text or HTML be required for every cell, but that doesn't prevent users from passing an empty string to it. Adding guidance would make this more explicit to implementing users, without them having to reference a separate body of documentation.

This was raised by a user via our support channels.

communityIssues.title: Do we need the govspeak HTML publication component?
communityIssues.body:
The [govspeak content (HTML publications) component ](https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/govspeak_html_publication) is a wrapper for the regular [govspeak](https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/govspeak) component with some extra CSS rules. It's used only in `government-frontend` on [HTML publication pages like this one](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/benefit-and-pension-rates-2025-to-2026/benefit-and-pension-rates-2025-to-2026).

Specifically, the differences are:

- extra spacing above headings (currently in the form of margin-top)
- a margin bottom to the overall component
- some styles for a specific table class (not sure how that's being added to the govspeak, the tables on the example link above don't have this class in its content)
- some miscellaneous things to do with `stat-headline` and `number`

I don't know the history behind this but it's obvious that HTML publications are meant to look slightly different from every other page type. My question is why does this one page type need to be different? Could we merge/adjust some of these styles into the regular govspeak styles, and retire this component? e.g.

- extra spacing between headings seems like either a good or bad idea everywhere, this could be dropped or merged into govspeak
- govspeak component now has a margin bottom option (component wrapper) so we could set that for the one instance in HTML publications
- need to check and see if the `financial-data` class is actually on any tables anywhere, if not could remove
- would need to check miscellaneous styles individually

communityIssues.title: Organisation logo image width needs adjustment

- width: 100%

ourIssues.title: Issues with Exit this Page keyboard shortcut and the iOS/iPadOS virtual keyboard
ourIssues.body:
## Description of the issue

The Exit this Page component includes a method of activating the exit functionality by pressing the <kbd>Shift</kbd> key three times (behind the scenes, three `keyup` events). We do not limit when this functionality works, so it's still possible to do this when focused on an input or textarea. This is by design, as we want the user to be able to use the function quickly and at any time. 

This does mean, however, that the function is exposed to devices that utilise virtual keyboards (aka, on-screen keyboards or software keyboards) when a text field is focused. This can be problematic, as the <kbd>Shift</kbd> function was only designed with hardware keyboards in mind and virtual keyboards can operate substantially differently than their hardware equivalents.

### An overview of iOS <kbd>Shift</kbd> operating modes

The <kbd>Shift</kbd> key on iOS has multiple modes of operation depending on the current context, attributes of the current input, and how it is pressed. In one context it is also replaced by a numbers and symbols toggle button, however this button is still treated as being a <kbd>Shift</kbd> key for the purposes of JavaScript events.

**When pressed for a short period of time**, the <kbd>Shift</kbd> key acts as a toggle switch, and changes between being 'on' or 'off' on alternating presses of the <kbd>Shift</kbd> key. The `keyup` event is fired on every second press (the 'off'), except in cases described below.

**When held down**, the <kbd>Shift</kbd> key acts transiently, being 'on' for as long as the user holds it down and turning 'off' once released. The user can press other keys when <kbd>Shift</kbd> is held down to type in uppercase. When used in this way, the `keyup` event is **not** fired when the user releases the <kbd>Shift</kbd> key.

The user can **tap <kbd>Shift</kbd> twice** in rapid succession to turn on Caps Lock mode. The user can press <kbd>Shift</kbd> a third time to turn Caps Lock mode off. When this is carried out, it's emitted as a `keyup` event by the <kbd>Caps Lock</kbd> key, not the <kbd>Shift</kbd> key.

When the user **enters numbers and symbols mode** on the keyboard, the <kbd>Shift</kbd> key is visually replaced by a button to toggle between the initial numbers and symbols view, and the extended symbols view. In this mode, tapping to view the extended symbols mode is treated as a <kbd>Shift</kbd> `keydown` event, and returning to the initial numbers and symbols view is treated as a <kbd>Shift</kbd> `keyup` event. These events are emitted to the webpage, in what feels like a bug in Safari or iOS. 

There are several situations in which **the <kbd>Shift</kbd> key is turned 'on' automatically**. When this happens, no `keydown` event is emitted to the webpage. When it is turned 'off', either automatically or by the user, no `keyup` event is emitted. 

> [!NOTE]
> The takeaway to remember from this is that <kbd>Shift</kbd> will _never_ emit a `keyup` event if the `keydown` wasn't initiated by the user, even if the `keyup` was. This holds true for all of the cases here. 

Situations where this can occur include:

* The input being empty when the user taps on it.
* The cursor being positioned at the start of a new sentence, line or paragraph when the user taps on the input.
* The cursor being positioned at the start of a new word, if the input has the `autocapitalize="words"` attribute.
* Always, if the input has the `autocapitalize="characters"` attribute.

There are a couple of situations where the virtual keyboard will **fire `keyup` events without user intent**. These include: 

* Turning <kbd>Shift</kbd> 'on' manually and switching to the numbers and symbols view will emit the `keyup` event.
* On an input where <kbd>Shift</kbd> will not turn 'on' automatically (e.g. in the middle of a word or sentence), manually activate <kbd>Shift</kbd>, close the virtual keyboard, and then tap on the input to open it again. <kbd>Shift</kbd> will be returned to the 'off' state and emit the `keyup` event.

In testing, we particularly noticed this being a problem on iOS and, presumably, are mirrored in iPadOS. 

> [!NOTE]
> These problems with the shortcut were only noted when using the virtual keyboard. The shortcut works as intended when using a hardware keyboard paired with the iOS/iPadOS device.

## Steps to reproduce the issue

1. Visit a page that has both the Exit this Page button and an input field.
2. Focus the input so that the virtual keyboard opens.
3. Attempt to activate the EtP functionality by tapping <kbd>Shift</kbd> at least three times.

## Actual vs expected behaviour

### Expected

The Exit this Page functionality is activated and the user leaves the page.

### Actual

It is very difficult to activate the EtP shortcut behaviour intentionally.

If the user is pressing the key rapidly, and assuming an initially empty input or textarea, the most likely scenario is:

1. <kbd>Shift</kbd> was already turned on by default. Tap 1 turns it off and does not emit a `keyup` event.
2. Tap 2 happens quickly enough that Caps Lock mode is activated. <kbd>Caps Lock</kbd> emits a `keydown` event. 
3. Tap 3 turns off Caps Lock mode. <kbd>Caps Lock</kbd> emits a `keyup` event.
4. Tap 4 turns Caps Lock mode back on.
5. Repeat.

It is possible to activate the function successfully if the user takes time to wait between button presses—roughly half a second between presses. This wait is exacerbated by the need to perform more taps than usual, requiring 3 before the indicator lights are first shown, and a total of 7 to activate the functionality.

In addition, there are seemingly many scenarios that can unintentionally add to the <kbd>Shift</kbd> key activation count or cancel an activation currently in progress, most commonly, accidentally tapping fast enough to enable Caps Lock mode.

## Environment (where applicable)

- Operating system: iOS 16.4
- Browser: Safari
- Browser version: 16.4
- GOV.UK Frontend Version: 4.7.0 (however testing took place prior to this release)

The hint text "Select all options that are relevant to you" applies to the set of checkboxes, and does not make sense in the context of the email address field.

backlog.title: Accessibility link
backlog.body:
What
Establish how best to name and link to information about the accessibility options available to users within services.
Is referring to 'Ease of access' (or similar) more likely to be recognised by users who could benefit from the information provided?
Why
As part of meeting the legal requirements for the accessibility, teams producing websites and applications are directed to publish an accessibility statement
Within this, services can give useful information to users about the controls available to the users, such as browser options to control text size and colours, certain assistive tools and so on.
Most services seem to do this through a link named 'Accessibility' page in the footer.
However, in a Slack discussion in the cross-government 'Accessibility' channel, members of the community shared examples where users:

do not recognise the term 'Accessibility'
do not think that it is relevant to them
do not bother to look because, from past experience, they expect it to contain technical information or jargon that isn't relevant

This means some users can miss out on information about ease of access that would make it easier for them to use a service.
Quotes from Slack discussion (as of now)
A user researcher at GDS, said:
[I've seen] "all of the above (when researching how users perceived accessibility statements for the GDS accessibility team). Particularly that users don't always associate the word with their needs, potentially consider it to be about physical access, don't expect it to contain anything useful for them, or are so used to those pages containing generic/jargony info that they don't bother to look."
A user researcher at Ministry of Justice, said:
"I’ve tested accessibility pages in the past. In usability testing users didn’t recognise the link and when prompted to look under it, didn’t think the information was relevant or helpful.
In the past, accessibility pages were largely a box-ticking exercise and had little valuable info for users. They usually consisted of a standard line about WCAG compliance (even if it was not true), HTML validation and browser keyboard shortcuts. The better ones linked to BBC’s 'my web, my way'.
I expect that even those who had looked there, over time learned not to waste their time.
Having observed recent discussions about accessibility statements, I think there’s still a risk of tick-boxing. That’s why any sample statements should include a massive caveat that they shouldn’t be copied and pasted and that you should first do the work, then write about it (in that order).
I think it would be interesting to get quant data on this with analytics."
A Front-End Developer and Accessibility Specialist at GDS, said:
"Bad discoverability was one of the reasons why Microsoft renamed their accessibility settings to “Ease of access”."
(But I don't know the source for this)
In the 'Apply for a Budgeting Loan' service, feedback about the usability of the service is broadly very positive but a small percentage of users consistently give feedback that they need larger text or for text to be read to them. For this service we know some of our user base struggle in terms of literacy and can be low in confidence and ability using technology. This service doesn't currently have an accessibility statement of its own but it seems that users have not read GOV.UK's accessibility statement about the options available to them.

ourIssues.title: Character count's character/word count functions should be customisable
ourIssues.body:
Following on from #1104, whatever 'default' way we use to count characters (code points, bytes, characters) ideally it should match the way that a service's backend validation will count them. For this reason, we should consider making the count function customisable.

For example,

```js
new CharacterCount($characterCount).init({ countFunction: string => string.length })
```

ourIssues.title: Character count component counts code points, not characters
ourIssues.body:
The character count currently uses `string.length` to establish the length of the user input. `string.length` counts code units, not characters, and this can lead to some confusing results when using certain strings.

![A single emoji (👩🏻‍🚀) counted as 7 characters within the character count component](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/121939/50347110-699b5c00-052c-11e9-8944-6ad62d0014b4.png)


You can see this by trying the following strings into the character component:

| String | Result                                                                                                                                  |
|--------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| cat😹   | The emoji is counted as 2 code units, and the length is reported as *5* characters.                                                     |
| cafȩ́   | Each combining mark is counted separately, and the reported length is *6* characters.                                                   |
| 👩🏻‍🚀    | Because this emoji includes both gender and skin modifiers and a zero-width joiner, this single character is counted as *7* characters. |

We should probably find a less naive way to count characters in strings, but we also need to work out how this will work with any backend validation or data storage on a service, which may already be using a different definition of a 'character' (for example, where the backend or storage treats one character as one byte).

Further reading:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Character_encoding
- http://developer.teradata.com/blog/jasonstrimpel/2011/11/javascript-string-length-and-internationalizing-web-applications
- https://dmitripavlutin.com/what-every-javascript-developer-should-know-about-unicode/#33stringlength

ourIssues.title: Improve Language Navigation guidance on not losing data in forms when navigating between languages
ourIssues.body:
<!--

  This is a template for any issues that aren’t bug reports or new feature requests. The headings in this section provide examples of the information you might want to include, but feel free to add/delete sections where appropriate.

-->

## What

Improve Language Navigation guidance on not losing data in forms when using the component so that it's clearer what the behaviour should be

> Make sure the user does not lose any data they’ve entered when they navigate to another language. Do not ask the user to re-enter information they’ve already given.

https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/language-navigation/

## Why

We have [had some feedback ](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/discussions/5620#discussioncomment-18582218)that it's not clear in practice if this means keeping the users currently inputted data on a page or just keeping the data from the overall user journey.

Since this is a non-standard thing to do, we think it's likely other developers will wonder what they're aiming for.

There's some potential improvements to this:
- improving the guidance so it's clear that it includes users' un-submitted input 
- guidance around explaining at a high level how to achieve this functionality, similar to what we do for Cookie banner and Form validation (for developers)

## Background

This content was originally added in response to HMRC's welsh language toggle guidance. They detailed why they chose to keep data between page views in some feedback of note:

> welsh users will toggle back and forth between languages to ensure understanding of unfamiliar words and/or to check that both journeys are the same

> welsh speakers familiar with uncommon english specific to the context benefit from both the ability to toggle easily, and from these terms being shown in brackets within the welsh service (to avoid having to do as much switching)

> users prefer english/welsh toggle to whole journey language switching and absence of feature to toggle within service (only being able to select at start) tested negatively

https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/discussions/5351#discussioncomment-17278309

## Who needs to work on this

Content designer, developer

## Who needs to review this

Content designer, developer

## Done when

- [ ] the guidance is clearer on exactly what data should be persisted
- [ ] we've considered if extended guidance is appropriate

ourIssues.title: Sentence on html5 validation is unclear
ourIssues.body:
Raising [as requested on Cross-gov slack](https://ukgovernmentdigital.slack.com/archives/C6DMEH5R6/p1748950286911109).

In the design system [guidance for the validation pattern](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/validation/#turn-off-html5-validation) it states:

> Do not add 'required' to your input fields.

There's two ways of reading this:

1. Do not use the 'required' attribute in html
2. Do not use the word 'required' in content

(3? could be both!)

The sentence is part of a section about not using HTML5 validation, so I _assume_ it means the first item. But this isn't explicit and probably should be.

I wanted to refer another team to the guidance for why they shouldn't use required attributes - but I think the line as written is ambiguous.

ourIssues.title: Review the use of aria-label on a <ul> element in the site navigation menu
ourIssues.body:
## What
We use an `aria-label` on our sub-navigation list `<ul>`. This causes HTML validation issues, so we need to make the call on whether we keep it as an exception, add an explicit `aria-role` to keep validation happy, or get rid of it and find another solution.

## Why
Previously, we added an `aria-label` to the main site nav's Community sub-menu to make a better experience for screenreaders:  https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/commit/4ff06e4961bcd4a147d580d1d5ac2736fe9f6ec3

Recently, we [added HTML linting](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/pull/2569), and it flagged this as `aria-label-misuse`.

If we assign an explicit `role` to the labelled list, the HTML validator is sated and complains no longer.

However, it's a bit unclear which `role` we'd want to add - `navigation` is out since this subnav is already contained within a `nav` parent, and `menu` [might not be right for this situation](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/pull/2569#discussion_r1115422380).

We could avoid this debate if we just find a solution that doesn't involve ARIA. First step would probably be to just remove the `aria-label` and test whether it reads fine in multiple screenreaders.

If it’s missing context without the aria-label, we could look at using a bit of ‘visually-hidden’ instead of an aria-label. Would need to test to see if it works consistently across all screen readers though.

## Who needs to work on this
Developer, Accessibility specialist(?)

## Who needs to review this
Developer, Accessibility specialist

## Done when

- [ ] We have a solution that is both valid HTML, and a good experience for screenreaders.
- [ ] We have implemented that solution (this will likely involve [removing the inline validation exception](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/blob/9ba07459f46a6e9738067c7ec90da6dd22f3a1b6/views/partials/_navigation.njk#L14))

ourIssues.title: Replace what's new Mailchimp signup form with a custom signup form using server-side validation
ourIssues.body:
## What

The 'what's new' email signup form should use GOV.UK Design System components, including using server-side validation to show form errors to the user.

As currently the Design System website is a set of static pages, this will require an additional server app to be able to:

1. serve the HTML form (possibly?)
2. receive the form submission
3. validate the form submission
4. generate a page with error messages and serve it to the user OR
5.  submit the request to the Mailchimp API

There are a number of ways to achieve this; the first part of this epic will be to choose one that fits our needs.

## Why

Currently the 'what's new' mailing list signup form is a regular hosted Mailchimp form. This has a number of downsides:

- the form HTML has accessibility issues
- the form error handling has accessibility issues
- the form design is not consistent with GOV.UK Design System
- the solution is tied to Mailchimp

We looked at using an embedded Mailchimp form, but this would require using JavaScript to do input validation and error handling.

We used the Mailchimp signup form as a 'minimum viable product' for the initial launch of the 'what's new' feature because: a) we had tested it in user research and found that users were able to complete the journey b) we hadn't yet got usage analytics to validate that an email list fulfils the user need.

However, for a permanent solution, server side validation is the best and only way to get an accessible and consistent experience for all users.

## Who needs to know about this

Product manager, Developer, User researcher (possibly)

## Done when

- [ ] we've scoped out the different options for server-side validation, and chosen one
- [ ] the 'what's new' signup form uses Design System components (design has already been done, see commit [5bca1b64a](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/blob/5bca1b64acb67a372f9cec84e37ba42277fd92dc/src/email-updates.njk))
- [ ] we have a server-side validation solution for the form input
- [ ] the form and validation are connected so that form errors are shown to the user using Design System components
- [ ] the form is reachable from the Design System website
- [ ] user journey to signup to emails has been validated with user testing (possibly?)

communityIssues.title: Machine Readable Metadata secretly handles (some) social media meta tags
communityIssues.body:
The [Machine Readable Metadata](https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/machine_readable_metadata) component, according to the documentation, only handles putting the JSON+LD schema blocks into frontend pages. However, it's also the component that puts in the social media meta tags (og:title, twitter:image, etc), and that isn't mentioned anywhere in the documentation.

(This was added here: https://github.com/alphagov/govuk_publishing_components/pull/335)

However, og:image is _also_ rendered by the [Public Layout](https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/layout_for_public) component, so if you include both you end up with two og:image meta_tags. I don't know if this is a problem?

So:
- At the very least, the documentation should be updated
- Arguably maybe the social media meta tags should be added by the [Meta Tags](https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/meta_tags) Component rather than this one?
- We also need to know if two og:image tags is a problem, and if so maybe fix it by removing from Public Layout?

communityIssues.title: layout_header does not translate into other languages properly
communityIssues.body: After `static` was removed from `frontend`, the `layout_for_public` component started to get translated on foreign language pages, which in turn translated the `layout_header` (super navigation header) component. It looks like the `Menu` button text tried to translate, but as translations don't exist for that text, it just output an empty string, making the button look broken. To fix this, we hardcoded the component to always render in English in https://github.com/alphagov/govuk_publishing_components/pull/5090. However we should fix the underlying issue so that the option to translate this component exists for the future. This also surfaces another blind spot in our visual regression tests, as if we were able to translate each component in our visual regression testing, this would have been spotted.

ourIssues.title: Radio and checkbox labels rely on the cursor changing on hover to show they can be clicked
ourIssues.body:
## Description of the issue

Radios and checkboxes can be activated by clicking their labels. The cursor will change when the mouse/trackpad/pointer is over the label to indicate this but it doesn't provide enough of a visual cue for low vision users.

This was reported by the 'Low vision' tester at the Digital Accessibility Centre (DAC), in an audit commissioned by GOV.UK Notify.

Their comment was:

> The radio button display provides a circular focus point which is easily accessed should a
> user navigate by placing the mouse pointer directly into the circle. Should a user, with low
> vision or mobility has difficulty doing this and find it easier to rely on clicking the text related
> to the button, they will realise that there is no additional visual cue or call to action to alert
> the user the text can be clicked to occupy the Radio button and therefore may not be
> functional.
> The addition of visual cue is important as some users may not have the vision or mobility
> skills to easily place the mouse pointer in the correct area to use this function. Underlining
> text or placing a border around the radio button hotspot will provide ideal addition visuals
> to alert the user of function.

They reported the same for checkboxes. They also noted [in another issue](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/2757) the difficulties in
relying on the cursor change alone for a cue to the clickability of anything:

> ...using the mouse to access a required link can prove problematic. With the mouse pointer
> frequently being lost, a low vision user heavily relies on call-to-action focus to ensure correct
> links are being accessed.

## Steps to reproduce the issue

Using a mouse/trackpad/pointer, hover over one of the labels in a radios or checkboxes component. If you do not have a visual impairment similar to the tester mentioned here, you should use something to hide the cursor, for example [this browser plugin](https://chrome.google.com/webstore/detail/auto-hide-cursor/jbbnnopgaidlnbefoiebogfaebmehbda?hl=en).

## Actual vs expected behaviour

It should be obvious that the label is clickable and when the cursor enters/leaves the clickable area without relying on being able to see the cursor. This was not the case for the tester because the only visual cue was the cursor changing.

## Environment (where applicable)

GOV.UK Notify currently uses version 2.13.0 but the tester mentions experiencing this issue on the [www.gov.uk](http://www.gov.uk/) website, so likely they were viewing pages using a more recent version.

The tester was using Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge on Windows (latest versions) for the audit but they mention experiencing this issue on mobile devices and other different screens. See their comment in the description for their exact words.

ourIssues.title: Visibility and clickability of links on white backgrounds an issue for low vision users
ourIssues.body: ## Description of the issue The link style doesn't have a sufficient contrast on a white background for low vision users and there is not enough of a visual cue to the link being clickable. This was reported by the 'Low vision' tester at the Digital Accessibility Centre (DAC), in an audit commissioned by GOV.UK Notify. They were talking about links in our side-navigation, which have no underline by default, but I think their comments apply equally to all uses of the link style. They were reporting on this side-navigation: Their comment was: > When viewing this page, I struggled to see the five links on the left-hand side of the page. > This affects me because of my eye condition the thin light blue text fades into the white > background causing them to become blurry therefore, preventing me from reading the > information provided. It would benefit me that the text is displayed in a darker colour and > made bold so they standout more clearly to read. > > The left-hand navigation links are displayed using a light blue contrast with the custom NTA > font. These links used throughout GDS products provide a difficult reading experience for > low vision users as the transparent look to the NTA font impacts text clarity. > With the difficult reading of links, using the mouse to access a required link can prove > problematic. With the mouse pointer frequently being lost, a low vision user heavily relies > on call-to-action focus to ensure correct links are being accessed. Displayed in a list, > navigating this list becomes difficult is no call-to-action focus is noticed. > In this example, an underline is presented on contact with the mouse pointer. The issue I > had with this is that I did not initially see it. The underline is thinly presented and displayed > with the same low contrast transparent blue. The call-to-action focus is not sufficient for > easy notification. > This can be improved by adding weight to the underline to produce a bolder and more > visible focus needed for accurate navigation to which would be welcomed throughout these > pages. Improved call-to-action enhances user/page interaction to increase overall UX of any > website. I think this can be summarised as the following issues: - the link style on a white background makes the text hard to read - the cursor changing over the clickable area of links is not enough of a cue to know they can be clicked - the link style on a white background makes the underline hard to see ## Steps to reproduce the issue Because the issue seems to occur for users with a visual impairment, I would guess that you would need to test with those types of users. ## Actual vs expected behaviour The tester expected to be able to read the content of the side navigation and identifying them as links but found problems reading the text and knowing they were clickable. ## Environment (where applicable) GOV.UK Notify currently uses version 2.13.0 but the tester mentions experiencing this issue on the [www.gov.uk](http://www.gov.uk/) website, so likely they were viewing pages using a more recent version. The tester was using Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge on Windows (latest versions) for the audit but they mention experiencing this issue on mobile devices and other different screens. See their comment in the description for their exact words.

ourIssues.title: Why do checkboxes and radios have transparent backgrounds?
ourIssues.body:
The following came from a question I asked on the design system slack channel.
https://ukgovernmentdigital.slack.com/archives/C6DMEH5R6/p1572279335253200

**TLDR:** checkboxes and radios have transparent backgrounds. This means they don't stand out visually against non white panels as text input elements do.

From thread:
---------
does anyone know why the checkboxes (and I assume radio buttons) have transparent backgrounds? Rather than a white background (which would probably be the default browser rendering of a standard checkbox).
**GOV checkbox (with transparent background):**
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/23551105/67845990-5e27a280-faf8-11e9-8e33-0bb7e1f6b0b5.png)
**Default checkbox (without GOV styling):**
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/23551105/67846092-86af9c80-faf8-11e9-8571-995a80aa3825.png)

**Anon 1:** 
I suspect that’s because they’re custom rendered rather than native checkboxes, and we want to support users who change their text and background colours.

11 replies

**Anon 2:**
Hi Dave,
This decision pre-dates the design system so I'll need to do a bit of digging to see if we can find out why - but my guess is something along the lines of what **Anon 1** said. Will come back to you.
Have you seen any problems around this, or are you just wondering?
After some investigation - it appears that his is the pertinent commit: https://github.com/alphagov/govuk_elements/commit/4972b81697fbf5b9ac12a211010c623e625ab3ab

**Dave Haigh**
I am looking at using small checkboxes as a filter for a list. The filters are located on a light grey panel (similar to the call to action blocks on GOV.UK guidance pages). As you can see in the screenshot the checkbox doesn’t stand out well as the background is transparent.

Im not sure on the answer to this but… should the scenario be:
- If user HAS NOT specified any browser background colour then they should be white;
- Else if user HAS a specified background colour in certain modes then they should be either transparent or that colour (when in that mode)
1. Is the above correct?
2. Is it possible?
3.Also, some other elements do not respect user specified background colours such as text inputs (they’re always white). Why are only the checks and radios transparent?

i’ve specified my background colour to be red (in any mode) in this screenshot:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/23551105/67846236-c5455700-faf8-11e9-868f-432708c3a31f.png)

**Anon 3**
I don’t really have a good answer for you other than that the radios and checkboxes in the Design System are based on those introduced in Elements back in 2016 by people that no longer work here. As **Anon 2** said, we don’t have the context of every historical decision. We could definitely look at changing that behaviour, but we’d need to test thoroughly to make sure they still work in all of these sorts of scenarios.

ourIssues.title: Prototype alternate CTAs for feedback on Feedback link component
ourIssues.body: ## What Currently, our component guidance seeks user engagement like this: ### Alternative We have the option of taking a different approach with Feedback link, which is likely to be shipped as our first "early access" component. For "early access" components, iterate this engagement section to instead be a call to action (CTA) for users to let us know if they're using the component. This would link through to a user research sign up form, and we could do targeted research to enable us to evolve a component from "early access" to "stable". ### Hypothesis A more prominent CTA will drive higher engagement rates for the component. ## Why - We will be unlikely to get the feedback we need to make an "early access" component stable if we can not identify who is using it. This is one a few ways we could identify services. - Most components which are "early access" will have limited to no research, deeming that section redundant - There is a clear pathway for when something moves to stable, the CTA is replaced by the standard "Research on this component" - Consideration: We can be clear about the insights we need from users ## Who needs to work on this @hazalarpalikli ## Who needs to review this @owenatgov @kellylee-gds Experimental squad (post-testing) ## Done when - [ ] Prototyped different options - [ ] Reviewed them as a squad - [ ] Selected a design to try

ourIssues.title: Button component without margin overhangs by 2px
ourIssues.body:
## Description of the issue

The button component uses a 2px box shadow to provide a visual bottom border. This is used primarily instead of an actual bottom border because the other borders are already defined and this would cause a bevelling issue between the bottom and left/right borders. This means that the button component 'overhangs' by 2px at the bottom.

By default the button component has a margin bottom of 32px, which accounts for this 2px and then adds spacing in line with the spacing scale. However on GOV.UK we use the button component without bottom margin in our search filters, where it is supposed to line up with the bottom of a wrapping element. Due to this 2px of box shadow it doesn't, and we have to insert 2px of padding somewhere to account for this.

This is a very small thing, but if there were a way of preserving the look of the button while allowing it to not have this 2px of overhanging box shadow it would make integrating the button component into edge case scenarios like this a little easier.

## Steps to reproduce the issue

Normal button appearance:

![Normal button appearance with margin beneath](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/8fa0aa19-b2de-458a-a989-d9c462484e67)

Button with zero margin applied to the bottom (note 2px overlap with containing element, highlighted):

![Button inside a highlighted form element showing 2px overlap with container when margin removed](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/76ebdc8f-353e-4036-80c0-6918477cc91a)

Use of button in GOV.UK search (mobile view) at bottom of containing element, note slight overlap/misalign with grey left border of container:

![GOV.UK search page on mobile showing button overlapping bottom of containing element by 2px](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/696e4503-ab9d-41f5-a0b3-3e48fb852f7b)

## Environment (where applicable)

- Operating system: N/A
- Browser: N/A
- Browser version: N/A
- GOV.UK Frontend Version: current (v5.6)

ourIssues.title: The expanded/collapsed state of conditional reveals is not available to all assistive technologies
ourIssues.body:
## What

As part of an internal accessibility audit of GOV.UK, conditional reveals† was flagged as failing WCAG 4.1.2:

> **4.1.2 Name, Role, Value**: For all user interface components (including but not limited to: form elements, links and components generated by scripts), the name and role can be programmatically determined; states, properties, and values that can be set by the user can be programmatically set; and notification of changes to these items is available to user agents, including assistive technologies. (Level A)

It was flagged as failing because:
- the additional 'role' of the checkbox or radio button is not clear
- changes to the expanded ‘state’ of the radio buttons is not available to assistive tech, and so users may be unaware that something else has changed on the page as a result of selecting a radio.

We use `aria-expanded` on these controls, but that is technically invalid according to the spec, which [only allows `aria-expanded` on certain roles](https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria-1.1/#aria-expanded). Some screen readers still announce the expanded state, but those that don’t have no reason to implement it because it’s against the spec. ARIA 1.2 (which is currently in draft) extends support of aria-expanded to checkboxes but not radios.

The fact that `aria-expanded` is not valid is recorded as a separate but related issue (https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/979).

As of [September 2019](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/979#issuecomment-528932826), this is known to affect:

- Voiceover (https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/989)
- JAWS (https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/935)

### Update

As of June 2021, we [removed conditional reveals from our accessibility statement](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/issues/6042#issuecomment-871527458).

---

† The [page being audited](https://webarchive.nationalarchives.gov.uk/20200911014618/https://www.gov.uk/email-signup?link=/world/switzerland) uses the conditional reveals in an unusual way, as what’s being revealed is effectively contextual help (like a hint) that would help the user to make the right choice. Whereas the way we intend the component to be used is [to reveal additional form controls that ‘follow on’ from the initial question](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/radios/#conditionally-revealing-content). We think that revealing text in this way is 'worse' in terms of accessibility, so we have a separate issue to discourage users from using conditional reveals to reveal text (https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/issues/1362)

ourIssues.title: Potentially not clear what we mean by 'question' in conditional reveal guidance, and why we require it
ourIssues.body:
## Related documentation
https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/radios/
https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/checkboxes/

Both pages have this section on Conditional reveals:

> You should only conditionally reveal questions - do not show or hide anything that is not a question.

## Issue

We had a support request that 'question' was ambiguous to them. In the example they were checking, the label was not worded as a question, so for example "Name of other benefit or expense".

It was also not clear why we have this guidance (it is because form elements are focusable, making it more likely that a screen reader user will discover it, compared to non-focusable content such as a paragraph).

ourIssues.title: Character count component reads out hints in an unintuitive order when initially focused
ourIssues.body:
When a the character count is rendered on a text areas the aria-describeBy attribute lists the ID (suffixed with "-info") of the character count text and the ID of the hint text of the textarea (suffixed with "-hint") in that order. 

example:
**aria-describedby**="char-count-info q-textarea-hint"

This means that screen readers read the information referenced by those ID's in that order. 
Character count info read 1st
Textarea hint read 2nd

![image](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system-backlog/assets/119854428/687a8725-0ed0-4566-83f6-0554a3afffcb)

## What
> Need to have configuration so that the "-info" ID is appended after the textarea "-hint" ID. 

## Why
When using a screen reader the character count below the textarea is read out first before the hint/description text above the textarea. This is counter intuitive to the page it should be read in order of appearance to help those needing to use screen readers

ourIssues.title: Hard-coded id for character count component
ourIssues.body:
`this.$countMessage = $module.querySelector('[id=' + this.$textarea.id + '-info]')`

Hey! Currently trying to implement your character count component. I am not using Nunjucks, so relying on copying the HTML from your examples (https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/character-count/). On further investigation as to why it was not working, even though my DOM was identical (or at least I though it was). The above snippet hard-codes `-info` onto the end of the `span` `id` (from `character-count.js`).

Nowhere does this appear to be documented (if it is, and I have missed this, accept my apologies and close this immediately)? It does seem somewhat brittle? Your own govuk-frontend version here https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/master/src/govuk/components/character-count/template.njk also manually adds `-info` onto the hint. 

Now whilst calling the Nunjucks macro would always works and you don't need to care that this behaviour is happening behind the scenes. Anyone using raw HTML or implementing it into another templating language, is bound to run into this issue? The example code snippets on your component pages seem to be mostly contrived names/ids so one would quite easily rely on that not being a hard and fast rule to make the component work.

I have mine all working now, so not a major problem for me anymore but thought I would ask the question.

Thanks

ourIssues.title: Character count component counts code points, not characters
ourIssues.body:
The character count currently uses `string.length` to establish the length of the user input. `string.length` counts code units, not characters, and this can lead to some confusing results when using certain strings.

![A single emoji (👩🏻‍🚀) counted as 7 characters within the character count component](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/121939/50347110-699b5c00-052c-11e9-8944-6ad62d0014b4.png)


You can see this by trying the following strings into the character component:

| String | Result                                                                                                                                  |
|--------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| cat😹   | The emoji is counted as 2 code units, and the length is reported as *5* characters.                                                     |
| cafȩ́   | Each combining mark is counted separately, and the reported length is *6* characters.                                                   |
| 👩🏻‍🚀    | Because this emoji includes both gender and skin modifiers and a zero-width joiner, this single character is counted as *7* characters. |

We should probably find a less naive way to count characters in strings, but we also need to work out how this will work with any backend validation or data storage on a service, which may already be using a different definition of a 'character' (for example, where the backend or storage treats one character as one byte).

Further reading:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Character_encoding
- http://developer.teradata.com/blog/jasonstrimpel/2011/11/javascript-string-length-and-internationalizing-web-applications
- https://dmitripavlutin.com/what-every-javascript-developer-should-know-about-unicode/#33stringlength

ourIssues.title: Tabs on mobile announce em-dash on contents list
ourIssues.body:
## Description of the issue

When using Talkback on Android and using the Tabs component (which collapses to use a Contents list on smaller screens) the each list item announced the em-dash as well which could create confusion for users.

Ideally this should be a presentational element, similar to how real bullet points work.

## Steps to reproduce the issue

1. Go to a page with Tabs component on it
2. Activate Talkback 
3. Read the content list

## Actual vs expected behaviour

Actual:
Em-dashes are being announced

Expected:
Only the content of the list should be announced

## Original reports

> Hope you are well. We recently had an accessibility audit and an issue was raised around confusing announcements associated with the tabs component which I wanted to make you aware of. When viewing the tabs on a mobile device, a screen reader reads outs the 'em-dash' which is displayed beside the tab name. 

 _Originally posted by @LucyGeddis in [#100](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/issues/5955#issuecomment-5604724373)_

> These are the details for the mobile devices and screen readers used:
> 
> - Android 15 – Samsung Galaxy S22 – Chrome 150 – TalkBack
> - iOS 26 – iPhone 13 – Safari 26 - VoiceOver
