ourIssues.title: Review list spacing
ourIssues.body:
## What
Evaluate spacing between list items in our list styles.

## Why
Whilst working on https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/issues/2862, we noticed that lists appear tightly spaced against the new typography scale. [See this comment](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/issues/2862#issuecomment-1772518434) for a light investigation. From a team discussion, we think there's value in experimenting with list spacing to assess if they should be more spaced out or not. There is a particular concern around:

- Lack of space afforded to bullet and number lists on mobile
- Similarities between list and paragraph spacing

## Timebox
1 sprint (2 weeks)

## Who is working on this?
TBD

Spike lead:
TBD

## Questions to answer
- [ ] How big should spacing be around lists?
- [ ] Does an increase or decrease in spacing impact other typographical elements eg: paragraphs

## Done when
- [ ] Questions have been answered or we have a clearer idea of how to get to our goal
- [ ] Findings have been reviewed and agreed with at least one other person
- [ ] Findings have been shared, e.g: via a write-up on the ticket, at a show & tell or team meeting

ourIssues.title: Tap targets on links within lists are too small
ourIssues.body:
## Description of the issue

When placing `govuk-link` classed links as list items within a `govuk-list` list, the tap targets on mobile device widths are too small. A Google Lighthouse audit reports these as 19px high and recommends 48px, although I believe the WCAG recommendation is 44px. At their current size and spacing they are difficult to tap individually. I can see that at desktop widths the `<li>` element receives a 5px `margin-bottom`, but a 0px margin at mobile widths.

## Steps to reproduce the issue

You can see an example of the list of links on this site: https://govuk-frontend-jinja.herokuapp.com Perform a mobile Lighthouse audit on it to get the report below: 
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2802973/105870712-71256d00-5ff0-11eb-9fc4-44cac3110e60.png)

## Actual vs expected behaviour

I am expecting the list items to receive either a larger tap target, or additional margin to space them out further. I am aware of the `.govuk-list--spaced` class, but I don't want the content spaced out further on desktop devices, only on mobile.

## Environment (where applicable)

- Operating system: Tested on MacOS, Windows and Android
- Browser: Tested on Firefox (MacOS, Windows, Android), Chrome (Windows, Android), Edge (Windows)
- Browser version: Firefox 84, Chrome 88, Edge 88
- GOV.UK Frontend Version: v3.10.2

ourIssues.title: Hint text for radio/checkbox groups gets read out repeatedly by VoiceOver
ourIssues.body:
## Description of the issue

When arrowing through a form with a radio (or checkbox) group that has a hint, VoiceOver on iOS reads out the hint text repeatedly.
While this is not a WCAG fail and is probably not a bug in the Design System itself, it can be annoying to screen reader users.


## Steps to reproduce the issue

Open our [inline radios example](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/radios/inline/) and arrow through the page (VO + right arrow).


## Actual vs expected behaviour

I don't know what is supposed to happen according to the spec, I only know what happens in all other major screen readers. I don't know if this means it's a bug in VoiceOver or just a different way how VoiceOver does things.

VoiceOver reads out the hint text:

* when arrowing to the legend
* (obviously also when arrowing to the hint text itself)
* when arrowing to the first radio button
* when arrowing to the second (and potential subsequent) radio buttons

The second and third are to be expected, the first and last not.
All other major screen readers only read the hint text when arrowing to the first radio button they encounter (and to the hint text itself).


## Environment

This happens with VoiceOver on iOS but also to some degree on macOS.
(It's less bad on macOS as the hint text doesn't get read out when arrowing to the legend.)

Tested in Safari on an iPad with iOS version 18.3.1 and a MacBook with macOS version 15.3.2.

A user has reported that this issue was not happening on iOS version 16.

ourIssues.title: NVDA does not read hints or error messages when tabbing to checkboxes
ourIssues.body:
## Description of the issue

This is an NVDA bug, but I'm filing an issue here because it affects the accessibility of GOV.UK Frontend so I thought you may want a record of it.

When a checkbox inside a fieldset gets focus, any hint or error message associated with the fieldset should be read out after the legend and before the checkbox label. They're associated with the fieldset via `aria-describedby`. However, NVDA only reads the legend and checkbox label, not the hint or error. This means that NVDA users may be unaware that the grouping has a hint or an error.

For example, the speech output for [this example](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/checkboxes/error/index.html) with a hint and an error is:

> What is your nationality?  grouping  clickable  British  check box  not checked    including English, Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish

Note that this only affects checkboxes. Radios use the same structure and are unaffected.

[An NVDA issue for this bug](https://github.com/nvaccess/nvda/issues/12718) has been open since 2021 but unfortunately it doesn't look like there's been much progress towards a fix. It looks like [this commenter](https://github.com/nvaccess/nvda/issues/12718#issuecomment-1533364655) has also come across this issue while using GOV.UK Frontend though.

## Steps to reproduce the issue

See CodePen at https://codepen.io/matteason/pen/PoyBwYM or one of the GOV.UK Design System examples (eg [checkboxes](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/checkboxes/with-none-option-in-error/index.html))

Open NVDA, navigate to the example page and tab through the form fields

## Actual vs expected behaviour

Hints should be read for all component types in the example, but they're only read for text inputs and radios

## Environment (where applicable)

- Operating system: Windows 10
- Browser: Firefox 112.0, Chrome 112.0.5615.138
- GOV.UK Frontend Version: 4.6.0

ourIssues.title: Textarea hints and error messages are not read out if a value is already present (JAWS/Chrome)
ourIssues.body:
## Description of the issue
When using JAWS, moving focus to a textarea that already has a populated value does not read out any elements associated with the textarea by `aria-describedby`.

## Steps to reproduce the issue
1. Create an instance of the textarea or character count component that: (a) has a default value of any length; (b) has an associated hint, error message, or both; and (c) does not have a threshold, if it's a character count. 
2. With JAWS running, navigate to the page in Chrome.
3. Apply focus to the textarea using either keyboard or mouse.
4. Listen to what JAWS reads out.

An existing example can be found in [the character count's error state example](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/character-count/error/index.html) in the design system. I've also made [a bare minimum example as a fiddle](https://jsfiddle.net/querkmachine/3z6drbto/).

## Actual vs expected behaviour
Actual behaviour: JAWS will read out the input label and that it is a textarea that currently contains text.

Expected behaviour: JAWS will read out the label, that it is a textarea that currently contains text, plus any hints and error messages associated with the input via `aria-describedby`.

The issue does not appear to occur with `<input>` elements (be they empty or populated), or with empty `<textarea>`s.

## Environment 
- Operating system: Windows 10
- Browser: Google Chrome
- Browser version: 99
- GOV.UK Frontend Version: 4.0.1

Tested in both JAWS 2021.2103.174 and JAWS 2022.2202.38. 

I could not reproduce this in Firefox or IE when using JAWS, and not in any browser when using NVDA 2021.2.

## What Consider updating hints and error messages to use paragraphs rather than spans and divs. https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/d5a3fa8c5e61dbc7ca0f7a8429cc8e6716ee7c32/src/govuk/components/error-message/template.njk#L3-L6 https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/d5a3fa8c5e61dbc7ca0f7a8429cc8e6716ee7c32/src/govuk/components/hint/template.njk#L1-L4 ## Why As raised by a user on x-gov Slack: > the error message is in a tag. Is there a reason why a `` is used, rather than a `
` or `

`, for example? The reason I ask is because I’ve been doing some testing with JAWS and I’ve found that there’s no pause between reading the hint text and the error message. So JAWS reads “For example 12 11 2007 error colon the date your passport was issued must be in the past”. Using a `

` didn’t make a difference, but using a `

` resulted in a pause between the hint text and the error message, so potentially making it a little clearer. It looks like hints used to be paragraphs, but [were changed to spans when the hints were moved inside the label](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk_elements/commit/5f631c113840bfd4cc3ed81de8fb311638457a92#diff-1968332cde003a71f281b5d33445bcb3a43d2ac1cee565f6bc0e0a0144cfb846) – presumably as [only phrasing content is permitted within a `label`](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/forms.html#the-label-element). Error messages, when they were added later, were also spans inside the label. We recently [updated hints to use divs rather than spans](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/commit/d92d3c8a990730213430b686d239fc7b278530a9) so that they can be used with flow content (for example multiple paragraph tags, or a list) Since [we moved hints and error messages out of the labels](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/pull/681), we should consider whether they should now by marked up as paragraphs instead. ## Who needs to know about this Developers, designers ## Done when - [x] Tested alternate form controls with error messages and hints marked up as paragraphs in assistive technologies - [x] Identified other potential issues cause by changing hints and error messages to paragraphs - [ ] Decision made and code change made - [ ] Check if the changelog for https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/1856 needs updating as a result of this work

ourIssues.title: Legend (and hint and error message) for the group of radios / checkboxes announced when focusing a conditionally revealed field whilst using VoiceOver
ourIssues.body:
Conditionally revealed controls are inside the `<fieldset>` that wraps the radios / checkboxes.

This could potentially cause confusion, as in VoiceOver the legend (and any other text associated with the fieldset using `aria-describedby`, such as a hint or error message) is read out when focusing the conditionally revealed content.

![Screenshot 2020-10-16 at 13 03 20](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/121939/96256125-fe980080-0faf-11eb-9da5-289e0c39a63e.png)

For example, when focusing the conditionally revealed 'email address' field in the example from the Design System (above), Voiceover with Safari (14) on macOS (10.15.7) announces:

> "Email address, edit text, How would you like to be contacted? Select all options that are relevant to you. You are currently on a text field. To enter text in this field, type."

The hint text "Select all options that are relevant to you" applies to the set of checkboxes, and does not make sense in the context of the email address field.

ourIssues.title: Make it easier to add a hint or an error message to a fieldset
ourIssues.body:
## What

If you want to use the fieldset component to group related fields, for example asking for a street address, you need to take care of including the hint / error message components separately and do extra work to associate them with the fieldset.

We do not provide any examples or guidance on how to do this, and it would be easy to get wrong (for example, by not creating the association with the fieldset)

It therefore seems like it would be useful if the fieldset component accepted `hint` and `errorMessage` objects and took care of this association itself.

## Why

This was requested by @edwardhorsford in https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/issues/778#issuecomment-459047140.

## Additional information

The radios, checkbox and date input components all use hints and error messages which are then associated with the fieldset using `aria-describedby`. However, this logic is handled (and therefore duplicated) within the individual components.

Moving this logic to the fieldset component _might_ allow us to simplify the repeated logic in the radios, checkboxes and date input components. However, it's not clear what should happen to the hint / error message [if you do not include a fieldset](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/62d3de38036b858b1dd85c5bd8c027830fab5a3d/src/components/date-input/template.njk#L79-L96).

ourIssues.title: Tell people not to use hints with small radios and checkboxes
Clarify the use of full stops in error messages and hints
ourIssues.body:
In the [Service Manual](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/design/writing-for-user-interfaces) we say "Headings and input field labels are sentence case, but not punctuated. Write other copy in full sentences, with a full stop at the end.". 

But the [error message example](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/error-message/) has no full stop.

More generally, we don't explicitly say whether hints and error messages should always, never or sometimes end in a full stop, and under what conditions.

Related issue: https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/issues/778

communityIssues.body:
Some components are named one thing but use a different name for their files, e.g.

- `Admin layout` template is named `layout_for_admin`
- `Form character count` template is named `character_count`
- `Form checkboxes` template is named `checkboxes`
- `Form date input` template is named `date_input`
- `Form fieldset` template is named `fieldset`
- `Form file upload` template is named `file_upload`
- `Govspeak content` template is named `govspeak`
- `Govspeak content (HTML publications)` template is named `govspeak_html_publication`
- `Form hint text` template is named `hint`
- `Form input` template is named `input`
- `Form label` template is named `label`
- `Public layout` template is named `layout_for_public`
- `Metadata block` template is named `metadata`
- `Form radio button` template is named `radio`

backlog.title: Progressive Web Apps (PWA) support
backlog.body:
What
Implementation of Progressive Web Apps (PWA) for GOV.UK services.
Why
There are some GOV.UK services that could be excellent PWAs, and enable services to:

send push notifications
allow users to access services when they’re offline
integrate services with other parts of a user’s phone, like geolocation

An example would be the Flood Information Service. To be able to send push notifications to customers when they are in an area at risk would be very useful indeed.
Anything else
Ideas for discussion/implementation:

Criteria for when PWAs are suitable for an existing service
How push notifications look and act for a service
How to ask for user permission for access to users phone/computer capabilities in the service
How to support users offline
Making PWA available to stores like the Windows Store
Best practises

That's the general "Menu" button as well as the buttons after each of the main navigation items. When you activate the main nav buttons they even visibly open the sub menu that shouldn't be reachable in the desktop view. Those buttons can also be explored by touch. Screenshot of the hidden "Get started" button being highlighted and activated with the "Get started" sub menu open underneath the service nav: This was first discovered as part of an [audit of the Brand Guidelines website](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-brand-guidelines/issues/138), which copies the Design System website functionality. ## Steps to reproduce the issue 1. At step 4 you shouldn't be able to open the mobile menu when it desktop view. ## Environment (where applicable) - Operating system: iPadOS 18.6 - Browser: Safari - Browser version: (not sure) I don't have a recent enough iOS version to see if it happens on current iOS as well. But I can confirm it does **not** happen with: * VO on iPadOS 15.8.3 * latest VO on macOS * latest TalkBack on Android * latest NVDA on Windows * latest JAWS on Windows That means it might well be due to a bug in iPadOS (and maybe iOS). ourIssues.title: Review the use of aria-label on a <ul> element in the site navigation menu
ourIssues.body:
## What
We use an `aria-label` on our sub-navigation list `<ul>`. This causes HTML validation issues, so we need to make the call on whether we keep it as an exception, add an explicit `aria-role` to keep validation happy, or get rid of it and find another solution.

## Why
Previously, we added an `aria-label` to the main site nav's Community sub-menu to make a better experience for screenreaders:  https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/commit/4ff06e4961bcd4a147d580d1d5ac2736fe9f6ec3

Recently, we [added HTML linting](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/pull/2569), and it flagged this as `aria-label-misuse`.

If we assign an explicit `role` to the labelled list, the HTML validator is sated and complains no longer.

However, it's a bit unclear which `role` we'd want to add - `navigation` is out since this subnav is already contained within a `nav` parent, and `menu` [might not be right for this situation](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/pull/2569#discussion_r1115422380).

We could avoid this debate if we just find a solution that doesn't involve ARIA. First step would probably be to just remove the `aria-label` and test whether it reads fine in multiple screenreaders.

If it’s missing context without the aria-label, we could look at using a bit of ‘visually-hidden’ instead of an aria-label. Would need to test to see if it works consistently across all screen readers though.

## Who needs to work on this
Developer, Accessibility specialist(?)

## Who needs to review this
Developer, Accessibility specialist

## Done when

- [ ] We have a solution that is both valid HTML, and a good experience for screenreaders.
- [ ] We have implemented that solution (this will likely involve [removing the inline validation exception](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/blob/9ba07459f46a6e9738067c7ec90da6dd22f3a1b6/views/partials/_navigation.njk#L14))

ourIssues.title: Research making the checkbox and radio button labels full width
ourIssues.body:
## What

Perform research with users as to whether making labels on checkboxes and radio buttons span the width of the container, thus increasing their touch surface, makes it easier to use these controls

## Why

Generally speaking, increasing the target area for a control makes the control easier for users to interact with.

We have some existing precendent for this in Frontend already: 

- Labels for other input types (text inputs, selects, textareas, etc.) are already full width.
- The Accordion activates expand/collapse functionality by tapping anywhere in the section header.
- The Skip Link component, when visible, is activatable by clicking anywhere in the component.

The GOV.UK team has had positive feedback when increasing target sizes for elements on the [homepage](https://insidegovuk.blog.gov.uk/2021/12/13/updating-the-gov-uk-homepage/) and [topic pages](https://insidegovuk.blog.gov.uk/2022/08/08/rolling-out-a-new-design-for-browsing-gov-uk-by-topic/) in the last year.

Various external design systems have full width checkbox and radio labels, some of which are based on or inspired by GOV.UK Frontend and have seemingly made the conscious choice to change it:

- ~~[USWDS](https://designsystem.digital.gov/components/checkbox/)~~ Update: Has since updated to no longer be full-width
- [NICE Design System](https://design-system.nice.org.uk/storybook/?path=/story/foundations-checkbox--default)
- [Transport for West Midlands Design System](https://designsystem.tfwm.org.uk/components/radios/)
- [GOLD Design System](https://gold.designsystemau.org/components/control-input/#checkbox-block) (formerly Australian Government Design System)
- [Atlassian Design System](https://atlassian.design/components/checkbox/examples)

Our inline labels date from the GOV.UK Elements days, and I couldn't immediately find any reason why they were implemented in this way at the time. We have stuck to that precedent in situations where a conflict or bug relating to the label sizing has arisen (e.g. #634).

We should validate our current approach and whether it best meets user needs when compared to alternative approaches.

## Assumptions

We've [previously found that users don't tend to click on checkbox or radio button labels](https://designnotes.blog.gov.uk/2016/11/30/weve-updated-the-radios-and-checkboxes-on-gov-uk/), even if they're styled to appear interactible. It could be assumed that the same applies here (if not moreso, as there isn't any visual indicator that interaction is possible). 

As a larger area of the screen will activate a checkbox/radio, there may be an increase in the number of accidental form inputs being made.

A seemingly 'empty' part of the page affecting a nearby input may be unexpected and cause confusion to users unless some other hint is present (e.g. a hover state). 

## Timebox
TBD

## Who is working on this?

Spike lead: TBD

Spike buddy: TBD

## Questions to answer

- [ ] Is there a tangible benefit to checkbox and radio button labels always being full width?
- [ ] Is there a tangible benefit to checkbox and radio button labels being full width in certain situations (e.g. on narrow screens)? 
- [ ] Are full width labels more likely to result in accidental and unwanted inputs?
- [ ] Is having a visually 'empty' area of the screen interactive unexpected or a source of confusion?

## Done when

- [ ] A review or prototype is produced with the modified checkbox/radio styles.
- [ ] User research has been carried out to see how these changes perform with users.
- [ ] Findings have been reviewed and shared with the team.
- [ ] Any follow up issues or actions have been written up.

ourIssues.title: Tweak design of button component on mobile (and maybe desktop, too)
ourIssues.body:
Currently our button components default to full width on smaller (mobile) screens. Because of this, its possible that the buttons are not as noticeable by users — many people have mentioned that they look like banners, not buttons, and this makes them easy to skip over.

Additionally, the top and bottom padding on the full width buttons is quite small which makes the text more difficult to read.

## Context

To solve the above issues and to generally improve the look of the buttons, we could:
- Make them responsive the width of the text, not the screen
- Improve the padding to make locating the text easier

## Alternatives

N/A

## Additional information (if applicable)

It would be great to do this around the time of the rebrand rollout, and ahead of the app release. Apps have chunkier buttons than our component and it would be beneficial for users if we brought them closer together

ourIssues.title: Provide guidance and examples for using product names in the header

communityIssues.title: Support OS-level accessibility text scaling
communityIssues.body:
## Description 
Over a third of mobile users customise their system level text size in their device settings for accessibility. While native mobile applications automatically adapt to these settings, web content inside standard or in app browsers remains at the default 16px base font size.

This creates a disconnect for users, most noticeably on the GOV.UK app which responds and resizes text to honour the OS type size setting, but when a user opens a web link in the app, the web content will not resize. Users are frequently forced to rely on manual pinch zoom on mobile, which goes against the following:

[WCAG 2.1 Success Criterion 1.4.4: Resize Text (Level AA)](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/resize-text.html)
[WCAG 2.1 Success Criterion 1.4.10: Reflow (Level AA)](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/reflow.html)

## Proposed Standard
Engineers from the BBC and Google Chrome drafted an opt-in web standard to solve this, which has landed in the W3C specification under [CSS Fonts Module Level 5 § 2 (Text-Scale meta element)](https://drafts.csswg.org/css-fonts-5/#text-scale-meta):

`<meta name="text-scale" content="scale">`
What it does: It tells the browser to multiply the root font size by the user’s OS and browser text scale factor, allowing relative units (rem, em) across our design system to scale proportionally.

Browser support: Works natively in Chromium (Chrome 146+). WebKit/Safari requires the @supports (font: -apple-system-body) fallback in CSS until native meta tag support is released.

Following discussion with the GOV.UK Design System team this change will ultimately need to land centrally in govuk-frontend and can then be implemented downstream. 

### Key considerations include:

Headings: Scaling all text strictly proportionally could make large headings (h1 at 48px) jump to 96px at 200% scale, rendering mobile screens hard to use. We could use clamp() or a capped scale for headings while letting body copy scale fully.

Tables: Wide data tables are already challenging on mobile screens. While [WCAG 1.4.10 exempts data tables](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/reflow.html) from 2D scrolling requirements, we need to ensure horizontal overflow containers remain functional.

Domain text size: Desktop users who previously customised domain browser zoom on gov.uk may see their zoom level compound with their OS setting until they perform a reset. So if someone with a 200% OS level zoom has previously visited and adjusted the text size to 200% and then post change they'll suddenly be at 400%.

## Next Steps for Publishing Components
Before this is formally adopted upstream, we could perform a spike in govuk_publishing_components to test and identify breaking layouts:

- Create a prototype branch adding <meta name="text-scale" content="scale"> to base templates
- Audit core publishing templates and components at 150% and 200% OS text scaling
- Document findings and share with the Design System

## Related Links
GOV.UK Frontend Issue: [alphagov/govuk-frontend#4933](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/4933)
W3C Specification: [CSS Fonts Module Level 5 – Text-Scale meta element](https://drafts.csswg.org/css-fonts-5/#text-scale-meta)
Josh Tumath: [Let's fix the web's text size](https://www.joshtumath.uk/posts/2026-07-02-lets-fix-the-webs-text-size/)
W3C CSSWG Explainer: [meta text-scale explainer](https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/blob/main/css-env-1/explainers/meta-text-scale.md)

communityIssues.title: Machine Readable Metadata secretly handles (some) social media meta tags
communityIssues.body:
The [Machine Readable Metadata](https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/machine_readable_metadata) component, according to the documentation, only handles putting the JSON+LD schema blocks into frontend pages. However, it's also the component that puts in the social media meta tags (og:title, twitter:image, etc), and that isn't mentioned anywhere in the documentation.

(This was added here: https://github.com/alphagov/govuk_publishing_components/pull/335)

However, og:image is _also_ rendered by the [Public Layout](https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/layout_for_public) component, so if you include both you end up with two og:image meta_tags. I don't know if this is a problem?

So:
- At the very least, the documentation should be updated
- Arguably maybe the social media meta tags should be added by the [Meta Tags](https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/meta_tags) Component rather than this one?
- We also need to know if two og:image tags is a problem, and if so maybe fix it by removing from Public Layout?

communityIssues.title: Whitehall overrides some component styles
communityIssues.body:
There are a few instances in whitehall's CSS where styles for gem components are being overridden, which violates our principle of [component isolation](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk_publishing_components/blob/main/docs/component_principles.md#a-component-is-isolated-when). 

If possible, these styles should either be applied directly to the components themselves (in the form of new options) or applied to parent elements of the components within the application, so they do not impact the appearance of the components themselves.

[_overrides.scss line 21](https://github.com/alphagov/whitehall/blob/main/app/assets/stylesheets/admin/_overrides.scss#L21) overrides `gem-c-summary-list` child elements:

- `.govuk-summary-list__key` is given a vertical align of top, which looks redundant and can potentially be simply removed (text is already vertically aligned to the top in this element)
- images are given `display: block`. This might be trickier to unpick although the use of this component doesn't normally include images, so this might be a custom application thing that could be added to the component defaults

[_overrides.scss line 44](https://github.com/alphagov/whitehall/blob/main/app/assets/stylesheets/admin/_overrides.scss#L44) overrides `gem-c-checkboxes` styles:

- there's a helpful comment here explaining the issue, which is to do with not showing checkboxes when JavaScript is enabled with the Add another component. The [component guide page for Add another](https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/add_another) doesn't show any examples containing checkboxes, so this could be something that could be part of the component with a documentation update

[_overrides.scss line 50](https://github.com/alphagov/whitehall/blob/main/app/assets/stylesheets/admin/_overrides.scss#L50-L59) overrides reorderable list styles:

- both overrides refer to a 'read only' version of the component, which seems like it should be an option within the component

[_document-collection-group-memberships-index.scss line 2](https://github.com/alphagov/whitehall/blob/main/app/assets/stylesheets/admin/views/_document-collection-group-memberships-index.scss#L2) overrides heading styles:

- it looks like the heading component is being positioned inline along with a list of items, presumably to make them all appear on one line together. Not sure which page this appears on, but it might be done better with some custom CSS specifically for this purpose, rather than components

[_edit-edition.scss line 33](https://github.com/alphagov/whitehall/blob/main/app/assets/stylesheets/admin/views/_edit-edition.scss#L33) overrides the warning text component:

- it's setting the margin bottom of the component to 0, which can be achieved without CSS by passing a `margin_bottom: 0` option to the component (warning text uses the [component wrapper helper](https://components.publishing.service.gov.uk/component-guide/warning_text#standard-options))

[_summary.scss line 47](https://github.com/alphagov/whitehall/blob/main/app/assets/stylesheets/admin/views/_summary.scss#L47) overrides the button component:

- it's setting the width of the button to `100%`
- this isn't an option on the component or in the Design System, it might be this could just be removed

ourIssues.title: Allow multiple components to be attached to an element
ourIssues.body:
## Related component Relates to any component that is initialised with the `data-module` attribute and might cross-over with another component that uses the same element. I've outlined this with a service-specific example because it's easier to describe, but my main concern here is with other component libraries which would benefit from seamless integration with the Design System, and where service teams have less say over the implementation details. ## Context Imagine my service has a bespoke component based by [Bootstrap's Popover component](https://getbootstrap.com/docs/4.0/components/popovers/). We initialise all our components following the Design System pattern, so in this case with a `data-module="app-popover"` attribute. I want to add a popover to a button, which I also want to behave like a [Button component](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/button/). This is a problem, since the Design System doesn't support multiple modules (if that's the right term?) being initialised from one element. I can't do `data-module="govuk-button" data-module="app-popover"` because that's invalid HTML. I could do `data-module="govuk-button app-popover"` (like class attribute syntax), but that won't work because the Design System [uses exact matches](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/dd748307ca612c73c2e60548419cee94d0cd636f/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/all.mjs#L55) when looking for attributes (`app-popover` could be made to work, but `govuk-button` won't) My suggestion is that the selector for initialising components is updated to `[data-module~="${Component.moduleName}"]`, which treats the attribute as a whitespace-separated list and matches if one entry in that list is the module. It would continue to work with exact matches, as the attribute would be treated as a list of one item. ## Alternatives ### Downstream components trigger upstream behaviour In the example above, the service's Popover component could be responsible for also initialising button behaviour on the element (i.e. `(new Button(this.$module)).init()`). However, if the Popover could also be applied to other elements (e.g. links, images) we wouldn't want to add button behaviour. The Popover component could apply this conditionally, if `$this.module.tagName === 'BUTTON'`, but this leads to hidden behaviour that's hard to opt-out of. #### Using ES2015 classes From v5, this could be achieved by extending the exposed JavaScript class: ```js export class Popover extends Button { constructor($module, options) { // GOV.UK Frontend button super($module, options) // Custom button things ... } } ``` This again creates a direct dependency on the Button component, which might not be desired if the component could be used by non-button elements too. It also creates a hierarchy, which could be complex if there are more than two components: if `Popover extends Button` and `SearchToggle extends Button`, then you have the same problem making an element both a Popover and a SearchToggle. ### Encourage other departmental and service-specific components to use a different attribute/approach In the example above, the Popover component might use the `data-app-module` attribute instead. Departmental component libraries could use e.g. `data-dft-module`. Since Design System components are prefixed `govuk-` in the value, I think it's reasonable to expect others to use the attribute with a different prefix. Also, there are already other components using this attribute so changing them would require changes to dependent services. ### Require one element per component/module In the example above, the Popover could be applied to a wrapping element, for example: ```html
``` This seems unnecessarily verbose to me, and requires introducing additional HTML elements to the DOM. ## Additional information (if applicable) ### Breaking change There is a breaking change risk: if a service already has whitespace-separated names in their `data-module` attribute then this would effectively "fix" them, but it _might_ cause unexpected behaviour if they've patched around it. For example, with my Popover component above, I might have added debouncing to the Popover code because govuk-button "wasn't working" and now have duplicate/conflicting behaviour. ### Components This doesn't align with Web Components, since each element can only be one component (e.g. `` or `

When you activate the main nav buttons they even visibly open the sub menu that shouldn't be reachable in the desktop view. Those buttons can also be explored by touch. Screenshot of the hidden "Get started" button being highlighted and activated with the "Get started" sub menu open underneath the service nav: This was first discovered as part of an [audit of the Brand Guidelines website](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-brand-guidelines/issues/138), which copies the Design System website functionality. ## Steps to reproduce the issue 1. At step 4 you shouldn't be able to open the mobile menu when it desktop view. ## Environment (where applicable) - Operating system: iPadOS 18.6 - Browser: Safari - Browser version: (not sure) I don't have a recent enough iOS version to see if it happens on current iOS as well. But I can confirm it does **not** happen with: * VO on iPadOS 15.8.3 * latest VO on macOS * latest TalkBack on Android * latest NVDA on Windows * latest JAWS on Windows That means it might well be due to a bug in iPadOS (and maybe iOS). ourIssues.title: Review the use of aria-label on a <ul> element in the site navigation menu
ourIssues.body:
## What
We use an `aria-label` on our sub-navigation list `<ul>`. This causes HTML validation issues, so we need to make the call on whether we keep it as an exception, add an explicit `aria-role` to keep validation happy, or get rid of it and find another solution.

## Why
Previously, we added an `aria-label` to the main site nav's Community sub-menu to make a better experience for screenreaders:  https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/commit/4ff06e4961bcd4a147d580d1d5ac2736fe9f6ec3

Recently, we [added HTML linting](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/pull/2569), and it flagged this as `aria-label-misuse`.

If we assign an explicit `role` to the labelled list, the HTML validator is sated and complains no longer.

However, it's a bit unclear which `role` we'd want to add - `navigation` is out since this subnav is already contained within a `nav` parent, and `menu` [might not be right for this situation](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/pull/2569#discussion_r1115422380).

We could avoid this debate if we just find a solution that doesn't involve ARIA. First step would probably be to just remove the `aria-label` and test whether it reads fine in multiple screenreaders.

If it’s missing context without the aria-label, we could look at using a bit of ‘visually-hidden’ instead of an aria-label. Would need to test to see if it works consistently across all screen readers though.

## Who needs to work on this
Developer, Accessibility specialist(?)

## Who needs to review this
Developer, Accessibility specialist

## Done when

- [ ] We have a solution that is both valid HTML, and a good experience for screenreaders.
- [ ] We have implemented that solution (this will likely involve [removing the inline validation exception](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/blob/9ba07459f46a6e9738067c7ec90da6dd22f3a1b6/views/partials/_navigation.njk#L14))

ourIssues.title: Hint text for radio/checkbox groups gets read out repeatedly by VoiceOver
ourIssues.body:
## Description of the issue

When arrowing through a form with a radio (or checkbox) group that has a hint, VoiceOver on iOS reads out the hint text repeatedly.
While this is not a WCAG fail and is probably not a bug in the Design System itself, it can be annoying to screen reader users.


## Steps to reproduce the issue

Open our [inline radios example](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/radios/inline/) and arrow through the page (VO + right arrow).


## Actual vs expected behaviour

I don't know what is supposed to happen according to the spec, I only know what happens in all other major screen readers. I don't know if this means it's a bug in VoiceOver or just a different way how VoiceOver does things.

VoiceOver reads out the hint text:

* when arrowing to the legend
* (obviously also when arrowing to the hint text itself)
* when arrowing to the first radio button
* when arrowing to the second (and potential subsequent) radio buttons

The second and third are to be expected, the first and last not.
All other major screen readers only read the hint text when arrowing to the first radio button they encounter (and to the hint text itself).


## Environment

This happens with VoiceOver on iOS but also to some degree on macOS.
(It's less bad on macOS as the hint text doesn't get read out when arrowing to the legend.)

Tested in Safari on an iPad with iOS version 18.3.1 and a MacBook with macOS version 15.3.2.

A user has reported that this issue was not happening on iOS version 16.

ourIssues.title: Investigate presence of both `/` trailed and non-trailed paths in GA
ourIssues.body:
<!--

  This is a template for any issues that aren’t bug reports or new feature requests. The headings in this section provide examples of the information you might want to include, but feel free to add/delete sections where appropriate.

-->

## What

Figure why the behaviour flow of Google Analytics revealed that we're tracking pages both with and without trailing slashes while users browse the site:
 - `/styles` and `/styles/`
 - `/patterns` and `/patterns/`
 - `/component` and `/components/`

This distinction would be fine for landing pages, as we don't control how other websites link to us. However, during navigation between pages of the design system, we should only see one format for the paths.

## Why

We likely have some form of redirect in place to make this transparent to users (at the price of an extra request, which would be great to avoid).  However, in the analytics, it muddies the data as:
- both URLs are the same page
- this doubling of pages pushes other pages out of the top X of the data, making it harder to review how users browse the Design System site

## Who needs to work on this

Developers

## Who needs to review this

Developers

## Done when

- [ ] We know why we're seeing both URLs on Google Analytics
- [ ] We've chosen and implemented a fix so we only track a single page

Are there any recommendations or real-world examples we should follow? Some ideas: - Define small Svelte components that configure the gov.uk classes, and use those. For example, a `TH` component would just wrap `` and pass through other attributes the user specifies. We'd have a separate `Button`, `StartButton`, `SecondaryButton`, [etc](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/button/). - Some precedent: https://github.com/govuk-react/govuk-react and https://github.com/PaulioRandall/svelte-gds-design-system - Ideally in CSS, there'd be a way to express something like `th { inherit from .govuk-table__header }`, but not that I can find - Do some CSS preprocessing magic to change some of the class selectors to HTML element selectors? - Use [Nunchucks](https://frontend.design-system.service.gov.uk/use-nunjucks/), which appears to be this sort of templating approach? CC @Pete-Y-CS and @ADD-William-WaltersDavis. A real example of manually specifying classes everywhere is in Will's project, https://github.com/ADD-William-WaltersDavis/planning_tool/blob/a586a944c31619ccc12f38f23b800263dbb0f703/components/HoverScores.svelte#L185. Thanks! (And apologies for not following the issue template; there wasn't any for questions. I'm on secondment to Active Travel England, don't have a gov.uk email, and thus can't join the Slack to ask there)

A reviewer asked why users should choose either `text` or `html`, as we hadn't specified this in the cookie content. I then learned that if users ever attempt to pass both `text` and `html`,  `html` will win every time.

We then decided to add this sentence to the `html` Description: "If you are not passing HTML, use `text`."

All of our components contain `text` and `html` options. However, it's only in the cookie banner content that we explain when to use one or the other.

ourIssues.title: Changing the colour palette used for graphs on GOV.UK/Design System
ourIssues.body:
## Context
<!-- What are you trying to do? Is this something you think should behave differently, or something that you currently cannot do? Is this related to an existing issue/bug? -->

The colours used in the existing charts that can be built using Govspeak do not meet the colour contrast requirements for adjacent colours (as set out in WCAG 2.1). The Analysis Function Support Team have developed accessible colour palettes to use with charts and would love to see these implemented in the charts created using Govspeak. 

I have published a webpage showing the [types of tables and charts that can be built using Govspeak](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/examples-of-visual-content-to-use-on-govuk). 

## Alternatives
<!-- Are you currently using a workaround / alternative solution instead? -->

In general statistics producers who use GOV.UK to publish content are frustrated with the technical capability they have to publish charts. Only horizontal bar charts can be created using Govspeak so they are very limited in what they can do in HTML. Many teams are still creating charts as images and then publishing them as PNGs, JPEGs or (at best) SVGs. Sometimes they publish a mix of charts created as images and charts created using Govspeak, sometimes all their charts are images. 

When it comes to colours, if they use the horizontal bar charts available in Govspeak they have no way of changing the colours. When they create charts as images they can choose whatever colours they want. 

This either leads to a mix of colour palettes being used (which isn't great), or they align all their charts with the Govspeak colour palette, which also isn't great as the adjacent colours do not meet the contrast requirements for adjacent colours, set out in WCAG 2.1. 

## Additional information (if applicable)
<!-- What evidence do you have that this meets the needs of users? It’s useful for us to know of any user research/testing you’ve done with this feature. -->

Making the Govspeak charts meet the contrast requirements set out in WCAG 2.1 won't make things 100% perfect for all users but it will definitely be an improvement for any users with access needs related to seeing adjacent colours. It is also a legal requirement. 

The colour palettes we have created are available within [this colours guidance](https://gss.civilservice.gov.uk/policy-store/data-visualisation-colours-in-charts/#section-5) (it is still technically in draft but should be signed off by the end of this week).

ourIssues.title: Include fingerprints in filename for image assets
ourIssues.body:
## What

Include a fingerprint in the filename for all of our image assets to make it easy for service teams to [treat them as immutable and cache them indefinitely](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Caching#cache_busting).

Update the page template and references in the stylesheet to point to the new images.

## Why

Although we allow customisation of the location of the images in both Sass (by setting `$govuk-images-path`) and Nunjucks (by setting the `assetPath` variable) it's non-trivial to change the filenames themselves – you'd need to either creatae a function that rewrites the filename in Sass or re-implement the entire `headIcons` block in Nunjucks.

Although there are only a handful of images in GOV.UK Frontend, the difficulty in adding fingerprints to them may cause issues for services with more images that are fingerprinted, preventing them from having a blanket caching strategy for all of their images.

It could also cause issues where the majority of images do have fingerprinted and teams are caching images indefinitely, without realising that our images do not have fingerprints.

## Further details

Note that if we use a hash of the file contents as part of the filename that would mean that any change to an image (including e.g. optimisations) could be a breaking change as teams would need to update the paths in their templates etc.

We could mitigate this by keeping previous versions of images between major releases, or consider using an alternative identifier that only changes if the image changes in a meaningful way (like a version number)

## Who needs to work on this

Developers

## Who needs to review this

Developers

## Done when

- [ ] Image assets in GOV.UK can be cached indefinitely (for example because they include a fingerprint in their filename that changes when the file contents change)
- [ ] References to those images have been updated
- [ ] We understand the impact on future changes to those images and what it means for versioning

ourIssues.title: Improve support for Windows High Contrast Mode and Internet Explorer 11
ourIssues.body:
<!--

  This is a template for any issues that aren’t bug reports or new feature requests. The headings in this section provide examples of the information you might want to include, but feel free to add/delete sections where appropriate.

-->

This builds on work by @chris-gds for the accordion component refresh in #2257.

## What

Add media feature `-ms-high-contrast` to media queries that change styles for Windows High Contrast Mode.

Add CSS property `-ms-high-contrast-adjust` where property `forced-color-adjust` is used.

For example, see draft PR #2290 

## Why

Internet Explorer 11 doesn't support the [`forced-colors` media feature](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@media/forced-colors) or the [`forced-color-adjust` property](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/forced-color-adjust), but it has equivalents in [`-ms-high-contrast`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@media/-ms-high-contrast) and [`-ms-high-contrast-adjust`](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/hh771863(v=vs.85)).

We can port fixes for High Contrast Mode such as improved focus states for radios and checkboxes (https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/pull/2264) that currently work in Edge / Chrome / Opera but not Internet Explorer.

According to the 2018 WebAIM survey of users with low vision, a higher percentage use Internet Explorer than Edge.

## Who needs to know about this

Devs

## Done when

- [x] GOV.UK Frontend has support for Windows High Contrast Mode and Internet Explorer 11 #2290 
- [ ] Documented how to add tweaks for Windows High Contrast Mode and other forced colour modes in future

ourIssues.title: Add content to Skip link guidance about problem caused by preservation of fragment identifiers between pages
ourIssues.body:
The skip link component adds a `#main-content` fragment identifier to the current URL. This can persist across pages causing an unexpected jump to the main content area on load. I'd like to add a warning about this to the guidance, along with tips about ways teams could write their code to avoid this. 

## Related component

https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/skip-link/

## Context

This problem has been seen to happen in the following scenario:
- the skip link was used, thereby adding `#main-content` to the current URL
- you leave the page via a successful form submission
- the form doesn't set the `action` attribute and so POSTs to the current URL
- the server uses [the POST -> Redirect -> GET pattern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post/Redirect/Get) to navigate to the next page

Given all that, the browser will preserve `#main-content` in the new URL[^1] causing the next page to jump to the start of the main content area when it loads.

This was picked up as an issue by the Digital Accessibility Centre (DAC) in a recent audit of GOV.UK Notify[^2], who stated that it failed [the WCAG 2.4.3 (Focus Order) success criteria](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG20/Understanding/focus-order).

Given [the POST -> Redirect -> GET pattern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post/Redirect/Get) is so commonly used in web apps, I think there's some value in making teams aware of this problem and helping them write their code in a way that stops it happening.

## Alternatives

N/A

## Additional information (if applicable)

Suggested changes, to stop the problem occurring are:
- setting the `action` attribute on the `<form>` tag to match the current URL, without `#main-content`
- setting the URL for the next page explicitly using the [Content-Location](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Content-Location) header

## References

[^1]: This is correct behaviour, as defined in [Handling of fragment identifiers in redirected URLs](https://www.w3.org/Protocols/HTTP/Fragment/draft-bos-http-redirect-00.txt)
[^2]: Issue 'ID: DAC_Focus_order_01' on page 19 of [the audit report](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jRkkL3AZj-7Q0uo7yfHUv_JF9q0Ecw6g/view?usp=sharing) (needs a GDS Google account for access)

ourIssues.title: Inconsistent print layout behaviour cross browser
ourIssues.body:
<!--
    Please fill in as much of the template below as you’re able to. If you're unsure whether the issue already exists or how to fill in the template, open an issue anyway. Our team will help you to complete the rest.

-->

## Description of the issue

When you print a page in chrome it looks different to when you print the same page in firefox or safari

Chrome uses the mobile breakpoint styles when printing - so grid columns become stacked vertically - however other browsers (firefox and safari) don't do this

A lot of HMRC services use a 2/3 grid area for their main content, but don't actually have anything in the remaining 1/3 of the layout

So when you print one of these in chrome, the 2/3 grid area expands to fill the whole width of the page (what they want). In firefox and safari however, the content still only takes up 2/3 with a gap on the right

For now they've patched it with this CSS to make the the print layout consistent between browsers
```
@media print {
    .govuk-main-wrapper > .govuk-grid-row > div[class*='govuk-grid-column-'] {
        width: 100%;
    }
}
```
The following screenshot shows how the print layout looks before applying this (top pdf on the right, with blue outlines added to it's layout elements) and after (bottom pdf on the right, with red outlines added to it's layout elements):
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/100650/228557746-c1377d6f-bcab-40d1-a2d8-0aac3e0f7341.png)

## Steps to reproduce the issue

Try printing this example from the design system in chrome, then try printing it in firefox

https://design-system.service.gov.uk/styles/layout/common-two-thirds-one-third/index.html

The print layouts will be different

## Actual vs expected behaviour

The team who raised this with us in HMRC expected the print layout to be consistent between browsers

Should there be anything in govuk-frontend to make the print layout consistent by default between browsers - or guidance in the documentation explaining why there can be a difference

ourIssues.title: Components assume the `govuk-visually-hidden` utility class will exist
ourIssues.body:
## Description of the issue

We provide an entry points for each individual component, the idea being that users should get all of the CSS they need to use that component, and ideally nothing more.

For example, including the character count component also includes the CSS for the:

- error message
- hint
- label
- textarea

However, it does _not_ include the `govuk-visually-hidden` utility class, which is used within the Nunjucks template.

From a quick check, it looks like this affects:

- Accordion (in the JavaScript)
- Character count (in the JavaScript)
- Error message (in the Nunjucks template)
- Exit this page (in the Nunjucks template and JavaScript)
- File upload (in the JavaScript)
- Footer (in the Nunjucks template)
- Pagination (in the Nunjucks template)
- Password input (in the JavaScript)
- Summary list (in the Nunjucks template)
- Warning text (in the Nunjucks template)

## Steps to reproduce the issue

Use the component-specific entrypoint to include just the CSS for any of the components listed above, then view the component

## Actual vs expected behaviour

Visually hidden text should be hidden, but it isn't because the `govuk-visually-hidden` utility class is not included in the CSS

ourIssues.title: Add `size` option to form input component labels
ourIssues.body:
<!--

  This is a template for any issues that aren’t bug reports or new feature requests. The headings in this section provide examples of the information you might want to include, but feel free to add/delete sections where appropriate.

-->

## What

Allow form field components to receive a new `size` option in their `label` or `legend` option for easily controlling the text size of their label or legend. The option should receive a t-shirt size and set the appropriate `.govuk-label--<T_SHIRT_SIZE>` or `.govuk-fieldset__legend--<T_SHIRT_SIZE>` on the label or legend.

For components using a `label` the option should be implemented by adding a [new option to our internal Label component](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/tree/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/label) and passing the option through. For those using a `legend`, the public Fieldset component should get an update first in a similar fashion.

The affected components are:
- [Character Count](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/character-count/template.njk) (forwarding the option to Textarea)
- [Checkboxes](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/checkboxes/template.njk) (forwarding the option to either Fieldset)
- [Date Input](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/date-input/template.njk) (forwarding the option to Fieldset)
- [Fieldset](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/date-input/template.njk)
- [File Upload](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/file-upload/template.njk) (forwarding the option to Label)
- [Input](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/input/template.njk) (forwarding the option to Label)
- [Label](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/label/template.njk)
- [Password Input](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/password-input/template.njk) (forwarding the option to Input)
- [Radios](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/radios/template.njk) (forwarding the option to Fieldset)
- [Select](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/select/template.njk) (forwarding the option to Label)
- [Textarea](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/textarea/template.njk) (forwarding the option to Label)

## Why

Different components use different tags for the "title" of the field. This requires the user to understand internal nuances (is it a `label` or `legend`) to change its size. Having an option abstracting this and letting the component work out if it's `.govuk-label--...` or `.govuk-fieldset__legend--...` that's needed is much easier.

## Who needs to work on this

Developers, Tech writer

## Who needs to review this

Developers, Tech writer

## Done when

- [ ] The new option is available on all the components listed above
- [ ] The option is documented consistently across components

ourIssues.title: Improve documentation of `beforeInput(s)` and `afterInput(s)` options of our form control components
ourIssues.body:
<!--

  This is a template for any issues that aren’t bug reports or new feature requests. The headings in this section provide examples of the information you might want to include, but feel free to add/delete sections where appropriate.

-->

## What

Research and document which kind of content is OK/not OK to put in the `beforeInput(s)` and `afterInput(s)` options of our form components, introduced in #4567 to ensure all users (especially those using assistive technology) get proper access to the content.

## Why

Because the content ends up inside a form field, where the control is associated to the label/legend and any error/hint, there's a risk that content injected through `beforeInput(s)`/`afterInput(s)` options gets missed when navigating from field to field, the focus skipping over the content to the next form field. 

This means we may want to suggest restrictions as to which content is suitable for these options, possible techniques to link the content so it gets announced when navigating from field to field, and possibly a warning to test thoroughly.

## Who needs to work on this

Developers, Accessibility specialist, possibly Designers

## Who needs to review this

Developers, Accessibility specialist, possibly Designers 

## Done when

- [ ] We've clarified how to best use the `beforeInput(s)` and `afterInput(s)` options of our form components.

ourIssues.title: Adjust components to scale with android system font size
ourIssues.body:
## What
Ensure as many of our components as possible are responding when viewing govuk-frontend web pages on android devices and adjusting android's system font size.

## Why
Govuk-frontend web pages should respect accessibility settigns and respond to them as expected.

## Steps to replicate
Tested in chrome on browserstack's Galaxy S23 instance as it's easy to notice the issue due to the device's large font size scale.

1. Go to the settings of the testing device and locate the setting to adjust device font size
2. Increase font size (recommend max in order to visualise issue more clearly)
3. Open a govuk-frontend web page on a browser on an android device eg: [the review app's announcements page](https://govuk-frontend-review.herokuapp.com/full-page-examples/announcements)

Notice that the breadcrumbs have not increased in size. Digging into the runtime styles, you will find that rem values of other elements on the page have adjusted in response to the font size change but the breadcrumbs haven't.

![Android browser showing an announcements page with scaled up font size except for the breadcrumbs element](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/assets/64783893/66ecb7d1-bf9e-459a-987c-8c85176a26b7)

## Notes
### Considerations from the spec

## What

Investigate whether we could enhance the password input component by using:

This was a late stretch goal that we didn't have time to complete during #4442, though some initial screen reader testing was carried out. 1 day(?)

This may vary depending on what the spike is, ranging from heavily involved (pairing) to less involved (reviewing/bouncing ideas off) -->

ourIssues.title: Improve the `title`s for pattern guidance pages

## Context

Pattern pages with compound titles do not have the entire title included within the `title` element.

|Page `h1`|Page `title`|
|:-|:-|
|Ask users for Bank Details|Bank details|
|Ask users for Email addresses|Email addresses|

Currently you must either look at the page's URL or click through to visit the page in order to see whether it is the desired page.

ourIssues.title: Voice Control bug with .govuk-visually-hidden
ourIssues.body:
Voice Control appears to have a bug with the 'say what you see' feature when using interactive elements which have partially obscured content. 

If the `.govuk-visually-hidden` is added to an entire element, it causes no issues. But if an interactive element has something like a `<span>` inside it to partially hide some content, such as a 'change' link on the 'check your answers' pattern, then the bug occurs. 

The issue appears to be that Voice Control does not adjust its view of the page based on what is visible, and is still maintaining a directory of the verbose versions of each element. 

For example:

Using Dragon and Windows Speech Recognition, when you say 'click change' both softwares recognise the change links as identical and each link is highlighted so the can select which one they want.

Using Voice Control, when you say 'click change' nothing happens. If you inspect each link for it's full label, you can then get Voice Control to work if you are verbose. For example, 'click change name' works, but just saying 'click change' does not. So it would only work by guessing the full link label.

The links do still work with 'show numbers' and you can still select them by using the grid, so it's unlikely to be a blocker. I have filled in a bug report with apple (FB8973238), but realistically I doubt they will fix it. 

Just wanted to raise it so people had sight of it.

ourIssues.title: Various issues under Chrome's Auto Dark Mode
ourIssues.body:
Since Chrome version 78, Google has included an experimental feature in the browser, initially named "Forced Dark Mode" and, as of writing, named "Auto Dark Mode for Web Content". 

This feature automatically modifies the appearance of webpages in order to create a "dark mode" version. This is done even if the page already supplies a "dark mode" via the `prefers-color-scheme` CSS media query. It also appears to ignore the `color-scheme` property. 

The flag comes with several different "enabled" modes (as of Chrome 99), which modify how Chrome is internally applying changes. Each mode results in subtly (sometimes radically) different resulting colours.

1. Enabled
2. Enabled with simple HSL-based inversion
3. Enabled with simple CIELAB-based inversion
4. Enabled with simple RGB-based inversion
5. Enabled with selective image inversion
6. Enabled with selective inversion of non-image elements
7. Enabled with selective inversion of everything
8. Enabled with increased text contrast

Most of these modes appear to work by first overriding neutral light background colours (such as white and light greys), and modifying any copy that it detects as existing on a modified background colour to maintain suitable contrast. Most other colours appear to be left intact. This method of alteration means that colours are not all modified in the same way: `$govuk-brand-color` in mode 1, for example, is unmodified when used as a background or border colour (#1d70b8), but is changed when it is used as a text colour (#61a1ee).

Mode 4 appears to simply invert all colours on the page, regardless of usage. 

I'm not sure how mode 1 is different from the others. It may be that this is an "automatic" mode where Chrome tries to determine which of the other seven modes works best for the given page and uses that one.

We have received at least one bug report raised by a user who was using Chrome's Auto Dark Mode feature for accessibility reasons (to make content easier to read with cataracts).

> RE the dark mode, it is now a function in Google Chrome that you can activate and it will force a dark version if the website can accommodate it. Not everyone does, BBC News for example still comes through with a traditional black text on a white background – but it works for many.

## Steps to reproduce the issue
In Google Chrome, go to `chrome://flags/#enable-force-dark` (this should jump you straight to "Auto Dark Mode for Web Contents") and enable the flag.

## Actual vs expected behaviour
Currently, a number of these modes produce colour combinations which fail the contrast requirements established in WCAG 2.1. 

Below is a non-exhaustive subset of issues currently identified in Auto Dark Mode.

### Text inputs and textareas
Text inputs are displayed with a grey background and black border in modes 1, 6, 7, and 8. This fails to meet the expected 1:3 contrast ratio for UI elements (at 1:1.68). 

![Screenshot of the design system input component, appearing grey on black.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160644743-7632dc27-cc56-4558-bd40-8fee1109717c.png)

They are displayed with a light grey background and white border in modes 3 and 5, which easily meets contrast ratio expectations.

They are displayed with the default white background and black border in all other modes.

### Input prefixes and suffixes

These are difficult to read in modes 2 and 4, where they are black on a dark grey background (1:3.23).

![Screenshot of the design system input prefix and suffix example, where the text is black on dark grey.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160646813-ac2ad0a1-083d-4ca0-b571-b1ecacd450e4.png)

These are much more difficult to read in modes 3 and 5, which renders it as black on an even darker grey (1.22).

![Screenshot of the design system input prefix and suffix example. The text is visually imperceptible from the background.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160650473-9c6f3529-5a06-4408-b20e-242b1c66a08e.png)

These are displayed with adequate contrast in other modes.

### Checkboxes and radio buttons
The border and selection states of checkboxes and radio buttons do not have sufficient contrast in modes 1, 6, 7, and 8 (at a pretty much imperceptible contrast ratio of 1:1.04)

![Screenshot of the design system checkbox component, illustrating insufficient contrast between the checkboxes and background, which are both dark grey.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160644218-1fc50370-249e-4e47-b73a-eab9a8b8ea34.png)

They are displayed with white borders and selection states in all other modes.

### Select

In modes 1, 6, 7, and 8, select boxes are rendered with a dark grey background and dark grey border (1:1.04).

![Screenshot of the design system select component, which appears to just be white text with no border or icon.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160648934-5554f80a-1794-40e1-a9b7-a7c16df83d29.png)

They are rendered with a black background and white border in all other modes.

### Skiplinks

In modes 1, 2, 6, and 7, skiplinks are rendered as white on focus-colour yellow, which does not meet contrast requirements (1:1.34).

![Screenshot of a white link on a bright yellow background.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160649767-19aecf58-2ea6-4517-9852-283a4c91f922.png)

In mode 4, it is white on light blue, which is also below expectations (1:3.24).

![Screenshot of a white link on a bright blue background.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160649982-3f7999be-3540-40c5-8d00-7b9350407360.png)

In mode 8, it is white on focus-color yellow, but additionally has a black text shadow/stroke effect applied, which makes it difficult to read.

![Screenshot of a white link with a thin, pixellated black shadow surrounding it, on a bright yellow background.](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1253214/160650309-a61034bd-d400-4ca3-b312-db890c382f19.png)

This is displayed with adequate contrast (albeit, in white on brown) in all other modes.

### Iconography

Most iconography fails to meet contrast requirements in virtually all modes. This includes:
- the open and close arrows on the Accordion component.
- the arrow on the Back link component.
- the arrows on the Breadcrumbs component.
- the exclamation icon on the Warning text component.

### Other components
The good news is that, for the most part, the majority of other components we have in GOV.UK Frontend are not as badly affected as those above, with various components such as Inset text, Error summary, and Notification banner maintaining their necessary visual presence and suitable contrast even with modified colours. 

## Environment
The results specified here were taken in Chrome 99, running on macOS 15.3, whilst the operating system was set to light mode. 

Interestingly, Chrome DevTools does not give any indication that a change to the page's appearance has taken place. All HTML and CSS content, including the user agent stylesheet, computed styles, and those returned through JavaScript, appear unmodified and are not aligned with the page's actual appearance when Auto Dark Mode is enabled.

ourIssues.title: Improve inconsistent screenreader behaviours for error summary/notification banner
ourIssues.body:
## What
The error summary and notification banner components are implemented in similar ways: using `role=‘alert’`, `aria-labelledby` and moving focus to the component with JavaScript. However, in our own testing and testing done by others, we have noticed that screenreader behaviour when announcing these components is extremely inconsistent ([link to testing spreadsheet here](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1KrgPdKf8M6zsNZcRPUG0r7H1-1aREW5QgnjhhfVHIag/edit?usp=sharing)).

We could investigate the following as some starting points:

- [ ] Test if we can reliably and consistently reproduce any of the issues below 
- [ ] Whether we're using `role='alert'` and `aria-labelledby` in the correct way
- [ ] If there are any other solutions to this problem that perform more consistently
- [ ] If the behaviour of `aria-live` / `role='alert'` is adequately defined in the specs

## Context
When building the notification banner component, it was flagged that `aria-labelledby` was redundant for the error summary component (and therefore on the alert versions of the notification banner too). However, when we tested this in various assistive tech, we found that removing `aria-labelledby` could 1) change the behaviour a lot (especially in Voiceover on Mac), and 2) in general, announcing of error summary/notification banner is extremely inconsistent between different screenreaders. 

In the short term, we decided not to remove aria-labelledbyfrom the error summary, and instead to add aria-labelledby to notification banners to make them consistent with the error summary.

## Related Issues

- [Inconsistent announcing of error summary/notification banner](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/1954)
- [Error summary is not focused correctly on second form submission with NVDA](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/2055)
- [Links within error summary are not consistently read out (Safari + Voiceover on MacOS Catalina)](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/2072)

This W3C issue is also slightly related and something we may want to follow up on if we think that the aria properties we're using need to be better defined in the spec, i.e: how things *should* behave on page load: https://github.com/w3c/aria/issues/1360

ourIssues.title: Consider changing or removing focus state for error summary and notification banner
ourIssues.body: ## What Decide on whether the notification banner, which is automatically focused when the page loads (for the error and success variants), should have a focus state and what it should look like. Decide whether the same treatment should be applied to the existing error summary component which behaves in the same way. ## Why We need to understand whether WCAG 2.1 1.4.11 Non-text contrast applies to this element. It's programatically focused on page load, but is not keyboard-operable – once focus has left the error summary, you cannot navigate back to it using the keyboard. The proposed 2.4.11 focus visible (at time of writing) [explicitly only applies to keyboard operable controls](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/focus-appearance-minimum.html#keyboard-focus): > Some elements can take focus (such as the target of a skip link), however, it is only when the element is operable by keyboard controls that this criterion applies. If this logic applies to 1.4.11, then the focus state of the error summary / notification banner does not need to meet contrast – in which case, is the yellow outline actually helpful? Or should we remove it entirely? If the focus state does need to meet contrast, then we need to revisit the focus state for both the error summary and the new notification banner component. ## Further detail The error summary currently has a yellow outline when focused. The proposed notification banner component will also take focus on page load (for the error and success variants), so we will presumably want to use the same approach. However, the yellow outline does not meet 3:1 colour contrast against the white background. Other components use a black border when focused (which then means it meets contrast), but because the error summary is focused on page load we want to preserve the border colour so that it suggests an error / success state as appropriate. ## Done when - [x] Understand how WCAG 2.4.11 applies to the notification banner and error summary components - [ ] Decide on focus state for notification banner - [ ] Decide on focus state for error summary

## Description of the issue
