ourIssues.title: Notification banner guidance has misleading line?
ourIssues.body:
## Related documentation

On the [notification banner](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/notification-banner/) page:

"Use a notification banner to tell the user about something they need to know about, but that’s not directly related to the page content."

## Suggestion

There are cases where you might use a notification banner that _is_ directly related to the page content, particularly when using a [green success banner](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/notification-banner/#reacting-to-something-the-user-has-done). So we might need to change the emphasis of that opening line so it doesn't mislead people.

## Evidence (where applicable)

A designer raised this when designing a page that allowed users to save changes to a content page. They wanted to show a message to confirm the saved changes to users, whilst staying on the same page. I think the green success banner is ideal for that use case. However, the content at the top of the page (about not being related to the page content) made them think this wasn't an option.

ourIssues.title: Investigate making it clearer that the Design System email address is not a generic government helpline
ourIssues.body:
Adding as I think we've discussed this before but never written it up.

## What

We very frequently receive emails from members of the public who have encountered issues with a GOV.UK service (or a government service generally) and are seeking support or updates. 

This is despite displaying a warning on our [get in touch](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/get-in-touch/) page stating that we are unable to help with these queries and providing instructions on how to contact the relevant government departments. 

## Why

This is not a high-volume issue (around a dozen emails a week or fewer), but it's a persistent one.

Members of the public often include Personally Identifying Information in these emails, unnecessarily exposing Design System team members to PII and requiring every member of the team to manually delete the offending emails from their inboxes to comply with data protection laws. In Zendesk, it also means that we need to go through the data redaction process before we can proceed to forward the ticket to user support.

In addition to dealing with the irrelevant ticket, these additional PII tasks are distracting for the whole team. They don't always happen in a timely fashion (if at all) due to members being on leave or on non-working days.

By reducing the quantity of unrelated support emails the team receives, we can alleviate this source frustration and help avoid unnecessarily holding personal data. 

A non-exhaustive list of potential ways to resolve this:

- Remove the contact page from search engine results, as (assumedly) this is where members of the public are finding it.
- Rewrite and/or reformat the existing warning text to make it _extremely_ explicit that we do not provide support or information to members of the public.
  - Consider harsher language in general, such as saying that emails from the public will be deleted and not responded to. 
- Use a more visually prominent component, such as a [Notification banner](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/notification-banner/), or bespoke styling, to display the warning.
- Consider not displaying the email address or link unless a user performs an action acknowledging the warning.

## Who needs to work on this

- Content designers
- Developers (potentially)
- Designers (potentially)

## Who needs to review this

- Content designers

## Done when

- [ ] Thing to do

ourIssues.title: Add 'select all' style functionality to checkboxes
ourIssues.body:
## Related component

- [Checkboxes](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/checkboxes/)

## Context

Checkboxes have the ability to have a 'None of the above' style option (in code, an `exclusive` option) that, when checked, automatically unchecks all other checkboxes in the same group.

Having a checkbox that can operate inversely, a 'select all' option that automatically checks all of the options, could be a useful complement to this. 

This could be used in cases where all or a majority of options are likely to be checked, without explicitly assuming that will be the case.

Potential questions this functionality might fit:

- Selecting dates/times when a user is available for an appointment
- Selecting names for invites, who can be notified of updates, emergency contacts, etc.
- Selecting contact methods
- Bulk selecting and editing in caseworking systems 

This was raised on crossgov Slack and [in the backlog discussion](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/issues/6042#issuecomment-429334420) as a piece of functionality teams often want or need. 

## Alternatives

Users can manually select all of the options relevant to them.

Some teams have resorted to recreating this functionality in their own code, in absence of it being part of the checkboxes component.

## Additional thoughts

### Placement in the list of options

Having the ability to 'select all' at the very top of a checkbox list is arguably the most useful placement: it means users can see it up-front and avoids the wastage of checking a bunch of boxes manually before realising there is an option to check them all at the bottom of the form. It also allows for the use case of checking all boxes and unchecking only those that aren't desired.

In a linear reading order, like a screen reader, having the option to 'select all' is less useful as the user will not yet have received context of what the options will be, whereas a sighted user could skip ahead to get this context.

### Deselect all

If checking the 'select all' option checks all of the unchecked checkboxes, should unchecking it uncheck all of the checked checkboxes too? (Try saying that quickly.)

This function is probably most useful in the caseworking example. I'm not sure if it's likely to be needed as much in a linear form process.

ourIssues.title: Consider adding documentation on `select[multiple]`
ourIssues.body:
The `<select>` HTML element has an alternative mode that allows for selecting multiple values, also known as a multi-select listbox. This is enabled using the `multiple` flag. We don't explicitly support using `multiple` with our Nunjucks macro, however service teams can still enable it through the attributes parameter. 

We do not support `multiple` in our CSS and discourage using it for a few reasons:
- Using multi-select is complicated, requiring the user to hold down one or more keyboard keys (<kbd>⌘ Cmd</kbd>/<kbd>⌃ Ctrl</kbd> or <kbd>⇧ Shift</kbd>) whilst clicking on options. This is difficult to convey and usually not well understood by users.
- Multi-select cannot be easily used with keyboard navigation alone, practically requiring a pointer device to use.
- Multi-select is not (to my knowledge) well supported by assistive technologies.

We may also want to include information on the `size` attribute, which we also do not support in Frontend's code, although it doesn't have the same pitfalls as `multiple`. 

## Related documentation
[Select](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/select/)

## Suggestion
A user has suggested adding documentation about `select[multiple]`; specifically, adding information on why we discourage using it and don't support it: https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/3317 

In most situations, we would probably recommend using [a list of checkboxes](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/checkboxes/) instead.

## Evidence (where applicable)

- [`<select>` your poison](https://www.24a11y.com/2019/select-your-poison/) on [24 Accessibility](https://www.24a11y.com/)

ourIssues.title: Add public API to make JavaScript components responsive to the same breakpoints as the CSS
ourIssues.body:
<!--

  This is a template for any issues that aren’t bug reports or new feature requests. The headings in this section provide examples of the information you might want to include, but feel free to add/delete sections where appropriate.

-->

## What

Create a public API so that custom components can easily observe a [MediaQueryList](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/MediaQueryList) matching one of GOV.UK Frontend's breakpoints. 

Proposed shape is two functions, in something like a `common/breakpoints` module (name up for change):
1. Make the [current `getBreakpoints` function](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/b0d62d49c76e5ce77bef7e0ed7eed6ac26f3c1d2/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/common/index.mjs#L16) public with a couple of tweaks:
   a. move the [error throwing currently do](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/main/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/tabs/tabs.mjs#L95-L100) from the components into the function
   b. this will allow to simplify the return value of the function to a string (never undefined as we'd throw if it is)
   c. cache the reading of the custom property from `document.documentElement` so we don't call `getComputedProperties` each time we need
2. Add a new `matchMedia(breakpointName, callback)` function (or better suited name) to replace the `setupResponsiveChecks` from the [Tabs](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/b0d62d49c76e5ce77bef7e0ed7eed6ac26f3c1d2/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/tabs/tabs.mjs#L92) and [ServiceNavigation components](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/blob/b0d62d49c76e5ce77bef7e0ed7eed6ac26f3c1d2/packages/govuk-frontend/src/govuk/components/service-navigation/service-navigation.mjs#L85).
   a. the function is responsible for creating a MediaQueryList observing a `min-width` media query for a given breakpoint, like the `setupResponsiveChecks` currently do, allowing components to pass in a callback that will be run when the media query is created and when there's change of whether the media query matches
   b. callback should receive either the whole MediaQueryList so it can react to whether the list matches or not 

Once those are in, use the new `matchMedia` function in our components so they don't need to create and store a MediaQueryList themselves and update their `checkSupported` static method so it checks the presence of the breakpoints and prevent initialisation of components.

## Why

It's a bit of logistics to read the breakpoint values from the DOM, throw errors and prevent component initialisation, and it's the same for both our responsive components and the mobile navigation on the Design System site.

## Who needs to work on this

Developers

## Who needs to review this

Developers

## Done when

- [ ] API for reading breakpoints has been implemented
- [ ] Component's `checkSupported` method has been updated
- [ ] Component's `setupResponsiveChecks` method has been replaced
- [ ] Frontend docs documentation for [creating your own components](https://frontend.design-system.service.gov.uk/building-your-own-javascript-components/) has an explanation on how to make components responsive
- [ ] MobileNavigationSection in the Design System site uses the public API

ourIssues.title: Add guidance around print styles and behaviour
ourIssues.body:
## Related documentation

No existing equivalent.

Should likely be a new page, but could be spread across several pages (colours, typography, accordion, tabs, details, etc.) otherwise. 

## Suggestion

The Design System doesn't currently provide any guidance relating to print styles. The only mention of them is on the [layout styles](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/styles/layout/), where there's a override class specific to hiding elements when printed.

This is a question that comes up on support channels and is discussed on Slack semi-frequently, and we have made various choices when developing styles and components that are undocumented. This guidance could also be useful for teams developing new components built on Frontend's code. 

### Things that could be documented

**Remember printing is expensive.** Ink and paper are not free (ink especially) for both users and the environment. Where possible, we should minimise how much of each is used by hiding superfluous elements on the page when printing (e.g. the site's navigation) and making considered decisions over the use and quantity of colour.

**Maintain the page's current state.** A user is often printing the page because they need a hard copy of some piece of information. This could be a particular section on a guidance page, a reference number for an application, or the answers they've provided to a service. Generally, don't alter parts page the user is likely to want to print, when they print it (e.g. expanding or collapsing accordion sections, changing tabs, blanking form inputs).

**Remove background colours.** Don't rely on the presence of a background colour for text contrast. If anything, we likely want to encourage proactively removing background colours to ensure the readability of any text placed on top of them. Use borders to preserve the separation and grouping of elements instead.[^FE]

**Don't use colour to convey information.** Pages may be printed in greyscale, making it difficult to determine the colours of elements. Supplement with text labels, shapes or patterns.

**Use system fonts.** Printers can occassionally struggle to correctly understand web font formats. Reset to a system font or font keyword (e.g. `sans-serif`) to avoid this issue.[^FE]

**Provide context for invisible information.** Some information is usually only visible within a browser, such as a tooltip expanding on an `<abbr>` or the browser status bar showing the URL that a link directs to. When printed, this important information can be lost. Use print styles to re-insert this content on the page.[^FE]

[^FE]: Already a thing GOV.UK Frontend or Frontend components do. Still good to include so teams don't inadvertently override it or forget to implement or test in their own styles.

### Caveats

A user's individual printer configuration will change what the output looks like, and each browser additionally handles things differently when printing, such as whether they respect media queries and what breakpoints they use for calculating them. In this regard, a content author doesn't have a huge amount of control over how some aspects of a page look when printed. Related issue: https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/issues/3441

backlog.title: Contribution submission for Exit this page component
backlog.body:
Formerly known as 'Hide this page component'
What
What are we proposing
We are looking to implement a component, using the existing button component, that allows vulnerable users of a Government service to quickly and safely hide the page and reduce the risk of Domestic Abuse incidents.
The functionality behind the component would allow a user to quickly hide the current page and open a new, ambiguous webpage, such as BBC Weather or another such website. This would lower the risk of drawing attention to browsing habits from a perpetrator.
Why
Why are we proposing this design pattern?

Domestic abuse is physical, sexual, psychological or financial abuse that takes place within an intimate or family-type relationship and that forms a pattern of forceful and controlling behaviour. This can include forced marriage and so-called ‘honour-based crimes.” Domestic abuse may include a range of abusive behaviours, not all of which are in themselves inherently ‘violent’

The biggest risk to a victim of Domestic Abuse is homicide and serious physical assaults - this is at its greatest risk when a victim is planning to flee or escape from the perpetrator. Often, one of the first things a victim will do is to speak to someone to make a disclosure about abuse. The second thing they will do is research and find help online, often using Government services.
We need to ensure that the risk is minimised for users when using online services. Although victims and survivors can be aware of the risks, it is the Government's responsibility to protect individuals using a service. Therefore, it is crucial that there is a consistency of approach in design and functionality across Government with this component.
What evidence do you have that it's needed by multiple services across government?
From conversations between the Department for Work and Pensions, Ministry of Justice, the Cabinet Office and Scottish Government, it is already clear that other services need to ensure that this design is available.
Services are already responding to the rise in Domestic Abuse during COVID-19 by building their own minimum viable solutions to allow users to quickly hide their webpages.
There are areas of the Government site, such as “Domestic Abuse: How to get help”, that a high risk user would access for support that does not include a way to hide their browsing. This is putting those users of this service at risk.
What evidence do you have that it meets the needs of the users of those services?
Speaking with subject matter experts (SME), it is critical that we offer this feature on the GOV.UK website. It is a feature that is provided by other organisations, such as:

Scottish Government - Domestic Abuse page
Refuge
Women’s Aid
Victim Support

Each website has varied design implementations, but ultimately addresses the same user need of being able to hide browsing habits quickly.
The Ministry of Justice have carried out some initial research with an SME to establish whether the proposed solution meets the user needs.
Have you checked that it doesn't already exist in the GOV.UK Design System?
There are no outstanding issues or tickets in the Design System backlog that refer to this type of component.
Anything else
What else has been done
The MoJ have iterated twice on the design component on our live service - looking at language, design and functionality.
There are several designs that are considered minimum viable products which have been released by the DWP (Child Maintenance Service) - Cabinet Office (Coronavirus Support) and the MoJ (Legal Aid Agency). The expediency of these releases has been due to the fact that by not having something, we are putting our users at risk.
The MoJ have carried out some early rounds of testing with an SME that have looked at design, functionality and various use cases from a range of user scenarios. This has all been documented and shared with DWP and CO to share research and findings.
Designs
We looked to extend the GOV.UK Button component to act as the interactive element that a user would press to exit the website.
The Design System suggests using red for any destructive actions undertaken on a GOV.UK website - as the intention for the 'Hide this page' button was essentially closing the webpage down, it would be deemed destructive. This has been adopted by DWP and the Scottish Government.
We decided to utilise the additional space available in the 1/3 column, which is usually reserved for additional information as it allowed us to present the button within immediate view for the user.
The button would then be "sticky" in position at the top of the page on smaller devices. This prevents any conflict with the GOV.UK 'Contents' link that is positioned at the bottom of the screen. It also removes potential accidental presses by a user who doesn't need to use it.
Feedback from SME on the design

Victims of Domestic Abuse are used to using their reptilian brain and are in fight or flight mode so the red would be a trigger for them to draw their to attention to it - Comment from SME

Content
The language used in the button has recently been changed in order to create a more unified style as we continue to work with DWP, Cabinet Office and the Scottish Government. The use of 'Hide this page' presented more of a sense of immediacy, as well as being more descriptive of what the button actually does when the user interacts with it, so we have moved away from the original 'Quick Exit'.
We also use a keyboard function for the user to be able to interact with the button which is controlled by pressing the 'Esc' key.
Behaviour and Functionality
We have explored several types of behaviour for the button, however in order to provide the greatest amount of safety for users we decided to implement functionality similar to other charities and organisations.
When a user interacts with the button, they are sent to a new browser tab that opens BBC Weather. The original tab that they were on doesn't close, but redirects to Google.
This component does not prescribe which websites are to be linked to. That is best done by the individual services and their user research combined with the knowledge of their user base. Google and BBC Weather are good neutral examples pending further research.
Accessibility
The Legal Aid Agency have had an Accessibility Audit on their service and this highlighted some improvements to the component. These were:

Ensuring the button text accurately describes it's purpose
Ensure the instruction "(Or press 'Esc' key)" is presented to all users when presented as a sticky element
Include visually hidden text at the top of the page to help users of assistive technology be aware of the leave page functionality
Differentiate betwixt mobile displays and PC displays zoomed in, so the information about using the escape key is not hidden for non-mobile narrow displays

These changes have been implemented in the latest version of the component, however we will be looking to further test the accessibility of the component as we continue to iterate on it.
MoJ Data Analytics
The 'Hide this page' button has been running as an MVP on the Check Legal Aid service since 14 April 2020. It has been used with a fair amount of frequency, however at present we are are yet to analyse the data in more detail.
The gaps in data recording were due to changes on the back-end of our service that caused GA to drop out.
Graph data since 14 April 2020

The below graph data also shows variations in spikes and lower use through the pandemic

ourIssues.title: Components assume the `govuk-visually-hidden` utility class will exist
ourIssues.body:
## Description of the issue

We provide an entry points for each individual component, the idea being that users should get all of the CSS they need to use that component, and ideally nothing more.

For example, including the character count component also includes the CSS for the:

- error message
- hint
- label
- textarea

However, it does _not_ include the `govuk-visually-hidden` utility class, which is used within the Nunjucks template.

From a quick check, it looks like this affects:

- Accordion (in the JavaScript)
- Character count (in the JavaScript)
- Error message (in the Nunjucks template)
- Exit this page (in the Nunjucks template and JavaScript)
- File upload (in the JavaScript)
- Footer (in the Nunjucks template)
- Pagination (in the Nunjucks template)
- Password input (in the JavaScript)
- Summary list (in the Nunjucks template)
- Warning text (in the Nunjucks template)

## Steps to reproduce the issue

Use the component-specific entrypoint to include just the CSS for any of the components listed above, then view the component

## Actual vs expected behaviour

Visually hidden text should be hidden, but it isn't because the `govuk-visually-hidden` utility class is not included in the CSS

ourIssues.title: Consider adding functionality to Exit this page to accept an array of redirects and use one at random
ourIssues.body:
## Related component

- [Exit this page](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/exit-this-page/)

## Context

Following a recent blog post I made about the Exit this Page component, a commenter suggested that users _always_ being directed to BBC Weather could raise suspicion in a vulnerable user. This is especially the case if they need to use the exit functionality several times in a relatively short period and are redirected to BBC Weather every time. 

To counter this, we could allow services to pass an array of multiple services into the EtP component and have the component choose one of these at random upon each activation to redirect to.

## Alternatives

A service could write server-side code to change the target for the EtP button on each page load, 

## Additional information (if applicable)

There would still need to be a 'main' redirect that exists as the `href` of the link used as a no-JS fallback. I'm not sure we have a defined format for passing an array via `data-*` attributes either, so this functionality may have to be limited to JavaScript configuration.

ourIssues.title: Exit this Page shortcut is sometimes aborted when combining Left Shift and Right Shift
ourIssues.body:
## Description of the issue

The Exit this Page shortcut is intended to be agnostic towards whether the user uses the Left Shift key or Right Shift key, so long as the user presses one of them three times.

However, it can misfire and abort the shortcut activation if the user mixes use of both keys. Rapidly alternating Left Shift and Right Shift keys can sometimes cause both to be registered as pressed at the same time. This triggers the `lastKeyWasModified` check, which is intended to avoid accidental activation when using the Shift key for regular typing, and thus aborts the shortcut.

This is very edge case-y, but it is something we can probably rectify in code.

## Steps to reproduce the issue

1. Open a page with Exit this Page functionality (e.g. [the Design System website example](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/exit-this-page/default/))
2. Press Left and Right Shift simultaneously. Alternatively, rapidly alternate pressing Left Shift and Right Shift.

## Actual vs expected behaviour

### Actual
The indicator light will briefly flicker on before disappearing, the shortcut having been aborted.

### Expected
The shortcut will not be aborted as the user has only pressed shift keys.

## Environment (where applicable)

Reproduced in the below, but likely applies to all browsers and operating systems that run the EtP JavaScript.

- Operating system: macOS 14.7
- Browser: Chrome 
- Browser version: 129
- GOV.UK Frontend Version: 5.6.0

ourIssues.title: Adjust components to scale with android system font size
ourIssues.body:
## What
Ensure as many of our components as possible are responding when viewing govuk-frontend web pages on android devices and adjusting android's system font size.

## Why
Govuk-frontend web pages should respect accessibility settigns and respond to them as expected.

## Steps to replicate
Tested in chrome on browserstack's Galaxy S23 instance as it's easy to notice the issue due to the device's large font size scale.

1. Go to the settings of the testing device and locate the setting to adjust device font size
2. Increase font size (recommend max in order to visualise issue more clearly)
3. Open a govuk-frontend web page on a browser on an android device eg: [the review app's announcements page](https://govuk-frontend-review.herokuapp.com/full-page-examples/announcements)

Notice that the breadcrumbs have not increased in size. Digging into the runtime styles, you will find that rem values of other elements on the page have adjusted in response to the font size change but the breadcrumbs haven't.

![Android browser showing an announcements page with scaled up font size except for the breadcrumbs element](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/assets/64783893/66ecb7d1-bf9e-459a-987c-8c85176a26b7)

## Notes
### Considerations from the spec
The likely reason this is happening can be found in CSS Mobile Text Size section of the CSS spec, specifically [2.2: Conditions that suppress adjustment](https://drafts.csswg.org/css-size-adjust/#default-adjustment-conditions). This section notes 4 reasons that would suppress text size adjustment. From initial testing, certain components can be 'fixed' by removing their block level positioning rules eg: components that have `display: inline-block`. We should be able to use `inline-block` on components and the text size adjustment not be suppressed. Recommend using the the spec in figuring out a solution.

### Impacted components
- Accordion
- Back link
- Breadcrumbs
- Button, and places consumed
    - Cookie banner buttons
    - Exit this page
- Checkboxes
- Details (not the content)
- File upload
- Some of the footer's links
- Header menu
- Notification banner
- Pagination
- Radios
- Select
- Table
- Tabs
- Tag
- Task list
- Text input, and places consumed
    - Date input
    - Password input

ourIssues.title: Update to 'Exit this page' default text may cause issues for voice control users
ourIssues.body: https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/pull/3989 updated the default content of the 'Exit this page' button to add 'Emergency' as visually-hidden text at the start of the button. Adding visually-hidden content to the start or middle of text on interactive elements can cause issues activating them for voice control users (eg Dragon, Apple Voice Control) because the label exposed to these tools ('Emergency Exit this page') doesn't match what the user will say ("Click 'Exit this page'"). Generally voice control needs an exact match on the start of the string, but anything extra at the end is fine - so making it something like `Exit this page in an emergency` would probably be OK. References: https://www.smashingmagazine.com/2022/06/voice-control-usability-considerations-partially-visually-hidden-link-names/#problems-with-partially-visually-hidden-text https://www.sarasoueidan.com/blog/accessible-text-labels/#improving-the-experience-for-screen-reader-users-whilst-keeping-it-accessible-to-speech-input-users I haven't tested yet but I have access to Dragon so I'll test in that to confirm ASAP. I just spotted this change in the v5 beta release notes and wanted to flag it as quickly as possible.

ourIssues.title: Issues with Exit this Page keyboard shortcut and the iOS/iPadOS virtual keyboard
ourIssues.body:
## Description of the issue

The Exit this Page component includes a method of activating the exit functionality by pressing the <kbd>Shift</kbd> key three times (behind the scenes, three `keyup` events). We do not limit when this functionality works, so it's still possible to do this when focused on an input or textarea. This is by design, as we want the user to be able to use the function quickly and at any time. 

This does mean, however, that the function is exposed to devices that utilise virtual keyboards (aka, on-screen keyboards or software keyboards) when a text field is focused. This can be problematic, as the <kbd>Shift</kbd> function was only designed with hardware keyboards in mind and virtual keyboards can operate substantially differently than their hardware equivalents.

### An overview of iOS <kbd>Shift</kbd> operating modes

The <kbd>Shift</kbd> key on iOS has multiple modes of operation depending on the current context, attributes of the current input, and how it is pressed. In one context it is also replaced by a numbers and symbols toggle button, however this button is still treated as being a <kbd>Shift</kbd> key for the purposes of JavaScript events.

**When pressed for a short period of time**, the <kbd>Shift</kbd> key acts as a toggle switch, and changes between being 'on' or 'off' on alternating presses of the <kbd>Shift</kbd> key. The `keyup` event is fired on every second press (the 'off'), except in cases described below.

**When held down**, the <kbd>Shift</kbd> key acts transiently, being 'on' for as long as the user holds it down and turning 'off' once released. The user can press other keys when <kbd>Shift</kbd> is held down to type in uppercase. When used in this way, the `keyup` event is **not** fired when the user releases the <kbd>Shift</kbd> key.

The user can **tap <kbd>Shift</kbd> twice** in rapid succession to turn on Caps Lock mode. The user can press <kbd>Shift</kbd> a third time to turn Caps Lock mode off. When this is carried out, it's emitted as a `keyup` event by the <kbd>Caps Lock</kbd> key, not the <kbd>Shift</kbd> key.

When the user **enters numbers and symbols mode** on the keyboard, the <kbd>Shift</kbd> key is visually replaced by a button to toggle between the initial numbers and symbols view, and the extended symbols view. In this mode, tapping to view the extended symbols mode is treated as a <kbd>Shift</kbd> `keydown` event, and returning to the initial numbers and symbols view is treated as a <kbd>Shift</kbd> `keyup` event. These events are emitted to the webpage, in what feels like a bug in Safari or iOS. 

There are several situations in which **the <kbd>Shift</kbd> key is turned 'on' automatically**. When this happens, no `keydown` event is emitted to the webpage. When it is turned 'off', either automatically or by the user, no `keyup` event is emitted. 

> [!NOTE]
> The takeaway to remember from this is that <kbd>Shift</kbd> will _never_ emit a `keyup` event if the `keydown` wasn't initiated by the user, even if the `keyup` was. This holds true for all of the cases here. 

Situations where this can occur include:

* The input being empty when the user taps on it.
* The cursor being positioned at the start of a new sentence, line or paragraph when the user taps on the input.
* The cursor being positioned at the start of a new word, if the input has the `autocapitalize="words"` attribute.
* Always, if the input has the `autocapitalize="characters"` attribute.

There are a couple of situations where the virtual keyboard will **fire `keyup` events without user intent**. These include: 

* Turning <kbd>Shift</kbd> 'on' manually and switching to the numbers and symbols view will emit the `keyup` event.
* On an input where <kbd>Shift</kbd> will not turn 'on' automatically (e.g. in the middle of a word or sentence), manually activate <kbd>Shift</kbd>, close the virtual keyboard, and then tap on the input to open it again. <kbd>Shift</kbd> will be returned to the 'off' state and emit the `keyup` event.

In testing, we particularly noticed this being a problem on iOS and, presumably, are mirrored in iPadOS. 

> [!NOTE]
> These problems with the shortcut were only noted when using the virtual keyboard. The shortcut works as intended when using a hardware keyboard paired with the iOS/iPadOS device.

## Steps to reproduce the issue

1. Visit a page that has both the Exit this Page button and an input field.
2. Focus the input so that the virtual keyboard opens.
3. Attempt to activate the EtP functionality by tapping <kbd>Shift</kbd> at least three times.

## Actual vs expected behaviour

### Expected

The Exit this Page functionality is activated and the user leaves the page.

### Actual

It is very difficult to activate the EtP shortcut behaviour intentionally.

If the user is pressing the key rapidly, and assuming an initially empty input or textarea, the most likely scenario is:

1. <kbd>Shift</kbd> was already turned on by default. Tap 1 turns it off and does not emit a `keyup` event.
2. Tap 2 happens quickly enough that Caps Lock mode is activated. <kbd>Caps Lock</kbd> emits a `keydown` event. 
3. Tap 3 turns off Caps Lock mode. <kbd>Caps Lock</kbd> emits a `keyup` event.
4. Tap 4 turns Caps Lock mode back on.
5. Repeat.

It is possible to activate the function successfully if the user takes time to wait between button presses—roughly half a second between presses. This wait is exacerbated by the need to perform more taps than usual, requiring 3 before the indicator lights are first shown, and a total of 7 to activate the functionality.

In addition, there are seemingly many scenarios that can unintentionally add to the <kbd>Shift</kbd> key activation count or cancel an activation currently in progress, most commonly, accidentally tapping fast enough to enable Caps Lock mode.

## Environment (where applicable)

- Operating system: iOS 16.4
- Browser: Safari
- Browser version: 16.4
- GOV.UK Frontend Version: 4.7.0 (however testing took place prior to this release)

ourIssues.title: Exit this page: Possibly note the `Clear-Site-Data` header
ourIssues.body:
### Discussed in https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/discussions/2932
Originally posted by **craigfrancis** July 9, 2023 Under the heading "Consider what to do with user session data", it might be worth noting that **some** websites might want to use the `Clear-Site-Data` header ([Specification](https://www.w3.org/TR/clear-site-data/), [MDN Article](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Clear-Site-Data)). This header helps if the user forgot to use Private Browsing Mode, and isn't familiar with clearing their browsing data (which in itself can be suspicious). This header does not clear the browsers history (as websites cannot/should-not be able to do this); but it does leave less traces of the website on the users computer (cookies, caches, localStorage, service workers, etc), which shows greater engagement with the website, and could include an active session showing a username and account details. I believe the Exit This Page link will need to use a redirect (i.e. go to a URL on the current website, which sets this header, and a Location header for the redirect). This will increase the loading time for the destination page, but loading time is always going to be a problem (and why a loading overlay is essential, because even a basic link to another website can take many seconds to begin loading - ref mobile phones with a poor connection, slow laptops running a virus checker, etc).

ourIssues.title: Improve the `title`s for pattern guidance pages
ourIssues.body:
## Context

Pattern pages with compound titles do not have the entire title included within the `title` element.

|Page `h1`|Page `title`|
|:-|:-|
|Ask users for Bank Details|Bank details|
|Ask users for Email addresses|Email addresses|
|Help users to Confirm an email address|Confirm an email address|
|Help users to Exit a page quickly|Exit a page quickly|

This can cause confusion, as some pages on the Design System website can have similar or identical `title`s in browser tabs and search result listings. 

|Pattern page `title`|Non-pattern page `title`|
|:-|:-|
|Cookies page|[Cookies](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/cookies/)|
|Dates|[Date input](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/date-input/)|
|Exit a page quickly|[Exit this page](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/exit-this-page/)|
|Passwords|Password input [in development]|

In instances where a pattern has a compound title (i.e. "Ask users for...", "Help users to...") these should be included in the page `title`. 

It may also be useful to include the name of the parent section ("Styles", "Components", "Patterns", etc.) somewhere within the page `title` on these child pages.

## Alternatives

Currently you must either look at the page's URL or click through to visit the page in order to see whether it is the desired page. 

## Additional information

Raised by a working group member during a working group meeting.

ourIssues.title: Propose a native HTP button to browser specs
ourIssues.body:
## What
Make a proposal to browser vendors/browser specs for them to incorporate a native hide this page button into browser software.

A potential way this could work is:
- Browsers look for an attribute on a a given page's `body` eg: `hide-this-page="true"`
- If the attribute exists, browsers display a hide this page button in the software, potentially with some messaging
- Upon activating the button, users are taken off the current website, similar to our current implementation of HTP
- Browsers can set the button to both bypass popup blocking and clear history from the domain the button was pressed on. These enhancements could potentially be managed by attributes in the `body`.

## Why
This is based on a hypothesis that by letting browser vendors handle this feature, they can ring-fence the functionality and more easily distribute it to users. During the HTP prototyping work, an issue we ran into was that certain enhancements weren't viable because they ran counter to browser rules. Examples of this were:

- Trying to erase the history of a service. We couldn't erase history completely and could only "erase" one page at a time, which didn't make a significant difference as most services are multi-page and would potentially give vulnerable users a false sense of security.
- A keyboard shortcut to activate the button. If the user uses the keyboard shortcut without interacting with the page ie: scrolling, clicking, moving focus etc, this triggers browser's popup blocker functionality as they presume this is an attempt to use malicious js to trick the user. This messes with the flow of HTP and at best confuses the user, at worst puts the user in danger.

From research into hide this page so far, it emerged that users already have existing strategies for covering their tracks and keeping anonymous online however it is often entirely down to that user to work out and manage successfully, putting them at further risk. There is an additional nuance that users may not realise they're at risk until prompted by online safety content. A broader hypothesis is that by browsers doing more to incorporate and promote online safety, it will both improve protection of users and make online safety a more prominent.

## Considerations
- This is not a proposal instead of the current HTP work but a long term solution to explore
- It may be useful to get backing on this before making the proposal from, eg, 1 or more W3C members and/or other government teams and charities
- This should be approached from the spec side over the browser vendor/software side
- This should probably be filtered into existing online anonymity and online safety spaces such as incognito mode

## Things to do
- [ ] Work out where this proposal needs to go
- [ ] Make contact with charities and gov teams who would have an interest in this
- [ ] Seek interest with w3C members
- [ ] Make proposal

ourIssues.title: Why do checkboxes and radios have transparent backgrounds?
ourIssues.body:
The following came from a question I asked on the design system slack channel.
https://ukgovernmentdigital.slack.com/archives/C6DMEH5R6/p1572279335253200

**TLDR:** checkboxes and radios have transparent backgrounds. This means they don't stand out visually against non white panels as text input elements do.

From thread:
---------
does anyone know why the checkboxes (and I assume radio buttons) have transparent backgrounds? Rather than a white background (which would probably be the default browser rendering of a standard checkbox).
**GOV checkbox (with transparent background):**
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/23551105/67845990-5e27a280-faf8-11e9-8e33-0bb7e1f6b0b5.png)
**Default checkbox (without GOV styling):**
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/23551105/67846092-86af9c80-faf8-11e9-8571-995a80aa3825.png)

**Anon 1:** 
I suspect that’s because they’re custom rendered rather than native checkboxes, and we want to support users who change their text and background colours.

11 replies

**Anon 2:**
Hi Dave,
This decision pre-dates the design system so I'll need to do a bit of digging to see if we can find out why - but my guess is something along the lines of what **Anon 1** said. Will come back to you.
Have you seen any problems around this, or are you just wondering?
After some investigation - it appears that his is the pertinent commit: https://github.com/alphagov/govuk_elements/commit/4972b81697fbf5b9ac12a211010c623e625ab3ab

**Dave Haigh**
I am looking at using small checkboxes as a filter for a list. The filters are located on a light grey panel (similar to the call to action blocks on GOV.UK guidance pages). As you can see in the screenshot the checkbox doesn’t stand out well as the background is transparent.

Im not sure on the answer to this but… should the scenario be:
- If user HAS NOT specified any browser background colour then they should be white;
- Else if user HAS a specified background colour in certain modes then they should be either transparent or that colour (when in that mode)
1. Is the above correct?
2. Is it possible?
3.Also, some other elements do not respect user specified background colours such as text inputs (they’re always white). Why are only the checks and radios transparent?

i’ve specified my background colour to be red (in any mode) in this screenshot:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/23551105/67846236-c5455700-faf8-11e9-868f-432708c3a31f.png)

**Anon 3**
I don’t really have a good answer for you other than that the radios and checkboxes in the Design System are based on those introduced in Elements back in 2016 by people that no longer work here. As **Anon 2** said, we don’t have the context of every historical decision. We could definitely look at changing that behaviour, but we’d need to test thoroughly to make sure they still work in all of these sorts of scenarios.

## What

As part of the work to [remove jQuery from the Jasmine tests](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk_publishing_components/issues/5248), we have found a few other areas for improvement, including:

- should we make further us of helpers, this could help reduce repetitive code in test files:

To help make our tests easy to maintain and to ensure we are making best use of Jasmine

communityIssues.title: Some components are not consistently named
communityIssues.body:
Some components are named one thing but use a different name for their files, e.g.

- `Admin layout` template is named `layout_for_admin`
- `Form character count` template is named `character_count`
- `Form checkboxes` template is named `checkboxes`
- `Form date input` template is named `date_input`
- `Form fieldset` template is named `fieldset`
- `Form file upload` template is named `file_upload`
- `Govspeak content` template is named `govspeak`
- `Govspeak content (HTML publications)` template is named `govspeak_html_publication`
- `Form hint text` template is named `hint`
- `Form input` template is named `input`
- `Form label` template is named `label`
- `Public layout` template is named `layout_for_public`
- `Metadata block` template is named `metadata`
- `Form radio button` template is named `radio`
- `Step by step navigation` template is named `step_by_step_nav`
- `Step by step navigation header` template is named `step_by_step_nav_header`

ourIssues.title: Hidden menu buttons reachable with VoiceOver on iPadOS
ourIssues.body: ## Description of the issue When using VoiceOver on iPadOS the hidden menu buttons in the header and service nav are all still reachable and can be activated in desktop view. That's the general "Menu" button as well as the buttons after each of the main navigation items. When you activate the main nav buttons they even visibly open the sub menu that shouldn't be reachable in the desktop view. Those buttons can also be explored by touch. Screenshot of the hidden "Get started" button being highlighted and activated with the "Get started" sub menu open underneath the service nav: This was first discovered as part of an [audit of the Brand Guidelines website](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-brand-guidelines/issues/138), which copies the Design System website functionality. ## Steps to reproduce the issue 1. Use VoiceOver with Safari on iPadOS 2. Open any page on https://design-system.service.gov.uk/ 3. Swipe forward within the menu to (wrongly) access a menu button 4. Double tap one of the buttons to (wrongly) open the mobile menu underneath ## Actual vs expected behaviour At step 3 you shouldn't be able to access those hidden buttons. At step 4 you shouldn't be able to open the mobile menu when it desktop view. ## Environment (where applicable) - Operating system: iPadOS 18.6 - Browser: Safari - Browser version: (not sure) I don't have a recent enough iOS version to see if it happens on current iOS as well. But I can confirm it does **not** happen with: * VO on iPadOS 15.8.3 * latest VO on macOS * latest TalkBack on Android * latest NVDA on Windows * latest JAWS on Windows That means it might well be due to a bug in iPadOS (and maybe iOS). And it would be worth isolating the exact problem.

## What

Review our use of `align-items: start` for `.govuk-service-navigation__container` and consider if we could have the children of `.govuk-service-navigation__container` be full width and expand the links to be full width on mobile.

backlog.title: Inbox pattern for mail, tasks or notifications
backlog.body:
What
Inbox design patterns for mail or notifications are common in commercial applications. The most pervasive patterns are a three-panel fluid layout for large & medium-sized screens and tabbed navigation with card components representing discrete messages for mobile.
We're testing the possibility of a cross-government inbox pattern to enable more rapid communication between departments and citizens.
Several components within the design system could be used to build an inbox-type experience. Modern inbox patterns are quite complex, setting a high standard for user interaction. Similar to driving a car—which is complex but, once mastered, offers significant benefits—these inbox patterns may not be easy or intuitive at first (or even accessible). However, their continuous development and widespread use have made them the standard way to manage complex tasks.
Why
Design System
Even though this will not be a reusable component it could be a keystone design pattern that connects to, possibly impacting, other patterns within the design system. This needs consideration from the design system community and input from other research and experiences.
Depending on the level of service integration into the inbox, many of the existing Design system components will be used including form design components and general service interactions.
Some related patterns would be

https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/summary-list/
https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/complete-multiple-tasks/
https://design-system.service.gov.uk/styles/layout/

And has the potential to impact some existing patterns changing them altogether

https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/contact-a-department-or-service-team/

ourIssues.title: Improve the `title`s for pattern guidance pages
ourIssues.body:
## Context

Pattern pages with compound titles do not have the entire title included within the `title` element.

|Page `h1`|Page `title`|
|:-|:-|
|Ask users for Bank Details|Bank details|
|Ask users for Email addresses|Email addresses|
|Help users to Confirm an email address|Confirm an email address|
|Help users to Exit a page quickly|Exit a page quickly|

This can cause confusion, as some pages on the Design System website can have similar or identical `title`s in browser tabs and search result listings. 

|Pattern page `title`|Non-pattern page `title`|
|:-|:-|
|Cookies page|[Cookies](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/cookies/)|
|Dates|[Date input](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/date-input/)|
|Exit a page quickly|[Exit this page](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/exit-this-page/)|
|Passwords|Password input [in development]|

In instances where a pattern has a compound title (i.e. "Ask users for...", "Help users to...") these should be included in the page `title`. 

It may also be useful to include the name of the parent section ("Styles", "Components", "Patterns", etc.) somewhere within the page `title` on these child pages.

## Alternatives

Currently you must either look at the page's URL or click through to visit the page in order to see whether it is the desired page. 

## Additional information

Raised by a working group member during a working group meeting.

ourIssues.title: Agree how to ensure that users don't lose information if they follow links in the cookie banner
ourIssues.body:
## What
As part of the cookie banner work we've been thinking about how teams should handle opening links in the cookie banner if the user is completing a transactional journey and could lose information they've entered in a form if they follow links in the cookie banner.

We have some information under [Opening links in a new tab](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/styles/typography/#opening-links-in-a-new-tab) about this so we could link to it from the cookie banner guidance if we though that would be useful. The content could say something like:

> If you show the cookie banner on a page where the user enters information into a form, [open the cookies page in a new tab](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/styles/typography/#opening-links-in-a-new-tab). 

Additionally, users could lose information if interacting with the cookie banner reloads the page (server side solution when JavaScript isn't enabled or the banner doesn't progressively enhance it). We could consider recommending that once the user has consented/rejected cookies, the hide button isn't shown if JavaScript isn't enabled (JS would unhide the button)/

It's possible that there's a wider pattern here about how teams should ensure that the information users enter in forms is retained safely. 

This card should be to decide what the scope of this work is.

## Why
We should provide guidance to teams on how to making sure that users don't lose information entered in a form if they follow links in the cookie banner. 

## Who needs to know about this
Content writer, technical writer, developer, service designer?

## Further detail
As well as the cookie banner, this relates to things like links in footers. However, it's possible that the proposed wider guidance is less relevant to user interaction patterns and would be more relevant for the [Service Manual](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual). 

## Done when
- [ ] We've agreed how to help teams to make sure that users don't lose information entered in a form if they click on links in the cookie banner
- [ ] We've created a follow up card if appropriate, or captured next steps in this card

backlog.title: Inbox pattern for mail, tasks or notifications
backlog.body:
What
Inbox design patterns for mail or notifications are common in commercial applications. The most pervasive patterns are a three-panel fluid layout for large & medium-sized screens and tabbed navigation with card components representing discrete messages for mobile.
We're testing the possibility of a cross-government inbox pattern to enable more rapid communication between departments and citizens.
Several components within the design system could be used to build an inbox-type experience. Modern inbox patterns are quite complex, setting a high standard for user interaction. Similar to driving a car—which is complex but, once mastered, offers significant benefits—these inbox patterns may not be easy or intuitive at first (or even accessible). However, their continuous development and widespread use have made them the standard way to manage complex tasks.
Why
Design System
Even though this will not be a reusable component it could be a keystone design pattern that connects to, possibly impacting, other patterns within the design system. This needs consideration from the design system community and input from other research and experiences.
Depending on the level of service integration into the inbox, many of the existing Design system components will be used including form design components and general service interactions.
Some related patterns would be

https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/summary-list/
https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/complete-multiple-tasks/
https://design-system.service.gov.uk/styles/layout/

And has the potential to impact some existing patterns changing them altogether

https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/contact-a-department-or-service-team/
https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/check-a-service-is-suitable/
https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/create-accounts/

There may also be existing inbox patterns that have been designed and tested internally for civil servants and gov departments that we can learn from when designing for a wider group of users.
Needs
The primary need is for citizens to receive communications from government departments that cover legal and functional requirements to implement policy. The government needs an official way to send these communications to individuals and organisations. Currently, this is done through physical letters sent to a mailbox at the person's residence, which is verified to be connected to their identity.
Although we have not yet researched the specific needs, we have a few initial assumptions that we will test during our work:

Persistent and Recoverable Communication: Citizens need a reliable way to receive government communications that won't be lost, destroyed, or missed (e.g., when moving). Physical letters can fail to meet this need.
Control Over Communication Preferences: Citizens should be able to manage their communication preferences with the entire government, rather than dealing with each department individually. This is especially important for those who need assistance or special accommodations.
Timely Action on Important Matters: Citizens need to act quickly on important issues. Physical mail can take up to a week for a round trip, delaying responses and potentially causing anxiety or stress for citizens. For the government, this leads to longer service delivery and issue resolution times.
Confirmation of Receipt: Government departments need to confirm that citizens have received communications, as this could affect their responses.

Anything else
Denmark has had a citizen mailbox since 2007 using a standard inbox design pattern and currently, the paradigm is being tested in Scotland.

https://en.digst.dk/systems/digital-post-app/
https://www.civtech.scot/demo-day-9-netcompany

backlog.title: Equality questions and WCAG 2.2 for long-term services
backlog.body:
I'm looking for some help and advice on adding equality questions to a service. My understanding is that equality questions are not attributed to the individual or their case/ application information. The GDS guidance says that, in line with new WCAG 2.2 requirements, you have to allow users to update any changes in their equality information, but without re-entering the same data again (redundant entry). I'm not sure how this is possible without linking a person's equality info to the individual? WCAG talks about applying 'redundant entry' per session - but the GDS interpretation is that a person can go back on a long-term service, and update equality info as it changes. I'm confused and would really appreciate some advice around this.
Originally posted by @francesporter-DWP in #5881 (comment)

ourIssues.title: Equality information pattern using potentially out of date examples
ourIssues.body:
I understand (via @StephenGill ) that the [equality information pattern](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/equality-information/) is based on the [GSS Ethnicity harmonised standard](https://gss.civilservice.gov.uk/policy-store/ethnicity-harmonised-standard/#telephone-questions-for-england)

The standard looks to be published in 2011, 10 years prior to the 2021 Census.

The above page looks to be outdated. [You can find the latest version here.](https://analysisfunction.civilservice.gov.uk/policy-store/ethnicity-harmonised-standard/)

On the updated site, there's a section noting that the standard is being updated and that for new equality monitoring services should use the Census 2021 options (more detail below).

Should the Design system examples be updated?

Relevant excerpts from the GSS guidance linked above:

> This means that the 2021 and 2022 Census questions are the most up to date way of collecting data about ethnic group at the moment.  But the question development for these approaches began in 2015 and we are aware that user needs may have changed since then.

> You should use the current ethnicity harmonised standard for existing data collections until we have finished our review.
> If you’re planning to include a new ethnicity question in your data collection and cannot wait for our review work to be completed, we recommend that you use the questions from the:
> * [2021 Census for England and Wales](https://www.ons.gov.uk/census/censustransformationprogramme/questiondevelopment/nationalidentityethnicgrouplanguageandreligionquestiondevelopmentforcensus2021#questions-recommended-for-census-2021)
> * current ethnicity harmonised standard for Northern Ireland

backlog.title: Help users to find the right service for them
backlog.body:
What
There are many examples of government services which serve similar (or the same) needs for people with slightly different circumstances.
In the case where we can rely on most users navigating to a high-level Start Page, but not to the individual service variants, we can ask users questions about themselves to and then present them with the options available to them.
n.b. This is related to the "Check a service is suitable for you" pattern but different in content. That pattern starts with a user thinking that a service is suitable for them, but possibly being incorrect. This pattern starts with a user needing a problem to be solved but not necessarily having any idea what their options are for solving it.
Why
I'm not sure which services this is currently part of, but I have a hunch that it should be part of more. I've seen some services early in development that are Brexit-related that do things like this, but can't currently put much info about them on here.
One live example is "Find out if you can settle in the UK".

backlog.title: Inbox pattern for mail, tasks or notifications
backlog.body:
What
Inbox design patterns for mail or notifications are common in commercial applications. The most pervasive patterns are a three-panel fluid layout for large & medium-sized screens and tabbed navigation with card components representing discrete messages for mobile.
We're testing the possibility of a cross-government inbox pattern to enable more rapid communication between departments and citizens.
Several components within the design system could be used to build an inbox-type experience. Modern inbox patterns are quite complex, setting a high standard for user interaction. Similar to driving a car—which is complex but, once mastered, offers significant benefits—these inbox patterns may not be easy or intuitive at first (or even accessible). However, their continuous development and widespread use have made them the standard way to manage complex tasks.
Why
Design System
Even though this will not be a reusable component it could be a keystone design pattern that connects to, possibly impacting, other patterns within the design system. This needs consideration from the design system community and input from other research and experiences.
Depending on the level of service integration into the inbox, many of the existing Design system components will be used including form design components and general service interactions.
Some related patterns would be

https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/summary-list/
https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/complete-multiple-tasks/
https://design-system.service.gov.uk/styles/layout/

And has the potential to impact some existing patterns changing them altogether

https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/contact-a-department-or-service-team/
https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/check-a-service-is-suitable/
https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/create-accounts/

There may also be existing inbox patterns that have been designed and tested internally for civil servants and gov departments that we can learn from when designing for a wider group of users.
Needs
The primary need is for citizens to receive communications from government departments that cover legal and functional requirements to implement policy. The government needs an official way to send these communications to individuals and organisations. Currently, this is done through physical letters sent to a mailbox at the person's residence, which is verified to be connected to their identity.
Although we have not yet researched the specific needs, we have a few initial assumptions that we will test during our work:

Persistent and Recoverable Communication: Citizens need a reliable way to receive government communications that won't be lost, destroyed, or missed (e.g., when moving). Physical letters can fail to meet this need.
Control Over Communication Preferences: Citizens should be able to manage their communication preferences with the entire government, rather than dealing with each department individually. This is especially important for those who need assistance or special accommodations.
Timely Action on Important Matters: Citizens need to act quickly on important issues. Physical mail can take up to a week for a round trip, delaying responses and potentially causing anxiety or stress for citizens. For the government, this leads to longer service delivery and issue resolution times.
Confirmation of Receipt: Government departments need to confirm that citizens have received communications, as this could affect their responses.

Anything else
Denmark has had a citizen mailbox since 2007 using a standard inbox design pattern and currently, the paradigm is being tested in Scotland.

https://en.digst.dk/systems/digital-post-app/
https://www.civtech.scot/demo-day-9-netcompany

This would connect and need to work with other Gov platforms

Gov.UK One login
Gov.UK Notify (has previously done some research on communicating with citizens)
Gov.UK Pay

Additional related components and issues
Generalised patterns such as cards and lists will be relevant in this work

https://design.education.gov.uk/design-system/dfe-frontend/components/card
https://designsystem.parliament.uk/components/cards/card/
#5852
UKHomeOffice/design-system#377

Mobile inbox patterns

https://www.simform.com/mobile-patterns/iphone/mailbox

Design History
A design history based on this work
https://github.com/alphagov/gov-mailbox-design-history
Figma file exploring the pattern
Figma file examining the inbox pattern
https://www.figma.com/design/zOdvURuLtLklNjP2f7zun0/GDS-Inbox-design-pattern-proposal?node-id=0-1&t=YTftxtJJQa2NG28c-1

ourIssues.title: WCAG 2.2: Start using a service ‖ Consistent Help
ourIssues.body:
## What

Consider adding or updating a screenshot of a start page to include visible help or contact information on the page, displayed in a consistent manner. Related to #2882. 

This is largely a usability suggestion and may not be necessary for WCAG compliance. 

### Resources

- [Start using a service pattern guidance](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/start-using-a-service/)
- [WCAG 2.2 criterion for 'Consistent Help'](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/consistent-help.html)

## Why

The new WCAG 2.2 Level A criterion 'Consistent Help' says:

> If a [Web page](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/consistent-help.html#dfn-web-page) contains any of the following help [mechanisms](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/consistent-help.html#), and those mechanisms are repeated on multiple Web pages within a [set of Web pages](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/consistent-help.html#dfn-set-of-web-pages), they occur in the same order relative to other page content, unless a change is initiated by the user:
> * Human contact details;
> * Human contact mechanism;
> * Self-help option;
> * A fully automated contact mechanism.

Although the intent of the criterion is that the contact information itself is consistently ordered with respect to the rest of the page (i.e. a help link is always in the same place in the footer, as described in #2871) we can go beyond this by advising that teams provide this information in a consistent order every time it appears.

For example, if a service has three contact mechanisms—phone, email address, post—these should be listed in the same order and format on all pages where it appears, such as the service start page, support pages, contact page, etc. 

## Who needs to work on this
- Content designer or technical writer

## Who needs to review this
- Accessibility specialist
- Content designer or technical writer

## Done when

- [ ] Guidance has been updated

ourIssues.title: Improve the `title`s for pattern guidance pages
ourIssues.body:
## Context

Pattern pages with compound titles do not have the entire title included within the `title` element.

|Page `h1`|Page `title`|
|:-|:-|
|Ask users for Bank Details|Bank details|
|Ask users for Email addresses|Email addresses|
|Help users to Confirm an email address|Confirm an email address|
|Help users to Exit a page quickly|Exit a page quickly|

This can cause confusion, as some pages on the Design System website can have similar or identical `title`s in browser tabs and search result listings. 

|Pattern page `title`|Non-pattern page `title`|
|:-|:-|
|Cookies page|[Cookies](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/cookies/)|
|Dates|[Date input](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/date-input/)|
|Exit a page quickly|[Exit this page](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/exit-this-page/)|
|Passwords|Password input [in development]|

In instances where a pattern has a compound title (i.e. "Ask users for...", "Help users to...") these should be included in the page `title`. 

It may also be useful to include the name of the parent section ("Styles", "Components", "Patterns", etc.) somewhere within the page `title` on these child pages.

## Alternatives

Currently you must either look at the page's URL or click through to visit the page in order to see whether it is the desired page. 

## Additional information

Raised by a working group member during a working group meeting.

ourIssues.title: Typography for labels on patterns with multiple fields
ourIssues.body:
Where patterns have multiple fields on a single page (rather than just one, where the label or legend doubles as the `<h1>`), it is currently unclear what typographic weight should be applied to the field labels (or legends).

[Addresses](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/addresses/) and [Bank details](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/bank-details/) suggest using regular weight, Address lookup (the video) and [Payment card details](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/payment-card-details/) suggest using `s`.

The Getting started page has a section on [styling options for labels and legends](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/get-started/labels-legends-headings/#styling-options-for-labels-and-legends) which also suggest that `m` is an option if needed.

Should the patterns in the Design System have consistency between them in typography (ie all use `s` or regular)? Or is there a reason for the differences?  And should those pages make clear whether the typography in the patterns can be changed if necessary, or whether they should be copied exactly as they are?

ourIssues.title: The names of some patterns can cause confusion when they appear as part of a sentence
ourIssues.body:
## What
Feedback from the cross-government working group following publication of '[Help users to understand the impact of an emergency on your service](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/understand-the-impact-of-an-emergency/)' to add single quotation marks when we reference page names.

Although feedback is for the emergency banner pattern this would also apply to all content on the Design System.

## Why

The pattern names are long, and this can make sentences that they appear in confusing to read. Starting the pattern name with an upper case letter is not sufficient, because it doesn't explicitly indicate the _end_ of the name.

Some options:
- live with it
- put quotes around pattern names
- put quotes around all document names
- put quotes around problematic instances only
- replace the name with a pronoun like 'this' or 'the pattern'

## Who needs to know about this

Stephen, Tim

ourIssues.body: ## What Review instances where we have a link to something's discussion page, asking for research, which replicates that same link in the contact panel at the bottom of our pages. At time of writing there are at least 8 instances of this: - [Accordion](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/accordion/#known-issues-and-gaps) - [Back link](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/back-link/#known-issues-and-gaps) - [Checkboxes](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/checkboxes/#research-on-this-component) - [Exit this page](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/exit-this-page/#known-issues-and-gaps) - [Images](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/styles/images/#research-on-images) - [Interruption page](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/interruption-pages/#next-steps) - [Navigate a service](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/navigate-a-service/#research-on-this-pattern) - [Radios](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/radios/#research-on-this-component) ## Why These links to a given style/component/pattern's github discussion space are intended as signoffs or CTAs for a page, however they're replicating the same link in the contact panel at the bottom of those same pages (the "Help improve this component" heading). backlog.title: GOV.UK Design System as an agent skill for Claude Code, Codex and Cursor
backlog.body:
I've packaged the Design System as an open source agent skill so coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and others) use it properly instead of from memory: https://github.com/chrisjohnleah/govuk-design-system-skill
It is generated from govuk-frontend 6.5.1, this repo and govuk-frontend-docs. Every component page carries the guidance, the macro options table and the exact HTML each example renders to, plus all 35 patterns and 13 styles. A single CHOOSING file compiles every "when to use" and "when not to use" so the agent picks the right component before it writes any markup.
The bit I cared most about: without the skill, an agent building a page for a charity used the crown, the GOV.UK header and GDS Transport. With it, the agent read "Using GOV.UK Frontend without GOV.UK branding" first and switched to the Generic header, a font override and its own icons. The skill leads with that decision.
Install: npx skills add chrisjohnleah/govuk-design-system-skill
A script regenerates everything from upstream, so it can track releases rather than drift.
Not affiliated with GDS. Happy to change anything the team would rather I did differently, especially around how the licensing of the crown and typeface is worded.

unmatchedBacklog.title: AI — we want your input (emerging patterns, use cases, research findings)
unmatchedBacklog.body:
Hello
We are starting a discussion about emerging design patterns for utilising AI in public services. This probably mostly covers generative AI, but other design patterns for making use of machine learning, data science, and similar technologies are also useful.
We’re doing this because there is a lot here! Many teams across government are experimenting with AI, and we are working out how to design for this. We need to work out how to surface AI-generated content to users, how to talk to them about accuracy, and how to design more dynamic interactions. A space to share learnings in the open seems like a good place to start 🥁
I work on the GOV.UK AI team, where we are experimenting how AI can help people navigate the complexity of government services and information. We have a ton of insights from testing so far, and we know that other teams do too. Most of our learnings come from experimenting with GOV.UK Chat. You can learn more about that in this blog post, or drop us a message if you want to chat more about it.
We’ll start by sharing some of our insights, but please join the discussion if you work in government and have things to share. Keep in mind that it’s all work in progress, and evolving fast!

unmatchedBacklog.title: Dark Mode
unmatchedBacklog.body:
What
GOV.UK needs a Dark Mode theme.
Why
I have written about why Dark Mode should be an inclusive design consideration.
2018: The Dark (Mode) Web Rises
2017: Apple Need a Dark Mode
2016: Molly Watt
Anything else
Some of the suggestions I've poked at in the past have always come with added complications. For example, how do we include an accessibility toolbar in a way that benefits the users who need it without getting in the way of those who don't.
The preference has always been to allow users to change website themes based on their own preferences using third-party and browser tools. This has always left a gap on mobile devices and often requires extra digital skill.
Safari Technology Preview has recently added a CSS media query prefers-color-scheme which can detect the system-level preference in MacOS Mojave of a light or dark theme. You can now easily write CSS custom to both and the user only has to declare a preference once to affect all websites (providing them adopt it).
Adoption and sharing of this by big websites (GOV.UK) will help spread awareness and prompt other platforms to add their own system-level preferences.
Check out a prototype: https://govuk-dark-mode.herokuapp.com. You'll need Safari Technology Preview and MacOS Mojave at time of raising this issue.
